en: Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣyam, Part I: [The First Compendium, titled "The Compendium of Characteristics"] Oṃ! Homage to the Three Jewels.
For what purpose has this treatise been commenced?
It is for the sake of producing skill (*kauśalya*) regarding the points of reflection, such as "how many" and "why," beginning with the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth.
For by means of this skill, two kinds of benefit are obtained: the benefit of mental attention (*manaskāra*) and the benefit of the definitive resolution of discussion (*sāṃkathyaviniścaya*).

In this regard, the benefit of mental attention (*manaskāra*) should be understood as being conducive to both serenity (*śamatha*) and the increase of insight (*vipaśyanā*). Conduciveness to serenity, moreover, arises from the ease of settling the mind in one-pointedness upon an object at will, due to the absence of doubt in one who has achieved proficiency in these points. Conduciveness to the increase of insight arises through the progression toward excellence in wisdom by means of examining the objects of knowledge in many ways.

The benefit of the definitive determination through discussion should be understood as arising from the attainment of fearlessness, due to the possession of the power to answer all questions regarding these points for one who is skilled in them.
Regarding the phrase "by way of manifesting the fivefold entity of the self": here, the "entity of the self" (*ātmavastu*) refers to the four aspects as the entity of the self;
however, it should be understood that the fifth is the "entity of the self" because it is the very characteristic of the self itself.
By the inclusion of the body together with its possessions, one should understand the inclusion of both the external and internal aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
That feeling and the other aggregates constitute "experience" and so forth will be made known in the exposition of their specific characteristics.
Consciousness is the "own-basis" (*svavastu*) of those [aggregates];
the meaning is that it is the basis for the body and so forth along with their possessions, and it is the entity characterized as a self (*ātman*).
For in the world, there is generally the grasping at a self with respect to consciousness,
and the grasping at what belongs to a self with respect to the remaining [aggregates].
"By means of the body and its appropriation" refers to the six sense faculties, beginning with the eye, and the six objects, beginning with form.
The sixfold experience—both past and present—is the sixfold consciousness; its "sustenance" consists in its being the basis and the object [of that experience].

Thus, the twelve sense objects (*indriya-viṣaya*) constitute elements (*dhātu*) by virtue of their function as supports (*dhāraṇatva*). Furthermore, the consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) should be understood as elements by virtue of their function as supports characterized by experience (*upabhoga-lakṣaṇa*).
For example, while past and present [faculties] such as the eye are maintainers of the characteristic of experience, future ones are not. //2//

Because they are merely gateways for the arrival [of consciousness], the twelve bases (āyatana) are established by the inclusion of only the sense faculties and their objects; however, the sixfold consciousness, which is characterized by experience, is not so included.
Grasping consists of desire and attachment;
therein, desire is longing,
while attachment is fixation.

Through desire (*chanda*), one grasps a future personal existence by way of longing, whereby one brings about the formation of future aggregates (*skandha*). Through attachment (*rāga*), one grasps a present personal existence by way of fixation.
Because one does not relinquish the present aggregates by means of it, these two alone are called "appropriation" (upādāna). In this regard, the explanation is the same as that for the aggregates.
Therefore, it should be understood that they are "dharmas with grasping" because they are associated with grasping.
Through contact with forms, their transformation should be understood;
"in a location" means in the space directly facing [the mirror];
"this and that" refers to the reflection of objects similar to the things to be known, such as a skeleton and so forth.
The designation "variegated" refers to the state of being perceived as such through various distinctions of color and shape.
The ripening of the fruit of wholesome karmas is the experience of pleasure;
that of unwholesome karmas is suffering.
For both [types of karma], the neither-painful-nor-pleasant [feeling] occurs;
for thus, the maturation (*vipāka*) of both wholesome and unwholesome [karmas] is the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which is always associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*) alone.
And that very equanimity is what constitutes the maturation here.

However, because pleasure and pain are born of maturation (*vipākaja*), they are metaphorically designated as "maturation. Regarding the objects that have been seen, heard, sensed, and cognized: "seen" refers to what has been experienced by the eye, and "heard" refers to what has been experienced by the ear.
"Thought" (*mata*) refers to that which has been personally inferred, thinking "it must be thus and so";
"known" (*vijñāta*) refers to that which has been individually experienced within oneself.
"Engages in conventional discourse" (*vyavaharati*) means to communicate through verbal expressions or to cause [others] to attain [understanding].
And "in various states" refers to states such as pleasure, pain, and so forth.
By the phrase "by which eye one has seen forms," he demonstrates its nature as an element (*dhātu*) by virtue of its being the sustainer of the experience of past consciousness;
by "one sees," it is shown by virtue of its being the sustainer of the experience of present consciousness;
and that storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) which is the accumulated seed of that eye, from which the eye will arise in the future, [is also indicated].
Furthermore, that which has arisen as a result of maturation (*vaipākya*) is also a twofold seed; it is called the "eye-element" (*cakṣurdhātu*) because it is the cause of the eye.
Regarding the statement that "the eye-element has sovereignty over visible forms," this is because external objects are produced through the sovereignty of the material sense-faculties.
It should be understood as being like those elements, and it should be applied accordingly: namely, the eye by which one will see visible forms, its seed, and so forth.
"And derived from the four great elements":
how is it derived matter?
It is so called because the four great elements act as the causes for its production, support, stability, maintenance, and growth.
Furthermore, the causality of the primary elements (*bhūta*) toward derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) is fivefold, with respect to its causal status:
(1) the causality of origination, because without them, that [derived matter] does not arise;
and (2) the causality of subsistence, because derived matter lacks the capacity to occupy a distinct location apart from the primary elements.
It is the cause of conformity because, through the transformation of the primary elements (*bhūta*), the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) supported by them undergoes transformation;
it is the cause of stability because, at the time of similar production, the primary elements sustain the continuum of derived matter by means of its non-interruption;
and it is the cause of accumulation because, during the period of functioning, the primary elements nourish the derived matter.
The establishment of the twenty-five forms, beginning with blue, should be understood through six aspects:

by way of characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), by way of configuration (*saṃniveśa*), by way of benefit and harm (*anugrahopaghāta*), by way of being the basis for action (*kriyāsaṃniśraya*), by way of the characteristic of action (*kriyālakṣaṇa*), and by way of adornment (*maṇḍana*). These apply respectively to the four, the ten, the eight, and each of the single [remaining] ones.
Among these, "open space" (*abhyavakāśa*) refers to that location which is devoid of any other obstructing tangible object (*spraṣṭavya*).
That which is seen as blue above is the sky.

The establishment of sound is by way of its characteristic, its benefit and harm, the differentiation of its causes, the differentiation of its teachings, and the differentiation of its conventional usage.
By way of its characteristic, it is the object apprehended by the auditory faculty.
By way of the differentiation of its teachings, there are three types, beginning with those well-known in the world.
The remainder should be understood according to their respective applications.
Among those, that which has the appropriated great elements as its cause is, for example, the sound of speech;
that which has the non-appropriated great elements as its cause is, for example, the sound of a tree.
That which belongs to both is, for example, the sound of a hand-drum;
it is well-known in the world and included within worldly speech. That which is brought forth by the accomplished ones is that which has been taught by the Noble Ones.
The imagined [nature] is taught by the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).
However, the noble and the non-noble conventional [natures] are to be understood with reference to the eight conventions, beginning with seeing.
The establishment of odor is by way of its specific characteristic, its benefit and harm, and its classification.
The determination of the tastes should also be understood in exactly this same way.

In this regard, the innate fragrance belongs to sandalwood and the like; the combined fragrance belongs to incense preparations and the like; and the transformational fragrance belongs to ripened fruits and the like.
It is established as a portion of the tangible through touching, weighing, contacting, pressing, and through conjunction, as well as through the imbalance or balance of the elements.
Coldness arises from the conjunction of water and wind;
stickiness arises from the conjunction of water and earth.
Rest, strength, and vigor result from the equilibrium of the bodily constituents;
moreover, vigor should be understood as fearlessness.
Satisfaction occurs in both ways.
The remaining states, such as hunger and so forth, should be understood as resulting from an imbalance of the elements.

The form that is by way of compression is the form of the atom (*paramāṇu-rūpa*). The form that is by way of space is that same [form] as previously described, but devoid of any other obstructive tangible objects.
The form that is by way of undertaking is non-informative form (*avijñapti-rūpa*).
The imagined [form] is the nature of a reflected image.
The form belonging to the realm of mastery is that which is the domain of those who meditate on the liberations.
The establishment of the aggregate of feeling is [to be understood] by way of its basis, its intrinsic nature, the synthesis of its bases, and its defilement and purification.
In this regard, bodily feeling is established by way of its association with a material basis,
while mental feeling is established by way of its association with a non-material basis; furthermore,
worldly feelings such as those accompanied by carnal desire are established by way of their defilement.
The establishment of the "unworldly" (*nirāmiṣa*) and other [types of giving] should be understood in terms of purification (*vyavadāna*).
That which is "disjoined from craving" (*tṛṣṇā-viyuktā*) should be understood as being both dissociated (*visaṃyuktā*) and conducive to dissociation (*visaṃyogya-anukūlā*).
For one who is unskilled in conventional usage and untrained in language, there arises a perception of "form" (*rūpa*) but not the perception that "this is form.
Therefore, it is called the "signless perception" (*animitta-saṃjñā*).

For one who has attained the signless realm (*animitta-dhātu*), where all signs such as form have ceased, the perception regarding the signless Nirvana is the "perception of the signless" (*animitta-saṃjñā*).

For one who has attained the meditative absorption of the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), there is the perception of the signless (*animitta-saṃjñā*) because, due to its lack of clarity, the object is not perceived as having signs.
The desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is "limited" because it is inferior; the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is "vast" because it is superior to that.
Because the spheres of infinite space and infinite consciousness are immeasurable due to their boundlessness,
the perceptions that take them as objects should be understood as "limited" and so forth.
This applies to all mental factors— excluding feeling and perception— as well as the formations dissociated from mind, since they are characterized by the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).
Since the others are preceded by that [volition], only volition itself is mentioned in its definition; thus, for the purpose of making known the cause, he says:
"by which one intends for the sake of wholesomeness," and so forth.
In this context, "wholesome" refers to faith and the other factors that will be explained later.
The afflictions (*saṃkleśa*) are passion (*rāga*) and so forth, as well as the primary and secondary afflictions (*kleśopakleśa*).
From the perspective of their distinct states, they are designated as formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*) within the states of formations impelled by volition (*cetanā*).
The exposition of mental factors such as volition (cetanā) should be understood by way of their characteristics and their functions.
Among these, the exposition of the characteristic of volition is that it is the mental formation (abhisaṃskāra) of the mind, which is mental action (manaskarma).
The exposition of its function is that its activity is to impel the mind toward what is wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral.
For it is thus:
the mind proceeds toward wholesome and other phenomena according to its formative activity (*abhisaṃskāra*).
It should be understood that the holding of the mind upon an object is the repeated directing of it toward that very same object.
For this very reason, one who has attained meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is said to have attained mental formation (*manaḥ-saṃskāra*).

Contact (*sparśa*) should be understood as having the aspect of that modification of the sense faculty which, upon the arising of consciousness, is conducive to the arising of feelings such as pleasure.
The "desire to act" associated with each [object] is intended to include the desire for all actions such as seeing, hearing, and so forth.
"Retention according to determination" is the conviction that "this is exactly thus and not otherwise.
For this very reason, one who is primarily focused on that cannot be diverted by others; it should be understood that the "familiar object" is something previously experienced.
Furthermore, the function of non-distraction of mindfulness is based on the non-distraction of the mind when there is a clear verbalization of the object;
it is the one-pointedness of the mind.
Its provision of a basis for knowledge arises from the knowledge of things as they truly are by one whose mind is concentrated.

The turning away of doubt occurs through wisdom by means of attaining certainty while discerning phenomena. Faith has the aspect of conviction regarding existence; it has the aspect of serene clarity regarding excellence.
When [the goal] is possible, it takes the form of aspiration,
thinking, "I am able to attain or accomplish it.
Since shame and the other [virtuous mental factors] are easy to understand, they are not analyzed in detail.

It should be understood that [wisdom] acquired at birth, that consisting of hearing and reflection, and that consisting of cultivation are, respectively, of the nature of maturation, scripture, and realization.
Discerning wisdom (*pratisaṃkhyā-prajñā*) accompanied by steadfastness—

such sūtra phrases as "possessing strength," "possessing vigor," "energetic," "firm in prowess," and "not casting off the burden regarding wholesome qualities"— are to be applied respectively to the objects of exertion, beginning with the armor-like [vigor].
Fulfillment is like the entry into the fundamental [state].
Accomplishment is the state of that very [state] being thoroughly refined.
The extraction of all obscurations is to be understood as resulting from the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*) by virtue of that [accomplishment].
Because the cultivation of all wholesome qualities is preceded by diligence and so forth, heedfulness is designated with respect to them.
Here, it should be understood that "outflows" (*āsrava*) refers to contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) as well as the objects that serve as the basis for those outflows.
Through the states of mental equanimity and so forth, the initial, middle, and final stages of equanimity (*upekṣā*) have been explained.
For thus, the mind endowed with equanimity is initially even because of the absence of imbalances such as laxity;
thereafter, it is smooth because it flows without volitional effort;
and finally, it remains effortless because there is no longer any apprehension of affliction.
Non-violence (*avihiṃsā*) should be understood as being nominally existent (*prajñaptisat*), because it is not distinct from non-hatred (*adveṣa*).
Its function is the production of suffering, because, under the influence of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), it brings about the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*).
It constitutes a state of non-contact (*asparśavihāra*), because one whose mind is full of malice dwells in suffering.
Lack of respect toward teachers and those possessed of virtues, as well as arrogance,
should be understood as the arising of suffering— that is, the arising of renewed existence.
Cognition that is perverted by false certainties is ignorance;
doubt is uncertainty;
and the arising of affliction is the manifestation of the defilements such as attachment.
It provides a basis for the arising of all afflictions in one who is deluded;
that is, doubt regarding the Jewels, and as appropriate, regarding the Truth of the Path and the Truth of Cessation.
Through that [doubt], there is no engagement with the side of the wholesome, because one who has not attained certainty does not begin [the practice].
The middle way is the knowledge of dependent origination, which avoids the grasping at permanence and annihilation.
Moral discipline and observances should be understood as being preceded by wrong views;
they result in the fruitlessness of effort because one does not attain liberation through them.
"There is no giving, there is no sacrifice, there is no performed deed, there is no good conduct, and there is no evil conduct"—this is the denial of cause.
"There is no ripening of the fruit of deeds consisting of evil or good conduct"—this is the denial of fruit.
"There is no this world, there is no other world, there is no mother, there is no father, and there are no spontaneously born beings"—this is the denial of action.
Because of the denial of the activity of going to and coming from other worlds, the activity of planting seeds, and the activity of linking rebirth,
there arises the destruction of existing reality by such claims as "there are no Arhats in the world.
Whatever other erroneous view exists besides that should be understood as false conceptualization.
The severance of the roots of virtue occurs through a specific false view alone, not every [false view].
Regarding the object of knowledge consisting of the five aggregates, the view of a real body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is that which superimposes the intrinsic nature of "self" and "mine.
The view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) is that which superimposes the distinctions of a self as being either eternal or non-eternal.
The misapprehension of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) is the superimposition of excellence upon a false view;
therein, the misapprehension of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is the superimposition of purity upon that very same [false view].
One [of these] is called "mostly" because it consists of false conceptualization, as it is not necessarily subversive [of reality].

In terms of their defining characteristics, [the view of self] consists of two: the view of grasping at extremes and false view; in terms of including their attendants, it consists of all [five views]. Form and the other [aggregates] are not the self.
Because they are of a different nature from that [self], for they do not possess the characteristics of a self;
the self does not exist in them, due to the fault of impermanence.
For there can be no dependent in the absence of a substratum. Thus, the self does not possess form,
because that would entail the fault of its lacking independence.
The self is not other than those [elements], because that would entail the fault of being bodiless;
for the conceptualization of a self is never perceived apart from the body.
There is the fault of lack of independence because one does not have mastery over them.
Furthermore, even if someone were to postulate a self of this kind, it would still not be tenable that the self is devoid of form and so forth.
Because there would be the fault of liberation occurring without effort;
for if the bondage of the body and so forth were absent, liberation would occur by its own inherent nature alone.

One regards form as the self; one regards feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as the self—these are the five views of a self. The remaining fifteen are views of what belongs to a self (*ātmīya-dṛṣṭi*).

The sense of "belonging to oneself" (ātmiyatā) arises through the connection [expressed as] "possessing form" up to "possessing consciousness," for it is by virtue of that connection that one becomes "possessor of that.
Alternatively, there is the sense of "belonging to oneself" in the form of "one's own form" up to "one's own consciousness," based on the self being the controller.
For whatever functions under the control of something—whether in its giving or its application—that is said to belong to it.
From form up to consciousness, there is a sense of "mine" through an inseparable mode of existence;
this is because of the conceptual construction that "this self is followed by, spread throughout, cast into, and has entered into every limb."

Furthermore, the state of having an unascertained object refers to the fact that for one who ascertains characteristics such as "this is form" and so forth, there is no room for the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*).
This is just as when someone suddenly perceives a rope as a snake; however, one who is ascertaining it as a rope would not perceive it as a snake.
Anger and the like should be understood as existing only nominally, because they do not exist apart from resentment and other such mental factors.
"Beyond that" means beyond anger.
Intolerance is the failure to endure harm.
It is the natural law (*dharmatā*) that one who conceals their faults experiences remorse.
And for this reason, it is called "dwelling in non-contact":

speaking words that are loud, intense, and harsh by way of piercing another's vital points; and speaking directly to their face; and "lack of austerity" (asaṃlekha) should be understood as the accumulation of requisites—even those not being used—due to stinginess.
The concealing of actual faults should be understood as shifting from one thing to another;
its function is to obstruct the attainment of correct instruction, because by not revealing oneself as one truly is, one becomes unfit for instruction.
The grasping at the signs of long life is due to the conceptualization thereof, preceded by the thought that one is immortal, which gives rise to pride in one's life.
Any one or another kind of contaminated prosperity—such as noble birth, power, physical beauty, intelligence, wisdom, wealth, or sovereignty—is to be understood [as the object].
Joyful gladness that is a portion of passion is a defiled, specific form of exhilaration.

For one who pursues a beautiful sign, it should be understood as a lack of tranquility of mind resulting from recollecting previous laughter, play, and amorous dalliances in accordance with passion; its function is to provide a basis for laziness in one who lacks faith.
(Abhidh-s-bh 8) Due to the absence of application and desire,
it should be understood as an unconscious conduct of body, speech, and mind in activities such as going forward and returning, because of a lack of correct reflection.
For in this way, due to his lack of knowledge regarding what is to be done and what is not to be done, transgressions arise for him.
Distraction of intrinsic nature refers to the five groups of consciousness,
because by their very nature they cannot be concentrated internally.

Distraction toward the external should be understood as the movement of the mind toward the qualities of sensual pleasure, away from the object of focus— such as hearing and other wholesome qualities— even when one is engaged in them.

Internal distraction (*adhyātmavikṣepa*) refers to sinking (*laya*), agitation (*auddhatya*), and relishing (*āsvādanā*), which cause the fall from meditative concentration for one who is indeed engaged in it.

Distraction regarding signs (*nimittavikṣepa*) should be understood as occurring when one who is engaged in wholesome practice gradually falls away from it due to the sign: "Others will regard me as possessing virtuous qualities.

Distraction of corruption (*dauṣṭhulyavikṣepa*) should be understood as resulting from the impurity of the side of the wholesome, because of the influence of corruptions such as ego-grasping (*ahaṃkāra*), whereby one forms notions of "I," "mine," or "I am" with respect to each feeling of pleasure and so forth as they arise.
First, "taking up" (udgraha) refers to the initial grasping;
"intermingling" (vyavakiraṇā) occurs thereafter, which is the mixing of the mental continuum by means of that [grasping].
"Making it a sign" (nimittīkāra) should be understood as the repeated conceptualization of that very same feeling.

Distraction of attention (*manaskāra-vikṣepa*) should be understood as occurring when one enters another meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), or when one resorts to another stage of meditation (*dhyāna*), by rising from a previous state.
Its function is to act as an obstacle to dispassion (*vairāgya*); this is said with reference to distraction that consists of secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
The sign of sleepiness is as follows: weakness, fatigue, and heaviness of the body.
It consists of attending to the sign of darkness,
disregarding all undertakings, repeatedly practicing sleep at that time, and inducing sleep in others through the power of mantras or by means of massage and the like.
The phrase "consisting of a portion of delusion" is for the purpose of distinguishing it from meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The statement regarding its being wholesome (*kuśala*) and so forth is made because it is not necessarily of the nature of delusion. "Time" refers to the middle watch of the night.
The opposite of that is the improper time.
It is appropriate at the proper time according to the authorization;
it may also be appropriate at an improper time for one who is ill, or for the sake of making the body serviceable for action.
The other is unwholesome. It should be understood that torpor (*middha*), which consists of secondary afflictions, provides a basis for the failure to perform what ought to be done.
Unintended action is preceded by intention; it is the performance of good or bad conduct.

The performance of what is undesired should be understood as occurring either when one is forced by others through physical compulsion, or due to being overcome by the afflictions (*kleśa*), as the case may be.
It is a part of delusion (*moha*) and is thus subsumed under the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
It persists for as long as one does not desist.
That which occurs after that time is "untimely.
That which is appropriate is "in the proper place"; that which is inappropriate is "out of place."

Or, depending on either volition (*cetanā*) or wisdom (*prajñā*), in the states of non-investigation and investigation respectively, *vitarka* is the mental verbalization in the mode of searching, and *vicāra* is the mental verbalization in the mode of examining. (Abhidh-s-bh 9)
Those same two, vitarka and vicāra, are connected [to the first dhyāna],
because of their establishment as coarse and subtle respectively.
For example: the abandonment of greed by means of non-greed, the abandonment of lack of faith by means of faith;
and dispassion is the antidote to attachment.
It acts as an obstacle to that [wholesome state], because it creates an impediment to its arising through that [affliction].

In the same way, it should be understood that for the secondary afflictions such as anger (*krodha*) and so forth, there is an obstruction to the side of joy belonging to one's own [practice of] loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the rest.
The exposition of the formations dissociated from thought (cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra) should be understood in terms of their basis, their intrinsic nature, and their designation.

The attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) and the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) are explained by way of their level (bhūmi), as well as by the two types of mental attention (manaskāra) preceded by the notions of "emancipation" and "abiding.
The state of non-perception (āsaṃjñika) is explained by these same factors, with the exception of mental attention.
The remaining [factors] are explained by means of three [aspects], beginning with the basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Among these, "of wholesome and unwholesome phenomena" is the explanation of the basis;
"accumulation and diminution" is the explanation of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
For thus, when there is an increase [of qualities], one is said to be "endowed with" superior faith and so forth;
when there is a decrease, one is said to be endowed with them in a weak degree.
"Acquisition," "attainment," and "possession" are designations; this is the explanation of the designation.
In this same way, it should be applied to other cases as well, according to what is appropriate.
"One who is free from passion for the Śubhakṛtsna [heaven]" means one who is free from passion for the third dhyāna.
"One who is not yet free from passion for what is above" means one who is not yet free from passion for the fourth dhyāna.
"Preceded by the perception of deliverance" means preceded by the perception of liberation.
"Of the non-stable" refers to those [minds] comprised within the active consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).

"Cessation" (*nirodha*) refers to the cessation of the activity of non-stable minds and mental factors for a period of time, brought about by the mind of meditative attainment (*samāpatti-citta*); it is a particular state of the basis (*āśraya*), so called because by means of this [state], [the activity] is ceased.

In the phrase "one who has not yet abandoned passion for the higher [realms] in the attainment of cessation," the mention of "not yet abandoned passion for the higher" is intended to exclude the Arhat who has abandoned passion for the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), since such an attainment is also possible for him.
And "of some immovable beings" refers to those comprised within the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*).

These two attainments (*samāpatti*) are explained by way of their level (*bhūmi*), mental application (*manaskāra*), basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*), intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and designation (*prajñapti*); the state of non-perception (*āsaṃjñika*) is explained by these same factors, excluding mental application.
The remaining [states] are explained by three factors only: basis and so forth.
The "homogeneous class" (*nikāyasabhāga*) is the continuum of the aggregates (*skandhasantāna*) belonging to a single birth.

The "determination of the duration of stay" is a specific capacity produced by karma, by which it is determined that one must remain in this homogeneous class for such a length of time—whether for a hundred years or a thousand years.
(Abhidh-s-bh 10)
"In each and every class of beings" refers to the classes of beings such as gods, humans, and so forth.
"In the similarity of personal existence" means in the state of belonging to the same category.

Although external matter also possesses a genus, the mention of the "homogeneity of the group" (*nikāyasabhāga*) alone is for the purpose of making known that this designation of characteristics applies specifically to the continuum of sentient beings.
For external form is characterized by dissolution and evolution, whereas internal [form] is characterized by birth, aging, and so forth.
Death should be understood as the destruction of the continuum.
Furthermore, these factors such as birth and the rest are not to be understood as occurring at every moment; rather, they are to be understood in terms of the states of the continuum.
A designation of intrinsic nature refers to such things as "eye," "ear," "god," or "human.
A designation of specific quality refers to such things as "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent" or "all sentient beings will die.
"Based on both of these" means based on the syllables that serve as the basis for designations of intrinsic nature and specific quality, such as *a*, *i*, *u*, and so forth.
And all this is just as follows: intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), particularity (*viśeṣa*), and the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of both;
all of that is conventionally expressed by means of these [three].
Therefore, these sets of names (*nāmakāya*), phrases (*padakāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*) have been established.
"By virtue of being non-translatable through synonyms" means that while [the word] "eye" (cakṣus) flows over— that is, can be expressed— by other synonyms such as *netra*, *akṣi*, *nayana*,
and *locana* because it is understood by those terms as well,
this syllable "A" cannot be made known by any synonym other than the synonym "A."
Therefore, because they do not pass away through transformation, they are called "immutables" (akṣara);
furthermore, "passing away" (kṣaraṇa) should be understood as "going" (gamana).

The establishment of activity occurs when there is no interruption of the continuum, because such a designation does not apply when a single moment has been severed. There is a diversity of cause and fruit: good conduct is the cause for a desired fruit, while bad conduct is the cause for an undesired one, and so forth;
thus, fruits have their respective causes individually and mutually.
The correspondence between cause and fruit, even though they are distinct, is that which is appropriate as the fruit of a particular cause—
for example, the perfection of wealth resulting from giving, and so forth.
It should be understood that the activity of each [cause] occurs individually, not simultaneously.
When the causal process proceeds as a continuous stream, that which therein is cause and fruit having arisen and ceased is designated as the past time;
that which has not yet arisen is the future time;
and that which has arisen but not yet ceased is the present time.
The metaphorical designation "direction" (*deśopacāra*) is applied to the cause and effect when they pervade space.
Furthermore, in this context, the cause and effect should be understood as being comprised of form (*rūpa*), because those that are formless lack the capacity to pervade space.

Regarding the term "number," it applies when there is a distinction between individual instances; for if there were an undifferentiated single essence, numbers such as two, three, and so forth would be untenable.

The convergence of causes, fruits, and conditions is as follows: for that which is called consciousness, it consists of the non-deficiency of the sense faculty, the arrival of the object within the range of appearance, the presence of the cognition thereof, and the manifestation of mental attention (*manaskāra*).
This should be applied similarly in other cases as well.

Thus, all these formations dissociated from mind (cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra) should be understood as existing only nominally (prajñaptisat), because they are designated in relation to the various states of conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra-dharma).
Among them, one [type] pertains to the state of accumulation and diminution of wholesome, unwholesome, and other factors;
three pertain to the state in which the mind and mental factors do not function.
There is one in the state of duration,
one in the state of similarity,
and four in the state of characteristics.
In the state of conventional usage, there are three;
in the state of non-attainment, there is one;
and in the state of cause and fruit, there are the remaining ones.
Furthermore, in this context, "cause and fruit" should be understood as all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
It is a cause because another arises from it;
it is a fruit because it arises from another.
When the aggregates and so forth manifest, the nourishment of their seeds is called "perfuming" (*vāsanā*).
It is "possessing all seeds" because it is endowed with the seeds for the arising of those very aggregates and so forth. In it, phenomena reside as seeds.
It is called the *ālayavijñāna* because sentient beings grasp it as a self;
it is the *vipākavijñāna* because it is produced by past karma;
and it is the *ādānavijñāna* because it repeatedly takes up a personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) at the moment of rebirth-linking.
Furthermore, this is called "mind" because it consists of the mental impressions (*vāsanā*) of all phenomena.
How is it known that this storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) exists?
Because, without it,
the appropriation [of the body], initial clarity, the seed, and karma would not be tenable.
Bodily experience, the two mindless attainments, and likewise death.

The detailed analysis of this summary verse (*uddānagāthā*) is as follows, according to the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*: the existence of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is to be understood through eight aspects. Namely:

because the appropriation of the basis (*āśrayopādāna*) would be impossible without the storehouse consciousness; because the initial arising [of the body] would be impossible; because a clear arising [of cognition] would be impossible; because its status as a seed (*bīja*) would be impossible; because karma would be impossible; because bodily experience would be impossible; and because the mindless attainments (*acittakasamāpatti*) would be impossible.
And because of the impossibility of the transmigration of consciousness.
For what reason is the appropriation of a basis not tenable?
It is said: for five reasons.

For instance, the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) has past formative predispositions (pūrvasaṃskāra) as its cause, whereas the active consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna), such as the visual consciousness and others, have present conditions as their cause.
As it has been stated in detail: "The arising of the consciousnesses occurs by virtue of the sense faculties, objects, and mental attention."
This is the first reason.
Furthermore, the six groups of consciousness, both wholesome and unwholesome, are perceived;
this is the second reason.
Furthermore, among the six groups of consciousness, no such category is found that could be comprised of neutral maturation (*avyākṛta-vipāka*);
this is the third reason.
Moreover, the six groups of consciousness function with specific, determined bases.
In that case, whichever consciousness proceeds by whichever basis, only that [basis] would be appropriated by it, while the remainder would be unappropriated; this is not logical.
Furthermore, even the state of being appropriated is not logical because of the dissociation from consciousness.
This is the fourth reason.
Furthermore, there follows the fault of having to repeatedly grasp a new basis (āśraya).
For instance, visual consciousness arises at one time and does not arise at another; the same applies to the remaining [sensory consciousnesses].
This is the fifth reason.

Thus, it is not tenable [that the self exists] because of its dependence on the causes of present conditions arising from past karma, nor because of being either wholesome or unwholesome, nor because of the non-perception of its birth, nor because of having a specific basis, nor because of the fault of repeated appropriation.
For what reason is the occurrence of an initial commencement not tenable?

If someone were to say, "If the ālayavijñāna exists, then there will be the simultaneous occurrence of two consciousnesses," he should be told this: "You perceive a fault where there is no fault at all."
For indeed, there is the simultaneous occurrence of two consciousnesses.
Why is that?
Because, for someone who simultaneously desires to see, and so forth, up to desires to cognize, the initial arising of one consciousness after another would not be logical.
For in that case, attention is no different [from other factors], as are the sense faculty and the object.

For what reason, if the simultaneous arising of consciousnesses does not exist, would the clarity of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that operates concurrently with the visual and other sensory consciousnesses be impossible?

For instance, at the time when one recollects a past experienced object, the activity of the mental consciousness is indistinct; however, the activity of the mind directed toward a present object is not similarly indistinct.
For this reason as well, either simultaneous occurrence is logical, or else the indistinctness of the mental consciousness [is to be explained].
For what reason is it impossible for the six groups of consciousness to serve as seeds for one another?
Because, immediately after a wholesome state, an unwholesome state arises; and immediately after an unwholesome state, a wholesome state arises.
Immediately after both of those is the indeterminate;
immediately after the inferior realm is the intermediate realm;
and immediately after the intermediate realm is the superior realm.
Thus, immediately after a superior realm, up to an inferior realm;
immediately after that which is with outflows, that which is without outflows;
and immediately after that which is without outflows, [that which is with outflows].
There is the contaminated, the supramundane immediately following the mundane, and the mundane immediately following the supramundane;
yet it is not tenable for these to function as seeds in such a manner.
Furthermore, even though the continuum has been interrupted for a long time, it would have to proceed after a long period; therefore, this too is not tenable.
For what reason is action not possible if there is no simultaneous arising of consciousnesses?
To explain: in brief, action is fourfold—representation of the receptacle world, representation of the basis, representation of "I," and representation of objects.
These representations are perceived as arising simultaneously moment by moment.
Moreover, it is not logical for a single consciousness in a single moment to possess such distinct and diverse functions as these.
For what reason is bodily experience not tenable in the absence of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*)?

For, in one who is either reflecting properly or improperly, or who is either in a state of mental composure or lack of composure, those various and manifold bodily experiences that arise in the body would not exist; yet they are indeed perceived.
Therefore, for this reason as well, the storehouse consciousness exists.
For what reason is it that without the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), the mindless attainments (acittā samāpatti) cannot occur?
For in such a case, whether one has attained the absorption of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) or the absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), consciousness would have departed from the body;
since it has not departed, death itself would occur.
As it was said by the Blessed One: "And his consciousness has not departed from the body."
For what reason is even death not tenable if the storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna) does not exist?
For it is thus: as one is dying, the consciousness abandons the upper part of the body while making it cold, or the lower part of the body.
Furthermore, the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) never fails to function.

Therefore, it is only through the departure of the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), which appropriates the body, that the cooling of the body and the lack of sensation in the body are observed;
this is not due to the cessation of the mental consciousness.
For this reason as well, it is not tenable.
It should be understood that the mind is defined by way of its etymology, its object, its association, and the time of its activity.
It is absent during the manifestation of the Path,
because ultimate knowledge is absolutely incompatible with the active manifestation of the view of a self.
Beyond that, there is the arising from the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*),
because it has not been abandoned by one in training (*śaikṣa*).
[This occurs] from the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*).
The state of being more peaceful in the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) is to be understood precisely from the non-occurrence of that [mental activity].
Since the mind that has just ceased is accepted [as the basis], the meaning is that it is considered "immediately preceding" (anantara).
The establishment of consciousness should be understood in terms of its basis, its object, and its intrinsic nature.

There is no separate establishment of specific characteristics for the elements (dhātu) and bases (āyatana), because the characteristics of the eye and so forth have already been stated within the exposition of the aggregates (skandha). Therefore, the elements are established by being extracted from the aggregates themselves.
From the elements come the sense bases.
As for that which is not included among the aggregates, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is established as being eightfold.
It should be understood that the threefold nature of suchness (*tathatā*) arises from the distinction of its bases and modes, not from a distinction in its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Because it is unchanging, it should always be contemplated as being devoid of self (*nirātmatā*).
"By way of the non-occurrence of affliction" means that by means of that object, the basis of affliction is rendered empty of affliction.
Even when it is said to be "afflicted," one should understand that the secondary affliction therein is merely adventitious.
What, then, is that adventitious secondary affliction?
The activity of the dependent mind (*paratantra-citta*), whose seeds of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*) have not been extracted, manifests in a dual form;
it is not the true nature (*dharmatā*) of the mind,
for the true nature of all phenomena is luminosity by nature (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara*).
Signs (*nimitta*) are elaborated as form, sensation, and so forth, up to awakening; because these have ceased therein, it is signless (*animitta*).
That which is real (*bhūta*) is that which is non-erroneous (*aviparīta*).
Its limit is its boundary, because no reality is sought beyond selflessness (*nairātmya*).
Space is the absence of form; that dharma which is the object of mental consciousness and is characterized by non-existence through the reversal of form—that is space.
Furthermore, its being an object of mental consciousness should be understood as occurring within the context of the *dharmadhātu*.

By the restrictive emphasis "of form alone" (*rūpasyaiva*), those factors common to feeling and so forth—namely, suchness, analytical cessation, non-analytical cessation, and impermanence—are excluded.
The absolute non-existence of things such as a rabbit's horn is not cognized by way of their opposite.
Because those very things do not exist at all;
even things such as a rabbit's horn are not the opposite of this existing form,
since they are common to [the category of] feeling and so forth.

Therefore, it is said that [the definition] applies only to the reversal of form (*rūpa*). By the statement of the characteristic of non-existence (*abhāva-lakṣaṇa*), there is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of feeling (*vedanā*) and the other immaterial factors,
for they do not have the characteristic of non-existence.
That which is cessation but not dissociation is due to the non-uprooting of the latent tendencies;
through the opposite, there is dissociation.
This dyad must be abandoned: the afflictions and the object that serves as their basis.
Furthermore, that "felt object" (vedita) is of two kinds: transformative and non-transformative, corresponding respectively to pleasure, pain, and neither-pain-nor-pleasure.
In that regard, the establishment of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) is due to the abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
The establishment of the imperturbable (*āniñjya*) and the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha*) follows respectively from the abandonment of the two kinds of feeling.
Therein, the abandonment of the afflictions is the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*) resulting from the removal of the dysfunctions (*dauṣṭhulya*) belonging to their side.
The abandonment of feeling is the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*) resulting from the removal of the hindrance to the meditative attainment that serves as its antidote.
For this very reason, in the second dhyāna, there is no establishment of the cessation of suffering as unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*),
because the transformative feeling has not been abandoned without remainder.
The ten material elements are subsumed within the aggregate of form; that same [aggregate] is subsumed within the element of phenomena (dharmadhātu);
and the seven consciousness-elements are subsumed within the sense-base of mind (manāyatana). Thus, all phenomena consist of these three.
When the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases have been thus established, this incidental matter is now explained.
Since the eyes, ears, and noses each exist as pairs, how is it that there are not twenty-one elements?
Although these are twofold, they do not constitute separate elements,
because both possess the same defining characteristic, namely the characteristic of the eye.
Because both possess the same functional nature, as they both perform the function of visual consciousness;
the same should be applied to the ear and nose.
However, the production of two [organs] for each [sense-field] is for the sake of the beauty of their basis.
Thus, a physical form with both sides well-proportioned and symmetrical is beautiful; it is not otherwise.
Does visual consciousness arise always depending on each eye individually, or rather on both?
It is said that it arises from both,
because of the clarity of perception.
Just as the perception of form is clear when both eyes are open, but not so when only one is, so too it should be understood here:
for example, in a single room, a single expanse of light that depends upon two lamps exists more clearly than if it depended on only one.
Such is the principle to be seen in this case as well.
When various objects are presented through each individual sense-door, do the consciousnesses arise in succession regarding those types of objects, or rather simultaneously?
It should be understood that there is only one simultaneous consciousness with manifold aspects.
When a morsel of food has reached the tongue, it should be understood that the tongue-consciousness and body-consciousness always arise simultaneously.
Because sound is subject to cessation, it does not travel to other locations through a series of successive productions in different places; rather, it occurs all at once.
Just as one observes the expansion of a lamp’s light while remaining fixed in its own place, so too should the expansion of sound be understood to arise.

As for the fact that a sound obstructed by something nearby is heard indistinctly, this should be understood as being due to the resistance of the sound, resulting from the mention of a slight opening in the obstruction.

Among the six consciousnesses, how many are conceptual and how many are non-conceptual? First, with respect to the three types of conceptualization, the single mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is conceptual.

The three types of conceptualization are: conceptualization of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavikalpa*), conceptualization of recollection (*anusmaraṇavikalpa*), and conceptualization of investigation (*abhinirūpaṇāvikalpa*).

Among these, conceptualization of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavikalpa*) is the conceptualization that takes the form of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) regarding presently occurring conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that are being experienced.
Conceptualization of recollection (*anusmaraṇavikalpa*) is that which takes the form of conditioned phenomena previously experienced.

Conceptualization of investigation (*abhinirūpaṇāvikalpa*) is the conceptualization that takes the form of inferential reasoning (*abhyūhana*) regarding past, future, and present objects that are not directly perceived.

Furthermore, there are seven types of conceptualization (*vikalpa*): conceptualization that flows spontaneously toward an object, conceptualization with signs, conceptualization without signs, investigative conceptualization, analytical conceptualization, afflicted conceptualization, and non-afflicted conceptualization.

Among these, the first conceptualization consists of the five groups of sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*), because they flow spontaneously toward their respective objects without elaborating upon the object.
Conceptualization with signs (*sanimitta*) is conceptualization that recollects intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because it takes present and past objects as its diverse focus.

Conceptualization without signs (*animitta*) is conceptualization whose object is the future and which takes the form of mental aspiration (*manoratha*). The remaining types of conceptualization should be understood as having the nature of investigative conceptualization (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*);
for instance, at one time, while deliberating, one investigates.
At one time he examines, at another time he becomes afflicted, and at another time he is unafflicted.
When consciousness is the specific cognition of form and so forth, for what reason is it called "eye-consciousness" and so on, rather than "consciousness of form" and so on?
Because five types of grammatical analysis are possible, the expression "consciousness of form" and so on is untenable.
How so?
Visual consciousness is consciousness in the eye;
this is because consciousness arises in the location of its support,
and because it exists when that [support] exists.
For when the eye exists, visual consciousness necessarily arises, because those who are not blind see even in darkness due to their non-blindness;
whereas it does not necessarily arise when the visible object exists, because the blind do not see it.
Visual consciousness is consciousness by means of the eye; for even when the visible object is unaltered, the consciousness undergoes transformation due to its influence.
This is just as in the case of one afflicted by the disease of jaundice.
Even when blue and other forms are present before the eye, only the perception of yellow occurs; thus,
it is "eye-consciousness" because the consciousness arises from the eye due to its connection with the seed of consciousness.
It is for the sake of the visual consciousness, because it is beneficial or harmful to it;
for in this way, the faculty undergoes either benefit or injury through the experience associated with that consciousness.

"Not of the object" means that eye-consciousness is [the cause] of eye-consciousness because both are included within the category of sentient beings, but it is not necessarily [the cause] of visible form.
Should it be understood that the eye sees forms, or rather that consciousness sees them?
It should be understood that neither the one nor the other sees,
because dharmas are devoid of activity.
However, when the totality of conditions is present, there is the designation of "seeing.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the eye possesses primacy in the seeing of forms by way of six aspects, and not consciousness.
By which six?
By way of being the cause of arising, because the eye arises from it;
by way of being its locus.
Because vision relies upon the eye,
and because its activity is unchanging, since the eye is always of a single homogeneous nature.
By way of independent activity,
because it does not depend on a collection of conditions for its production at every moment;
and by way of beautiful activity.
Therefore, it is because of the excellence of its basis;
and from scripture, because of the statement, "having seen forms with the eye.
And all this as described is not possible for consciousness alone.
Its state of having a fluctuating activity, however, should be understood as arising in many different ways.

Just as the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is established among the elements (*dhātu*) and the sense-bases (*āyatana*), why is it not likewise established among the aggregates (*skandha*)? Because the meaning of "aggregate" is impossible [in that case].
The meaning of "aggregate" has been explained as the sense of a "heap," based on the concise grouping of forms (*rūpa*) and so forth according to their categories such as past and so on.
And since that [characteristic] is not possible for what is eternal, there is no establishment of the unconditioned within the aggregates.
For what reason are those very same phenomena taught separately by way of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*)?
It is for the purpose of generating in those to be trained skill in teaching through both summary and detailed exposition.
For instance, those two which were taught in brief as form (*rūpa*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) in the exposition of the aggregates are presented in eleven ways within the elements and bases.
And as they have been taught by Vyāsa after dividing them into seven parts according to their respective applications,

those [factors] therein such as feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth, which were treated individually, are here subsumed within the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*) as the element and base of mental phenomena (*dharmadhātu-āyatana*).
Furthermore, it should be understood that the exposition of the aggregates (*skandha*) is by way of establishing [phenomena] according to their mere characteristics;
the exposition of the elements (*dhātu*) is by way of establishing the apprehended, the apprehender, and the act of apprehension;
and the exposition of the sense-bases (*āyatana*) is by way of establishing the mere apprehended and apprehender as the gateways for the act of apprehension.
The incidental discussion is concluded.
From this point forward, the explanation of the meaning of the root text itself should be observed.
The "final eye" of an Arhat refers to the last [eye] at the time of parinirvāṇa;
therein lies the element (*dhātu*).
Because the eye of another is not a cause [for one's own];

for when an ordinary person born in the formless realm falls from there and is reborn in a realm possessing form, the eye will arise from the seed of the eye residing within the *ālayavijñāna*, and not so for a noble one (*ārya*), because of their non-returning.

It must be stated here that the body-element is not the body for an ordinary person born in the formless realm; for while there is a body-element for such a person, it is not a body, because bodies such as those in the egg-stage and so forth have come into existence, and because that which has lost its body is no longer living.

It may be that there is the mind-element (manodhātu) but not the mind (manas); this refers here to one who has entered the attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñisamāpatti), because the afflicted mind (kliṣṭamanas) exists [there].
"Born," "become," and "ceased" refer respectively to birth, growth, and decline.

This is said with reference to the noble disciple (*ārya-śrāvaka*), who by means of a mind belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*) cognizes phenomena belonging to the formless realm, those of his own level, and those that are untainted (*anāsrava*).
An outsider, however, an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), cognizes only those belonging to his own level.
But here, a certain follower of the Dharma, by virtue of the cultivation of what he has previously heard, takes even higher levels as objects for the sake of producing that [knowledge].
As is form, so is experience; for from the two—sense faculty and object—which are to be experienced as pleasure and so forth, there arises the feeling of pleasure and so forth.
As one feels, so one perceives; for one grasps the signs according to the experience. As one perceives, so one intends; for one performs karma in accordance with one's perception.

Just as one intends, so does consciousness proceed toward this or that [state], because consciousness transforms according to its formative activity (*abhisaṃskāra*) with respect to objects and various destinies.
That in which one is defiled or purified is the body together with its sense faculties;
that by means of which there is experience is, respectively, that which is "with worldly attachment" (*sāmiṣa*) and that which is "free from worldly attachment" (*nirāmiṣa*), and so forth.
"By which formative activity of grasping signs" refers to that which proceeds either improperly or properly;
"that which becomes afflicted or purified" refers to the arising of the mind's dysfunction or its lack of dysfunction.
The classification of form and the other aggregates into categories such as past and so forth should be understood as being based on eleven types of craving. These are:

craving of dependence, craving of delight, craving of attachment, craving for food, craving for sense objects, craving for sensual pleasure, craving for meditative attainment, craving for the suffering of misconduct, craving for the happiness of good conduct, distant craving, and proximate craving.
The past and other [temporal] categories should be applied respectively as the objects (*ālambana*) of this craving (*tṛṣṇā*).

There is another classification: the past and so forth are to be understood accordingly through the distinctions of what has arisen and what has not arisen; the distinction between the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the grasped (*grāhya*); the distinction between that which is directed outward and that which is directed inward; the distinction between the afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) and the non-afflicted (*akliṣṭa*); and the distinction between the remote (*viprakṛṣṭa*) and the proximate (*saṃnikṛṣṭa*).
These are to be understood as follows:
therein, that which has arisen is the past and the present;
that which has not yet arisen is the future.
That which is directed outward belongs to the stage of non-concentration;
that which is directed inward belongs to the stage of concentration.
The remainder has not been analyzed because it is easy to understand.

"By way of having the characteristic of the vastness of suffering" means that, based on form and so forth, there is an expansion of sufferings such as birth and so on. "Carrying the burden of affliction" is because the afflictions and other defilements depend upon form and so forth.
For example, in the world, it is observed that the metaphorical designation "aggregate" (*skandha*) is applied to that part of the body by which a burden is carried.
"One carries a burden with the shoulder."
The meaning of "the seed of all phenomena" refers to the sense of cause with respect to the *ālayavijñāna*.

The meaning of "maintaining the state of cause and effect" refers, respectively, to the six consciousness-elements and the elements of the sense faculties and their objects among the eighteen elements.

It should be understood that by means of the inclusion of all types of phenomena, the other elements (dhātu) taught in other sūtras—such as the earth element and so forth—are also included within these very eighteen [elements] as appropriate.
Furthermore, the meaning of "basis" (āyatana) should be understood as the sense of being a seed and the sense of the inclusion of all types of phenomena.
The fact that the aggregates of form and so forth are like a mass of foam should be understood from their appearing as non-existent, empty, void, and lacking essence.

Furthermore, the meaning of these scriptural phrases is to be understood through the words "by way of non-self," and so forth, which serve respectively as the antidotes to the inversions of self, purity, pleasure, and permanence.

The establishment of the three questions—“How?”, “How many?”, and “For what purpose?”—is for the sake of abandoning confusion regarding characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and entities (*vastu*), as well as superimposition (*samāropa*).

In this regard, confusion regarding [the nature of] substantial existence (*dravyasat*) is abandoned by the explanation of the characteristic of what is substantially existent. Confusion regarding the entity itself is abandoned by the statement that “all [of these] are substantially existent,” for the purpose of relinquishing the dogmatic adherence to a self-substance (*ātma-dravya*). And by the phrase “for the purpose of relinquishing [that adherence],” superimposition is abandoned.
The same should be applied elsewhere as well.

That which is independent of verbal expression is the objective domain of the sense faculties; for example, when there is the apprehension of an object after it has been differentiated by a name, such as "form" or "feeling.
That which is independent of anything else is, for example, where that cognition occurs without depending on another object.
It is not as in the case of jars and the like, where the cognition of a jar and so forth arises in dependence upon color and other qualities.
That which has defilement as its object exists conventionally in the sense that it functions as defilement;
this is for the purpose of abandoning the attachment that the self is the cause of defilement.
The object for the sake of purification is the ultimate reality (*paramārthasat*), in the sense that it is the sphere of supreme knowledge;
all phenomena are ultimately real because they are not distinct from suchness (*tathatā*).
That by which one is defiled and purified should be understood as the mental factors (*caitasika*), such as attachment (*rāga*) and so forth, as well as faith (*śraddhā*) and so forth.
Furthermore, that which is the "state" therein refers to the formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*) designated upon the states of form, mind, and mental factors.
And that which is purification should be understood as the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) purification.
And that [object] is as appropriate [to each case].
Furthermore, the object of the thirteenfold consciousness has been demonstrated by this as the "knowable" (*jñeya*).

Moreover, that consists of knowledge derived from hearing (*śrutamaya-jñāna*), knowledge derived from reflection (*cintāmaya-jñāna*), mundane knowledge derived from cultivation (*laukika-bhāvanāmaya-jñāna*), and ultimate knowledge (*paramārtha-jñāna*).

The knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of phenomena, subsequent knowledge, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, the knowledge of cessation, the knowledge of the path, the knowledge of destruction and non-arising, and the knowledge of the Mahāyāna— these and others, such as the knowledge of resolute belief and so forth, are to be understood according to their respective order.
In that context, knowledge of another's mind is "knowledge of another" because its object is the mind of another self;
knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) is "lower knowledge."

Subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) is the knowledge of the higher [realms], because it arises after the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*). It is so called because it first arises with respect to the truths.

Regarding the knowledge of thorough examination (*vidūṣaṇā*), the knowledge of arousal (*samutthāpanā*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda*), the knowledge of culmination (*niṣṭhā*), and the knowledge regarding great purposes (*mahārtha*): these should be connected [to the term "knowledge"] as "the knowledge of their thorough examination" up to "the knowledge of great purposes.
Furthermore, their status as "great purposes" is due to their being for the benefit of both oneself and others.
In that regard, it is non-conceptual through the five groups of sensory consciousnesses;
it is conceptual through the mental consciousness;
and it is the cause through the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna).
From the perspective of their engagement, consciousness is distinct from them; from the perspective of the cause, they are the sense faculties and their objects;
from the perspective of the effect, they are the consciousnesses;
and from the perspective of the discordant factors and their antidotes, they are "with lust" and "free from lust," "with hatred" and "free from hatred," and so forth.

In terms of subtle distinctions, there are seven types based on the classification of representations that are difficult to discern. These seven types of representations difficult to discern are as follows: (1) the representation that is not consciously perceived; (2) the representation of the receptacle world, because its form is undifferentiated at all times; and (3) the representation of manifold forms, which consists of many diverse forms within a single [consciousness]. Its subtlety arises from the fact that it is difficult to establish [its specific nature] due to this variety.

The representation of coexistence refers to consciousnesses arising at the same time; their subtlety consists in the difficulty of establishing how they individually discern their respective objects. It should be understood that "subtlety" is the term governing all [the following cases]. Regarding the representation of the rapid transformation of the adversary and its antidote: how is it that the mind, which is bound by the entire collection of fetters such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth, becomes momentarily and simultaneously free from passion and the like?
How is the representation of latent impressions (vāsanāvijñapti) perfumed by the mind through the performance of actions?
That latent impression is neither something other than that [mind],
nor is it merely that [mind] itself.
And regarding the granting of the fruit, there is the gradual acquisition of its activity.
How is it that the consciousness at rebirth— which is permeated by karma capable of producing a physical existence (*ātmabhāva*) of many kinds—
suddenly awakens a certain latent impression (*vāsanā*) of that karma during the indistinct state of death and [manifests] in one [particular form]?
"I shall form a rebirth-linking in [this] existence.

Since it is difficult to establish how the mind of an Arhat— liberated from informative action (*vijñapti*), supreme, free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), having attained the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and having transcended all forms of contaminated conduct (*sāśravacaryā*) appropriate for cyclic existence— continues in this manner, its subtlety (*sūkṣmatva*) should be understood.
By the mention of "the seer" and so forth, it should be understood that the inclusion of the seer, the hearer, the smeller, the taster, the toucher, and the cognizer is intended.
That which is to be known through supernormal knowledge (*abhijñeya*) is the object of the six supernormal knowledges (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*).
Because it is characterized by the excellence of movement, the supernormal knowledge of psychic power (*ṛddhy-abhijñā*) is "to be known" by way of its transition into that object.
[The others are so called] because one enters into the conduct [of beings] through the knowledge of the signs of those who possess passion and so forth.
It is [known] by way of arrival through the knowledge of coming from the succession of past births;
by way of departure through the knowledge of going toward future arising;
and by way of escape through the knowledge of the means for liberation from the three realms.
All [objects] are to be known through direct higher knowledge (*abhijñeya*), because the final three have everything as their object.

In that context, "possessing form" (*rūpī*) means that form is the essential nature (*ātmasvabhāva*) of that phenomenon; therefore, it is "possessing form," not because it is conjoined with another form.
As for the statement "it has the intrinsic nature of form" (*rūpasvabhāva*),

he shows that it possesses the quality of being "form" (*rūpitva*) both by way of its dependence on the primary elements (*bhūtāśrayataḥ*) and by way of its association with other forms (*rūpāntarayogāt*).
This is because derived form (*upādāyarūpa*) is associated with the form of the primary elements, and the primary elements are mutually associated with one another.
"Arising from joy" means that its very nature is such that joy itself is its arising;
it is not, however, as in the case of feeling and so forth, where prior joy is the arising and present contact and so on are the conditions.
Because it possesses spatial extension (*sapradeśa*) due to having parts;
because it pervades space through its proximity to the cardinal directions;

because it can be designated as being "in this direction" through the teaching of location; and because it serves as an object of cognition for one situated in a particular place, since its sphere is that of location.

Because of the common range of both [types of] beings in a certain location, there is the state of being an object (*ālambana*) for two kinds of beings due to the presence of a forest; because of the common range of both [types of] beings, there is the equal state of being an object for two kinds of beings due to the presence of a forest. However, it is not so for those who are formless (*arūpin*), because they cannot be apprehended by others according to their own self-experience.
Furthermore, in terms of connection, visual consciousness and the others also possess the nature of form (*rūpitva*) in a successive manner.
Because of the connection with the material sense-faculties;
because of their persistence, since the seeds of form persist in ordinary beings even in the formless realms;
and because of their manifestation, since applied and sustained thought manifest upon their respective objects.
"By way of affliction" means by the deformation and oppression of the five aggregates through the contact of hands and so forth, as well as by grief and so forth, as appropriate;
"by way of attainment" means by the determination of the meaning of the teaching;
"by way of the establishment of accumulation" means because of the establishment of the atom as having parts, beyond which no further form exists.

From the perspective of being outward-turned, the form belonging to the desire realm arises from craving for the objects of sensual pleasure; from the perspective of being inward-turned, the form belonging to the form realm arises from craving for the mind of meditative attainment. For this very reason, its nature as "mind-made" (manomaya) should be understood.
From the perspective of duration, it belongs to ordinary persons because there is no established limit to their past and future ends.
From the perspective of limitation, the form (*rūpa*) of one in training (*śaikṣa*) is limited because their cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) has been brought to its end.
From the perspective of time, the form of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is [limited] because only the present existence remains.
From the perspective of manifestation, the form of the Buddha and others is [limited] by virtue of its being merely a display and not being fully established (*aniṣpanna*).
In that regard, all material forms are [to be understood] by way of their being subject to affliction;
the remaining [categories] are to be understood accordingly.
Furthermore, the six divisions of material form, beginning with outward-directedness, should be understood as being common to feeling and the other aggregates.
"The division of the remaining [categories] is like that of form (*rūpin*).
How so?

Just as it was stated in detail that "possessing form" (*rūpin*) is so because of its nature as possessing form, so too "visible" (*sanidarśana*) should be applied in detail because of its nature as being visible.

In that regard, all [factors] are with demonstration (*sanidarśana*), because even formless factors (*arūpin*) are considered "with demonstration" due to their connection with all demonstrations and so forth.

It "covers" (*āvṛṇoti*) and is "covered" (*āvriyate*) in the sense of being an obstacle to movement. While it would have been sufficient to say only "it covers," the statement that it is also "covered" is for the purpose of establishing that visible form, such as light, possesses resistance (*sapratighatva*). For such [form] is indeed covered and does not cover; this is its genus, this is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), is the meaning.

"Above the atom" means that a single atom is non-obstructive. "Form that does not function by the power of meditative concentration" means that it is non-obstructive because it functions through the power of concentration, like a deity with an even mind.
"A basis for provocation" refers to that physical basis or object upon which hatred arises.
And by this sense of being "with resistance" (sapratigha), all [factors] are understood as being with resistance;
or, as the case may be, they are understood through the remaining [senses], according to their respective application.
They are "with-outflows" (*sāsrava*) by way of being identical with outflows, because they are endowed with the intrinsic nature of outflows.

They are "with-outflows" by way of connection with outflows, because the mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) that arise simultaneously with them, as well as the eyes and other sense faculties, are respectively associated with outflows and serve as the basis for outflows.
They are "with-outflows" by way of bondage through outflows, because wholesome states that are with-outflows bring about renewed existence (*punarbhava*) under their influence.
Because they are connected with the outflows (*āsrava*), even those belonging to other stages serve as the basis for the depravity (*dauṣṭhulya*) of the outflows of other stages.

"Because they are conducive to the outflows" means that although the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) are accompanied by the depravity of the afflictions, they are established as being without outflows (*anāsrava*) because they are turned away from all existence (*bhava*).
Because they are the antidotes to that;
and because, by way of the continuity of the outflows (*āsrava*), the aggregates (*skandha*) of Arhats have arisen from the afflictions (*kleśa*) of previous births.
The five aggregates are with outflows (*sāsrava*).
