Fifteen elements are with outflows, excluding the final three.
Ten bases are with outflows, excluding the final two.
It consists of a portion of the three realms and two bases, excluding the noble path along with its attendants and the unconditioned.

Passion and the like are "conflicts" (raṇa) because they are the causes of battle, such as the taking up of weapons; as many as there are contaminated (sāsrava) phenomena, so many are "with conflict" (saraṇa), and so forth—this is to be understood in the sense of being their consequence.
Attachment and the other [afflictions] are "the bait" because they are the causes for clinging to renewed existence.
How is it that hatred is a cause for clinging to renewed existence?
Because one clings to renewed existence through hatred toward the dharmas conducive to purification.
Greed refers to attachment and other afflictions that cause one to be intent upon the qualities of sensual pleasure.
By what kind of hatred is there such intentness?
By hatred toward renunciation.
The manifestation and non-manifestation [of phenomena] through one's own volition (kāmakāra) is not possible for the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), because it is eternal.

Since that which is neither conditioned nor unconditioned is not distinct from these two—as it has been said: "These two are the conditioned and the unconditioned"—how then can this duality exist in such a manner?
It should be said that it is "conditioned" (saṃskṛta) in the sense of being present through the exercise of will;
it is "unconditioned" (asaṃskṛta) in the sense of not being produced by karma and afflictions.
It is not distinct from these two, nor is it separate from them.
"Appearing as that" refers to the aspect included within the three realms;
for appearances such as *tathatā* (suchness) are exclusively supramundane (*lokottara*) because they are entirely unfamiliar [to worldly consciousness].
This is stated with the exception of one portion of the aggregates comprised by right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), and the appearances of the supramundane obtained subsequently (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*).
And that, with the exception of the unconditioned, should be understood as a portion of the three elements and two bases.
The Noble Path is the antidote to the three realms.

Furthermore, because it serves as the antidote to the fourfold distortions— such as the notion of permanence and so forth— for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, it is non-conceptual by virtue of being non-erroneous and free from conceptual construction.

Because it serves as the antidote to the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) of all phenomena such as form for Bodhisattvas, it is non-conceptual by virtue of being free from proliferation and conceptualization;
the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), however, is non-conceptual because all conceptualizations have ceased to appear. "Arising at the beginning" refers to the time of rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi*).
That which arises from continuity occurs from that point onward.
That which arises from accumulation is produced by four kinds of accumulation caused by sleep, food, celibacy, and meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
That which arises as a basis is the internal faculty (*indriya*).

That which arises from transformation is the modification of the faculties that is concordant with the arising of pleasant feelings and so forth. That which arises from maturation is the state of being decayed. That which arises from decline pertains to one who, having passed away from a happy destiny, is being reborn in an unhappy destiny.
That which arises from distinction is the opposite [of the former].

That which arises from luminosity pertains, as appropriate, to the gods of the *Kṛīḍāpramoṣaka*, *Manaspradūṣaka*, *Nirmāṇarati*, and *Paranirmitavaśavartin* realms, as well as to the gods of the Form and Formless Realms, because of their great abundance of joy and their mastery over enjoyments and dwellings.
That which arises without radiance is other than that;
that which arises through transition occurs during the state of movement;
and that which arises with seeds exists, excluding the final aggregates of an Arhat.
The final aggregates arise without seeds;

the objects of knowledge that arise as reflections, manifestations of mastery, and illustrations are, respectively, the similar form, the form pertaining to liberation, and the form pertaining to the Tathāgata;
and those that arise through succession exist within the continuity of births.
The characteristic of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arises through momentary destruction at every instant.

It arises through conjunction and disjunction in the states of union with or separation from the pleasant and unpleasant, as well as in the mind’s states of being with passion or free from passion, and so forth.
It arises through change of state in the stages such as the *kalala* and others, and in the stages such as illness and others.
The world of sentient beings arises through death and rebirth;
the receptacle world arises through the processes of dissolution and evolution;
and the existence of the prior period arises during the prior period.
That which arises at the time of death is the existence at the time of death (maraṇakālabhava);
that which arises in the interval is the intermediate existence (antarābhava);
and that which arises at the moment of rebirth-linking is the existence of birth (upapattibhava).

It is a portion of the aggregate of form (*rūpa*) and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra*), characterized respectively as the sense faculties (*indriya*) and the associated mental factors (*saṃprayukta*).
It is also a portion of the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), having the nature of the associated factors.
It should be understood as the "experiencer-self" (*bhoktātman*) in the sense of perceiving desirable and undesirable objects.
The eye, the ear, and the mind grasp their objects without reaching them;
the other sense organs grasp their objects by reaching them.
That which is born of the five sense organs grasps its respective object—each determined individually—which is present and possesses its own specific characteristic.
That which grasps its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), as well as all objects at all times, is that which is produced from the sixth faculty.
With reference to the arising of consciousness through the assembly of conditions, the designation of a "grasper" (subject) should be understood as a conventional metaphor,
and not as an ultimate reality, because all phenomena lack functional activity. Furthermore,
that which is a grasper is also an object of grasping, since even the eyes and other sense organs are objects of mental consciousness.
The restriction "only within the domain of the grasper" is intended to exclude the mental factors (caitasika).

The non-external orientation of that which is comprised of [wisdom] consisting of hearing, reflection, and the practice in accordance with that Dharma should be understood as being due to its having the outflowing Dharma as its cause, and because it takes nirvāṇa and so forth as its object by virtue of that [cause].
Furthermore, the outflowing dharma (*niṣyandadharma*) should be understood as the teaching that follows from the realization of the Buddhas and others.

There are four elements: the element of olfactory consciousness, the element of odor, the element of gustatory consciousness, and the element of taste. There are two bases (*āyatana*): the base of odor and the base of taste; these, along with a portion of the others, are comprised within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
"Of ten elements" refers to the seven consciousness-elements and the elements of form, sound, and mental phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
"Of four bases" refers to the bases of form, sound, mind, and mental phenomena.
"By way of the employment of cause and fruit" means, respectively, because of having arisen and because of having ceased.

"By way of transcending the activity of affliction and purification" means that, like present passion and so forth, or faith and so forth, there is an absence of the capacity for the mind's affliction or purification.
Or, "by way of the destruction of the appropriation of causes" means that it has perished after having deposited its latent impression (*vāsanā*).

It should be understood that memory, conceptualization, and so forth function as causes by virtue of being merely objects of focus (*ālambana-mātra*), because at the present time the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of their fruits exist and non-exist— due to the presence of the latencies (*vāsanā*) deposited therein and the absence of the substances (*dravya*) that deposited them.
A single portion of all [phenomena] consists of those excluding the future, the present, and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The phrase "non-arising when a cause exists" is for the purpose of distinguishing [conditioned phenomena] from the unconditioned;
for the latter, although it is non-arisen, it does not possess a cause,
because its nature is not established through the acquisition of its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Because the cause and fruit have not yet been utilized, that seed has not fulfilled its function, and because it has not yet arisen.
Furthermore, it is because of the utilization or non-utilization of cause and fruit, and because of being irreversible and non-abiding;
and because the designation of the past and future occurs by depending upon the present as the basis for manifesting the past and future.
Regarding that state... (Abhidh-s-bh 27)
That which is yet to be attained is the future;
that which has been attained is the past.
This is because the eye and other faculties exist as the bases for consciousness and so forth through the presence of their functional activity (*kāritra*).

By virtue of the section concerning the exposition of the past, this is also made known: for what reason did the Blessed One establish only the three bases of discourse (*kathāvastu*)—the past and so forth—and not *nirvāṇa*?
The meaning is that because *nirvāṇa* is to be personally realized (*pratyātmavedanīya*), it is inexpressible; therefore, it cannot be spoken of.
This is because the conventional usages of "seen," "heard," "thought," and "cognized" have as their basis the past, future, and present.
Of ten elements— namely, the consciousness elements and the elements of form, sound, and phenomena—
and of four bases— namely, the bases of form, sound, mind, and phenomena— it is within those very [bases], such as faith and the rest.
"By nature, without deliberation" means by its own inherent tendency (*svarasena*), that is to say, without the power of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and so forth.

"The inclination (*ruci*) becomes established" means that it is not merely the inclination alone that is acquired through birth (*upapattiprātilambhika*), but rather [the inclination] together with those qualities such as faith (*śraddhā*) and the rest.
The cultivation of the wholesome refers to all wholesome factors consisting of hearing and so forth; this should be understood as follows:

by means of [the results of] rebirth in heaven and birth in a wealthy family, he shows the cause of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*); and by means of the acquisition of what is conducive to purification (*vyavadāna-anukūla*), he shows the cause of attainment (*prāpti*).

The counteragents to the [ten] defilements and so forth will be explained later. Any other affliction or secondary affliction that gives rise to misconduct is as follows: that which belongs to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) is non-abandonable (*anaiḥsargika*);
however, that which gives rise to misconduct and is abandonable (*naiḥsargika*) is unwholesome (*akuśala*).
That which is other than those should be understood as obscured-unneutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).
For example, one establishes a shrine preceded by violence, where goats, buffaloes, and so forth are slaughtered;
or one established with wrong views, where those seeking merit or seeking boons undergo affliction through fasting and the like.
Whether it be "projecting" (*ākṣepaka*) or "completing" (*paripūraka*), this is with reference to the miserable destinies (*durgati*);
however, in the happy destinies (*sugati*), it is only "completing," by which one who has been reborn here experiences calamities such as poverty.
The factors that obstruct the wholesome are, for instance, frequent gatherings in groups and so forth.
The eight elements are the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, odor, taste, and tangible-object elements;
the eight bases are those very same ones.
By the phrase "of one whose mind is neither defiled nor serene," he demonstrates the opposite of the wholesome and the unwholesome.
They are "appropriated by those very [factors]" because they function as mental chatter (*manojalpa*) through taking on their aspects.

They are called the "habitual tendencies of expression" (*abhilāpavāsanā*) of those very [factors], meaning that the habitual tendencies of the mind, through the body and so forth, exist for the sake of the future occurrence of expression.

That which is "aroused by the mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*) appropriated by them" refers to the forms of expressions such as names and so forth, belonging to one whose mind is neither defiled nor serene.

Regarding one whose mind is neither afflicted nor unwholesome: if his mind is neither afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) nor wholesome (*kuśala*), then it is neutral (*avyākṛta*), such as that pertaining to deportment (*airyāpathika*) and so forth; otherwise, it is wholesome or unwholesome as the case may be.
Just as one distinguishes [the former] by saying "not through discernment" because it is wholesome,
and [the latter] by saying "with an unafflicted mind" because it is unwholesome;
so too, one partakes of medicine through discernment for the sake of health, as an antidote to all diseases.

The transformation-mind (*nirmāṇacitta*) that is innate (*sahaja*) is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) by way of being a natural outflow (*niṣyanda*) of realization; it is that mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitasika*) by which a transformation is emanated for the sake of sport.
However, when it is for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings, it should be understood as wholesome (*kuśala*).
By way of illustration, [the Buddha] demonstrates what is wholesome and so forth for the sake of those to be trained (*vineya*). How is there a demonstration of the unwholesome?
By manifesting as thieves and the like, and for the purpose of terrifying other beings, demonstrating such things as the cutting off of hands, feet, and heads.
"Of one who has not yet abandoned passion" means one who is not even disconnected through partial detachment and has not attained meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Otherwise, [the stage of] *anāgamya* would result in being connected with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). It should be understood that partial detachment exists because, upon attaining concentration, there is the abandonment of the *dauṣṭhulya* (corruption) which is the adversary to the delight in abandonment (*prahāṇābhirati*).
In this context, external form and so forth are associated with the desire realm because they are produced through the sovereign influence of the karma of those who have not yet abandoned passion.

The statement regarding their arising from the sovereign influence of the common karma of all sentient beings is made because, even among those in the form and formless realms, there exist "seed-holders" due to the karma of those who have not abandoned passion.
The four elements are the elements of odor, taste, nose-consciousness, and tongue-consciousness.
Two bases are the bases of odor and taste;
they consist of a portion of the other [bases], excluding those belonging to the realms of form and formlessness, as well as the untainted.
This is stated by setting aside the four elements and the two bases mentioned immediately above.
A portion of the other aggregates, elements, and sense-fields— excluding those belonging to the desire and form realms as well as the untainted—
is [the object] of the four aggregates beginning with feeling. (Abhidh-s-bh 29)

Of the three elements— the mind element (*manodhātu*), the mental-object element (*dharmadhātu*), and the mind-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*)— and of the two bases— the mind base (*manāyatana*) and the mental-object base (*dharmāyatana*)—
it is a portion [of these] excluding those belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Partial detachment refers to the abandonment of up to the eighth type of affliction with respect to a particular stage;
complete detachment results from the abandonment of the ninth.

Alternatively, with respect to detachment from the view of a self-identity (*satkāya*), it should be understood that partial detachment pertains to one in training (*śaikṣa*), while complete detachment pertains to one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

It should be understood that detachment through penetration occurs by means of the path of seeing; detachment through impairment occurs by means of the mundane path; and detachment through eradication occurs by means of the supramundane path.

In the phrase "ten types of detachment" (*daśavairāgyāṇi*), the meaning of *vairāgya* should be understood as "disfavor" or "antipathy," and not necessarily as "abandonment. Regarding "one who has attained a higher station [feeling aversion] toward a lower station": this refers to one who has attained a superior position, such as the status of a city magistrate, feeling aversion toward a lower position, such as that of a village headman.
Regarding "nirvāṇa for the foolish": this is because they do not know its peaceful nature and because of their attachment to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyābhiṣvaṅga*).

For one who has attained the path of seeing and has fully understood the suffering inherent in conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) within the three realms, there arises a weariness toward all contaminated (*sāsrava*) things.

It should be understood that the analysis of the terms *prakṛti-vairāgya* (natural detachment) and *prahāṇa-vairāgya* (detachment through abandonment) follows this pattern: *prakṛtyā vairāgyam* means "detachment by nature," and *prahāṇena vairāgyam* means "detachment through abandonment."

The "wholesome state of one training" (*śaikṣa*) refers to that of one engaged in liberation; it should be understood as pertaining to one who has been engaged for the sake of liberation starting from the stage of having accumulated the provisions (*saṃbhṛtasaṃbhārāvasthā*).
Furthermore, the stage of having accumulated the provisions should be understood as the stage of the factors conducive to liberation through realization (*ādhigāmikamokṣabhāgīyāvasthā*).
This concerns ten elements (*dhātu*): the elements of consciousness, form, sound, and mental phenomena (*vijñāna-rūpa-śabda-dharmadhātu*).
Of the four bases— namely, the bases of visible form, sound, mind, and mental phenomena—
for one who has reached the culmination in the trainings; that is to say, for an Arhat who has reached the culmination in the training of higher ethics, higher mind, and higher wisdom.
"The wholesome and so forth of an ordinary person" refers to [the states] of one who has not yet applied himself to liberation;
for he is called a "learner" (*śaikṣa*) because he is still training in the precepts.
Regarding "the afflicted and the neutral of a learner," here "afflicted" means either unwholesome or obscured-neutral, as the case may be.
Furthermore, the indeterminate should be understood as the non-obscured indeterminate.
The imagined afflicted view is preceded by hearing false doctrines and consists of the five views.
The inclusion of the term "imagined" is for the purpose of excluding the innate *satkāya-dṛṣṭi* (view of a self-identity) and *antagrāha-dṛṣṭi* (view of extremes).
What kind of *antagrāha-dṛṣṭi* is innate?
The view of annihilation (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) is that which causes terror in one engaged in clear realization, such as thinking, "Then what is my self?
The bases of views (*dṛṣṭisthāna*) are the factors co-arising with views and their seeds; the bases of doubt (*vicikitsāsthāna*) should be understood in the same way.

Furthermore, those afflictions and secondary afflictions that are mistaken regarding views—those that proceed by way of views and those that have them as their objects, such as attachment (*rāga*) and so forth—are also included.
A portion of all [dharmas] is to be abandoned by cultivation, excluding those that are untainted (anāsrava).

By way of the opposite of those [dharmas] to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*), "with outflows" (*sāsrava*) means that they are other than the imagined defiled views and so forth; this is the meaning.

Furthermore, here, by the inclusion of the term "with outflows," it should be understood that the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) are also included, in the sense that they are followed by the persistence of functional rigidity (*dauṣṭhulya*).
A portion of all [these dharmas], excluding those to be abandoned by seeing and the untainted (*anāsrava*), [is the object].
A portion of the aggregates is not to be abandoned:
namely, the supramundane path and that which is subsequently attained from it;
as well as a portion of ten elements and four bases.
Thus, it is both conditioned and unconditioned.
Of what nature are the form and sound elements that are not to be abandoned?
They have the nature of the wholesome bodily and vocal actions of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
(Abhidh-s-bh 31) "Conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces," and so forth.
In this regard, the statement "when this exists, that comes to be" is based on the fact that the arising of conditions occurs without any volitional effort.
The meaning is that when the condition is present, the fruit arises; however, there is no volitional effort on the part of the condition toward the production of the fruit.
"Because this arises, that arises" is said with reference to the fact that the condition arises in dependence upon impermanence.
For no effect is established as arising from a cause that lacks productive capacity; thus,

based on the fact that formations (*saṃskāra*) have ignorance (*avidyā*) as their condition and so forth, and that they arise from conditions possessing efficacy, even though these conditions are devoid of agency and impermanent, it is not the case that every fruit arises from just any condition whatsoever,
but rather from one that is efficacious.
That is to say: from ignorance come volitional formations, and so on, up to birth, from which come aging and death.
Those same twelve factors, beginning with ignorance, which have been analyzed, when again condensed, become four factors, beginning with the projecting factor (*ākṣepāṅga*).

Furthermore, this much alone is to be taught in the exposition of the process of existence (*pravṛtti*): namely, at the time of the cause, that by which [the result] is projected and that which is projected; and at the time of the fruit, that by which it is actualized and that which is actualized—all of this is to be understood as being indicated by these factors.

In this context, the projecting factors are ignorance, volitional formations, and consciousness, because they project the name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling through the meaning of mental impression by means of karma preceded by non-knowledge regarding the truths, for the sake of the actualization of future birth. The projected factors are name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling.

By means of that mental impression (*cittavāsanā*), for the sake of the production of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth in the future through the sequence of mutual dependence between the preceding and succeeding [moments], there is the nourishment of the seed.
The factors that bring about this production are craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*).

Through craving and so forth—which have not been abandoned—there arises, with respect to the realms of desire and so on, a desire-attachment (*chandarāga*) preceded by delight in the various modes of good and bad conduct regarding those realms.

When consciousness is accompanied by grasping (*sopādāna*), at the moment of death, because of the manifestation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from other actions that correspond to desire and attachment for the giving of a fruit, there arises the limb of "arising" (*abhinirvṛtti*), namely birth, old age, and death. This occurs because, when the latent impressions of other actions have manifested in that manner, *nāmarūpa* and so forth are produced within a particular homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*)— distinguished by various types of destinies, modes of birth, and so on— just as they were projected.
The mention of birth, aging, and death is for the purpose of inducing revulsion by way of [focusing on] the three characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*).
Aging and death are treated as a single member because death can occur even without aging.

However, this is not the case in the womb-born (*jarāyuja*) mode of birth, where the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) and so forth cannot arise without name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and the other factors; thus, it should be understood that these are established as separate members.
The establishment of the status of the members [of dependent origination] is based upon four conditions.
Among these, first, ignorance is the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) by virtue of being their previously arisen latent impression;

this is because it exists at that time as the active manifestation of those karmas produced within a continuum permeated by that [ignorance], which possess the capacity to construct renewed existence.
From the perspective of impelling force, it is the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*),
because the stream of formations continues to proceed by means of that specific impelling power;
from the perspective of mental attention (*manaskāra*), it is the objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).
In the state of delusion (*mūḍha*), because it serves as the object for improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*) through its priority and other such qualities,
it is the sovereign condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) by way of coexistence; for, through its sovereignty, it causes the volition (*cetanā*) associated with it to construct a distorted object.
Ignorance deludes sentient beings regarding existence; because it obscures that [existence], there is a lack of thorough knowledge of the past, future, and middle limits as they truly are.
It is precisely for this reason that one doubts: "Did I indeed exist in the past time, or did I not exist? and so forth.
And it is the condition for the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), because by its power there is the accumulation of karma leading to renewed existence.
The formative forces differentiate beings among the destinies (*gati*),
because of the variety of beings' transitions between different destinies through the power of karma.
And these [formative forces] become conditions for consciousness by nourishing the seed for the future production of name-and-form;
consciousness, moreover, maintains the bondage of karma.
The formative forces (saṃskāra) arise together with the latent impressions of benefit;
furthermore, they serve as the condition for name-and-form (nāmarūpa),
because through the descent of consciousness (vijñāna) into the mother’s womb, name-and-form undergoes growth.
Name-and-form causes sentient beings to grasp at a personal existence, because through its cessation, sentient beings are born into another category of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*).
The status of name-and-form as the condition for the six sense bases and so forth should be understood as the arising of subsequent members based upon the reliance on preceding members.
The six sense bases constitute the completion of the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*).
And it causes sentient beings to grasp [objects],
because when that [grasping] ceases, there is no deficiency of the other sense faculties;
furthermore, it serves as the condition for contact (sparśa).
Contact impels sentient beings toward the enjoyment of sense objects,
because through that medium they enjoy the three kinds of objects— those to be experienced as pleasant and so forth—
and it also serves as the condition for feeling.
Feeling causes sentient beings to engage in the enjoyment of birth, because through it they experience the maturation of desired and other types of karma;
furthermore, it serves as the condition for craving.
Because craving arises by way of the longing for association with that [feeling] and so forth;
craving draws sentient beings toward birth, since by its power the stream of future births remains uninterrupted.
And it becomes the condition for grasping (*upādāna*), because through the gateway of craving for enjoyment, desire and passion (*chandarāga*) arise toward sense pleasures and so forth.
Furthermore, grasping causes consciousness to become possessed of grasping (*sopādāna*) in order to take up renewed existence (*punarbhava*).

It serves as the condition for existence (*bhava*) because, due to the restriction of karmic latencies (*vāsanā*), there is the reconnection (*pratisaṃdhi*) with a new birth characterized by specific destinies such as the hells; and it is through its power that the latencies of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) gain their functional activity.
Furthermore, becoming (bhava) directs sentient beings toward renewed existence (punarbhava),

because it brings about the immediate transition to another state of rebirth; and it serves as the condition for birth (jāti), since it results in the manifestation of a new group-homogeneity (nikāyasabhāga).
Birth brings forth sentient beings through the sequence of name-and-form and so on, by inducing successive subsequent states;
furthermore, it serves as the condition for old age and death.
Once birth has occurred, because there is the possibility of change and destruction in its continuity,
old age and death repeatedly join sentient beings with the transformation of their vitality and the transformation of their life-force,
by joining them with the destruction of youth and lifespan.
The inclusion of consciousness within the defilement of karma is because the limb of consciousness is produced by the latencies of formative forces (*saṃskāra-vāsanā*);
its meaning of being "without an agent" is because it is devoid of a creator such as Īśvara;
and its meaning of "having a cause" is because it has ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth as its causes.
The meaning of "devoid of a sentient being" is because it is itself without self;
the meaning of "dependent on others" is because it is subject to conditions;
the meaning of "without agency" is because conditions are devoid of activity.
The meaning of impermanence (*anitya*) is non-eternality; the meaning of momentariness (*kṣaṇika*) is the failure to persist beyond the time of its arising;
and the meaning of the uninterrupted continuity of cause and effect is that the moment of the effect arises simultaneously with the cessation of the moment of the cause.
The meaning of the grasping of corresponding causes and fruits is that everything does not arise from everything.
The meaning of diverse causes and fruits is that from a cause of a single or manifold kind, effects of one or many kinds are produced.
The meaning of specific causes and fruits is that there is no production of fruits within a different continuum.
Furthermore, by means of these very points, the fivefold profundity of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) should be understood:
profundity of cause, which is through two points as an antidote to the doctrines of an unequal cause and no cause;
and profundity of characteristic, which is through one point, namely, the absence of self (nirātmakatā).
The profundity of arising consists of two points: because the fruit arises from conditions, yet even in that arising it is not produced by them.
The profundity of abiding consists of two points: because there is no actual abiding for those things that appear to abide.
The profundity of activity consists of four points: because the activity of cause and fruit is difficult to discern.
In this context, it should be understood that the non-perishing of the fruit of action consists in the fact that even without an agent, there exists the action and the experience of its fruit.
Dharma is not self-made, because that which has not yet arisen does not exist such that it could be made by itself; nor is it made by another, because conditions lack agency;
nor is it made by both, for the same two reasons.
It is not produced without being caused by either self-action or action by another, because causes and conditions possess the capacity to bring about the arising of a fruit.
Another formulation:
it is not self-made because it depends upon conditions;
nor is it made by another, because even when conditions are present, there is no production for that which lacks a seed.
It is not produced by both, because those two are devoid of agency;
nor is it arisen without a cause, because of the existence of the power of seeds and conditions.
For it is also said:

"Because it has its own seed, it does not arise from another; because it depends on that [seed], it does not arise from itself; because it is devoid of volition, it does not arise from both; and because of its capacity, it does not arise without a cause. Thus, dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) would be profound even when two alternatives are rejected—namely, that it arises neither from itself nor from another—let alone in a case where all four alternatives are rejected.
Therefore, its supreme profundity is to be understood.
(Abhidh-s-bh 35) From the distinction of the arising of consciousness: "Dependent upon the eye and forms, visual consciousness arises," and so forth.
From the distinction of etymological derivation: with reference to the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*), [it is said that consciousness arises].
"Conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces," and so forth.
Regarding the distinctions in the arising of external things: depending on the seed there is the sprout;
depending on the sprout there is the stalk.
Likewise, the flowers and fruits are not to be joined [to the trees],
because the great earth and so forth arise in dependence upon the sovereign power of the collective karma of all sentient beings, through the distinctions of the cycles of dissolution and evolution;
and because sentient beings remain within the three realms in dependence upon the four types of nutriment, through the distinctions of sustenance by food.
[The distinction] is by way of the differentiation between the divisions of desirable and undesirable destinies, because one goes to good or bad rebirths in dependence upon good or bad conduct;

by way of the distinction of purification, because the aids to penetration arise in dependence upon the aids to liberation, up to the sequential attainment of arhatship through the paths of seeing and cultivation;
or else, because right view arises in dependence upon the voice of another and internal wise attention, and from that [right view] up to the exhaustion of all outflows.
Based on the distinction of power, the specific qualities such as the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) arise in dependence upon realization.
Through these various distinctions, the dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is to be understood in detail.

"Conformable and reverse order of affliction" refers to the sequence of the process of evolution (*pravṛtti*); thus, the teaching in forward order beginning with "conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces" (*avidyāpratyayāḥ saṃskārāḥ*) should be understood.

The teaching in reverse order, concerning the establishment of the truths (*satyavyavasthāna*), should be understood as: "old age and death, the origin of old age and death, the cessation of old age and death, and the practice leading to the cessation of old age and death."

[Regarding "in the direct and reverse order of purification"]: for example, "from the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations," and so forth, is the exposition in the direct order of purification.
From the exposition in the reverse order: "In the absence of what do aging and death not come to be? From the cessation of what does the cessation of aging and death occur?"*

The causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) formations (*saṃskāra*) is, respectively, the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) and the wholesome latencies (*kuśala-vāsanā*).
Furthermore, the storehouse consciousness is of two kinds: that which is maturational (*vaipākika*) and that which is produced by effort (*ābhisaṃskārika*).
Among these, the maturational [storehouse consciousness] is the causal condition for those [formations] acquired at birth (*upapatti-prātilambhika*).

The formative [seeds] of those who engage in practice should be understood as the causal condition for another storehouse consciousness in the future. Furthermore, the formative storehouse consciousness should be known as perfumed by the manifestation of the active consciousnesses belonging to that same lifetime. The perfuming of the wholesome should be understood as the perfuming of the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*).

It should be understood that, because it possesses the characteristics of the phenomena that flow from their acceptance of the supramundane, the latent predisposition for those [phenomena] serves as the cause for supramundane dharmas.
Furthermore, by the passage beginning with "also by way of intrinsic nature," he demonstrates that there are six causes which constitute the causal condition (*hetupratyaya*).
Among these, the establishment of the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*) is according to its intrinsic nature and its subdivisions.
It should be understood that the establishment of the co-existent, associated, homogeneous, omnipresent, and ripening causes is to be known respectively through the remaining terms.
With reference to the intrinsic nature of causes, since they are established as the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*), it should be understood that all causes are included within the efficient cause.
However, they are established separately for the purpose of elucidating specific distinctions such as "concomitants" (*sahāya*) and so forth.

Regarding the divisions of the efficient cause, that which was taught—such as the totality of conditions for consciousness (*vijñānasāmagrī*) and so on—should be regarded as merely illustrative examples.
This is for the purpose of inferring other similar things by means of that direction.
In this context, the cause of arising is that from which the effect manifests after having not previously existed;
the cause of persistence is that which ensures the non-interruption of the continuity of what has arisen.
The cause of support is due to the prevention of falling;
the cause of manifestation is due to the revealing of that which is obscured;
the cause of transformation is due to bringing about a change in its continuum.
It is a cause of separation because it effects a bifurcation of the connection;
it is a cause of transformation because its constituent parts move to another location;
and it is a cause of cognition because, through it, one infers what is beyond the reach of the senses.
It is the cause of conviction because one attains right certainty through it;
it is the cause of attainment because one reaches realization through it;
and it is the cause of conventional usage because, by grasping signs according to their designations, one becomes attached and subsequently engages in worldly discourse.

The causal condition of dependence (*apekṣākāraṇa*) is so called because it serves as the cause for the arising of desire elsewhere. The causal condition of projection (*ākṣepakāraṇa*) is so called because it impels the successive states that arise one after another in a continuous sequence. The causal condition of actualization (*abhinirvṛttikāraṇa*) is so called because it generates that which arises immediately thereafter.

The cause of appropriation (*parigrahakāraṇa*) is because it strengthens that which produces its own seed; the cause of attraction (*āvāhanakāraṇa*) is because it draws [the result] toward itself in accordance with that [seed];
the cause of specific determination (*pratiniyamakāraṇa*) is because, through their distinct intrinsic natures, they function as mutual results.
A cooperative cause (*sahakārikāraṇa*) is so called because it depends on other causes for the accomplishment of its own effect;
an opposing cause (*virodhikāraṇa*) is so called because it creates an obstacle.
The non-contradictory cause should be understood as the opposite of that.

For example, as with the primary elements (*bhūta*) and the derivative matter (*bhautika*), these arise according to what is possible; however, it is not necessarily the case that all four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are present in every aggregate, nor is derivative matter such as visible form (*rūpa*) always present.
Therefore, whatever exists in a particular place arises together with it, and not without the other.
The co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*) is established by way of the necessity of companionship.
This should be understood as a mere illustration— namely, the primary elements (*bhūta*) and the derivative matter (*bhautika*)—
because there is a rule of mutual inseparability (*avinābhāva-niyama*) between mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitasika*).
If this were so, the associated cause (*saṃprayuktahetu*) would not be established as distinct [from the co-existent cause],
because minds and mental factors are already included within the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*).
Even though this is the case, it is nevertheless [established] by way of another meaning.

Those phenomena which attain their object through simultaneous existence (*sahabhāva*) and not through the deficiency of even one of them, are established as the associated cause (*saṃprayuktaka-hetu*) by virtue of their concordant functioning,
and not merely by way of coexistence; for example, the mind and its mental factors (*caitasika*).
"Of those previously cultivated" means those practiced in the past or previously manifested.

"The subsequent progression that becomes increasingly more nourished in the future limit" is to be understood as the distinguished arising in a future time of those [dharmas] whose seeds have been fully nourished by them and which follow their lineage.
Thus, this homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) is established as the cause for the nourishment of similar things.

The pervasive cause (*sarvatragahetu*) does not merely serve for the nourishment of what is similar; rather, through the cultivation of any affliction such as attachment (*rāga*), there occurs the strengthening of the continuity of all [afflictions] such as aversion (*dveṣa*). Therefore, its establishment should be understood in the sense that it acts as an obstacle to the attainment of liberation by making the bonds firm.

Furthermore, the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) is established in the sense of "appropriation" because it projects a ripening that is comprised within the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*), which is exclusively dissimilar [to its cause] in the future and is non-obscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
The inclusion of "wholesome with outflows" (*kuśala-sāsrava*) is because those without outflows (*anāsrava*) do not project [such a result], as they are contrary to rebirth.

"Also by way of immediate succession and contiguity" means that contiguity does not necessarily refer to the contiguity of moments; rather, in this context, contiguity should be understood as the contiguity of other states of mind.

For otherwise, in the case of the mindless attainments (*acittika-samāpatti*), the mind of emergence would not have the mind of entry into attainment as its immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), yet it does so.
Therefore, within a single continuum, a preceding mind is the immediately preceding condition for a subsequent mind when it is not separated by another mind.
Just as this applies to the mind, so too should it be understood for the mental factors.

"Also by way of the immediate succession of the arising of similar and dissimilar mind and mental factors": wholesome mind and mental factors are the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for wholesome mind and mental factors that have arisen immediately after them—whether they are similar (wholesome) or dissimilar (unwholesome or neutral). In the same way, wholesome and neutral [factors] should be applied to their own respective categories and others.

For example, those belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) are the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for those that have just arisen in the desire realm, as well as for those in the form and formless realms and the untainted (*anāsrava*).

In the same way, those belonging to the form realm and so forth should be applied respectively to those that have just arisen in the form realm and so forth, and to those in the desire realm and so forth.
Is it indeed the case that every state of mind arises immediately after every [preceding] state of mind, or is there a specific restriction?
It is said: there is.
If one were to state that "immediately after this particular mind, such-and-such a mind arises," there would be much to be said;
therefore, regarding the arising of the mind in general, only its defining characteristics are established.
That is to say, the arising of the mind should be understood as occurring through ten powers: the power of familiarity, the power of aspiration, and the power of application.

By the power of meditative attainment, the power of penetration, the power of the cause, the power of the object, the power of mindfulness, the power of mental attention, and the power of rebirth-linking;
furthermore, the power of familiarity is threefold: weak, medium, and intense.
It is weak because the signs of entry into, remaining in, and emerging from meditative attainment have not been clearly discerned;
it is middling because they have been discerned but not yet well-mastered;
and it is superior because they have been discerned and well-mastered.

In this regard, it should be understood that through the power of weak familiarity, there is the successive attainment (*anupūrvasamāpatti*) of the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
Through middling [familiarity], there is the skipping attainment (*vyutkrāntakasamāpatti*) by means of the "single-interval" (*ekāntarika*) yoga.
Through superior [familiarity], it should be understood that one attains all [stages] according to one's wish, skipping over them in both forward and reverse order.

One who has attained the second dhyāna through the power of aspiration, having entered the first dhyāna, if he so desires, brings to manifestation an emergence-consciousness belonging to the level of the second dhyāna; if he does not desire it, he brings to manifestation either a wholesome consciousness of the desire realm or an unobstructed-neutral one. This should be applied in detail to other cases as well.
By the power of application (*prayoga*), immediately after a wholesome mind of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), for the first time, a mind of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) arises.
Immediately after the wholesome [mind] of the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), the fundamental [concentration] (*maula*) arises;
immediately after the wholesome fundamental [concentration], the mind of one who has entered the second dhyāna arises, and so forth, in detail, up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
By the power of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), for one who has entered a pure attainment (*śuddhaka*), sometimes only the pure state arises and sometimes the afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) state.

By the power of momentum (*āvedha*), for one who has emerged from concentration and is practicing, the mind belonging to the level of concentration continues uninterrupted through moments of non-concentration until it is lost due to the manifestation of afflictions that are contrary to it.
Thus it is said.

Furthermore, the manifestation of a mind associated with afflictions that are contrary to that [state] should be understood as occurring through four powers, beginning with the power of the cause (*hetu*). Among these, first, by the power of the cause, if there is an obscuration that necessarily leads to falling away from the stage (*bhūmi*):
It becomes previously accumulated:
either by the power of the object, if an object characterized by beauty and so forth—which is conducive to the arising of passion and the like—appears with its power intensified;
or by the power of mindfulness, if one elaborates upon past objects through acts of recollection and mental construction.
If, by the power of mental attention (*manaskāra*), one attends to any particular auspicious sign through the mental attention of investigation (*mīmāṃsā-manaskāra*);

and by the power of rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi*), there are nine death-minds associated with craving for personal existence (*ātmabhāva-tṛṣṇā*), belonging respectively to each of the three realms—the desire, form, and formless realms.

Among these, it should be understood that for one who dies in the desire realm and takes rebirth-linking specifically within the desire realm, the death-mind is associated with craving for a personal existence belonging to the desire realm.
For one who forms a rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi*) in the form or formless realms, [the mind] belongs to the form or formless realm.
Likewise, for one who passes away from the form or formless realms and is being born there or elsewhere, six minds are to be applied.
Furthermore, that craving for personal existence (*ātmabhāva-tṛṣṇā*) is innate, has an unspecified object, and is unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Its objective support (ālambana) should be understood as the class of personal existence (ātmabhāva-jāti), without distinction of its specific modes.
By virtue of that, there is immediately thereafter the reconnection (pratisaṃdhi) of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) in the intermediate state (antarābhava).
Even for noble ones (ārya) who have not yet abandoned desire, this craving (tṛṣṇā) continues to operate until, at the time of death, they reach the stage where perception becomes indistinct.
Having discerned this, they suppress it with its antidote.
However, for noble ones who are free from passion, because their antidote is more powerful, that [affliction] does not manifest at all even though it has not been abandoned;
yet, due to the power of its latent tendency (*anuśaya*), there is rebirth for them.

Furthermore, the moment of linking rebirth in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is always exclusively unobscured-indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), because it is a result of maturation (*vipāka*).
From that point onward, [the mind] may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate, according to the circumstances.
Setting aside the mind at death,
it should be understood that the mind of death belonging to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is always defiled, just like the existence at death (*maraṇabhava*);
furthermore, the reconnection of rebirth (*upapattipratisaṃdhi*) is always exclusively unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
However, for Bodhisattvas who are taking birth through the power of their vows, it should be understood that everything, beginning with the mind at death, is exclusively wholesome.
The discussion concerning the immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya) is concluded.
The objective support (*ālambana*) of the five groups of consciousness (*vijñānakāya*) is by way of having a delimited object,
because the five groups of consciousness have restricted objects;
the objective support of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is by way of having an undelimited object.
Because mental consciousness has all phenomena as its object,
it takes as its objective support those objects that are not characterized by conceptual differentiation for those whose perceptions have not yet been developed;
this is because they are impossible to express in words or characters.
It should be understood through the object of conceptualization as its basis, and by the opposite of that.

With respect to having a basis consisting of a real entity (*savastuka-viṣaya-ālambana*), it is the object of [the other afflictions], excluding views, the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*), and the factors associated with them;
with respect to having a basis consisting of no real entity (*avastuka-viṣaya-ālambana*), it is the object of those [factors] that were excluded.
Because they have the self as their basis;

because they take real entities as their objective support—excluding those that take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their objective support, those that are universal (*sarvatraga*) across different realms and stages, those whose objects are not restricted, and those that take the past and future as their objective support;

and because they take conceptual constructs (*parikalpa*) as their objective support—the objective support of those [defilements] other than these excluded ones is the objective support of the excluded ones.
Because they take only one's own conceptual construction as their object,
those [cognitions] having aspects such as permanence have a perverted object;
those having aspects such as impermanence have a non-perverted object.
For those who have not yet abandoned the obscuration of the knowable, the object of focus is obstructed;
for those who have abandoned the obscuration of the knowable, the object of focus is unobstructed.

Regarding the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*), its determination should be understood through its characteristics, its classifications, its stability, its thorough knowledge, and its abandonment; thus is the establishment of the object-condition to be known.
How is it defined by its characteristic?

That object which is the cause for the arising of those mental states and mental factors that manifest as its appearance, and which, once arisen, serve to bring about the conventional expression and internal realization of the adherence to that object— that is the characteristic of having that as its objective support.
How [is it] by way of classification?

There is an unreal objective support (*asad-ālambana*), such as that of perverted minds and mental factors, and the objective supports of the past, the future, dreams, reflections, illusions, and so forth. There is a real objective support (*sad-ālambana*) for those other than these.

The object that is without an object of perception consists of form, the factors dissociated from mind, and the unconditioned. The object that has an object of perception consists of the mental states and mental factors.
An object of rightness is, for example, the wholesome.
An object of falsity is, for example, that which is afflicted (*kliṣṭa*). An object that is neither right nor false is, for example, that which is unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
A proper object (*yoniśa ālambana*) is, for example, that of wholesome mental states and mental factors (*cittacaitasika*).
Improper objective support refers, for example, to that of the afflicted states. Neither-proper-nor-improper objective support refers to those states free from both.

Homogeneous objective support refers, for example, to the wholesome and so forth of the wholesome and so forth; likewise, for those belonging to their own level, there is an objective support belonging to their own level; for those with outflows, there is an objective support with outflows; and for those without outflows, there is an objective support without outflows.

A dissimilar object of focus (*visabhāgālambana*) is, for example, unwholesome states and so forth for wholesome states and so forth, or states belonging to another level for those belonging to another level, and the uncontaminated for the contaminated and vice versa.

A diverse object of focus (*nānātvālambana*) is, for example, the mind and mental factors accompanied by applied and sustained thought (*savitarkavicāra*). A unitary object of focus (*ekatvālambana*) is, for example, [the mind and mental factors] without applied or sustained thought (*avitarkāvicāra*).

The extensive objective support is that of the mental states and mental factors belonging to those practicing for the sphere of non-perception, as well as those of the spheres of infinite space and infinite consciousness.

The condensed subtle objective support is that of those belonging to the sphere of nothingness. The ultimate subtle objective support is that of those belonging to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

The afflictions (*kleśa*) are the object (*ālambana*), because they are apprehended by means of that [object]. Phenomena (*dharma*) are the object, such as the noble ones' sets of names (*nāmakāya*), sets of phrases (*padakāya*), and sets of phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*).
Meaning (*artha*) is the object, which is the meaning dependent upon those [phenomena].
A limited object of focus is, for example, the Śrāvakayāna; a vast object of focus is, for example, the Mahāyāna;
and a sign-based object of focus is, for example, the signs of calm abiding, exertion, and equanimity.

The signless object of focus (*animitta-ālambana*) is, for example, nirvāṇa and the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*). The reality object of focus (*tattva-ālambana*) is, for example, suchness (*tathatā*) and the truths consisting of the sixteen aspects. The dwelling object of focus (*vaihārika-ālambana*) is, for example, the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
The object of mastery is, for example, the qualities beginning with the liberations and ending with the knowledge of all aspects.
The momentary object is, for example, that which belongs only to this life for those beyond training (aśaikṣas). The conforming object is, for example, that of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
How is it established?
It is so established because the objective support (*ālambana*) is not ultimately real.
Furthermore, the objective support should be understood as non-real for four reasons: because it is the cause for contradictory cognitions, (Abhidh-s-bh 42) [and so forth].
By means of the perception of consciousness without an object,
by the consequence of the absence of error even without effort,
and by the conformity with the threefold knowledge.
Consequently, the apprehender (*grāhaka*) is also not established.
Knowledge is threefold: the knowledge of mastery (*vaśitājñāna*), the knowledge of insight (*vipaśyanājñāna*), and non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpajñāna*).
Regarding these, there are examples of four causes.

It is maintained that for hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and gods, there is no establishment of an external object, because their minds differ even with respect to the same thing, according to their respective merit. // 1 //

Likewise, in the past and so forth, in dreams, and even in the two kinds of reflections, [consciousness arises] because its objects do not exist and because it is joined with those non-existent objects as its support. (2)
If the object were established as an object [independently], non-conceptual cognition would not exist;
and in the absence of that, the attainment of Buddhahood would be entirely impossible. // 3 //

Because when a Bodhisattva has attained mastery, through the power of resolute conviction, such a state of being is perceived upon the earth and other elements by those who practice meditation. // 4 //

For the wise one here who has perfected discernment and attained meditative concentration, there is [the state of non-conceptualization] through the mental engagement with all phenomena and also because objects appear in that very way. (5)

For when cognition proceeds without conceptual construction, because all objects do not appear, one must admit the non-existence of objects; and since those [objects] are absent, representation [too] is non-existent. //6//
How is it known through full comprehension?
It is through the knowledge of the characteristics, the distinctions, and the states of things as they truly are.
How is it [attained] through abandonment?
It is through the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*) by means of both the Śrāvaka-yāna and the Mahāyāna.
Through the transformation of the basis in the Śrāvaka-yāna, there is liberation from the objects of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, but there is no attainment of mastery over them.

But through the Mahāyāna transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*), both [conditions] are present. Thus is concluded the determination of the objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) according to the text.
Regarding the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) by way of its foundation: the wind-circle and so forth are the dominant conditions for the water-circle and so forth.
The receptacle world is [the support] of the world of sentient beings; the primary elements are [the support] of derived matter;
the sense faculties are [the support] of consciousnesses, and so forth.
From the perspective of the sovereign condition of projection (*āvedhādhipatita*), there is the karma common to all sentient beings regarding the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*),

as well as past contaminated karma (*sāsravakarma*) regarding its maturation (*vipāka*), and so forth; from the perspective of the sovereign condition of coexistence (*sahabhāvādhipatita*), there is the mind (*citta*) with respect to mental factors (*caitasika*), and attention (*manaskāra*) with respect to the mind.
"Contact is [the dominant condition] for feeling," and so forth.
Beyond this, the establishment of dominance (*adhipati*) should be understood with reference to the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*).
Among these, by way of dominance over their respective objects, there is dominance for the faculties of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Because form and so forth are produced through their predominance;
because of the predominance of procreation, [the female and male faculties exist],
since entry into the womb occurs through their predominance.
The life-faculty [is predominant] by way of being the sovereign over its own station, because by its power one remains within the homogeneous class of beings;
the faculties of pleasure, pain, mental joy, and equanimity [are predominant] by way of being the sovereign over the enjoyment of the fruit.
Because of that basis, there is the experience of desirable and undesirable maturation;
and by virtue of mundane purification, there are the faculties of faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom,
because through them the afflictions are suppressed.

The establishment of the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known" should be understood as being due to the sovereignty of supramundane purification,
because by means of them the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are completely eradicated.
It should be understood as "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) because of the continuous arising of the faculty and its object, which are not devoid of consciousness and are similar to it;

that is, because the faculty, accompanied by consciousness and resembling it, arises in a continuum with respect to objects, that faculty is called "homogeneous" in the sense of having a resemblance to the functioning of consciousness.
It is "similar-to-that" (*tatsabhāga*) because of the continuous arising of what is devoid of consciousness and resembles itself.

The continuous arising of a faculty that is dissociated from consciousness, by way of its own similarity [to its predecessor], should be understood as "functionally similar" (*tatsabhāga*) in the sense of having a resemblance in the characteristics of the faculty.
This constitutes a portion of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), characterized by the five faculties beginning with the eye.
It is likewise the five material elements and bases (*dhātu-āyatana*) beginning with the eye.
Regarding "the form that is the basis for the arising of feeling": that form depending upon which feeling arises is called "appropriated" (*upātta*).
This constitutes a portion of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), comprising the sense faculties together with their physical bases.
It consists of the five material elements and bases, such as the eye and so forth.
And a portion of four—namely, visible form, odor, taste, and the tangible—is inseparable from the sense faculties.
The six [faculties], beginning with the eye, [are predominant] by virtue of their sovereignty over the apprehension of objects,
because it is through their sovereignty that the mind and mental factors proceed toward objective supports such as visible form.
The female and male faculties [are predominant] by virtue of their sovereignty over the continuity of the lineage.
From that, there proceeds the lineage of sons, grandsons, and so forth.
The remainder should be understood as it was explained in the context of the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
A portion of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) consists of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and the male and female faculties.
A portion of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) is characterized by the faculties of life, faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
There are twelve elements (*dhātu*), namely the elements of the faculties and their corresponding consciousnesses.
There are six internal bases (*āyatana*).
A portion of the sphere and base of the dharma-element, the life-faculty, the [faculties of] pleasure and so forth, and the five beginning with faith.
Painful feeling (*duḥkhā vedanā*), being of the nature of suffering, is the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*) by its very own characteristic.

However, the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*artha*), as well as the mental factors associated with them, which serve as the causes for the arising of that [painful feeling], should be regarded as the suffering of suffering because they are to be experienced as painful.
Because mental distress arises from the transformation of pleasant feeling and those phenomena to be experienced as pleasant, that transformation is the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).
In this regard, the transformation of the mind through attachment should be understood as the suffering of change, as it is said: "one who is overwhelmed by a transformed mind."

Neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling associated with the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), as well as the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) conducive to that feeling, are permeated by the state of dysfunction (*dauṣṭhulya*) due to the suffering of change and the suffering inherent in conditioned existence.

Because they are not liberated from these two types of suffering, they at times assume a state of pain and at times a state of pleasure; they do not remain exclusively in a state of neither-pain-nor-pleasure at all times.
Therefore, because they lack security due to being bound by impermanence, the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) should be understood as pertaining to the aggregates,
and to the three elements— the mind element, the phenomena element, and the mind-consciousness element.
And of the two bases— the mind base and the phenomena base—
setting aside one part characterized by the untainted (*anāsrava*),
all others [are included].

The maturation (*vipāka*) of the unwholesome and of the wholesome-with-outflows (*sāsrava*) is the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) together with its associated mental factors in the future; therefore,
by means of that maturation, both of those [categories] among the aggregates are said to possess maturation.
Of the ten elements— namely, the elements of consciousness, form, sound, and mental phenomena—
and of the four bases— namely, the bases of form, sound, mind, and mental phenomena— one part is neutral, excluding the untainted (anāsrava) portion.

Other than the *ālayavijñāna*, that which is the eye and so forth, as well as pleasure, pain, and so forth, receives the designation "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*) because it is produced from that [store-consciousness].
That which arises through transformation is the "transformational" (*pāriṇāmika*), namely, edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*).
At the time of transformation, because it nourishes the sense faculties and the great elements,
nutriment derived from objects (*viṣayaja*) consists of contact (*sparśa*); for, through contact based on desirable objects, it benefits the physical basis (*āśraya*).
The nutriment of mental volition (*manaḥ-saṃcetanā-āhāra*) is "pertaining to hope" (*āśika*),
because it sustains the physical basis through the power of hope bound to a desired object.
The nutriment of consciousness (*vijñāna-āhāra*) is "pertaining to grasping" (*aupādānika*), because of its nature as grasping.
Because the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) is established through the power of the appropriation (*upādāna*) of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*);
for indeed, when separated from that [consciousness], the basis (*āśraya*) becomes putrid.
Furthermore, all four nutriments (*āhāra*) are collectively established by means of four distinctions.
For example, there is that which abides in an impure basis, such as ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*),
because they are bound by all fetters;
and there is that which abides in both pure and impure bases, such as those in training (*śaikṣa*) and ordinary persons belonging to the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpyāvacara*).
Because its bonds are still remaining,
it abides in a pure basis for the Arhats, owing to their complete liberation from all bonds.
It is the demonstration of the stability of the Buddhas and of the Bodhisattvas who have attained great power;
for their stability is merely a demonstration based on the influence of nutriment.

A portion of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is the perfected nature (*niṣpanna-svabhāva*), which is "with superior" (*sottara*)— that is, excluding *nirvāṇa*— because it is the foremost of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-agratva*) and because pure suchness (*tathatā*) has that as its characteristic.
In brief, the classification is threefold;
it should be understood with respect to the three natures according to the principle of the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*).
Among these, the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is that non-existent nature of a self and so forth which is imagined by depending upon the aggregates (*skandha*) and other bases.
The dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) consists of those very aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, upon which that false conceptualization of a self and so on has proceeded.
The perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is suchness (*tathatā*), characterized by being free from existence and non-existence,
because it is characterized by the presence of selflessness (*nairātmya*)— the absence of a self and so on— within the aggregates and other phenomena.
The differentiation by characteristic (*lakṣaṇaprabheda*) refers to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena,
such as "form" (*rūpa*), "feeling" (*vedanā*), and so forth.
The differentiation by mode (*prakāraprabheda*) refers to their specific distinctions (*viśeṣa*).
"Substantially existent" (*dravyasat*) and "existent as a designation" (*prajñaptisat*), and so forth;
the differentiation of the basis (*āśrayaprabheda*) refers to the diversity of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so on with respect to each individual existence (*pratyātmabhāva*).
(Abhidh-s-bh 46)
The differentiation of the continuum refers to the alteration of the specific characteristics of the aggregates and so forth, even within a single personal existence.

The distinction of being "outwardly directed" refers primarily to that which belongs to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*); the inclusion of the word "primarily" (*bhūyasā*) is for the purpose of excluding those factors produced by the natural outflow (*niṣyanda*) as well as those consisting of hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintā-maya*).
The classification is completed.

By way of inclusion through characteristics, the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is included by the aggregate of form alone, and so on in detail up to the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), which is included by the sphere of phenomena alone.
By way of inclusion through elements (*dhātu*), all aggregates, elements, and spheres are included within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*),
because all of them exist therein as seeds.

By way of inclusion by genus (*jātisaṃgraha*), all [factors] such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth are included within the aggregates (*skandha*), even though they are mutually distinct in their own-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), because they belong to a single genus through the sense of being a "heap" (*rāśi*) and so on.

In the same way, it should be understood that the eyes and so forth are included within the elements (*dhātu*) and the sense-bases (*āyatana*), because they are endowed with the sense of being the basis for experience and maintenance, and the sense of being a gateway for arising (*āyadvāra*).

By way of inclusion by state (*avasthāsaṃgraha*), although the aggregates are of a single genus, when restricted to states such as pleasure (*sukha*) and so on, those in a state of pleasure are included only by other states of pleasure, and not by states of suffering (*duḥkha*) and so forth.
In this way, the states of suffering and the states of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure are subsumed by those very states themselves.
As it is with the aggregates (*skandha*), so it is with the elements (*dhātu*) and the sense-bases (*āyatana*).

By means of the inclusion of their associates, the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), when taken together with its associates—feeling (*vedanā*) and the rest that depend upon it—is subsumed by all five aggregates.
In this way, feeling and the other aggregates, when taken individually along with their attendants, are subsumed within the five aggregates.
Likewise, it should be understood that the elements and the sense-bases, when taken individually along with their attendants, are each subsumed by all the elements and all the sense-bases.
By way of partial inclusion, the aggregate of ethical discipline is subsumed by one part of the aggregate of form.
The aggregates of concentration and wisdom are included within a portion of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).
The realms of desire, ill-will, and harmfulness are included within a portion of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
The sphere of infinite space and the others are included within a portion of the spheres of mind (*manāyatana*) and phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).

Having established this, it should be understood that however many phenomena are included within the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases in various sūtras, they are included therein either by way of inclusion in one or another [category] or by partial inclusion.
By way of complete inclusion, the aggregate of suffering is included within the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*),
and the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is included within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).
The sphere of non-percipient beings is comprised of ten spheres, excluding the spheres of odor and taste.

Having established this, one should understand that the "complete inclusion" refers to the exhaustive inclusion of all phenomena—however many are comprised within the aggregates, elements, and spheres—in other sūtras.
By way of mutual inclusion, each aggregate is comprised of the elements and the spheres.

In this same manner, according to their respective applications, the elements (dhātus), aggregates (skandhas), and sense-bases (āyatanas) should be understood in detail as being subsumed within the aggregates and elements.
Furthermore, the characteristic of inclusion (*saṃgraha-lakṣaṇa*) should be understood as being of six kinds, following what is well-known in the world. What, then, are these?

Inclusion by way of location (*padasthāna-saṃgraha*) is as it is said in the world: "humans are included within Jambudvīpa" or "wild animals are included within the forest"; likewise here, the inclusion of visual consciousness and the others by means of the eye and the other [faculties] should be understood.

Inclusion by way of binding (*nibandha-saṃgraha*) is as a load of wood and so forth is bound by a rope and the like; likewise, the inclusion of the sense-faculties such as the eye by means of the body.

Inclusion by way of a common object (*tulyārtha-saṃgraha*) is, for example, like trustworthy people who share all their purposes and act toward the same object at the same time, being mutually associated (*saṃprayukta*). Inclusion by way of appropriation (*upādāna-saṃgraha*) is, for example, like a master’s possession of his own slaves and so forth; likewise, the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) [appropriates] the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*).
Inclusion by way of non-dispersal (*avisāra-saṃgraha*) is, for example, like water [held] by a jar; likewise, meditative concentration (*samādhi*) [holds] the other minds and mental factors.
Comprehension by way of condensation is like the gathering of rivers into the ocean; likewise, it is the inclusion of the eye and other [faculties] within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
Regarding this comprehension by way of condensation, one should understand that there are eleven kinds of inclusion.

In the location of a single atom (*paramāṇu*), there is an inseparability (*avinirbhāga*) of all constituent parts (*deśin*)—namely, visible form (*rūpa*) and so forth—that are contained within that one atom; this should be understood as their occupying the same location.
Above the level of a single atom, there is a mutual mingling of all constituent parts, just as water and earth atoms mingle with one another in turbid water.
Furthermore, there is a mutual conjunction (*samavadhāna*) among the constituent parts themselves as they aggregate, just as one lump of clay meets another lump of clay on a wall.

The association of coexistence (*sahabhāva-saṃprayoga*) refers to the momentary aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth existing within a single personal continuum (*ekātmabhāva*). The association of performing a function (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-saṃprayoga*) refers to those engaged in a single purpose acting in relation to one another.

The association of concordant engagement (*saṃpratipatti-saṃprayoga*) occurs by way of another nature (*parabhāva*) and not by way of its own nature (*svabhāva*); for example, one mind does not associate with another mind.
"Feeling by means of another feeling," and so forth.
