It is not [the case] for two contradictory things, such as passion and hatred, or the wholesome and the unwholesome, and so forth.
Nor is it [the case] for things belonging to dissimilar times, such as the present and the future, or the past and the present.

There is no [association] between factors belonging to different realms (*dhātu*) or levels (*bhūmi*), such as those belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), or those belonging to the first and second dhyāna levels, and so forth.

Universal association (*sarvatraga-saṃprayoga*) refers to the association with the six [mental factors], beginning with feeling (*vedanā*), which occurs in all states; for these cannot exist without one another.

Habitual association (*ucita*) pertains to certain [factors] among those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), as well as to wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral factors that are exclusively mundane (*laukika*), according to their respective possibilities.

The phrase "of the first and those subsequent" is intended to indicate that supramundane [states] produced in the first moment and those produced in the second and subsequent moments are of a previously non-existent kind (*apūrvajātīya*) and thus unfamiliar.

(Abhidh-s-bh 48) Possession (*samanvāgama*) by way of its characteristic is as previously stated: namely, for wholesome and other dharmas, there is the designation (*prajñapti*) that "possession" (*prāpti*), "acquisition" (*pratilambha*), and "endowment" (*samanvāgama*) refer to their increase and decrease.

Regarding "possession of seeds," one born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is endowed with the afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) belonging to the three realms; this should be understood as referring to an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who is not free from passion.

But one who is free from passion (vītarāga) regarding a certain level, whether born on that level or on a higher one, is not possessed of the defilements belonging to that level because he is free from passion for it; yet he is possessed of them in terms of latent tendencies (anuśaya), respectively, because they have been suppressed by their antidotes but not yet eradicated.
Furthermore, as for the wholesome states acquired at birth (upapattiprātilambhika), he is possessed of those belonging only to the level where he was born.

"One who has attained the antidote to the three realms" means one who has attained the supramundane path. Regarding the phrase "for whichever type the antidote has arisen," this refers to afflictions such as the intense [grade] to be abandoned by cultivation; one is no longer possessed of the possession of the seeds of each respective [affliction], because they have been uprooted through their latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).

The possession of mastery refers to the wholesome states resulting from application, such as those consisting of hearing and so forth; for even though their seeds exist, it is impossible to bring them into manifestation without the nourishment of the seeds produced by their repeated practice during that very lifetime.
It also includes certain neutral states, such as the minds of abiding in tranquility (*śamatha*) and the transformative mind (*nirmāṇacitta*).
"Because of the deficiency of the causes for liberation, they lack the causal endowment in an absolute sense.
This means they lack the causal endowment for attaining liberation.
But what, then, is the cause for attaining liberation?

When the corruption of the afflictions (*kleśadauṣṭhulya*) is thus established within suchness (*tathatā*), it can be eradicated provided that one obtains conditions favorable to the antidote; this is called the "cause" in the sense of being a potentiality (*bhavyatā*).
From the opposite case, one should understand the deficiency of the cause.

(Abhidh-s-bh 49) II The second compendium, titled "The Determination of the Truths": [It consists of] that which is born from the birth of sentient beings and that which is based upon birth; namely, the world of sentient beings that is born.
And wherever one is born in the world of the vessel (*bhājanaloka*),
both of these are said to be suffering.

By stating that "both the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*) and the world of the vessel are produced by karma and afflictions (*kleśa*) and have karma and afflictions as their dominant condition," he makes known the reason for the suffering-nature of those two worlds, the world of sentient beings and the world of the vessel.

Furthermore, having previously explained the definition of the truth of suffering by summarizing it as "birth is suffering" and so forth, he now begins to analyze the meaning of the exposition stated in the Sūtra concerning the truth of suffering,

taking into account that birth is suffering because it involves the suffering of conflict, the suffering of change, and the suffering of being the basis for other sufferings; specifically, in the sense of experiencing the pain of bodily compression and the affliction of various impure substances while sitting between the stomach and the large intestine in the mother's womb, or while emerging from the womb.
And because, when birth exists, there is the subsequent attachment to the sufferings of old age and so forth, respectively.
The six types of suffering become eight by dividing the suffering of transformation into three kinds.

The statement that illustrates the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*) by means of birth and so forth is made in the sense of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of those phenomena that are to be experienced as painful. The statement that illustrates the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*) by means of separation from the beloved and so forth is made in the sense of the specific characteristic of the transformation (*vipariṇati*) of phenomena that are to be experienced as pleasant, whether already attained or not yet attained.
By the phrase "the five aggregates of clinging are suffering" (Abhidh-s-bh 50)...

The statement elucidating the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā) is made in the sense of being inseparable from duality, being accompanied by impermanence, and being subject to acquisition and security (yoga-kṣema).
"Birth is suffering," and so forth, refers to suffering by way of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*),
because it is the object of worldly knowledge.
"The five aggregates of clinging are suffering" refers to suffering by way of ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
Because it is the object of supramundane knowledge by way of the suchness of its arrangement.
Regarding the general characteristic of suffering, those aspects by which yogis investigate the truth of suffering are as follows: as impermanent, as suffering, as empty, and as non-self.
In this regard, the truth of suffering is to be understood as impermanent by means of twelve kinds of characteristics.

Furthermore, its characteristic of non-existence (*asallakṣaṇa*) means that the truth of suffering never exists with the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a self (*ātman*) or what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*); this is the meaning of "the truth of suffering is impermanent.
This is because the prefix *a-* has the sense of negation, and the word *nitya* has the sense of "all times" (eternality).

The characteristic of destruction (*vināśa-lakṣaṇa*) of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is their non-existence after having existed. The characteristic of transformation (*vipariṇati-lakṣaṇa*) is the occurrence of a continuity that is dissimilar [to its predecessor]. The characteristic of separation (*viyoga-lakṣaṇa*) is the loss of mastery over one's own nature regarding things remaining in that very state; it should also be understood as, in some cases, being appropriated by others.
The characteristic of proximity is impermanence being experienced at that very moment;
the characteristic of nature is that which one will necessarily experience;
and the characteristic of the moment is the necessity of destruction immediately after the acquisition of self-existence.
The characteristic of continuity is the occurrence through the process of coming and going within beginningless saṃsāra.

The characteristic of illness, old age, and death consists of the imbalance of the elements, such as baldness and so forth, as well as the application of the piercing [of the vital points] at the time of stability.
The characteristic of the occurrence of the mind and mental aspects is the state of being established or not established in terms of the opposition between the adverse factors and their remedies.

The characteristic of the perfection of enjoyments is the transience of all worldly prosperity, which, by its very nature, has a miserable end. The characteristic of the destruction and formation of the receptacle world consists in the repeated dissolution and arising of the great earth and so forth through fire and the other elements—
namely, by the cosmic destructions (*saṃvartanī*) of fire, water, and wind, which consist respectively in burning, moistening, and drying.

When the world-structure has been formed down to the limits of the first, second, and third dhyāna-stations, those intermediate spaces above them that remain— the intervals between the second, third, and fourth dhyānas— should be understood as their respective "summits. But then, by what means do the destruction and formation (*saṃvartavivarta*) of the celestial palaces belonging to the level of the fourth dhyāna occur?

They do not arise through anything external; rather, those celestial palaces are produced together with all those beings as they are being born, and they cease together with them as they are passing away.
That itself should be understood as their period of dissolution and evolution;
it means that by this, the departure of the kalpa occurs—that is, its completion.
One intermediate kalpa is the period of decrease, being the nineteenth [period] during the time of evolution.
There are eighteen increases and decreases;
beyond that, there is one final increase.
Death occurs through the exhaustion of the lifespan with respect to timely death, because the projected lifespan has reached its completion.

Regarding untimely death due to the exhaustion of merit, it should be understood as resulting from the impairment of the cultivation of karma that projects that lifespan, by way of relishing meditative attainments (*samāpatti*). Regarding death through the exhaustion of karma,

it should be understood as occurring because, having been reborn in that particular realm, the karma to be experienced in subsequent lives has either been exhausted or is absent, and thus there is no further arising in that state.
Or, suffering is of eight aspects, such as the suffering of oppression and so forth.
Impermanence pertaining to the factor of arising is existence after having not existed;
and that [arising] consists in the nature of affliction for those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that belong to the side of suffering.
Thus, based on that impermanence, the suffering of suffering is discerned;
it is the non-existence resulting from the factor of decay,
and that is undesirable for those conditioned phenomena belonging to the side of pleasure.
Thus, by depending on that [suffering of change], the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*) is discerned.

Furthermore, because the continuous arising of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) accompanied by functional rigidity (*sadauṣṭhulya*) is undesirable, and their passing away is also undesirable, the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*) is discerned by depending on impermanence that pertains to both these aspects.

With reference to the impermanence of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and the transformation of conditioned phenomena, it was said by me: "Whatever is felt here, that is of the nature of suffering. This should be understood as the underlying intention (*abhisaṃdhi*) behind the statement that even pleasant and neutral feelings are suffering. However, because a painful feeling is already well-known in the world as being suffering, no further intention is stated regarding it.
It should be understood that the underlying intention is that those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) in which birth and so forth are perceived are suffering because they are impermanent;
otherwise, even the Path would be suffering due to its impermanence.

The characteristic of emptiness is the non-existence of a self—characterized by permanence and so forth, and existing as an entity distinct from the conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*)—within those conditioned factors; and it is the existence of selflessness (*nairātmya*), characterized by a nature devoid of that [self] at all times, within those same conditioned factors. Both of these are called emptiness.
The emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) is based on the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*),
because that [nature] is non-existent by its very own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Likewise, the emptiness of existence (*tathābhāva-śūnyatā*) is based on the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Because it does not exist in whatever manner it is conceptually constructed;
for, based on the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), its nature is emptiness, since its very essence is emptiness.

Furthermore, the characteristic of non-self (*anātmalakṣaṇa*) is the state of those very conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) being devoid of the characteristic of a self as it is imagined by proponents of a self (*ātmavādin*).

The impermanence characterized by destruction and so forth is well-known, but the momentariness characterized by instantaneousness is not well-known for all conditioned phenomena; therefore, that must be established.
In this regard, the momentariness of the mind and mental factors is well-known in the world; thus, by means of that, the momentariness of form, which is not yet established, is proven.
How so? By virtue of being appropriated by the mind;
for the body is appropriated by the momentary mind.
In what sense?
On account of their sharing a single destiny (*ekayogakṣematā*);
for it is only when accompanied by consciousness that the body comes into being, and through the departure of consciousness that it becomes putrid.
Therefore, because it shares a single destiny with the mind, its momentariness should be understood to be like that of the mind.
Furthermore, this is based on its dependence upon the mind;
for a transformation of the body is observed through a transformation of the mind in states such as pleasure, pain, attachment, and aversion.
Therefore, because the body conforms to the mind which undergoes change at every moment, the momentariness of the body is established;
this is based on its being produced through the sovereign influence of the mind,
for it is well known that the body together with its sense faculties is the support of the mind.
Furthermore, it is never observed that whatever serves as the basis for the arising of something can function as its support without itself undergoing destruction;
for example, fuel and seeds are the bases for fire and sprouts, respectively.
Therefore, since the mind has a basis at every moment, it is established that it perishes at every moment.
Based on the fact that [all things] arise through the sovereignty of the mind—
for all internal and external form arises through the sovereignty of the mind—
it should be understood that because the cause is momentary, the effect is also momentary.
"Those causes and those conditions for the arising of form are themselves impermanent;
how indeed could form, having arisen in dependence upon impermanent causes and conditions, be permanent?"— according to these words of the Sūtra—
and also on account of its being subject to the mastery of the mind.
Furthermore, matter is under the control of a mind distinguished by its power (*prabhāva*),
because [matter] is transformed according to that [mind's] will.

Therefore, since there is a different resolution at every moment, momentariness is established because of arising as something else. Furthermore, it is based on the observation of transformation at the end;
for indeed, without a change in nature at every moment, a sudden transformation of form at the end would not be logical.
And that [destruction] is perceived;
therefore, because the final transformation of form is caused by the progressive increase of momentary changes within its own continuum, it is established that form is momentary.
Furthermore, this is based on the fact that once produced, it perishes by its own inherent nature without depending on any further condition.
The destruction of everything that has arisen occurs by its own inherent nature (*svarasa*) without depending on any further conditions.

Therefore, since destruction—which does not depend on other conditions—is necessarily present, there is no distinction such that it does not belong to an entity at the very moment it arises but only happens later.
Consequently, it is established that because everything that perishes perishes as soon as it has arisen, all things are momentary (*kṣaṇika*).

The meaning of "derived" (*upādāya*) is the state of depending upon a single spatial point (*ekapradeśa*), because that which is independent of the location of the primary elements lacks the capacity for separate, autonomous existence.
There exists a composite consisting of a single primary element, such as, for example, a dry lump of clay.

There is that same moist lump of clay which consists of two elements; there is that same warm one which consists of three elements; and there is that same lump of clay, both moist and warm, which consists of all [four] elements during the state of motion.
There exists a collection consisting of a single derived form, such as light;
one consisting of two derived forms, such as sound, odor, or wind;
and one consisting of three derived forms, such as smoke.
This is because it is produced by a specific excellence of form, odor, and tangibility;
furthermore, in this context, the specific excellence of tangibility should be understood as lightness.
It consists of the four derived forms of matter (*upādāyarūpa*), such as, for example, a lump of molasses.
The [aggregate] consisting of the five derived forms (*upādāyarūpa*) is, for example, that very same [aggregate] together with sound.
Thus, in other cases as well, whatever primary element (*bhūta*) or derivative form (*bhautika*) is perceived therein, it should be understood that it exists there and not elsewhere.
The statement that "an atom is bodiless" means that it is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) and is a mere conventional designation (*vyavasthānamātra*).
Because there is no limit to [further] reduction.

However, the definition of an atom (*paramāṇu*) is established by means of the intellect through the differentiation of its limits; that is, the definition of an atom is made based on as much reduction of parts as can be divided by the intellect.
But what is the reason that an atom is thus defined even though it is bodiless?
Based on the cultivation of the dissolution of the notion of a "lump" (*piṇḍasaṃjñā*):

for when form is analyzed into its constituent parts by the intellect, the notion of this entire form as a single lump disappears; thereby, there arises conformity with the entry into the selflessness of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya*).
And because it involves entering into the non-establishment of the substance of form (*rūpadravya*):

for when form is thus analyzed by the intellect, one realizes that it becomes nothing at all; having understood this, one enters into the non-establishment of the substance of form, since through this entry into representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*), there is conformity with the entry into the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).

The vast suffering that is unrefined belongs to those in the desire realm who have not accumulated roots of merit; it should be understood as "vast" because the desire realm is characterized by all states of suffering and birth, and as "unrefined" because it is unobstructed due to the non-accumulation of roots of merit and because one goes to every state of existence, respectively. That same suffering is "refined" for those who have produced the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*).
Because it is necessarily fixed toward final nirvāṇa.
That very suffering pertaining to the desire realm—whether attenuated or unattenuated—is for those who have planted roots of merit through worldly detachment;
it is, respectively, so called because it is determined by the transcendence of the suffering of suffering and so forth, and because it is not ultimate.
In this way, the "moderately austere" and other levels should be applied accordingly;
it is called "the presence of great austerity" because it is present for the purpose of removing the suffering within the mental continuums of many sentient beings.
The death of a wholesome mind and so forth should be understood as referring to the state of the final moment of consciousness at the time of passing away, which is associated with self-attachment;
it is "mind-made" because of its being born spontaneously,
since it has nothing but the mind as its cause.
A *gandharva* is so called because it "rushes" (*arvaṇāt*) by means of its odor; the meaning is that it goes to the place of rebirth by following the scent.
It remains for up to seven days, or it passes away sooner if it obtains the conditions for rebirth.
If it does not obtain them, after passing away beyond seven days, it returns once more to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) itself.

In this way, up to seven times; beyond that, he may turn back once if the conditions for rebirth are present— specifically, if a monk who has attained the fourth dhyāna but harbors the conceit of having attained arhatship finds himself in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of that level, and upon the manifestation of powerful conditions for rebirth, he acquires the false view that denies liberation, whereby he produces an intermediate state existence in hell, just as before, and while remaining there, he accumulates karma.
Due to the force of previous momentum (*pūrvāvedha*), there arises the manifestation of volitions (*cetanā*) such as wholesome ones;
he perceives beings of a similar class with whom he previously practiced that wholesome or unwholesome conduct, and he recognizes himself as being among them, just as in a dream.
Furthermore, the form of his prior existence (*pūrvakālabhava*) is produced in the place where he has been reborn.
Thereafter follows the formation of the sense faculties, according to the sequence of dependent origination beginning with name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), as it has been said:
"First there is the *kalala*; from the *kalala* arises the *arbuda*."
From the *arbuda* stage the *peśī* is born; from the *peśī* the *ghana* is born.
From the *ghana* stage, the secondary branches arise: hair of the head, body hair, nails, and so forth;
as well as the material sense faculties and the minor marks, in their proper sequence.
The truth of origination is that from which suffering arises.
What, then, is that?
It consists of the afflictions and the karma governed by the afflictions; the meaning is that these are "with outflows" (sāsrava).
If this is so, for what reason did the Blessed One specify craving alone in the exposition of the origin?
Because of its universality and preeminence.
Craving is universal with respect to objects because it pervades all objective bases—whether already attained or not yet attained—across all forms of personal existence.
Craving for a self-existence already attained; craving for renewed existence regarding what is not yet attained;
and that which is accompanied by delight and lust regarding sense objects already attained.
It should be understood as "delighting in this or that" regarding objects not yet attained.
It is "pervasive across all states" because it follows after the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) existing in the three states, such as the state of suffering-as-suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).
Among these, when those [phenomena] in the state of suffering-as-suffering have been attained, there is the craving for separation (*viyoga-tṛṣṇā*).
There is the craving for non-union regarding things not yet attained;
and there is the craving for non-separation and the craving for union regarding things that exist in a state of changeable suffering,
distinguished by whether they have been attained or not.
In states characterized by the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), there is delusion and craving,
because these states are produced by the corruption of the afflictions (*kleśa-dauṣṭhulya*) and are not produced by feelings that are neither painful nor pleasant (*aduḥkhāsukha-vedanā*).

It should be understood that the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is specifically in the state of the suffering of conditioned formations, and within it, craving proceeds through the pleasure of self-delusion.
It is "pervasive across the time periods" because it follows along in all three time periods:
first, it follows in the past time period by way of the aspect of retrospection; in the future, by way of the aspect of longing.
In the present, it functions through the mode of attachment;
it is universal across the realms because it pervades the three realms by means of craving for the desire, form, and formless realms;
and it is universal across the searches because, by that [craving], one searches for sense-pleasures, existence, and false religious practices.

Not being liberated from the realm of desire (kāmadhātu) due to the quest for sensual pleasures (kāmaiṣaṇā), one produces suffering right there. Likewise, through the quest for existence (bhavaiṣaṇā), one produces suffering in the realms of form and formlessness (rūpārūpyadhātu).
And through the quest for a false holy life (mithyābrahmacaryaiṣaṇā), not being liberated from saṃsāra, one wanders therein.
It is universal in its modes because it follows the modes of eternalism and nihilism, due to the two types of craving: for existence and for non-existence.

The division of views (*dṛṣṭi*) is fivefold: the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the esteeming of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and the esteeming of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
(Abhidh-s-bh 56) The characteristic of being unpacified is to be understood as the general characteristic of the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Furthermore, that [unpacified state] is of six aspects, namely: lack of pacification due to distraction, lack of pacification due to perversion, lack of pacification due to restlessness, lack of pacification due to sloth and torpor, lack of pacification due to negligence, and lack of pacification due to lack of shame.
and //

Furthermore, the latent tendency of the afflictions (*kleśānuśaya*) remains unabandoned because the corresponding functional rigidity (*dauṣṭhulya*) has not been eradicated; and an object conducive to the afflictions—such as something provocative to passion—comes into range; and there, improper attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*) is present, which, with respect to that object, grasps at signs of beauty and so forth, thereby being conducive to the arising of passion and the like.

Ignorance (*avidyā*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*) also have higher levels as their objects; however, it should be understood that those levels are not their direct objects in the same way that one's own level is.
Rather, the determination of them as having those [higher] levels as objects should be understood as occurring because they function through the medium of conceptual construction (*parikalpa*).
In this context, ignorance has higher levels as its object when it is associated with views.

View refers to the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), excluding other views; for it is not observed that one who is fixated on "I" with respect to conditioned factors belonging to another level [possesses such a view].
Furthermore, a defilement belonging to a higher level does not have a lower level as its object.
Because one is free from passion (*vītarāga*),
those two [the cessation and the path] are not objects for that [knowledge],
since they are to be personally realized (*pratyātmavedanīya*) by means of supramundane knowledge (*lokottara-jñāna*) or the subsequently attained knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*).

While it should have been stated that "its object of apprehension (ālambana) is that which is imagined (parikalpita)," the statement "its object of apprehension is the imagining thereof (tat-parikalpa)" is used because the imagined is not distinct from that [act of imagining].
Attachment is not associated with aversion,
because it is impossible for two things that are diametrically opposed to exist together in one place;
nor is it associated with doubt.
For one whose intellect is established in doubt does not reach a firm determination.
However, it should be understood that this [doubt] is associated with pride and the other [defilements], because they are not mutually contradictory.
Hostility is not associated with pride or with views.
For indeed, one who is obstructed regarding a particular object does not attain elevation through it, nor is he able to investigate it;
in this same way, other cases should also be applied accordingly.

Anger and the other [afflictions] do not associate with one another; thus, those that are mutually contradictory do not associate with those that are contradictory—for example, those belonging to the category of attachment (*rāga*) do not associate with those belonging to the category of hostility (*pratigha*).
However, those that are not contradictory do associate just as the afflictions do. (Abhidh-s-bh 57)

It should be understood that lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) are associated with all unwholesome states, because the manifestation of unwholesome things is impossible without disregard for oneself and others.
In this way, torpor and the other [secondary afflictions] are to be applied to all defiled states,
because defilement is impossible without such factors as lack of functional fitness (*akarmaṇyatā*).
The exposition of the fetters (saṃyojana) should be understood through the description of that by which, in whatever manner, and upon which object one is fettered.
What does it fetter?
First, the fetter of attachment (anunaya-saṃyojana), which has the nature of passion for the three realms, fetters [beings].
In what manner does it bind?
It binds one who possesses that [affliction], when there is no revulsion toward the three realms, when non-virtue is being practiced, and when virtue is not being practiced.
To what does it bind?
Regarding the production of suffering in the future,
the same should be applied to the fetter of aversion and the others.
One who is conjoined with the fetter of ignorance does not correctly discern the phenomena of suffering or the phenomena of their origination.
Because they do not fully understand the defects of the contaminated conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that constitute both fruit and cause,

one who is fettered by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) seeks a false refuge, thinking: "This is my liberation," "This is my liberation," "I shall become liberated and eternal," or "I shall be annihilated," even though for the Buddhists there is no such [non-Buddhist] liberation.

One who is bound by the fetter of adherence imagines and adheres to a false means of deliverance; having abandoned the Noble Eightfold Path, one seeks purification through the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the ascetic rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) preceded by it.
The statement that the bonds of passion and so forth are like the bonds of the suffering of change and so on is because they underlie feelings such as pleasure.
For one bound by an external bond obtains two things: he cannot go, and even while sitting, he does not obtain the power to act according to his will in his intended movements.
By analogy with that, the internal bondage of passion and so forth should be understood.
For one who has not desisted from the quest for sensual pleasures, the latent tendencies of sensual lust and aversion persist;
this is because, through that gateway, those two [tendencies] reach full growth.
They falsely deliberate upon liberation and the means to liberation respectively by means of three views and two graspings, as it was explained regarding the fetters (*saṃyojana*).

(Abhidh-s-bh 58) Excluding the six afflictions beginning with attachment (*rāga*), the other afflicted mental factors belonging to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*)— such as anger (*krodha*) and so forth— are to be understood as the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*).
They are called "outbursts" because they repeatedly envelop the minds of practitioners with agitation, thereby obstructing the side of wholesome qualities.

Furthermore, the side of the wholesome consists of the cultivation of the signs of tranquility (*śamatha*), exertion (*pragraha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) at their appropriate times, as well as the ethical discipline (*śīla*) based upon them that is comprised within the purity of the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
In that regard, at the time for tranquility, lethargy and torpor (*styāna-middha*) act as an obstacle, because they bring about an internal contraction [of the mind].
At the time of exertion (*pragraha*), there is agitation and regret,
because they bring about outward distraction;
at the time of equanimity (*upekṣā*), there is envy and avarice.

Because one who possesses those [two] experiences repeated trembling of the mind through the grasping of self-conceit regarding the perfection of oneself and others, there is a lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and a lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*) at the time of purifying one's ethical conduct; for such a person, there is no sense of shame in any way toward the occasions of transgression.

The establishment of the floods (*ogha*) and yokes (*yoga*) should be understood according to their sequence in terms of the meaning of affliction (*saṃkleśa*), purification (*vyavadāna*), excellence (*guṇa*), and deficiency (*vaiguṇya*).
By way of the connection between the supported (*āśrita*) and the support (*āśraya*): the flood of views (*dṛṣṭy-ogha*) is the supported, and the flood of ignorance (*avidyā-ogha*) is the support.
When there is delusion, it arises from a distorted investigation regarding liberation and its means.
Due to the two types of clinging— clinging to views and clinging to rules and observances— the heterodox teachers dispute with one another because they hold manifold opinions therein;
however, due to the clinging to the doctrine of a self, they do not dispute with one another.
Since all [non-Buddhists] agree on the existence of a self,
the heterodox outsiders dispute with the followers of this Dharma by means of their adherence to the doctrine of a self,
because the latter are proponents of selflessness (*nairātmya*).

Covetousness and the others are called "bonds of the body" (*kāyagrantha*); these should not be understood as bonds of the physical body, but rather as bonds in the sense that they fetter the body whose nature is a concentrated mind.

Based on a distinct view, one becomes dogmatically attached, thinking, "This alone is the truth; all else is vain. As one examines the objects of knowledge, the mind becomes distracted due to this improper examination of what is to be known.
From what is it distracted?
Because of the vision of knowledge as it truly is by one whose mind is concentrated.

They are called "hindrances" (*nivaraṇa*) because they obscure the mind so that the side of wholesome qualities (*kuśalapakṣa*) does not become manifest; the meaning is that they create an obstacle to the engagement in what is wholesome.

Sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) creates an obstacle to delighting in the life of renunciation (*pravrajyā*), because through the longing for the enjoyment of sense objects, one finds pleasure here and there.
Malice [is an obstacle] to right practice in response to exhortation;
for when one is exhorted by fellow practitioners regarding the points of training,
one fails to train correctly due to a mind of malice.

Stiffness-and-torpor, restlessness-and-remorse, and doubt [are obstacles] to calm abiding and exertion, respectively, because— as previously explained— they bring about contraction and distraction, and so forth. Doubt is an obstacle to equanimity.
Because it is impossible to disregard [an object] without a definitive determination.
The establishment of the "barrenness" (khila) should be understood in the sense of being difficult to penetrate by means of the factors that constitute the antidote,
because it has become barren through habituation in other lifetimes.
They are called "impurities" because they are the causes for the perception of impurity in immoral conduct.
They are called "destructions" (nighā) because they repeatedly destroy [beings] in saṃsāra through the connection with birth, aging, and death.
The arrows are so called because they pierce by way of craving and doubt, entering into the enjoyments of existence and into treasures.
By taking possession of many requisites, one makes oneself "possessing something" (sakiñcana); because of being joined with fear and so forth, they are called "those who have something" (kiñcanā).
They are called "misconducts" (*duścarita*) because they carry along unwholesome practices such as the taking of life;
and greed, hatred, and delusion are established as the roots of the unwholesome precisely because beings engage in misconduct through these gateways.

In this regard, those who seek enjoyments commit misconduct out of greed for the sake of some material gain; those who cannot endure the offenses of others commit misconduct out of hatred due to the conceptualization of harm as a cause;
and those such as the ritualists commit misconduct out of delusion because they hold perverted views due to their attachment to false doctrines.
They are called outflows (āsrava) because they cause the mind to flow away and disperse.
They are called "afflictions" (vighāta) because they cause physical and mental distress.
Having grasped improper signs and secondary characteristics, they burn the body and the mind; therefore, they are called "torments" (*paridāha*).

The *upāyāsas* (distresses) are so called because, having caused beings to form an attachment and fixation toward objects such as form, they afflict them with grief and other emotions when those objects undergo transformation.
They are called *raṇas* because they cause [beings] to clash (*raṇayanti*) through the taking up of weapons and so forth.
Because they cause great torment through unrighteous passion and so forth, they should be understood as "fevers," just like [physical] fevers.
In this context, unrighteous passion (*adharmarāga*) is attachment to unwholesome courses of action (*akuśalakarmapatha*).
Improper greed (*viṣamalobha*) is the pursuit of sense objects through unjust and unrighteous means.
False dharma (*mithyādharma*) should be understood as a poorly expounded doctrine and discipline (*dharmaninaya*).
They are called "foresters" (vanasāḥ) because they cause the forest of the formative forces rooted in birth to grow.
They are called "hindrances" because they obstruct the application of wholesome qualities by means of dependence on the body and so forth;
furthermore, this dependence on the body and the rest refer to the five mental hindrances.
Attachment is erroneous with respect to both objects and views; thus, it is to be abandoned through cultivation and abandoned through vision, respectively.
Since attachment has as its object merely what is beautiful, even that attachment toward sentient beings should be understood as being erroneous solely by way of the object.
Likewise, since aversion has as its object merely what is disagreeable, even when it operates toward sentient beings, it should be understood as being erroneous solely by way of the object.

Pride (*māna*) is to be understood as being perverted with respect to sentient beings and views, because it functions in such modes as "I am superior to one who is inferior," and so forth; thus, it is perverted toward sentient beings.

The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) are perverted with respect to the knowable (*jñeya*) by way of superimposition (*samāropa*) and denial (*apavāda*), as the case may be.

The adherence to precepts and vows (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and so forth are perverted with respect to views, because through the very defect of a view, one adheres to precepts and vows as being the means to purification.
Doubt is a misconception regarding the antidote, because it causes the intellect to be divided with respect to the truths.
Thus, all ten afflictions constitute the cause for both suffering and its origin,
and those two [truths] are their locus.
Therefore, they are said to be "erroneous" because they are mistaken regarding that causal basis and foundation.

They are also to be seen as erroneous regarding cessation and the path due to the production of terror; for one who, under the power of the afflictions, delights in saṃsāra, there arises a fear and a perception of falling from the perspective of purification.
Furthermore, they are to be understood as erroneous regarding cessation and the path due to their distorted conceptualization.
Because there is a misconception regarding that [reality], due to its being falsely conceptualized by the non-Buddhists in other ways.

Attachment belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) associated with the five groups of sensory consciousness (*pañcavijñānakāyika*) is conjoined with pleasure (*sukha*); that associated with the group of mental consciousness (*manovijñānakāyika*) is conjoined with joy (*saumanasya*);
all [types of attachment] are conjoined with equanimity (*upekṣā*) at the time when the continuity ceases.
However, it is not associated with suffering or mental distress,
because it functions in the mode of joy.
Resistance associated with the five groups of consciousness is conjoined with suffering;
that of the sixth [consciousness] is conjoined with mental distress; all [of them] are conjoined with equanimity as before, and they are not conjoined with pleasure or joy.
Because it proceeds in the form of dejection.
Pride is not associated with pleasure in the desire realm, because of the absence of [mental factors] belonging to the five groups of sensory consciousness.
How, then, is it associated with pleasure in the first and second dhyānas?
[It is] by means of pleasure belonging to the mental level (*manobhūmika*).
How is there pleasure belonging to the mental level there? That which is called "the pleasure of joy" (*prītisukha*).
As it has been said: "What is joy (*prīti*)?

It is the satisfaction of the mind, the elation of the mind, the gladness of the mind, the pliancy of the mind, which belongs to one whose basis has been transformed (*parivṛttāśraya*), and which rests upon the transformed consciousness (*parivṛttivijñāna*); it is a pleasant feeling, a sensation belonging to the category of feeling.
What is bliss (*sukha*)?"

"That which, for one whose basis has been transformed, is the gratification of the basis through the support of the basis—residing in the *ālayavijñāna*—is the pleasant feeling belonging to sensation.
This means the following:
when a pleasant feeling arises in the first and second dhyānas, it gladdens that collection of mind and mental factors with which it is associated by way of the aspect of joy.
It gladdens the basis, which has the nature of the *ālayavijñāna*, with the bliss of pliancy (*prasrabdhi-sukha*).
Therefore, because it performs both functions, it should be understood that it is established in two ways: as joy (*prīti*) and as bliss (*sukha*).
Consequently, pride (*māna*) when associated with that [pliancy] is said to be associated with both bliss and mental ease (*saumanasya*).
False view in the desire realm is associated with both mental distress (*daurmanasya*) and mental joy (*saumanasya*),
because one experiences dejection or elation upon seeing the fruitlessness of those who have performed good or evil deeds.
It is not associated with physical pleasure (*sukha*) or pain (*duḥkha*).
Because every kind of vision belongs to the level of the mental faculty (*manobhūmika*).

Doubt (*vicikitsā*) is not associated with mental joy (*saumanasya*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), because for one whose mind is undecided, there is no joy in the absence of tranquility (*nairvṛtya*).

In the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), even for those who practice meditation while dominated by doubt, joy and bliss (*prītisukha*) indeed continue to follow through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*); therefore, in that realm, it is also associated with both bliss and mental joy.

This same principle should be understood to apply to unique ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*) as well, beginning with its association or non-association with pleasure (*sukha*) and mental joy (*saumanasya*).

All afflictions are associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*) by way of reaching a state of indifference and thereby undergoing cessation; for, as the continuity of afflictions becomes increasingly weaker until its momentum is exhausted and it comes to rest, one must understand that at the very end, there is necessarily an association with equanimity through the gateway of indifference.
In the realm of form (rūpadhātu), [the afflictions] belong to the four groups of consciousness, because there is an absence of olfactory and gustatory consciousnesses therein.
Pride and the others belong exclusively to the group of mental consciousness, because they function by way of comparative evaluation.
Pride functions in only one part [of the mind] because it proceeds toward elevation by means of only a certain aspect [of oneself].

In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), ten [defilements] are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśanaprahātavya*); these are those which are mistaken regarding their causal basis (*nidāna*) and objective support (*padasthāna*). In the same way, it should be understood that those which are mistaken regarding origination (*samudaya*) and so forth, as appropriate, are to be abandoned by the vision of those [truths]. Indeed, are those [defilements] which have a certain object (*ālambana*) abandoned with respect to that very object? (Abhidh-s-bh 62)
They should be understood as being "misconceived.
It is not necessarily so, because those [afflictions] which have the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object do not adhere (*anuśaya*) to a tainted (*sāsrava*) entity.

Since there is an absence of hostility (*pratigha*) in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), it should be understood that there are exactly nine [afflictions] to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and the other [truths].
Likewise in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*),
what is the innate view of a self-identity (*sahajā satkāyadṛṣṭi*) that is to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanāprahātavyā*),
based upon which the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*) still manifests even for a noble disciple (*āryaśrāvaka*) who has already generated the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*)?
As it has been said: "O Venerable Dāsaka, I do not regard these five aggregates of clinging as self or as belonging to a self;

however, regarding these five aggregates of clinging, there exists in me the conceit 'I am,' the desire 'I am,' and the underlying tendency 'I am'—which are unabandoned, unrecognized, unceased, and not cast out."

Just as a nurse’s garment, though thoroughly washed with alkaline substances and the like while it was defiled, remains free of stains yet continues to retain a mere trace of odor caused by its previous soaking— an odor that must be removed once again by perfuming it with fragrant substances— in the very same way,

even for a noble disciple (*ārya-śrāvaka*) who has abandoned the impurity of the imagined view of self-existence (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) through the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*), a perception of a self persists; this is produced by the habituation of former attachments and lacks any determinate objective basis.
Furthermore, as for that which is to be abandoned through the cultivation of the path:
it should be understood that the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) includes the innate view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*),
by means of which the mind turns back from *nirvāṇa* out of fear, thinking, "In that case, what then is my self?"
Attachment and the other [afflictions], excluding those belonging to the category of views, are to be abandoned through cultivation.

The thorough knowledge of the basis for that [affliction] consists in the fact that the underlying tendency (*anuśaya*) of the afflictions has not been abandoned, and so forth, as previously described.
Thorough knowledge of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the recognition: "This affliction that has arisen is of the nature of a defilement of the mind.
Thorough knowledge of its disadvantage (*ādīnava*) is the recognition that it leads to harm for oneself, harm for others, and harm for both.
One produces fault pertaining to the present life, one produces fault pertaining to future lives, and one produces fault pertaining to both the present and future lives;
and one experiences the mental suffering and dejection born thereof. Having thus understood through these three modes, the arisen affliction is abandoned by means of non-acceptance.
But the path is cultivated for the sake of the non-arising of that which has not yet arisen.

"By means of mental attention with an undifferentiated object" means by means of an object that is mixed [with all phenomena], in the form of the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena.
If the abandonment of afflictions occurs through the knowledge of selflessness alone—namely, "all phenomena are without self"—for what purpose are the aspects such as impermanence taught?
They are not for the sake of abandoning the afflictions; rather, they are for the sake of preparing (*parikarma*) the aspect of selflessness.

For the aspect of selflessness (anātmākāra) emerges by departing from the aspect of impermanence (anityākāra), as it has been said: "That which is impermanent is suffering; that which is suffering is selfless.
For this very reason, the establishment of the supremacy of the aspect of selflessness is determined.

With reference to the unsurpassed states, there are three unsurpassed states: the unsurpassedness of knowledge (*jñānānuttarya*), the unsurpassedness of the path (*pratipadānuttarya*), and the unsurpassedness of liberation (*vimuktyānuttarya*).
Among these, the unsurpassedness of knowledge is the knowledge of selflessness (*nairātmyajñāna*).
Beyond that is the search for another knowledge:
the unsurpassed excellence of the path, which is easy and brings swift super-knowledge,
because it is the foremost of all paths.
The unsurpassedness of liberation consists in the liberation of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) that is unshakable,
because it is distinguished above all other liberations.
These three types of unsurpassedness should be understood as referring, respectively, to the path of seeing, the path of cultivation, and the final path.
The activity of perception (*upalabdhi-karma*) refers to the seeing of forms and so forth by the eyes and other [faculties].

The activity of function (*kāritra-karma*) refers to the supporting and so forth of earth and other [elements], or whatever constitutes the specific characteristic-function (*svalakṣaṇa-kṛtya*) of each; for example, "the transformation of form" (*rūpaṇā*) is the function of form, and so on.
Action preceded by resolve and intention refers to actions of the body and so forth;
transformative action refers to the ornaments and such produced by goldsmiths and others;
and action of attainment refers to the realization of nirvāṇa and so forth by means of the noble path and so forth.

However, in this context, since it is intended that action (*karman*) primarily refers to volitional effort (*vyavasāya*), both the action of attainment (*prāpti-karman*) and the action of performance (*kāritra-karman*) are also possible.
According to the Sūtra, it should be understood that the statement "the actions of body and so forth are the paths of action" is an explanation given according to their primary importance,
since the preliminary applications and other stages are also included within the actions of body and so forth.
It should be understood that three, four, and three paths of action are, respectively, characterized by the actions of body, speech, and mind.

The basis (*vastu*) of killing and so forth is, as appropriate, a being counted among sentient beings or that which is not counted among sentient beings, depending upon which killing and so forth proceed.
The intention (*āśaya*) regarding that basis consists of the intention of perceiving it as such, and the intention of the desire to perform that course of action (*karmapatha*).
The preliminary effort (*prayoga*) is the undertaking, by means of body, speech, or mind, either by oneself or through others, for the sake of that action.
The afflictions are greed, hatred, and delusion, occurring either collectively or individually as appropriate.
Reaching completion is the fulfillment of each respective action through its respective application, whether at that very moment or at a later time.
In that regard, the basis of taking life is a sentient being; the intention is the desire to kill one who perceives them as such;
and the application is the act of killing by means of weapons and so forth.
The affliction consists of greed and so forth.
Reaching the conclusion means that the living being dies immediately after or subsequently due to that preparatory effort.
We shall explain the object and the completion of taking what is not given;
the remainder should be applied accordingly as appropriate.
The object of taking what is not given is that which is possessed by another, whether classified as a sentient being or as a non-sentient thing.
The culmination of that act is its consummation.

Regarding sexual misconduct, the object is a woman who is either forbidden or permitted; it is also performed through improper means, in an improper place, at an improper time, or with one who is not of the proper measure. Furthermore, every male and every neuter being is an object. Culmination is the mutual union of the two.
The basis of false speech consists of what is seen, heard, sensed, or cognized, as well as what is unseen, unheard, unsensed, and uncognized.
The intention is the desire to speak otherwise than the truth. The culmination is the communication of this to the assembly or the opponent.
The basis of divisive speech consists of sentient beings who are either united or divided.
The intention is the desire to create a rift among them such that they do not reconcile. The culmination is the communication of the division to those being split.
The objective basis of harsh speech consists of sentient beings who have become the cause for malice; its completion is the actual utterance of those harsh words.
The objective basis of frivolous chatter consists of matters associated with what is meaningless.
The completion of that [action] is its verbal expression.
The object of covetousness is the wealth and utensils belonging to another. The intention consists of the desire for that, held by one who perceives it as such.
The preliminary application (*prayoga*) is the deliberation regarding its acceptance;
the culmination (*niṣṭhāgamana*) is the determination regarding its acceptance.
The objects (*vastu*) of malice (*vyāpāda*) are sentient beings who serve as the cause for the intent to strike them down.

Reaching the culmination is the determination to abandon [the object]. The basis (*vastu*) of false view is an existing thing (*sann-artha*). The intention (*āśaya*) is the inclination of one who perceives that [non-existent thing] as real.
Reaching the culmination is the certainty regarding the negation.

Intentionality through being commanded by another is, for example, when someone, though unwilling, having been forcibly commanded by others, intentionally practices what is unwholesome. Intentionality through being persuaded by another is, for example, when someone, as if unwilling, being persuaded and exhorted by others while being led to accept it as beneficial, intentionally practices what is unwholesome. Intentionality without full understanding is, for example, when someone who is ignorant of virtues and faults and lacks firm resolve, intentionally practices what is unwholesome by mere whim.

Volition based on fundamental attachment (*mūlābhiniveśa-saṃcetanīyatā*) is, for example, when someone, overcome by unwholesome roots such as greed and so forth, with a mind possessed [by them], intentionally commits an unwholesome act through intense attachment. Volition based on perversion (*viparyāsa-saṃcetanīyatā*) is, for example, when someone who desires the Dharma, yet holds a view of improper causes, intentionally commits an unwholesome act for the sake of a desirable fruit in the future.

In these cases, even though an action is performed through the first three types of volition, it is not accumulated (*naiva upacīyate*); therefore, its maturation (*vipāka*) need not necessarily be experienced.
However, regarding the two latter types of intentional actions, if they have been both performed and accumulated, their maturation (*vipāka*) will necessarily be experienced.

Accumulation (*upacaya*) should be understood as the increase of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), which is the nourishment of the seeds of maturation within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

The restriction of karmic activity is determined by previous actions alone; thus, the continuum of maturation is projected such that [it is fixed] that "in this life, this person must perform this action. Transgressing that limit, one performs that action, for which even the Blessed Buddhas are not capable of creating an obstruction to its performance, because the transformation of the continuum of results follows the restriction of causes.
The certainty regarding the experience of the maturation (*vipāka*) of intentional action (*saṃcetanīya-karma*) is as previously described.
Regarding the certainty of the state (*avasthā-niyama*), the state is also determined by [the classification of] actions to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-vedanīya*) and so forth;

that is, it is determined such that "by this maturation one must experience the result in the present life," "by this [one must experience it] upon rebirth" (*upapadya*), or "by this [one must experience it] in another subsequent period."

The ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) of the weak, medium, and intense unwholesome paths of action is to be understood as [rebirth] among animals, hungry ghosts, and in the hells. The outflowing fruit (*niṣyandaphala*), for those who have passed away from the states of woe and been reborn among humans, is the misfortune of both the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) and its possessions (*parigraha*), corresponding respectively to each [unwholesome path] beginning with killing and taking what is not given.
For example, short lifespan, poverty, and so forth, according to the circumstances.
The dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*) is the deterioration of external things, such as crops and the like, each corresponding respectively to its cause.
For instance, through the dominance of killing, beings become weak in vitality, and so forth.
As stated in the Sūtra: "By practicing, cultivating, and frequently performing all ten unwholesome paths of action, one is reborn in the hells;
this is their fruit of ripening (*vipākaphala*).
If, however, one comes to the state of humanity among men,"
Through the taking of life, one becomes short-lived; through taking what is not given, one suffers the loss of wealth;
through sexual misconduct, one has a rival wife;
and through false speech, one is frequently subjected to slander.
Through malicious speech, he suffers the alienation of friends; through harsh speech, he hears unpleasant sounds;
and through frivolous chatter, his words become unacceptable.
Through covetousness, there is intense passion; through malice, intense hatred;
and through wrong view, intense delusion.
This is because of the predominance of delusion in her;
this is their outflow-result (*niṣyanda-phala*).
Through the excessive practice of taking life, external things become weak in vitality.
Through taking what is not given, there is an abundance of lightning and dust;
through sexual misconduct, they are covered in dust;
and through false speech, they are foul-smelling.
Through false speech, the land becomes uneven with highs and lows; through harsh speech, it becomes saline, arid, and desolate, a wretched and evil terrain;
through idle chatter, the seasons undergo irregular transformations.
Through covetousness, they have subtle fruits;
through malice, bitter fruits;
and through wrong view, small fruits or no fruit at all.
This is their sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
The ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of the ten wholesome paths of action is [rebirth] among gods and humans. (Abhidh-s-bh 66)
The outflow fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) is the excellence of the acquisition of a personal existence (*ātmabhāva-parigraha*) corresponding respectively to each of those very [actions].
Just as the three fruits, beginning with the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*), were established for the unwholesome paths of action,
so too the three fruits for the wholesome and other contaminated (*sāsrava*) paths of action should be applied accordingly among gods and humans.
By a single karma one projects a single personal existence (*ātmabhāva*),
because by a single karmic moment the seed for the maturation (*vipāka*) of only one birth is nourished;
[and] by one [karma] one projects many.
Because it nourishes the seeds of maturation over many lifetimes by that very [action],
one [birth] is projected by many [moments of action];
for through many moments of karma, the seed of that very same [birth] is nourished again and again.
The manifold projects the manifold, because through many [factors] acting in mutual dependence, there is the nourishment of the seeds for the succession of births.
For what reason is wholesome karma associated with the realms of form and formlessness called "imperturbable" (*ānijya*)?

Just as a wholesome root that fulfills [the requirements for rebirth] in the desire realm— even when directed toward another destiny— bestows its maturation elsewhere, the wholesome roots associated with the realms of form and formlessness do not do so.

Because it bestows its fruit through restriction to a specific level (*bhūmi*), the giving of its maturation (*vipāka*) is called "immovable" (*aniñja*) in the sense of being unshakable; and because it belongs to the level of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmika*), it is also [called] immovable in the sense of being unshakeable.
For one who is deluded regarding the ripening of results, non-meritorious formations arise;
because these are exclusively afflicted, when ignorance is present, there is no opportunity for right view—which has the mode of conviction regarding the ripening of results.
For one who is deluded regarding the reality of things, meritorious and imperturbable [formations] arise; "the reality of things" refers to the four noble truths.

In that regard, delusion persists as a latent tendency even for those with wholesome minds who have not yet seen the truths; under its influence, because they do not thoroughly understand the three realms as they truly are in their nature of suffering, they give rise to meritorious and neutral formative forces that become the cause for renewed existence.
However, this is not the case for those who have seen the truths, because of the absence of delusion regarding the reality of things.
Therefore, they are said to have that as their cause.
The preparation for taking life occurs through greed in the case of butchers and the like;
through hatred alone in the case of those desiring to avenge an enmity;
and through delusion in the case of sacrificial priests and the like.
The culmination [of killing] occurs through hatred alone, because it is impossible to destroy another being without mercilessness.
In this same way, harsh speech (*pāruṣya*) and the others should be applied accordingly.
How, then, is there an application of covetousness (*abhidhyā*) and the others by means of greed (*lobha*) and the rest?
In this regard, it has been stated that the path of action of covetousness (*abhidhyā*) is the determination to appropriate the wealth and requisites of another.

If one desires those very same wealth and requisites and forms a volitional impulse (*abhisaṃskāra*) to appropriate them, then its preliminary application (*prayoga*) is established as being through greed (*lobha*).
Alternatively, if one acts with the thought, "Let him not have these," it is established as being through hatred (*dveṣa*).
Furthermore, it should be understood that an application [of effort] based on the delusion that there is no fault whatsoever in appropriating what belongs to another is likewise improper;
other cases should be applied in the same way.

It should also be understood that karma which is mutually dominant is common [to all], by the power of which sentient beings become the causes for the transformation of one another’s minds and mental factors.
Action belonging to the side of the remedy should be seen as stronger than action belonging to the opposing side,
because by the power of the remedy, even the fruit of the opposing side that has been projected is brought to a different state.
Furthermore, all wholesome intentional action should be seen as stronger than unwholesome action when it possesses the power of the remedy.
However, for one whose power of the counteractive (pratipakṣa) is weak, the unwholesome is stronger than the wholesome.
Furthermore, all wholesome and unwholesome karma without distinction that has a fixed maturation (niyatavipāka) and has not been abandoned by the Noble Path (āryamārga) is said to be strong.
Unwholesome karma associated with the desire realm (kāmadhātu) is strong by its very nature.
Because it has a vast retinue consisting of the primary and secondary afflictions (*kleśa-upakleśa*),
even that which was previously practiced is powerful, since the continuum (*saṃtati*) has been permeated by it.
Furthermore, that which pertains to those established in the stages who are of full maturity,
because it produces intense devotion and faith;
and even that which is incurable for those whose nature is not to attain final nirvāṇa.
Because it cannot be removed by its opposite;
furthermore, in terms of the field, such as the killing of one's mother and so forth;
and in terms of the mental formation, such as the vow for great enlightenment and so forth—these should be understood as powerful karma.
Powerful karma should be understood through nine aspects.
Namely: in terms of the field, if the field is one that possesses qualities and is worthy of offerings;
and in terms of the substance, if the object to be given is excellent and abundant.
In terms of intrinsic nature, it is from giving that morality arises, and from morality that cultivation arises, and so forth.
In terms of basis, it is when the agent of meritorious deeds is free from passion.
In terms of mental attention, it is when the mental attention is accompanied by intense clarity.
In terms of intention, if there is the intention for nirvāṇa;
in terms of companionship, if it is accompanied by other bases of meritorious action;
and in terms of frequent practice, if it has been performed or repeatedly reflected upon again and again.
If it is done by many people, whether performed by oneself or caused to be performed by others.

If one were to say: "In whatever way this person, this individual, performs and accumulates karma, in that very way he experiences its maturation"— if this were so, there would be no living the holy life (*brahmacaryavāsa*),
and no opportunity would be discerned for the complete destruction of suffering or for making an end to suffering.

How is it that this does not constitute living the holy life (*brahmacaryavāsa*)? Because one who has intense afflictions (*tīvrakleśa*) observes the precepts while accompanied by physical pain and mental distress through deliberate reflection (*pratisaṃkhyāya*). If its maturation (*vipāka*) were likewise experienced with such physical pain and mental distress, then the observance of those precepts would be in vain.

Furthermore, if those who commit adultery and other such acts were to experience the ripening of their results with the same pleasure and mental satisfaction as they felt while committing the misconduct, then abstaining from it would be in vain; for this reason, one does not dwell in the holy life.
And how is it that no opportunity is perceived for the complete destruction of suffering and for making an end to suffering?
Precisely because the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), which serves as the proximate cause (*upaniṣad*) for that [liberation], results in the ripening of suffering.

And this being so, the ripening of karma accompanied by pleasure is itself accompanied by pleasure; that of karma accompanied by suffering is accompanied by suffering; and that of karma accompanied by neither-suffering-nor-pleasure is accompanied by neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
The restrictive rule has been prohibited.

In this context, by the statement "according to how it is to be felt, according to how it is to be felt," and so forth, it is authorized that for wholesome and unwholesome [karma] accompanied by pleasure, there is a ripening of pleasure and so on in the future, as appropriate, for that which is to be felt as pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant; likewise,
for [karma] accompanied by pain or neither-painful-nor-pleasure that is to be felt as pleasant and so on, a ripening of pleasure and so on is authorized.
The restraint of one who has gone forth is fivefold, ranging from the restraint of a *bhikṣu* to the restraint of a *śrāmaṇerī*.
It is established with reference to an individual whose conduct consists of seclusion from misconduct and seclusion from sensual desires;
for such a person is capable of abstaining from taking life and from unchaste conduct for as long as they live.

The restraint of laymen and laywomen pertains to conduct characterized by seclusion from misconduct, but not to conduct characterized by seclusion from sensual desire. For this very reason, for them, abstinence from sexual misconduct is established for as long as life lasts, but not abstinence from unchaste conduct. The restraint of the fast (upavāsa-saṃvara), however, is neither conduct characterized by seclusion from misconduct nor conduct characterized by seclusion from sensual desire.

For this very reason, the restraint of fasting for a day and night (ahorātrika-upavāsa-saṃvara) has been prescribed for them, for the purpose of gradually practicing both [the lay and monastic precepts].
Just as eunuchs and impotent persons are prohibited from being lay followers (upāsaka), because they are unfit to attend upon the community of monks and nuns.

Likewise, even for those with both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*), because they are capable of honoring both sides through the manifestation of the afflictions (*kleśa*) of both women and men, they are not mentioned separately.

The meditative restraint (*dhyānasaṃvara*) is the abstention from immorality (*dauḥśīlya*) on the part of one who is free from passion for sense pleasures— even if only through partial detachment— once the seeds [of those passions] have been impaired by the antidote that suppresses the desire-realm afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), such as greed and the like, which give rise to immorality.

It should be understood that for one who has become free from passion for the third dhyāna, there is an even greater impairment of the seeds of those very factors that give rise to immorality, by means of the antidote consisting in distancing.

However, for one who has become free from passion for the fourth dhyāna, it should be understood that the restraint of conduct is not established in the formless realms because of the absence of matter there.
(Abhidh-s-bh 69) Butchers (*aurabhrika*) are those who, having killed animals, make their livelihood by selling them.
In the same way, poultry-sellers (*kaukkuṭika*) and others are to be applied according to the circumstances as appropriate.
Elephant-trappers bind elephants in the forest and tame them; snake-charmers live by taking up snakes and performing their tricks for a livelihood;
and slanderers live by harming others through malicious gossip.
"Whether by birth or by undertaking that action" refers respectively to one born into such a family and one not born into such a family.
Non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) is defined as the determination to habitually engage in those actions, preceded by the application of body and speech.

The actions of one who is free from both the aforementioned restraint and non-restraint—such as giving, kind words, and so forth, or striking with a stick or a slap—are called "neither restraint nor non-restraint."

Karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) is that which ripens in the very same birth in which it was performed. Karma to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*) is that which ripens in the immediately following birth,
such as the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*).

For one who has only a single immediate transgression (*ānantarya*), it is logical that its maturation (*vipāka*) occurs immediately thereafter; but for one who now has many such transgressions, how is the experience of their maturation?
The maturation of all of them is experienced simultaneously.
For thus, the physical basis of one who has committed many acts of immediate retribution is produced as exceedingly delicate,
and the causes are manifold, intense, and diverse, by virtue of which one experiences abundant sensation.

Furthermore, these categories— such as karma to be experienced in the present life (dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya) and so forth— are established based on the commencement [of ripening], not with reference solely to the fact of being experienced in that [specific] lifetime.
That for which the ripening begins to mature in that very birth is "to be experienced in the present life."

That which begins to ripen in the very next birth is "to-be-experienced-in-the-next-birth" (*upapadyavedanīya*); that which begins to ripen after skipping over the next birth is "to-be-experienced-in-a-subsequent-birth" (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*). And having established this, it is said in the *Hācittāvadāna*: "The experience of the maturation of an immediate (*ānantarya*) karma occurs through repeated death and rebirth in hell."
It becomes conformed.
Black karma with black ripening is unwholesome, because it is afflicted and because its ripening is undesirable.
By contrast, the white [action] has a white ripening; it is the wholesome [action] pertaining to the three realms.
"Black-and-white" refers to that which has black-and-white ripening; it means the ripening associated with the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) is a mixture of wholesome and unwholesome.
How can one [action] be both wholesome and unwholesome?
It is not so here (Abhidh-s-bh 70).

It is stated that those two are one by way of the necessity of the moment of engagement (*pravṛtti-kṣaṇa-naiyamyena*); however, one must understand that the intended meaning here is that "action" (*karman*) is a single entity by virtue of its underlying intention (*āśaya*) and its application (*prayoga*).
And since those two are mutually dissimilar with respect to their blackness or whiteness, a single action is established as "black-and-white.

In that regard, it is black by way of intention but white by way of application, as for example when someone, desiring to deceive others, gives gifts with a sincere disposition (*bhāva*) merely for the sake of inspiring confidence in them, even to the point of going forth into homelessness (*pravrajati*).

In terms of application it is black, but in terms of intention it is white; for example, when someone, desiring to turn a son or a disciple away from what is harmful and wishing to establish them in what is beneficial, with a mind of compassion, at that time becomes afflicted through harshness of body or speech.

Karma that is neither black nor white leads to the exhaustion of karma; it is the untainted (anāsrava) karma within the paths of preparation (prayoga-mārga) and the uninterrupted paths (ānantarya-mārga), because these paths of preparation and uninterrupted paths serve as the antidotes for abandonment.
In this context, it is "not black" due to the absence of the stains of afflictions (kleśa), and it is "white" because of its absolute purity.
It is without ripening because it is opposed to *saṃsāra*.

It leads to the exhaustion of karma; for by means of that untainted (*anāsrava*) karma, the latencies (*vāsanā*) for the yielding of ripening of this threefold tainted (*sāsrava*) karma—black and so forth—are completely eradicated.

Furthermore, with reference to the nature of all untainted (*anāsrava*) karma as being respectively an obstacle or a favorable condition, one should understand the systematic arrangement of crookedness (*vaṅka*), faults (*doṣa*), and impurities (*kaṣāya*), as well as those things conducive to purity (*śauceya*) and those conducive to sagehood (*mauneya*), in their proper order.
In this context, "crookedness" (*vaṅka*) refers to the actions of body, speech, and mind that act as obstacles to the arising of the eightfold path that is straight.
"Fault" (*doṣa*) refers to those actions of body and so forth by which, when the mental continuum is corrupted, such obstructive karma arises.
"Stains" (*kaṣāya*) refer to actions of body and so forth based upon the views of non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).
Because it is embraced by the turbidity of lack of faith (*aśraddhya*), which is the opposite of clarity regarding the Buddha’s teaching;
another synonym is that it is "crooked" (*vaṅka*) in the sense of being contrary to the middle way, as it does not fall into the extremes of eternalism or nihilism;
and it is a "fault" (*doṣa*) in the sense of an aversion toward the establishment of purification, as it is embraced by the view of denial (*apavāda-dṛṣṭi*).
It is called "impurity" (kaṣāya) in the sense that it is embraced by the view of a self-identity and acts as an obstacle to the vision of the reality of selflessness.
Purifications (*śauceya*) are those actions of body, speech, and mind comprised within perfectly pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) and comprised within straight view (*dṛṣṭi*),
because they are free from the stains of failure in ethical discipline and view.
