Silences (*mauneya*) are the untainted (*anāsrava*) actions of body, speech, and mind of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), because these are the actions of the sages (*muni*).
With reference to the perfection of giving, the phrase "he will become a giver" demonstrates his habit of constant giving,
because he gives again and again by virtue of that character;
and the phrase "to śramaṇas, to brāhmaṇas," and so forth, demonstrates his impartiality in giving.
Because of giving to all supplicants without distinction;
it is the nature of giving that fulfills desires through food, drink, and so forth,
by relinquishing all types of requisites according to their wishes.

One who has relinquished all attachments, one whose hand is ever outstretched, one who delights in renunciation, one who frequently performs sacrifices, one who is perfected in giving, and one who delights in the distribution of gifts—by these terms, in their respective order, the non-reliant nature of giving and the other qualities should be understood.
Furthermore, the non-reliant nature of giving should be understood as not being dedicated toward the enjoyments of future existence.
By the phrase "attained through exertion and vigor" with reference to the excellence of the gift (*deyasaṃpad*), he shows that the object to be given is not acquired through extortion.
For what is acquired through extortion is attained without exertion or vigor,
since it is obtained by remaining in one's own place while falsely denying the deposit of another.
By the phrase "acquired through the strength of one's own arms," it is indicated that the object to be given was not seized from others;
for what is seized from others is not acquired through the strength of one's own arms, since it is taken away from them after they have acquired it with great difficulty by various means.

By the phrase "not discarded by sweat or impurities," it is indicated that the object to be given is unspoiled and pure; the meaning is that it has not been cast off or abandoned due to sweat or impurities.
By the word "righteous" (*dhārmikaiḥ*), it is indicated that the object to be given is appropriate.
Because it is free from improper things such as weapons, poison, and intoxicants;
by the phrase "obtained through Dharma," he shows that the objects to be given are those acquired righteously, since they have been earned by avoiding wrong livelihoods such as cheating with scales.
By undertaking ethical discipline (*śīla*) without impairment, one becomes "possessed of ethical discipline" (*śīlavat*) through that application.
That restraint which is directed toward liberation is the Prātimokṣa restraint;
for it serves as the means for departing from cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
He is perfected in conduct because his deportment and other behaviors are beyond reproach by the virtuous.
He is perfected in his range of activity because he avoids the five improper spheres of activity.
The five improper spheres for a monk are: a marketplace, a brothel, a tavern, a royal court, and a *caṇḍāla* settlement as the fifth.

Because he trains with intense reverence even toward those offenses that are merely proscribed (prajñapti-sāvadya), just as toward those that are naturally unwholesome (prakṛti-sāvadya), he perceives danger even in the slightest faults.
Having undertaken the training in its entirety, he trains in the precepts; thus he is said to be one who trains in the bases of training.
Hereafter, the meaning of that which was taught by the Blessed One in various sūtras concerning ethical discipline (*śīla*)—beginning with "one is restrained in body"—is now explained.

In this context, one is "restrained in body and speech" because, being embraced by clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*), one acts correctly and intentionally in walking back and forth and so forth, exactly as permitted.
One is "endowed with the perfection of body and speech" because, by not committing any transgressions, one does not violate ethical discipline.
The conduct of body and speech is completely pure because, by relying on meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the stain of immorality is removed through the power of concentration.
It is wholesome conduct of body and speech because it is exclusively virtuous, being unmixed with afflicted discursive thoughts (*kliṣṭa-vitarka*).
It is irreproachable conduct of body and speech because it is praised by the virtuous, as it is not dedicated toward existence (*bhava*) or enjoyments (*bhoga*).

The conduct of body and speech is non-afflictive because it does not cause distress to others through self-exaltation and the like, nor through contemptuous association. It is conformable because it accords with the attainment of nirvāṇa by bringing about the Noble Path. It is appropriate because it serves to suppress one's own faults and conceal one's virtues.
His conduct of body and speech is appropriate because it is worthy of being approached due to his habit of supporting his fellow practitioners of the holy life (*sabrahmacārin*).
His conduct of body and speech is fitting because he serves teachers and those who stand in the place of teachers with humility as is required.
His conduct of body and speech is respectful because he receives instruction with deference, being free from the dogmatic clinging to his own views (*svadṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).

The conduct of body and speech is "unafflicted" because it is free from self-mortification, being devoid of adherence to painful austerities and coarse practices. The conduct of body and speech is "without regret" because there is an absence of remorse, due to having no subsequent regret regarding the renunciation of enjoyments and the undertaking of activities. The conduct of body and speech is "free from remorse" because, with respect to the side of wholesome qualities, one strives to accomplish as much as possible without being satisfied with a mere trifle, owing to an absence of remorse.
Action is their own; thus they are "those for whom action is their own.
But how is action their own? It is by virtue of their experiencing the ripening of the action performed by themselves.
For that which is not shared with others is indeed called "one's own.
Actions are their inheritance; thus, they are the heirs to actions.
How is it that actions constitute their inheritance?

In that experience of the ripening of what one has done oneself, because wholesome and unwholesome karmas are mutually inherited, there is a distribution of desired and undesired fruits according to each being's own [actions]. Furthermore, from where did those beings who experience the ripening of the desired and undesired fruits of their own performed actions first arise? Are they causeless, or do they have causes such as primordial matter (prakṛti) or a Lord (īśvara)? To this he says: "They have karma as their womb" (*karmayonīya*); the meaning is that for these beings, karma alone—avoiding both the absence of a cause and an unequal cause—is the womb for their arising.
Thus, with respect to both engagement and withdrawal, they have action as their refuge;
because they rely upon untainted action for the sake of abandoning tainted action, action itself becomes their refuge.
Regarding what was said—that the maturation of karma for sentient beings is inconceivable—it should not be understood as being inconceivable in every respect.

How, then, is it conceivable, and how is it inconceivable? It is conceivable that the desirable or undesirable maturation of wholesome or unwholesome karma occurs in happy or miserable destinies; however, it is inconceivable in other ways. (Abhidh-s-bh 73)
Because it is possible [to describe] and because it brings about qualities such as right view,
the diversity of the various types of physical forms, colors, and so forth of the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) of sentient beings through this karma is inconceivable;
for it is impossible [to fathom], and because anyone other than an omniscient one would bring about defects such as madness.
That very [action] is inconceivable by way of its locus (*sthāna*), basis (*vastu*), and so forth.
Among these, the *locus* is the place where one stands while performing an action, such as in a village or a city, and so on.
The *basis* is the object upon which the action is directed, whether it be classified as a sentient being or as a non-sentient thing.
The cause of the wholesome, unwholesome, and so forth, consists of the wholesome and unwholesome roots as appropriate.
The maturation (*vipāka*) is that very diversity of personal existence (*ātmabhāva*).
The karma that brings about the diversity of external phenomena is inconceivable.
Indeed, because the worldly inquiry— "By what kind of karma was the sharpness of thorns and such things produced?"— is not included [within the scope of rational analysis],

action associated with jewels, mantras, medicinal herbs, and secret formulas is inconceivable. Among these, that which is associated with jewels refers to the flowing of water from moonstones (*candrakānta*) and the like.

That which is connected with mantras is the absence of burning and so forth in those who have been consecrated by them; that which is connected with medicinal herbs is the curing of a patient by means of those [herbs] taken [by him];
and that which is connected with the application of manual techniques is the removal of fever and so forth through various such manual applications.
Furthermore, the power and activity of all yogins is inconceivable.
How so?
By the power of their minds, they cause the great earth to tremble or fly up into the sky, and so forth.
The activity performed by Bodhisattvas through their masteries (*vaśitā*) is inconceivable.

For example, through mastery over life (*āyur-vaśitā*), Bodhisattvas, having sustained the formative forces of life (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*), remain for as long as they wish. Through mastery over mind (*citta-vaśitā*), they enter meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) according to their desire. Through mastery over requisites (*pariṣkāra-vaśitā*), they rain down immeasurable and priceless provisions for sentient beings.
Through mastery over karma, they transform karmas that were to be experienced in other realms, stages, destinies, births, or conditions into something else.
Through mastery over rebirth, even while dwelling in the meditative absorptions (dhyāna), they are born in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) without ever falling away from them.
Through mastery over resolve (adhimukti), they resolve upon earth and so forth as being like water and the like.

Through mastery over their vows, they bring forth, according to their wish, incalculable great vows that accomplish the welfare of both themselves and others. Through mastery over supernatural powers, for the sake of attracting sentient beings, they display immeasurable miraculous feats of psychic power.
Through mastery over knowledge, they reach the ultimate limit of excellence regarding the Dharma, its meaning, its etymological explanations, and their eloquence.

Through mastery over phenomena (*dharmavaśitā*), they are able to simultaneously satisfy the minds [of beings] by establishing the teachings— such as the *sūtras* and so forth— in various names, phrases, and syllables according to the needs of all sentient beings;
such is the inconceivable activity of the Buddhas in performing their Buddha-deeds.
How so?

All the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, having reached the state of effortless spontaneity and attained the single flavor of the *dharmadhātu*, perform every task that must be accomplished for sentient beings—whenever, however, and to whatever extent it is required. Thus, the sphere of the Buddhas is inconceivable.

It is the *hetu* (cause) because it is the cause that nourishes the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of rebirth. It is the *samudaya* (origin) because it is the cause for the collective arising of sentient beings who possess accumulated latent impressions within the classes of beings such as gods, by way of a resemblance to their respective forms and natures.

It is the *prabhava* (source) because it is the cause for the intense emergence of all modes of existence—such as the realms of rebirth (*gati*) and birth-places (*yoni*)—individually within each continuum, extending up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
The condition for the attainment of another, unprecedented personal existence through the passing away of the previous personal existence is called "cause" (hetu-pratyaya).
If that cessation were other than the formations due to their subsistence, it would be unrelated and thus a separate entity.
If it were not other, it would possess the characteristic of affliction.
Therefore, it is neither both nor neither.
Furthermore, in this context, "conceptual proliferation" (*prapañca*) means thinking in an improper manner—that is, by way of a non-path, an illogical, and an unjust method;
it refers to thinking otherwise than how one ought to think. But how, then, should it be thought?
By such modes as "peaceful," "sublime," and so forth.
He is without ornaments because those who are purified by wisdom lack the ornaments of specific qualities such as the [mundane] sciences and so forth.
The statement "the abandonment of all without remainder" is the summary;
the remainder is the detailed explanation.
For this very reason, it is said that [the following] is based on the remaining words.
Because of their instruction regarding that [path],
how is there abandonment without remainder? It is through the abandonment of both the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) and the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
In this context, "relinquishment" (pratiniḥsarga) refers to the abandonment of the active outbursts (paryavasthāna),
because of the avoidance of what has already arisen;
"extinction" (vyantībhāva) refers to the abandonment of the underlying tendencies (anuśaya).
Because there is absolutely no arising in the absence of the root,

that [cessation] is further established as twofold through the distinction between the antidotes of the path of seeing and the path of cultivation— namely, destruction (*kṣaya*) and detachment (*virāga*).
Among these, "destruction" refers to the state of detachment achieved by means of the path of seeing.
Because only a small portion of the mass of afflictions remains,
there is detachment through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), since that path is characterized by the attainment of detachment from the various stages (*bhūmi*).
Furthermore, when one is dissociated from both of those, suffering is ceased in the future through the attainment of the state of non-arising;
and in this present life, mental distress is stilled.
Because it does not manifest,
he says "cessation" (*nirodha*) and "quiescence" (*vyupaśama*) with reference to the abandonment of suffering which is the fruit thereof.
However, he says "disappearance" (*astaṃgama*) with reference to the natural subsiding of those sentient beings who have arisen from previous karma and afflictions.
Having done so, it should be understood that the abandonment of all [defilements] without exception has been taught.
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is so called because it is the opposite of the conditioned, due to the absence of arising, passing away, duration, and change.
It is difficult to see, as it is the objective range of the eye of wisdom belonging solely to the Noble One (*ārya*).

It is immovable because it is stable due to no longer wandering through the destinies such as the hells; it is unbending because it does not bend toward states of existence due to the absence of craving for the realms of desire, form, and formlessness;
it is deathless because of the absence of the aggregates that serve as the basis for death.
It is "without outflows" because of the absence of outflows;
it is a "refuge" because it is the basis for the bliss and joy of liberation;
it is an "island" because it serves as dry land within the great ocean of saṃsāra.

It is a protection (*trāṇa*) because, upon its attainment, all calamities such as birth and so forth are eliminated. It is a refuge (*śaraṇa*) because it is to be resorted to as the locus for the non-binding nature of the intention and application produced by it.
It is the ultimate resort (*parāyaṇa*) because it is the locus for attaining supreme nobility; the meaning is that it is the objective support for the means of attaining arhatship.
It is "unfailing" because, being unborn, there is no possibility of its falling away;
it is "free from fever" because there is an absence of the torment caused by the frustration of all desires;
it is "without burning" because it is cool due to the complete subsiding of all burning afflictions such as grief.
It is secure (*kṣema*) because it is the basis for dwelling in the noble state, free from the fear of disease, old age, and death;
it is auspicious (*śiva*) because it is the basis for all wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma*);
and it is golden (*sauvarṇaka*) because it is the objective basis for supramundane happiness.
It is a *svastyayana* (auspicious path) because it serves as the objective support for attaining that state through the practice of ease;
it is health (*ārogya*) because it is free from the diseases of the afflictions and other obscurations;
it is immovability (*āniñjya*) because it is free from the distractions of the manifold proliferation of all sense objects.
Nirvāṇa is the object of focus for the peaceful and blissful dwelling that results from the departure of perceptions of form and so forth.

Furthermore, with reference to the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*), synonyms such as "unborn" (*ajāta*) and so forth should be understood in the sense of being the opposite of the characteristics of suffering (*duḥkhalakṣaṇa*).
For suffering arises there, within various classes of beings, through the linking of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhibandha*);
thereafter, it increases through the full development of the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*).
And that suffering is produced by the impelling force of past karma and afflictions;
furthermore, that present suffering serves as the basis for the formation of other existences through karma and afflictions.
Consequently, by way of non-interruption, there occurs the continuous arising of renewed existence.

Therefore, by way of its opposite, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering should be understood, respectively, as unborn, unbecome, uncreated, and unarisen. Furthermore, with reference to the truth of cessation,
it has the characteristic of peace.
With reference to the dissociation from the aggregates of grasping, which have the characteristic of being unpeaceful due to the suffering inherent in conditioned formations;
with reference to the characteristic of excellence, which consists in having a nature of intrinsic purity and bliss through dissociation from the suffering of afflictions;
and with reference to the characteristic of transcendence, which consists in having a nature of eternal benefit.
Because it is not subject to recurrence and because it is secure, it is respectively termed "beneficial" and "wholesome," as these qualities are possible therein.

The truth of the path is that by which one thoroughly understands suffering, and so forth; its definition should be understood in terms of its functional role regarding the truths. The statement "the path is fivefold" is made in terms of its classification.
It should be understood that there are five divisions, based on the section concerning the Truth of the Path together with its retinue.

In that context, the path of accumulation consists of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and so forth; through its fulfillment, one attains the fitness of the mental continuum for the sequential stages beginning with "Heat" (*uṣmagata*), for the vision of the truths, and for the abandonment of their obscurations.

Alternatively, it should be understood that other wholesome factors conducive to enlightenment (*aupaniṣadakuśala*), such as freedom from regret (*avipratisāra*) and so forth, also constitute this path.

Heat (*uṣmagata*) is the concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), together with their associated factors, which has attained illumination regarding the truths within one's own person. It should be understood as Heat when, through a concentrated mind,
there is a clear manifestation of the meaning by way of mental verbalization (*manojalpa*) of the Dharma— such as the Sūtras and so forth— which is governed by the truths,
and when both calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) are present.
The increase of that [heat] is the "Summits" (*mūrdhan*), established for the purpose of further advancement beyond it.
Patience (*kṣānti*) is the concentration that has entered and followed after one part.
How does it become "entered into one part"?
Because it is characterized exclusively by the non-existence of the apprehended object (*grāhyabhāva*).
How is it "conforming to one part"? Because it abides in a manner conducive to the penetration of the non-existence of the apprehending subject (*grāhakābhāva*).
The supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) is that immediately following which the supramundane path (*lokottaramārga*) first arises.

The path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) should be understood as characterized by non-conceptual calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), occurring immediately after the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*).
It is also the knowledge of the equality of the object and the subject; for by means of it, one penetrates suchness (*tathatā*), which is the absence of the grasped and the grasper.

It is also the knowledge of dharmas that takes as its object that which has internally removed the conventional designation of "sentient being" (*sattva-saṃketa*) and the conventional designation of "dharma" (*dharma-saṃketa*), having entirely removed both types of conventional designations.
How is it that there is knowledge of phenomena as objects of support from which the conventional designation of "sentient being" has been personally removed?

Because, within one's own continuum, one does not conceptually construct the signs of a self. How is it that there is knowledge of phenomena as objects of support from which the conventional designation of "phenomenon" has been personally removed?
Because he does not conceptualize the signs of dharmas such as form within his own continuum,
how is it that there is knowledge of dharmas which has as its object the removal of both types of conventions from everything?
It is because he does not conceptualize the signs of self or dharmas without distinction in all cases.
Furthermore, the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) in its detailed classification consists of the sixteen moments of acceptance (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) regarding the [four] truths.

Among these, the acceptance of the dharma-knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣāntiḥ*) is the knowledge that investigates the teachings— such as the sūtras and so forth— which pertain to the truth of suffering while one is on the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*).

Taking as its predominant condition the application of attention that is thorough (*yoniśo-manaskāra*), there arises a supramundane wisdom (*lokottara-prajñā*) whose nature is right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), which directly experiences the suchness (*tattva-tathatā*) of the truth of suffering within one's own continuum. By means of this, one abandons the twenty-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the three realms that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering.
Therefore, it is called "receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering" (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*).

Through that patience (*kṣānti*), because of the abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*) to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, the basis (*āśraya*) is transformed. Immediately thereafter, the knowledge (*jñāna*) by which one experiences that transformation of the basis is called "dharma-knowledge regarding suffering" (*duḥkhe dharmajñāna*).
Both of these—the initial patience and knowledge—are the "conformity" (*anvaya*) for all noble qualities (*āryadharma*) of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

Therefore, because of their collective realization, there arises—taking that as its object—an untainted wisdom (*anāsravā prajñā*) that is personally and directly experienced (*pratyātma-pratyakṣānubhāvinī*), which consists in the subsequent acceptance of knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkhe anvayajñānakṣānti*). This is the conviction that "this is the lineage (*anvaya*) of the noble dharmas.
That knowledge by which one subsequently experiences that acceptance of subsequent knowledge is called "subsequent knowledge" (*anvayajñāna*).
For the supramundane path has two objects: suchness (*tathatā*) and correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).

Among these, suchness is the object of the path belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), while correct knowledge is the object of that belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).

Therefore, this is said: through the receptivities (*kṣānti*) and knowledges (*jñāna*) regarding the dharma-knowledge, there is the realization of the apprehended (*grāhya*); through the receptivities and knowledges regarding subsequent knowledge (*anvaya*), there is the realization of the apprehender (*grāhaka*).
That person described by the Blessed One as the sixth "dweller in the signless" (*animittavihārin*) should be understood as abiding in these receptivities and knowledges.
Because of the non-apprehension of all signs,
these sixteen moments of mind, comprised of [patience and] knowledge, constitute the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
since one sees each of the noble truths, previously unseen, through four [moments].

And here, a mental moment (cittakṣaṇa) should not be understood as the mere appearance or manifestation of an entity; rather, it is that duration by which the completion of the arising of knowledge regarding the object of knowledge occurs. For example, "suffering is to be fully known" constitutes a single mental characteristic.
In this way, [the truths] such as "origination is to be abandoned" and so forth are explained.
Furthermore, all that has been elaborated in detail concerning the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) should be understood as being merely a formal establishment (*vyavasthānamātra*),
because the supramundane state (*lokottarāvasthā*) is to be personally realized within oneself (*pratyātma-vedanīya*).

For the entire truth of the path is to be understood through four aspects: by way of formal establishment (*vyavasthāna*), by way of conceptualization (*vikalpata*), by way of direct experience (*anubhava*), and by way of fulfillment (*paripūri*).

Among these, "by way of formal establishment" means that Śrāvakas and others, having attained the culmination of their respective realizations, establish the truth of the path for others—by means of the collections of names, phrases, and phonemes—through the subsequently attained knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) for the purpose of enabling others to attain it.
Thus, regarding the truths, there are the patiences (*kṣānti*) and the knowledges (*jñāna*), and so forth;

these are practiced through conceptualization, as those engaged in clear realization (*abhisamaya*) repeatedly cultivate what they have conceptualized according to the established order by means of worldly [wisdom].

Experiencing it thus through repeated practice, they personally experience from the beginning that supramundane state free from conceptual proliferation called the path of seeing; having perfected it, thereafter, once they have completed the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*), up until the finality of realization—
They attain [these].

Furthermore, having reached the culmination of realization, they establish the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*) by means of the subsequently attained knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). It should be understood that this wheel of the path (*mārgacakra*), possessing these four aspects, proceeds again and again through mutual dependence.
As for what was said— that "the dustless, stainless Dharma-eye arises regarding phenomena"— that was stated with reference to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
because for the first time it has the nature of the noble eye of wisdom (*āryaprajñācakṣus*) regarding the truths.
In that regard, it is "dustless" by means of the receptivities to the teachings (*dharmakṣānti*).
By means of those [knowledges], there is freedom from stain through the abandonment of the dust of the afflictions;
by means of the knowledges of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), it is free from stain because of the arising of a basis that has abandoned those [afflictions] and the stains that obscure them.

Furthermore, with respect to the purity of the path through thorough knowledge and abandonment, respectively, in these very two stages of receptivity and knowledge, it should be understood as "dustless" and "stainless."
The passage beginning with "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*) and so forth should also be understood as referring specifically to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),

because it is spoken immediately after the realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*) for those to be trained. In that context, the "truths seen" (*dṛṣṭadharma*) are [realized] by means of the receptivities to the teachings (*dharmakṣānti*).
Through those [knowledges], because of the penetration of reality;
they have attained the Dharma by means of the knowledges of the Dharma,
because of the direct realization of the transformation of the basis (āśrayaparivṛtti) through them.
They have realized the Dharma through the patiences of subsequent knowledge (*anvayakṣānti*),
because they experience both [the Dharma and its subsequent realization], thinking, "This is the lineage of the noble dharmas.
They have thoroughly penetrated the Dharma through the cognitions of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).
By all [of these], one has "crossed over doubt" because of having completed all that is to be known; by all the patiences (*kṣānti*) and knowledges (*jñāna*),
when the fruit is attained through the supramundane path, there is no longer any uncertainty regarding one's own attainment, which had been long desired.
"Crossed beyond doubt" regarding supreme realization refers to all [the Buddhas],
because for one in that state, there is no longer any disagreement among others concerning the attainment of further distinctions.
"Not dependent on another" means that in the cultivation of the path, he is self-sufficient due to his own skill, even without the instruction of others.
He is not led by others because, through the attainment of verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*), he cannot be diverted from the Teacher’s teaching by other non-Buddhist sectarians even in future lives.

He has attained fearlessness regarding the teachings because, with respect to his realization, he lacks the mental cowering found in those of evil intent or false pride when faced with questions concerning the Dharma.
The path of cultivation is the mundane path.
In this context, the mundane path consists of the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*).

Furthermore, these meditative absorptions and formless attainments should be understood in terms of affliction (*saṃkleśa*), purification (*vyavadāna*), establishment (*vyavasthāna*), and purity (*viśuddhi*).
How is it [defined] from the perspective of defilement?
There are four neutral roots: craving (*tṛṣṇā*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), pride (*māna*), and ignorance (*avidyā*).

Because the minds of those who are defiled by these are turned toward all the obscured-neutral afflictions and secondary afflictions belonging to the realms of form and formlessness through the gateway of afflicted meditation (*kliṣṭadhyāna*).
Therein, it is defiled by craving through the defilement of relishing,
due to the relishing of the pleasure of pliancy;
it is defiled by views through the practice of meditation dominated by views.
Having fixed upon meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), one becomes defiled by pride through the arising of views regarding the past eons and so forth,
because one proceeds toward arrogance due to that attainment of distinction while being absorbed in meditation characterized by pride.

One is afflicted by ignorance through the state of being absorbed in doubt; because, despite the desire for liberation, one fails to penetrate reality and thus gives rise to doubt regarding that specific attainment, wondering whether it is liberation or not.
How [are they] from the perspective of purification?

The pure meditative absorptions (dhyāna) and formless attainments (ārūpya), even when mundane, are called "purified" because, being wholesome, they are free from the stains of the outbursts of affliction (paryavasthāna).
How is it established? First,

the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) are established in four ways, according to the distinctions of their factors (aṅga), attainment (samāpatti), measure (mātra), and the absence of perception (asaṃjñākaraṇa).
The formless attainments [are associated] with [the factors] excluding three members.
Furthermore, with reference to what are vitarka and the others established as factors within the dhyānas, even though other dharmas are present?
It is because the factors consisting of the counteragent, the benefit, and the basis for both are fully accomplished by that many alone.
In the first dhyāna, applied thought (vitarka) and sustained thought (vicāra) are the factors of the antidote,
because through them there is the abandonment of thoughts of sensual desire, ill will, and cruelty, and so forth;
joy (prīti) and bliss (sukha) are the factors of benefit.
When the opposing factors have been countered by applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), one attains the joy and bliss born of seclusion from them; thus,

one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*) is the factor that serves as the basis for both, because the activity of applied thought and the others proceeds by the power of reliance upon meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Likewise, in the second dhyāna, internal clarity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*) is the factor that serves as the antidote, because it acts as the counteragent to applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*). Joy (*prīti*), bliss (*sukha*), and one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*) are the remaining factors, as previously described.
In the third dhyāna, equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension are the factors of the antidote, because they counteract joy;
bliss and one-pointedness of mind are the remaining factors. (Abhidh-s-bh 80)
Respectively,
in the fourth dhyāna, the purity of equanimity and the purity of mindfulness are the factors of the antidote, because by means of these two, pleasure is countered.
The feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant is the limb of benefit;
one-pointedness of mind is the limb common to both.
Furthermore, how is it that there are seven mental orientations (*manaskāra*) for one entering the first dhyāna?
By means of the mental orientation belonging to the stage of meditative concentration, through seeing the defects and so forth in the realm of desire, one perceives its coarse characteristic;
and due to the absence of those [defects], one perceives the peaceful characteristic in the first dhyāna.

This is called the mental application that experiences the characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedanīya-manaskāra*), and it should be understood as being interspersed with hearing and reflection (*śrutacintā*). Thereafter, having transcended both hearing and reflection, it takes as its object the signs of the characteristics of coarseness and tranquility (*audārika-śānta-lakṣaṇa-nimitta*) exclusively through the mode of cultivation (*bhāvanākāra*).

Cultivating calm abiding and insight again and again, one resolves upon the coarseness and tranquility as they were previously investigated; this is the attention consisting of resolution (*adhimokṣika*).
Through the practice of that, the attention accompanied by the path of abandonment for the first time is the attention of seclusion (*prāvivekya*).

Because he has abandoned the highest degree of the afflictions and because the functional rigidity (*dauṣṭhulya*) associated with them has been removed, that yogi from then on delights in abandonment and perceives the benefits of abandonment. Touched by the joy and bliss of limited seclusion,
he from time to time gladdens his mind with an inspiring mental attention, precisely for the sake of pacifying lethargy, drowsiness, and restlessness.
This is the attention that gathers delight (*ratisaṃgrāhaka*).

For one who is thus correctly applied, because he is supported by the application to the side of the wholesome (*kuśalapakṣa*), when the outbursts of the afflictions belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) do not manifest, there occurs an examination by means of mental attention toward auspicious signs conducive to their arising, for the purpose of discerning whether they have been abandoned or not yet abandoned; this is the attention of investigation (*mīmāṃsāmanaskāra*).

For one who thus cultivates the counteragent through investigation, there arises—by means of temporary application—the mental engagement of the counteragent that has reached the culmination of the preliminary practice for the first dhyāna, leading to dissociation from all afflictions belonging to the desire realm;
this is called "the culmination of the application.
Immediately following that, there arises that which is associated with the actual first dhyāna, which is "the fruit of the culmination of the application."
Therein, having thoroughly understood through the [meditation] characterized by discernment what is to be abandoned and what is to be attained, one directs the mind toward abandonment and attainment.
Through the [meditation] consisting of resolute conviction, one undertakes the correct application for that purpose.
Through the [meditation] characterized by seclusion, one abandons the intense afflictions.
By means of the [attention] that gathers delight, one abandons the middling type of affliction;
by means of the [attention] that investigates, one establishes the mind in the state of being free from pride regarding attainment;
by means of the [attention] culminating in application, one abandons the mild type of affliction.
Through the fruit of the culmination of application (*prayoganiṣṭhāphala*), one experiences the fruit of cultivation (*bhāvanāphala*) of these well-cultivated mental attentions (*manaskāra*).

Just as there are seven mental attentions for the attainment of the first dhyāna, so too should they be applied accordingly up to the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

Furthermore, the characteristic of coarseness (*audārikalakṣaṇa*) in all lower stages, up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), should be understood briefly as twofold: by way of dwelling in greater suffering and by way of dwelling in lack of tranquility.
And the state of having a shorter lifespan should be understood as the opposite of that; the characteristic of tranquility belongs to the higher stages.
(Abhidh-s-bh 81) The determination of the degrees of the dhyānas is due to their being cultivated as weak, medium, or intense;
thus, the fruit of each dhyāna is rebirth in three ways.
For example, there are the Brahmakāyikas, the Brahmapurohitas, the Mahābrahmans, and so forth, as previously described.
However, in the formless realms (ārūpya), because it is impossible for there to be a spatial arrangement of distinct celestial palaces, such a classification of rebirth is not established.

Nevertheless, even among those [beings], there exists a distinction of high and low at the time of rebirth—due to the differences in lifespan and other factors—based on whether their cultivation was weak, middling, or intense.
And there is inferiority or excellence according to the distinction of being predominantly afflicted or non-afflicted.

The establishment of designations refers to the names of the meditative absorptions (samādhis) categorized within the fourth dhyāna— names that are innumerable and inconceivable. For instance, however many meditative absorptions comprised within the first dhyāna the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and the Bodhisattvas who have attained great power enter,
even the names of those absorptions are unknown to Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
And from where would they know their number, or how could they attain them?
As it is stated in the *Prajñāpāramitā*: "A hundred samādhis have been accomplished.
Likewise, it is so in those various other Mahāyāna sūtras as well.
How is it [purified]?

The meditative absorptions (dhyāna) and formless attainments (ārūpya) of the ultimate limit (prāntakoṭika) are called "purity" because they lead to the excellence of functional flexibility through the attainment of these states at will for the sake of producing extraordinary qualities (vaiśeṣikaguṇa).

The supramundane path on the path of cultivation consists of the eight subsequent knowledges (*anvaya-jñāna*) regarding suffering and the other [truths], as they were described in the context of the path of seeing.
The meditative concentration associated with these is comprised within the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), the first dhyāna, up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

The sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) should be understood as exclusively mundane, because its mental activity is not fully clear due to the indistinctness of perception, and because it cannot serve as a support for the noble path, which functions with supreme clarity.
For this very reason, because perception (*saṃjñā*) is dull therein, it is called "signless" (*animitta*) in the sense that the object is made signless.
But how is it known that the Noble Path does not exist in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*)?
Because it was said by the Blessed One: "As long as there is attainment through perception (*saṃjñā-samāpatti*), so long is there penetration to full knowledge (*ājñā-prativedha*)."
The attainment of cessation is supramundane because it is acquired subsequent to the noble path;
it is "elicited" among humans, which means it is produced for the first time there.
The manifestation [of a previously produced attainment] occurs later either among humans or upon being reborn in that very same life in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
How can an noble disciple (*ārya-śrāvaka*) who has attained the formless attainments (*ārūpya-lābhin*) and is free from passion for the form realm be reborn in the form realm?
It is not necessarily the case that one who is free from passion for the form realm must enter the formless attainments.

Therefore, in this regard, there is a fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika): Is everyone who is free from passion for the realm of form one who has attained the peaceful liberation of the formless realm?
Or is everyone who has attained the peaceful liberation of the formless realm one who is free from passion for the realm of form? (Abhidh-s-bh 82)
The first alternative: one who, relying on the *anāgamya* stage, is free from passion for the realm of form (*rūpa-vītarāga*).

The second alternative: a noble one (*ārya*) who has attained the fourth dhyāna and does not seek rebirth in the noble realms, having set aside the path of abandonment (*prahāṇa-mārga*), relies upon the path of distinction (*viśeṣa-mārga*) to attain the peaceful liberations (*śānta-vimokṣa*) of the formless realm.
The third alternative: that same person, seeking dispassion (*vairāgya*), relies upon the path of abandonment to attain the peaceful liberations of the formless realm.

The fourth [alternative] is: setting aside these modes, why does it not manifest for those born in the formless realms? Because the Noble Ones, desiring to dwell in a peaceful abiding, bring this [attainment] forth and manifest it after having achieved it among human beings.

However, those born in the formless realms dwell, without any effort at all, in the most peaceful liberations that are the result of maturation; therefore, they do not undertake further effort for the sake of bringing those [liberations] into manifestation.

The path— whether weak, medium, or intense— is further divided into three types each, such as the weak-weak and so forth, and is thus established as having nine types, in order to indicate the gradual abandonment of those [afflictions] to be eliminated through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
But what is the reason that an intense affliction is abandoned by a weak-weak path?

For that [craving], being excessively characterized by a failure of shame (*hrī*) and a lack of modesty (*apatrāpya*), manifests within the continuum of one who is utterly shameless; moreover, it is easily observed and easy to distinguish. Therefore, like a gross stain, it is removed even by a slight counteragent (*pratipakṣa*).

However, this other [affliction], which is difficult to distinguish and manifests as something subtle and latent within the continuum—the extremely mild affliction (*mṛdumṛdu-kleśa*)—is like a fine stain and is removed only by a great power of the counteragent.
Thus, it should be understood that the classification of the types of counteragents is established by way of the inversion of the types of their opposites (*vipakṣa*).

The path of application (prayogamārga) is that path, when cultivated, by which the basis (āśraya) is gradually transformed through the removal of the factor of depravity (dauṣṭhulyāṅga) belonging to each respective category of afflictions—beginning with the highest-of-the-high (adhimātrādhimātra) and so forth; this is called the path of application within the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).

But that [path] by which, immediately following [the preparatory path], the basis (āśraya) is transformed into one free from that corruption (dauṣṭulya)—due to the removal of the remaining corruption belonging to that category of afflictions and their side—this is the path of immediate succession (ānantaryamārga).
The path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) is that by which one personally experiences the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*).

The special path (*viśeṣamārga*) consists of those paths of preparation (*prayogamārga*), uninterrupted paths (*ānantaryamārga*), and paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) belonging to one who effects the abandonment of the remaining afflictions subsequent to that.

Another formulation is this: the "special path" (viśeṣamārga) is the path of one who, setting aside the preparatory application for the abandonment of afflictions, contemplates the teachings such as the Sūtras;
or, it is the path of one who dwells in the contemplation of the teachings previously contemplated and realized; or, it is the path of one who enters another meditative attainment;
or again, it is the path of one who brings forth special qualities such as the superknowledges (abhijñā), or dwells by means of them.
Having thus explained the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) in detail, the cultivation of the path (mārgabhāvanā) is now described as a related topic.
There are four kinds of cultivation of the path with respect to the right efforts (samyakprahāṇa), as appropriate:
therein, cultivation for the sake of acquisition is "cultivation of acquisition" (pratilambhabhāvanā).
Because of the acquisition of wholesome dharmas through that [practice],
cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is itself the act of cultivation; it is "cultivation as practice" because of the repeated exercise of the wholesome dharmas already acquired.
Cultivation for expulsion is "expulsion cultivation," because it expels unwholesome dharmas from the state of their active manifestation;
cultivation of the antidote is "antidote cultivation."
Because it brings about the state of non-arising for unwholesome dharmas that have not yet arisen.

Another formulation: when the path arises, it deposits its own latent predisposition (*vāsanā*); that predisposition is "cultivation through acquisition" (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*), because from it there follows an even more intense attainment of subsequent [moments].
The actual manifestation of this very path is "cultivation through practice" (*abhiniṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*).
Because it brings about the cessation of the dysfunctions (*dauṣṭhulya*) that are its own adversaries, it is the cultivation of expulsion (*nirdhāvana-bhāvanā*).
Because the basis (*āśraya*) has been transformed, the establishment [of those factors] in a state of non-arising in the future is the cultivation of the antidote (*pratipakṣa-bhāvanā*).
Furthermore, the fourfold classification of the antidote, beginning with revulsion (*vidūṣaṇa*), should be understood.

In this context, the counteragent of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇā-pratipakṣa*) is the vision of the defects (*ādīnava*) in contaminated conditioned phenomena (*sāsrava-saṃskāra*), because it reviles the aggregates of clinging (*upādāna-skandha*) through such aspects as being like a disease or an abscess.
The counteragent of abandonment (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*) consists of the paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) and the uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*).

The path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) is the counteragent of support (*ādhārapratipakṣa*), because by means of it one maintains the attainment of abandonment through the elimination of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
The counteragent of distancing is the path subsequent to that,
because by means of it, the previously abandoned afflictions are rendered distant.

Furthermore, the path is established as being of eleven kinds through its divisions, such as the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣya*). That is to say, there is the path of examining the object (*vastu*), which consists of the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*);
for, by means of these, one first examines the objects of the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena through aspects such as the foul (*aśubha*) and so forth.

The path of exertion consists of the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*), because through them one initiates vigor for the sake of abandoning obscurations after having examined all objects. The path of preparation for meditative concentration (*samādhi*) consists of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).

Likewise, for one whose obscurations have not yet been purified, the path of application for clear realization consists of the faculties (*indriya*), because through these— namely, the gateways of zeal, energy, mind, and investigation— one brings about the pliancy (*karmanyatā*) of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

For one who has thus performed the preparatory work for concentration, [the path] consists of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), such as "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and those above it, because they serve as the dominant conditions (*adhipati*) for the full attainment of the Noble Path.

The path conjoined with clear realization consists of the powers (*balāni*), because for one who has attained sovereignty, there immediately follows the application of patience and the supreme mundane dharmas (*kṣāntyagradharma*), which are not overcome by their opposites such as lack of faith, for the sake of penetrating the truths.
The path of clear realization consists of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅgāni*).
Therefore, because of the direct realization of reality within oneself from the very beginning,

the Noble Eightfold Path is the path of purification and deliverance; for beyond that, by means of it, one proceeds toward purification through the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation.
For this very reason, the sequence of these factors conducive to awakening (bodhipakṣa) should be understood as follows:
the path, distinguished by its basis and faculties, consists of four modes of progress (pratipad).

Among them, the difficult mode of progress is based on the preparatory stage (anāgamya) and the formless realms (ārūpya), respectively, due to the deficiency of either calm abiding (śamatha) or insight (vipaśyanā).
The [attainment] based on the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) is pleasant because it proceeds through the union of the two [tranquility and insight].
For those of dull faculties, there is slow direct knowledge (dhandhābhijñā) regarding both of these bases—whether they are painful or pleasant.
For those of sharp faculties, there is swift direct knowledge (kṣiprābhijñā) regarding those very same two.
The path that purifies the three trainings consists of the four bases of dharma.

Among these, non-covetousness and non-malice are the purification of the training in higher ethics (*adhiśīla*), because one does not violate the precepts of training by way of being free from attachment and aversion.
Through right mindfulness, there is the purification of the training in higher mind,
because when the object of focus is not forgotten, the mind becomes concentrated.
Through right concentration, there is the purification of the training in higher wisdom.
Because one who possesses a concentrated mind knows things as they truly are.
The path that brings forth all virtues is calm abiding and insight,
because from them all mundane and supramundane virtues are accomplished.
The path that subsumes the path consists of the three faculties.
In this regard, the path of preparation and the path of seeing are subsumed under the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*);

the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is subsumed under the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*); and the path of completion (*niṣṭhāmārga*) is subsumed under the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).

Furthermore, the establishment of the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣya-dharma) should be understood through five aspects: by way of their object (ālambana), their intrinsic nature (svabhāva), their companions (sahāya), their cultivation (bhāvanā), and the fruit of their cultivation (bhāvanā-phala).
In that regard, the objects of the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are, in their respective order, the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena (*dharma*).
For what purpose, then, are these established as such objects?
Because those whose cognitions are perverted—

Since ordinary people (*bāla*), for the most part, depend upon the body endowed with sense faculties and, while experiencing pleasure and so forth, conceptualize that they are characterized by perception and are thus afflicted or purified by self-attachment and so on, as well as by faith and so on— it is for the sake of correctly examining the characteristics of those objects from the very beginning that the fourfold establishment of the objective supports (*ālambana*) should be understood.
By their intrinsic nature, they are wisdom and mindfulness, respectively,
because of the mention of the contemplation of the body and so forth, and because of the mention of the foundations of mindfulness.
In terms of association, the mind and mental factors are conjoined with those two.
Cultivation is the contemplation of the body and so forth within the body and so forth, internally, externally, and both internally and externally.
In that regard, the internal body consists of the faculties of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body,
because they are comprised within the internal sense bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*) and are reckoned as belonging to sentient beings (*sattvasaṃkhyāta*).
The external body consists of external forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.
Because they are comprised within the external sense bases (*bāhyāyatana*) and because they are reckoned as non-sentient (*asattvasaṃkhyāta*).

The internal-external body consists of the sense bases such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, which are connected to the sense bases of the eye and so on and serve as the physical supports for the faculties;
this is because they are reckoned as sentient (*sattvasaṃkhyāta*) and because they are comprised within the external sense bases.
And the internal material sense-bases belonging to another's continuum constitute the internal-external body,
having taken as authoritative both the establishment of the sense-bases and the establishment of the continuum.
Contemplation of the body as the body through its similarity is "contemplation of the body within the body" (*kāye kāyānupaśyanā*),
because one determines the natural image of the body by following the observation of the conceptual reflection-body.

Internal feelings and so forth arise based on the internal body, either by having the eye and other [senses] as their object or by arising from their own basis. External feelings and so forth arise based on the external body,
either by having form and other [objects] as their object or by arising from another's basis.
Internal-external feelings and so forth arise based on the internal-external body,
either by having as their object external bases belonging to one's own continuum or by having as their object internal bases belonging to another's continuum.

Languor of the mind (*cetaso līnatvam*) consists of self-contempt regarding the attainment of excellence; despondency (*viṣāda*) is weariness due to excessive outflow; exhaustion (*parisrava-parikheda*) is the inability to endure the oppression caused by disturbances such as gadflies and mosquitoes; and contentment with a mere trifle (*alpamātra-saṃtuṣṭi*) is the refusal [to strive further], thinking, "Enough for me with that much of the side of virtue."

Remorse for an offense (*āpattivipratisāra*) is the regret following a transgression of the training rules by one who acts without clear comprehension during activities such as going out and returning.

Abandoning the burden (*nikṣiptadhuratā*) is the failure to bring to completion the application to the side of wholesome qualities, as originally undertaken, due to the fault of negligence (*pramāda*).
The fruit of the applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) is, respectively, the eradication of the perversions of purity, pleasure, permanence, and self:
through the cultivation of the foul (aśubha),
and through the knowledge that whatever is felt here is suffering.
This is because consciousness is understood to be different at every moment due to distinctions such as its basis and its object,
and because one examines it as being merely phenomena of affliction and purification that are devoid of functional activity.
Furthermore, the result of these [foundations of mindfulness] is, respectively, the entry into the Four Truths.
One enters into the Truth of Suffering by means of the foundation of mindfulness of the body,
because the body is characterized by *dauṣṭhulya* (corruption), which has the nature of the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*).
For in this way, the pliancy (*prasrabdhi*) which serves as its antidote arises specifically within the body itself.
One enters into the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*) by means of the application of mindfulness to feelings (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*),
because craving for conjunction and so forth has as its basis feelings such as pleasure and the like.

Through the application of mindfulness to the mind, one enters the truth of cessation; for one who perceives that there is no self and that it will not be mere consciousness alone, there is no fear of nirvana due to the absence of the apprehension of the annihilation of a self.
Through the application of mindfulness to phenomena, one enters the truth of the path.
Because one cultivates the qualities that serve as antidotes in order to abandon the qualities that are their opposites;
furthermore, the fruit of these [applications of mindfulness] should be understood as the disjunction from body, sensation, mind, and phenomena respectively,
since by cultivating them, the functional rigidity (dauṣṭhulya) associated with the side of the body and so forth is removed.

Regarding the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the object of the first is the unarisen adverse factor (*vipakṣa*), because through it one generates the desire for the non-arising of unarisen evil and unwholesome states. For the second, the object is the arisen adverse factor.
The antidote for the third [hindrance] is that which has not yet arisen;
the object for the fourth is that which has already arisen—this should be applied according to the Sūtra.
By means of the phrases beginning with "he generates desire," the cultivation of vigor together with its basis is elucidated.
In this context, desire (*chanda*) is the basis,
because exertion (*udyoga*) is preceded by it.

When one cultivates the mere antidote with an object that is independent [of other factors] through mental attention (*manaskāra*) upon the signs (*nimitta*) of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and so forth, then one is said to "exert oneself" (*vyāyacchate*).
When, upon the arising of the secondary affliction of dullness (*laya*), one uplifts the mind through mental orientations such as those conducive to clarity (*prasadanīya*) in order to remove it;

and when, upon the arising of the secondary affliction of restlessness (*auddhatya*), one holds the mind by means of withdrawal (*pratyāsaṃkṣepa*); at that time, it is said that "one exerts vigor" (*vīryam ārabhate*).

For this very reason, immediately following [the mention of vigor], he says "one uplifts the mind and exerts oneself" (*cittaṃ pragṛhṇāti pradadhāti*) in order to demonstrate the means for removing dullness and restlessness.

The fruit of the first and second right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) is the abandonment of all adverse factors (*vipakṣa*) without remainder, because by means of those two, one abandons— respectively as they arise— the evil, unwholesome states that have arisen and those that have not yet arisen.
The fruit of the third is the acquisition of the counteragent (*pratipakṣa*).
Because of that, there is the arising of unarisen wholesome dharmas;
for the fourth, there is the increase of the antidote, because of that, there is the production of the expansion of arisen wholesome dharmas.

The objective support for the bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) refers to the tasks to be performed, such as the supernormal powers (ṛddhi) and so forth, by means of perfected meditative concentration (samādhi).

Concentration through desire (*chanda-samādhi*) is that which, having relied upon devoted application (*satkṛtya-prayoga*), touches one-pointedness of mind; for "devoted application" is so called because it is an application with intense desire and intense respect. Concentration through vigor (*vīrya-samādhi*) is that which, having relied upon continuous application (*sātatyaprayoga*), touches one-pointedness of mind.
That is called vigor which applies itself constantly and never at any time fails to apply.

Concentration of mind (*cittasamādhi*) is that which, by virtue of having relied upon the cultivation of concentration in previous lives, results in the mind’s natural transformation toward concentration because its seeds have been fully nourished; thus it touches upon one-pointedness of mind.

Furthermore, it should be understood that the instruction beginning with "he generates desire for the cultivation of the right abandonments" is intended solely to illustrate the accomplishment of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
Here, the sequence of the text should be understood as: "he exerts the mind" and "he uplifts the mind."

In this context, concentration of mind (*cittasamādhi*) means that by applying the mind, one touches [the object]; the meaning is that by individually holding, calming, and withdrawing the very mind within the mind, one attains it.
Concentration of investigation (*mīmāṃsāsamādhi*) means that by exerting the mind; the meaning is that one uplifts the mind by way of the gateway of insight into phenomena (*dharmavipaśyanā*).
Cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is the repeated practice of the eight formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*), beginning with zeal (*chanda*).
Furthermore, these eight formative forces of abandonment are divided into four groups, as follows: those consisting of exertion, namely zeal, effort, and faith.
In this context, zeal (*chanda*) is the basis of exertion (*vyāyāma*),
while faith (*śraddhā*) is the cause of zeal.
For it is one who has a desire for something that exerts effort for the sake of attaining it.
And there can be no longing for that [object] without a firm conviction regarding its existence and so forth.
The supportive factor is pliancy (*prasrabdhi*),
because it provides assistance to both body and mind.
The [application] based on binding consists in mindfulness and clear comprehension, because the mind abides one-pointedly through the non-forgetting of the object,
and because there is discernment when there is negligence, respectively.
The counteractive [factors] are volition and equanimity;

because of the abandonment of sinking and excitement produced by the formative forces of mental restraint and exertion, and because of the imitation of the signs of shamatha and so forth that are free from secondary afflictions.
The cause of contraction is sinking, which occurs through the gateway of laziness for one who is devoid of vipaśyanā.

The cause of distraction is the mental upliftment (*sampragraha*) characterized by agitation in one who is devoid of the perception of the foul; contraction (*saṃkṣepa*) is the inward shrinking characterized by the sign of torpor (*styāna*);
and distraction (*vikṣepa*) is the dispersal toward sense objects characterized by the pursuit of the sign of the beautiful (*śubhanimitta*).
Insight into phenomena (*dharmavipaśyanā*) relies upon the sign of analytical observation (*pratyavekṣaṇānimitta*), which is a cultivation conducive to withdrawal;
it is the analytical observation of the substantial entities of hair and so forth as being impure, which is conducive to non-distraction;
and it is the perception of light (*ālokasaṃjñā*), which is conducive to both.

And this was said by the Blessed One with reference to these [states] in their proper order: "My zeal shall not be too slack, nor too over-exerted; it shall not be withdrawn within, nor distracted outwardly."
Thereafter, one will possess the perception of the east and the perception of above and below;
with an open and unobstructed mind, one will cultivate a mind accompanied by radiance, and my mind will not be subject to darkness.
This is the fruit, because it accomplishes qualities such as supernormal powers (ṛddhi) according to one's wish.
The four noble truths are the objective support for the faculties, because they take on those aspects by being comprised within the preparatory application for the clear realization of the truths.
The fruit is the arising of the path of seeing after a short period of time due to that predominance, and at that very same time, the continuum's possession of the levels conducive to penetration.
The objects of focus and so forth for the powers are the same as those for the faculties.
However, there is a distinction regarding the fruit.

For it has been stated that these [factors] additionally involve the removal (*nirlekha*) of their opposites, such as lack of faith (*āśraddhya*) and so forth; for this very reason, although they are equal in terms of their object (*ālambana*), intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and other qualities, they constitute a distinct category among the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣa*) due to a specific excellence in their purpose.
The object of the limbs of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*) is the four noble truths as they truly are; the ultimate meaning is that this is the object of purification.
The intrinsic nature consists of seven factors, beginning with mindfulness.
Among these, mindfulness is the factor of support.

Investigation of phenomena (*dharmavicaya*) is the limb of essential nature, because it has the characteristic of enlightenment (*saṃbodhi*), due to the verbal expression of all wholesome qualities by one whose mindfulness is present.
Vigor is the limb of departure, because by means of it one proceeds as far as the goal can be reached;
joy is the limb of benefit.
Because it nourishes the continuum through that [joy],
pliancy (*prasrabdhi*), concentration (*samādhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are the factors of non-affliction;
therein, one is not afflicted by means of pliancy.
Because of the flowing out of corruption by that [wisdom],
one is not defiled in meditative concentration;
for one established therein, there occurs a transformation of the basis.
Equanimity is undefiled because its intrinsic nature consists in a state free from covetousness and dejection.

By these four phrases— beginning with "one cultivates the mindfulness factor of enlightenment based on seclusion"— the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment, which have the four truths as their respective objects, is elucidated.

For instance, for one who takes suffering as an object by way of its aspect of suffering, because of the seeking of detachment from it, that object of suffering is said to be "based on detachment. For one who takes the origin of suffering—characterized by craving—as an object by way of its aspect of the origin of suffering, because of the seeking of dispassion toward it, that object is "based on dispassion.
For one who takes the cessation of suffering as an object by way of its aspect of the cessation of suffering, because of the seeking of its realization, that object is "based on cessation."
The practice leading to the cessation of suffering is called relinquishment (*vyavasarga*),
because by means of it, suffering is cast off.
For one who takes that as an object in such a manner, because of the pursuit of its cultivation, that object is said to have been transformed into relinquishment.
The fruit is the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing,
because the factors of enlightenment have the nature of the path of seeing.
The object of the path-factors is the very suchness (*yathābhūtatā*) of the truths as they were seen, subsequent to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) consists of the eight factors beginning with right view.
Among these, right view is the factor of discernment (*paricchedāṅga*).
Right intention is the limb for communicating to others because, through it, one determines reality according to one's own experience; for,
having established it according to one's realization, one brings forth speech.

Right speech, right action, and right livelihood are the factors for inspiring confidence in others, because by means of them, others sequentially ascertain the purity of the view and so forth of the practitioner who has attained realization.
Among these, through right speech— by means of answering questions and determining discussions in accordance with his realization— the purity of his vision is made known.

Purity of ethical discipline (*śīla-viśuddhi*) consists in the perfection of conduct through right action (*samyak-karmānta*) in advancing, retreating, and so forth; purity of livelihood (*ājīva-viśuddhi*) consists in the seeking of robes and other requisites according to permission and in accordance with the Dharma through right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*).
Right effort (*samyag-vyāyāma*) is the limb for purifying the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), because by means of it, all fetters (*saṃyojana*) are abandoned without remainder.
Right mindfulness is the limb for purifying the obscurations of the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*),
because through it, by not losing sight of the signs of right tranquility (*samatha*) and so forth, there is no opportunity for secondary afflictions such as lethargy (*laya*) to arise.
Right concentration is the limb for purifying the obscurations to the distinguished qualities (*vaiśeṣikaguṇa*).
Because it brings about qualities such as the superknowledges (*abhijñā*),
cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is like the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*); for example, "he cultivates right view based on seclusion," and so forth.
And the meaning of those words is to be understood in accordance with what has been previously explained.

The explanation of the meaning of the "practices" (*pratipad*) and the "bases of the Dharma" (*dharmapada*) should be understood as previously stated. The practice that is difficult (*duḥkhā pratipad*) relies respectively on the *anāgamya*, the formless realms (*ārūpya*), and is characterized by a deficiency in either calm (*śamatha*) or insight (*vipaśyanā*). The practice that is easy (*sukhā*) relies on the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) because it proceeds with both [calm and insight] joined together (*yuganaddha*). The "slow superknowledge" (*dhandhābhijñā*) belongs to those with dull faculties (*mṛdvindriya*) who rely on either of these two—the difficult or the easy practice. The "quick superknowledge" (*kṣiprābhijñā*) belongs to those with sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*) who rely on those same two.
Śamatha is the ninefold abiding of the mind.
Among these, *sthāpanā* (placement) is the binding of the mind internally by withdrawing it from external objects and bringing about non-distraction.

*Saṃsthāpanā* (continuous placement) is the further contraction of that very mind—which was initially bound, yet remains restless and coarse—by means of continuity and refinement upon that same object.
The re-collection (*pratisaṃharaṇa*) of that mind which has been distracted outwardly due to the loss of mindfulness is "establishment" (*avasthāpanā*).

It is the application of established mindfulness so that, from the very beginning, that mind does not wander outwardly. It is "taming" (*damana*), which is the non-extension of the mind by taking as predominant the perception of the defects (*ādīnava-saṃjñā*) in forms and other objects that are previously signs of distraction.

*Śamana* (calming) is the non-extension [of the mind] by seeing the disadvantage in discursive thoughts (*vitarka*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) that cause agitation of the mind. *Vyupaśamana* (quelling) is the non-endurance of the occurrence of discursive thoughts and so forth when they arise due to a lapse of mindfulness. *Ekotīkaraṇa* (making one-pointed) is the stabilization of a continuous flow of samādhi that is flawless and uninterrupted through volitional effort (*abhisaṃskāra*).
Concentration (*samādhāna*) is the proceeding of the flow of mental concentration without distraction, through non-effort and spontaneity due to thorough cultivation.

Vipaśyanā is, for example, that which discriminates phenomena, and so forth. In that regard, one discriminates by way of the full extent of existence (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) the object for purifying conduct, the object for skillfulness, or the object for purifying afflictions; and one thoroughly discriminates by way of the mode of existence (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*).
By means of conceptual mental attention accompanied by wisdom, he forms a mental image and reflects upon it; investigating and scrutinizing it, he enters into thorough examination.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "there are four paths based on calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*)," this refers to the instruction on the four paths.
Among them, the first, having attained calm abiding, settles the mind while sitting down itself and brings it to concentration;

however, because he has not yet attained insight, he relies upon that concentration and, while remaining seated, subsequently investigates those phenomena and so forth, up to the point of thorough examination.
The second [type] should be understood as the opposite. The third obtains neither and applies itself to both. How so?
By means of grasping what has been heard, one applies oneself to non-distraction, and based on that, to calm abiding;
in the fourth [case], it is because of the attainment of both.

The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) is that faculty which exists during the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*) as comprised by the levels conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), and during the fifteen mental moments of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*);
namely, the faculty of mind (*manaindriya*) and the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*).

Depending on the basis, such as the *anāgamya* stage and so forth, it consists of whichever one among the faculties of pleasure (*sukha*), mental ease (*saumanasya*), mental distress (*daurmanasya*), or equanimity (*upekṣā*) is possible. Furthermore, the faculty of mental distress (*daurmanasyendriya*) should be understood as being comprised of the longing for higher liberations following the stages conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) at the time of preparatory practice (*prayoga*). Because these ten types of faculties function toward the full knowledge of a reality not previously known, they are called the "faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown'" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*).

These same ten faculties, from the sixteenth moment of mind on the path of seeing up to the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*), are called the faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*) within this path of training (*śaikṣamārga*),
because there is no further object of knowledge to be previously unknown.

Furthermore, these same nine faculties— excluding the faculty of mental distress (*daurmanasyendriya*)— are called the faculty of "one who has already known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) on the path of no-more-training (*aśaikṣamārga*).
This is because it is the faculty of one who has already realized [the truth], that is, an arhat.
This will also be explained in the context of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*):
when the path belonging to a higher stage is being cultivated through its manifestation, the roots of virtue belonging to lower stages— even if not currently manifest— also undergo cultivation.
Because they have attained mastery over them;
furthermore, mastery should be understood as the power gained through the manifestation of intense application.
The path of culmination is for the sake of the complete subsiding of all forms of functional rigidity; such is the detailed explanation.
In that regard, there are twenty-four types of all-pervasive functional rigidity (*dauṣṭhulya*).

They are as follows: the pervasive functional rigidity of verbal expression, which consists of the latencies (*vāsanā*) of attachment to the names of all phenomena such as the eye and so forth, residing within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), persisting from beginningless time;
this is what is called the "latency of conceptual proliferation" (*prapañcavāsanā*).
Since phenomena such as the eye and so forth proceed again and again accompanied by attachment to their names,
the "corruption of experience" (*veditadauṣṭhulya*) is the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of tainted feelings (*sāsrava-vedanā*).
The "corruption of afflictions" (*kleśadauṣṭhulya*) is the underlying tendency (*anuśaya*) of the afflictions.
The depravity of action (*karmadauṣṭhulya*) is the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of contaminated actions (*sāsrava-karma*).
The depravity of maturation (*vipākadauṣṭhulya*) is the lack of functional flexibility (*akarmaṇyatā*) resulting from maturation.
