The depravity of the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇadauṣṭhulya*) is the intensity and protracted duration of the afflictions.

The depravity of the obstruction of karma (*karmāvaraṇadauṣṭhulya*) is the state of being shrouded by karmas that obstruct the path, such as the immediate retributions (*ānantarya*). The depravity of the obstruction of maturation (*vipākāvaraṇadauṣṭhulya*) is the acquisition of a self-existence, such as that of a hell-being, which is incompatible with the clear realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*). The depravity of the hindrances (*nivaraṇadauṣṭhulya*) is the state of being overwhelmed by sensual desire and other factors that obstruct application to the side of the wholesome (*kuśalapakṣa*).

The corruption of discursive thought (*vitarka*) is the state of being overwhelmed by thoughts of sensual desire and the like, which act as obstacles to delighting in the life of renunciation (*pravrajyā*). The corruption of food is the unsuitability for spiritual practice (*prayoga*) caused by eating either too little or too much. The corruption of sexual intercourse is the affliction of body and mind produced by the union of two persons.

The corruption of dreams is the dullness of the physical basis caused by torpor. The corruption of disease is the lack of well-being caused by an imbalance of the bodily elements. The corruption of old age is the lack of mastery caused by the transformation of the primary elements.
The corruption of death is the agitation of all the sense-faculties in one who is dying.
The corruption of exhaustion is the aching of the limbs caused by excessive travel and the like.
The firm corruption consists of these very same things, such as the corruption of verbal expression and so forth, as they occur, in those who do not possess parinirvāṇa.
The gross, medium, and subtle dysfunctions (*dauṣṭhulya*) should be understood as belonging respectively to the realms of desire, form, and formlessness.
The dysfunction that is the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa-dauṣṭhulya*) is the adversary to the enlightenment of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
The depravity that is an obstacle to meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) is the adversary to the realization of the nine successive attainments;
the depravity that is an obstacle to the knowable (*jñeya*) is the adversary to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
Thus, the path of culmination (*niṣṭhāmārga*) consists in the cessation of all these depravities according to their respective applications.

As it has been said: "Through the fulfillment of his liberation of mind (*cetovimukti*), through the fulfillment of his liberation by wisdom (*prajñāvimukti*), and through the subsiding of the bodily dysfunctions (*kāyadauṣṭhulya*), he possesses mindfulness as a cause; thus his first gateway becomes well-tamed, well-guarded, well-protected, well-restrained, and well-spoken—namely, with respect to forms cognizable by the eye, and so on, up to mental phenomena cognizable by the mind."
The diamond-like samādhi (vajropama-samādhi) should be understood as the final stage of the path of abandonment within the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).
That samādhi is "uninterrupted" because its flow is not severed by the mundane path (laukika-mārga) in the interim.
It is "firm" because it is unbreakable by any obscurations (āvaraṇa), and because it is essential due to its capacity to shatter all obscurations.
It is "of a single flavor" because it is non-conceptual and of a single flavor;
it is "all-pervading" because its object is the suchness that is common to all that is knowable.
To illustrate this meaning, the Blessed One said: "For example, a great mountain of solid rock is unbroken, without fissures, without cavities, a single mass, and well-compacted."
For one who has attained the path capable of sustaining the uninterrupted revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*),
the revolution of the basis of the mind is the true nature (*dharmatā*).
It is that revolution which arises from the removal of all adventitious secondary afflictions from the mind that is luminous by nature.
The meaning is the revolution of suchness (*tathatā-parivṛtti*).

Revolution of the basis of the path (*mārgāśraya-parivṛtti*) means that previously the mundane path is transformed into supramundane status at the time of clear realization (*abhisamaya*); it is then called "with training" (*śaikṣa*) because there remains further work to be done.
However, when one has eliminated all adverse factors through detachment from the three realms, then the complete revolution of this basis, which has the nature of the path, is established.

The transformation of the basis consisting of the removal of corruption should be understood as the transformation of the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) through the departure of all latent tendencies of the afflictions.
When there is destruction, or regarding that object, whatever knowledge there is is called "knowledge of destruction" (kṣayajñāna).

This means that when the origin [of suffering] has been extinguished without remainder, the knowledge belonging to one in that state, which has the cessation of the cause as its objective support, is "knowledge of destruction."

Thus, when there is non-arising—either with respect to that object or in general—the knowledge of that [state] is the "knowledge of non-arising. This means that when the nature of the absolute non-arising of all suffering exists in the future, the knowledge which has another truth as its object, or rather, the knowledge which has the non-arising of the truth of suffering as its object, is the knowledge of non-arising.

The ten factors of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) refer to the five aggregates, beginning with the morality of one beyond training. Among these, right speech, right action, and right livelihood constitute the aggregate of morality (*śīlaskandha*) of one beyond training; right mindfulness and right concentration constitute the aggregate of concentration (*samādhiskandha*).
Right view, right intention, and right effort constitute the aggregate of wisdom;
right liberation constitutes the aggregate of liberation;
and right knowledge constitutes the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Furthermore, there are four aspects and four characteristics of the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*).

In that regard, it is called the "path" (*mārga*) because one seeks (*mārgayati*) the meaning of reality by means of it. It is called the "right method" (*nyāya*) because it serves as the antidote to afflictions that are not in accordance with reality.

It is a "path" (*pratipat*) because it leads to the non-perversion of the mind—toward the realization of reality—for one who has been perverted by misconceptions such as impermanence due to the fault of not understanding reality. It is "leading to liberation" (*nairyāṇika*) because of its departure toward the eternal, ultimate state of transcendence.
Regarding the truths of suffering and so forth, there are sixteen aspects, such as impermanence and the rest, which are both mundane and supramundane.

Among these, the mundane ones have not entered into the object of knowledge (*jñeya*); they are characterized by obscurations and conceptual construction, respectively, because of the non-penetration of suchness (*tathatā*), because of the persistence of the latent tendencies of the afflictions (*kleśānuśaya*), and because of the proliferation (*prapañca*) by way of verbal expression.
By contrast, the supramundane [cognitions], being well-entered and free from obscuration, are distinguished from mundane ones by their non-conceptual nature.
But how do these, while not conceptualizing, become entered into the objects of knowledge?
Because, abiding in these, one sees the meaning of impermanence and directly experiences it.
But one does not perceive it as "impermanent" by way of the proliferation of verbal expression;
in this same manner, it should be applied to the aspects of suffering and so forth.

(Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya 95) (The third compendium, titled "The Determination of Dharmas") Regarding the determination of dharmas, dharma consists of the twelvefold division of the word of the Buddha.

In this regard, a *sūtra* is that which is spoken in prose by way of indicating the intended meaning. But for what reason does the Tathāgata not teach that intended meaning by fully expanding upon it? He says: seeing ten advantages, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma by way of indication and establishes it easily.
For by the teachers,
having established the object to be attained in many ways, it is established concisely and without difficulty.
He teaches with ease, because he causes a great expansion of meaning to be understood through a small [amount of words],
such as when he says "he establishes" or "he thoroughly establishes," and so forth.
The listener also grasps [the teaching] easily; through reverence for the Dharma, they quickly fulfill the accumulations, because—
having understood that "this Dharma is to be realized through cultivation"— they fulfill the accumulations of faith and so forth by means of respect for that Dharma once aspiration has arisen.
One swiftly penetrates the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) because the wisdom of one who practices with such reverence has become sharp;
one attains verified clarity (avetyaprasāda) regarding the Jewels.
Through the thorough comprehension of the well-established nature of the teaching, one generates serene confidence toward the teacher and others;

and by contemplating the intended meaning with intense application, one touches the supreme dwelling in happiness in the present life, due to the attainment of a particular state of joy upon having gained that understanding.
Through the definitive resolution of discourse, he satisfies the minds of the virtuous by elucidating hidden meanings;
for this very reason, he is reckoned as a "wise man," a "wise man."
The meaning is that his fame spreads in all directions.
Both of these should be regarded as a single benefit resulting from the final realization.
The sūtra of definitive meaning is the prophecy, because it explains through the disclosure of intentional terminology.
An *udāna* is that which is uttered by one whose mind is uplifted, such as: "When these phenomena arise," and so forth.

The *nidāna* is whatever has been spoken with reference to a specific person, whether it be the laying down of a training rule together with its origin (*sotpattika-śikṣā-prajñapti*) or a discourse on the establishment of rules;
for example, "In this nidāna, in this context," and so forth in detail.
(Abhidh-s-bh 96) An *avadāna* is that which is spoken with an illustrative example; the meaning is that it clarifies and makes manifest the intended sense (*artha*).

*Vaipulya*, *vaidalya*, and *vaitulya*—these are synonyms for the Mahāyāna. Because it is endowed with seven kinds of greatness (*mahattva*), it is called the "Great Vehicle" (*mahattvayāna*). The seven kinds of greatness are as follows: (1) greatness of the objective support (*ālambana-mahattva*), because the path of the bodhisattva has as its objective support the immeasurable teachings of the Dharma found in the *Śatasāhasrikā* and other sūtras.
The greatness of practice consists in the practice of all that benefits oneself and others;
the greatness of knowledge consists in the knowledge of the selflessness of persons and phenomena;
and the greatness of vigor consists in the application of hundreds of thousands of various difficult feats throughout three great incalculable eons.
The greatness of skillful means consists in not abiding in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa.
The greatness of attainment consists in the realization of immeasurable and incalculable qualities, such as the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, and the unique qualities of a Buddha.
The greatness of activity consists in the performance of the work of a Buddha by manifesting enlightenment and so forth for as long as saṃsāra endures.
Instruction (*upadeśa*) is the exposition of the meaning of the *sūtras* and so forth by means of the unerring characteristic of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).

The *nidāna* is the Vinaya Piṭaka, which comprises the formulation of the training rules (*śikṣāprajñapti*) together with their origins; its appendages, such as the *avadānas*, should be understood as belonging to it.

The marvelous phenomena (*adbhutadharma*) are included within the Bodhisattva Sūtra Piṭaka, because they are specifically endowed with inconceivable, vast, and distinguished powers. The *upadeśa* (treatises) in both the Śrāvaka Vehicle and the Mahāyāna constitute the Abhidharma Piṭaka.

The establishment of the Sūtra Piṭaka is for the sake of counteracting the secondary affliction of doubt; it is taught through the discourses (sūtra), verses (geya), and so forth, with the purpose of cutting off the doubts—both those already arisen and those not yet arisen—of those to be trained.
The establishment of the Vinaya Piṭaka is for the sake of counteracting the secondary affliction of devotion to the two extremes;
this is because it prohibits the accumulation and enjoyment [of goods] and so forth, while permitting [the use of] garments worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold].
Furthermore, the two extremes are the extreme of devotion to the pleasure of sensual desires and the extreme of self-mortification.
The systematic presentation of the Abhidharma serves as the antidote to the secondary affliction of adhering to one's own views,
because it establishes the characteristics of phenomena in detail therein.
Furthermore, by relying on the Sūtra Piṭaka, those to be trained become proficient in the three trainings,
because these are extensively elucidated therein.
Relying on the Vinaya, they accomplish the training in higher ethics and higher mind;

for, by relying on the instruction in the path of training in the Prātimokṣa restraint, they purify their ethical conduct, and through the sequence beginning with freedom from remorse produced by that purification, they achieve concentration of the mind.
Relying on the Abhidharma, they accomplish the training in higher wisdom.
Because therein the means for the discernment of phenomena (dharmapravicaya) are taught in detail, for this reason also the establishment of the three baskets (piṭakatraya) is justified.
Furthermore, by relying on the Sūtra Piṭaka, there is the analytical understanding of the words and their meaning;
by relying on the Vinaya, there is the realization of both,
because the Vinaya is characterized by the practice of the training.
Therefore, it is called the "basis" (*padasthāna*) for the direct realization of the Dharma and its meaning, in the sense of being a support.

By relying on the Abhidharma, through the mutual determination of discussion and the enjoyment of the Dharma, there comes to be a dwelling in contact; for therein, the specific characteristics and the true nature (*dharmatā*) of phenomena are explained in many ways.
These very three baskets constitute the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma,
which were compiled by the Elder Ānanda with reference to the Śrāvaka Vehicle.
Furthermore, what is the measure of a single *dharmaskandha*? A *dharmaskandha* consists of a count of one thousand; this means its number is a thousand.
If that is so, why is it not simply called "that which has a count of a thousand"?
This is for the purpose of making known the rationale for establishing the single aggregate (*skandha*) as a thousandfold.
For in this way, through an increase starting from one, there arise the numbers ten, hundred, thousand, and so forth;
these numbers of ten and hundred should be seen as the foundational bases (*upaniṣad*) for those [higher numbers].
For example, ten hundreds make a thousand; a hundred thousands make a hundred-thousand (*śatasahasra*); and a hundred hundred-thousands make a *koṭi*.
Thus, in all subsequent numbers, one of these two numbers—ten or a hundred—is necessarily the basis for the next.
Therefore, these very [topics], when combined, are established as one aggregate of Dharma (*dharmaskandha*) consisting of one thousand [verses].
By this calculation, there are eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma, which amount to eight crores and four million.
Of what is this Dharma, comprised within the Three Baskets (piṭaka), the domain?
It means that it is the domain and object of the mental states and mental factors (citta-caitasika) consisting of those born of hearing (śrutamaya) and so forth.
In connection with this, the objects and other characteristics of the mental states and mental factors—such as those possessing an object—are established with reference to the Dharma.
In that regard, what is the object of their [cognition] concerning the Dharma?
It is the teaching of the Sūtras and so forth, which means the teaching of the Sūtras and other texts as comprised within the collections of names, phrases, and phonemes.

The aspect (*ākāra*) refers to those categories of objects such as the aggregates (*skandha*) upon which the teaching is based; it should be understood that the mind and mental factors possess those very aspects. The basis (*āśraya*) consists of the communication of others, mindfulness, and latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).

In that regard, at the time of the teaching, the basis is the communication of another, which is what is called "from the voice of another"; after that, the basis is mindfulness, because one practices by recollecting according to what was heard;
and after that, the basis is the latent impression (*vāsanā*), because it appears later through the power of the cultivation of practice even without that recollection.

As for the association (*samprayoga*), it is the mutual assistance of the mind and mental factors in their correct engagement with objects such as sūtras, by way of the aspects of meanings associated with the aggregates and so forth.
The classification of the object (*ālambana*) is fourfold, beginning with the pervasive object (*vyāpyālambana*).
Furthermore, the pervasive object is fourfold according to the distinctions of conceptual images (*savikalpapratibimba*) and so forth.
Among these, "attention consisting of resolute belief" (*adhimuktimanaskāra*) is that attention which is exclusively mundane.
The mental engagement with reality (*tattvamanaskāra*) is both supramundane and that which is subsequently attained.

It consists of two aspects: by way of the full extent of existence (*yāvadbhāvikatā*), there is the determination of all knowable things as many as there are entities among all phenomena, such as the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*);
and by way of the mode of existence (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*), it is well-known through these various modes.
For example, by way of the truths, those very aggregates, elements, and sense-fields are to be known as suffering and so forth, up to the path, according to their respective possibilities.
By way of aspects, each individual truth is to be known through four aspects; and without distinction, all are to be known through the aspect of suchness.

Alternatively, according to the section on the summaries of the Dharma (*dharmoddāna*), all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are to be known as impermanent, up to being peaceful, [which is] nirvāṇa;
or, according to the section on liberation (*vimokṣa*), they are to be known as empty, up to being signless (*animitta*).
The perfection of the task is the perfection of the basis, because for one whose basis has been transformed, there is the manifestation of objects without error.
Regarding the exposition of the mode of being as it truly is (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*), sixteen types have been stated, as well as three modes of liberation; these are mutually inclusive.
How so?
Among the sixteen aspects, two are the aspects of emptiness—the aspect of emptiness and the aspect of non-self.
Six are the aspects of wishlessness—the aspect of impermanence, the aspect of suffering, and the aspects of cause, origin, production, and condition.
Because of their lack of aspiration toward the three realms,
the remaining eight modes of signlessness [are established], since it is impossible to take the aspects of cessation and the path as signs.
The object for purifying conduct consists of the foul and so forth for those whose conduct is dominated by passion and the like,
because through it, excessive passion and other such afflictions are pacified.
The factors such as ignorance moisten the factors such as volitional formations;

for their arising is neither without cause nor from discordant causes such as Īśvara. Such knowledge is skill in dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Even though things have only [other] phenomena as their causes, a corresponding fruit arises from a corresponding cause.

For example, the knowledge that the maturation of good conduct is desirable and that of bad conduct is undesirable—such as this—is to be understood as skill in the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna-kauśalya*).
The object for the purification of afflictions, with reference to the mundane path, is the coarseness and tranquility of the lower and higher stages,
because by means of it one suppresses the outbursts of the afflictions;
with reference to the supramundane path, it is, in brief, suchness.
Vyāsa [taught] the four noble truths,
because by that [means] the underlying tendencies are eradicated.
In connection with the investigation of the teachings such as the sūtras and so forth, four reasonings are described, because those [teachings] are investigated by means of them.
In this context, the reasoning of dependence (*apekṣā-yukti*) refers to the dependence of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) upon conditions for their arising;
for example, the arising of a sprout depends upon the seed, water, and soil, and consciousness depends upon the sense faculty, the object, and mental attention (*manaskāra*), and so forth.

The principle of cause and effect is as follows: for example, the state of being the basis for visual consciousness and so forth on the part of the eye and other [faculties]; the state of being the objective support for them on the part of visible forms and so forth;
the act of cognizing visible forms and so forth by means of visual consciousness and so forth;
and the fashioning of gold and so forth by artisans such as goldsmiths, and so on.

The instruction of the thesis and so forth is that which does not contradict direct perception and other means of valid cognition regarding the object to be proven, which is comprised of the specific nature established by the reasoning of logical proof (*upapattisādhanayukti*).
The reasoning of the nature of things (*dharmatāyukti*) is, for example, burning by fire and moistening by water; such is the well-known nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
As it has been said: "The eye, though perfected, is empty of what is permanent, up to and including what belongs to a self.
Why is that? Because this is its very nature.

The investigation of names (*nāma-paryeṣaṇā*) is the analytical inquiry that because the sets of names and so forth exist only as designations (*prajñapti*), their own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not ultimately established. The investigation of things (*vastu-paryeṣaṇā*) is the discernment and examination that the aggregates and so forth are not established in the same way they are expressed by the sets of names and so forth. The investigation of the designation of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-prajñapti-paryeṣaṇā*) is the discernment that within the relationship between the signifier and the signified, there is merely the designation of intrinsic nature serving as the cause for conventional usage.
The relationship between the signifier and the signified is,
furthermore, the state of being the cause for mutual comprehension.
For instance, when one who is proficient in linguistic usage hears merely the signifier, a comprehension of its signified arises by way of memory.
Furthermore, having apprehended the denotable object,

when there is a well-established relationship such as "in the expression of that [object]," the investigation which states that the mere designation of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)— such as "eye" and so forth— becomes the cause for conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding things like jars and lumps of clay,
is called the "investigation into the designation of intrinsic nature" (*svabhāvaprajñaptiparyeṣaṇā*).

The investigation of the designation of specific qualities (*viśeṣaprajñaptiparyeṣaṇā*) is the discernment that, within the very same relationship between the designator and the designated, the causes for conventional usage consist merely in the designation of specific characteristics— such as permanence or impermanence, superiority or non-superiority, materiality or immateriality, visibility or invisibility, and so forth.
The four thorough cognitions of reality as it is are the cognitions of the non-apprehension of names and so forth, just as they were investigated.
For one engaged in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the stage of yoga (*yogabhūmi*) consists of five aspects, beginning with the basis (*ādhāra*).

Among these, the "basis" refers to the kind of extensive learning (*bāhuśrutyam*) that serves as the foundation for calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) by means of its connection to the object of focus; that is called the basis.

Furthermore, this refers to the hearing of the discourses (*sūtra*) and so forth, which have been mastered by one who has accumulated the necessary provisions (*saṃbhṛtasaṃbhāraḥ*) with a view toward the clear realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*).

The "foundation" is the appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manaskāra*) directed toward that [learning]; for by means of it, one directs the mind toward that great learning with a mental aspect that perceives the meaning without error. The "mirror" is the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) together with its signs, which takes that great learning as its object.
The meaning is that its form is a reflection that shares the same nature as the object to be known (*jñeyavastu*).
Furthermore, its status as a mirror should be understood from the fact that by means of it, the image of the object to be known is examined.

"Light" (*āloka*) refers to the knowledge of the non-apprehension of the grasped and the grasper, which is comprised within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), because it functions as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Furthermore, how does a bodhisattva, engaged in a single stage of yoga, avoid touching upon non-apprehension?

A bodhisattva who has accumulated the equipment of merit and wisdom, having emerged from incalculable eons, brings about meditative concentration by properly attending to the heard teachings in accordance with that penetration.

When his mind is thus concentrated, he contemplates the reflection of the object of knowledge; perceiving that this reflection is not other than that concentrated mind, he turns away from the notion of an external object within that reflection and focuses on its form as being merely his own mental representation.
At that time, by abiding in his own mind alone, having become one whose mind is established within, he thoroughly realizes the non-existence of any graspable object.
And then, because of the absence of the object to be grasped (*grāhya*), the subject that grasps (*grāhaka*) is also not fully established; thus, one realizes its non-existence as well.
Thereafter, one personally attains a non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) that is free from the perception of the intrinsic nature of both.
It is with reference to this very point that the Blessed One said, "seeing the mind as a reflected image," and so forth.
The basis is the transformation of the basis;
the meaning is that the basis is completely purified through the removal of functional rigidity (*dauṣṭhulya*).
This stage of yoga should be understood as being explained both in terms of its cause and its fruit.
In this regard, the explanation of the cause is given by means of the four factors beginning with the basis, while the explanation of the fruit is given by the final one.
Regarding what was said by the Elder Ānanda— “O Venerable Śāriputra, a monk endowed with five qualities receives [the teachings] lightly”—
in that sutra, it should be understood that by means of those same five qualities, the four [qualities] beginning with receiving lightly are to be applied as appropriate.
How are there four?
One who is skilled in the Dharma grasps it quickly because of his great learning, for the most part by means of distinct words and phrases.
One who is skilled in the meaning grasps much.

Because he knows the characteristics of the Abhidharma and so forth, and because he compiles extensive texts by means of the subject matter of discourses concerning the aggregates, elements, and so on;
being skilled in phonemes and proficient in etymological analysis, he grasps what has been well-learned.

Because he knows the etymologies of words and is not attached to local dialects such as "self" or "self," and because he knows how to follow conventional usage by grasping the meaning of texts without error; because he is skilled in connecting the past and the future, he does not let what has been grasped perish;
and because he knows the Buddha’s intentional meaning—that one must subsequently emerge from existence by relying on the dharmas previously grasped—he extracts the essence through realization.

In this sūtra, when it is said, "A monk who dwells in the Dharma, a monk who dwells in the Dharma," the Blessed One has demonstrated that dwelling in the Dharma occurs through the complete dwelling in hearing, reflection, and cultivation (*śruta-cintā-bhāvanā-vihāra*), and not by means of any single preliminary application (*prayoga*) alone.

In that context, those who are preoccupied with mastery, recitation, and teaching, and who are preoccupied with discursive thought (*vitarka*), are engaged solely in hearing and reflection and not in cultivation; because they abandon yoga and so forth, they are not dwellers in the Dharma.
They are thus established.

Even someone who, without having recourse to hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintā*), would be solely engaged in cultivation (*bhāvanā*), is not established as one who dwells in the Dharma (*dharma-vihārī*).

For this very reason, starting with the monk who dwells in the Dharma, and after stating in detail that "here a monk masters the Dharma—the discourses (*sūtra*), the verses (*geya*), and so forth"—it is subsequently said: "he does not abandon yoga," and so on.
It is so that it may be understood that, having relied upon hearing (*śruta*), reflection (*cintā*), and cultivation (*bhāvanā*), one dwells in the Dharma by means of both [the latter] abidings.

Through such statements as "one does not abandon yoga," the aspect consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*) is demonstrated by way of both application to meditative concentration (*samādhi-prayoga*) and lack of contentment with that application.
This is the application to meditative concentration (*samādhi-prayoga*).

Furthermore, it is shown to be twofold: that which is comprised of constant and respectful application, indicated by the phrase "he does not abandon yoga"; and that which is comprised of non-erroneous application, indicated by the phrase "he does not abandon mental attention.
Lack of contentment is shown by the phrase "he does not abandon internal mental tranquility (*śamatha*)."
Its non-abandonment should be understood as resulting from not relishing that [attainment] and from the application of further tranquility (śamatha).
For what reason is the Vaipulya called the Bodhisattva-pāramitā-piṭaka in other sūtras?
Because therein the perfections (pāramitās) are explained by way of their enumeration, up to their mutual determination.
In that regard, number is twofold:
the number of enumeration and the number of mere measure.
"The six perfections" is the number of enumeration.

Because the two paths of a bodhisattva’s worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and ultimate excellence (*niḥśreyasa*) are subsumed by three and three [perfections] respectively, there are exactly six perfections—neither more nor fewer. This enumeration consists of that alone;
the threefold prosperity consists of great wealth, great selfhood, and a great faction.
Among these, the fruit of the perfection of generosity is great wealth.
The fruit of the perfection of ethical discipline is its great nature, because through ethical discipline one attains the excellence of the physical form of a Sugata.
The fruit of the perfection of patience is its great faction.
Because through patience one attains the state of being approachable by all people.
The path to the supreme good is threefold: the means for applying oneself to the side of virtue by overcoming the afflictions,
the means for maturing sentient beings,
and the means for bringing about the realization of the qualities of a Buddha.
For without even one of these, the supreme welfare of a bodhisattva cannot be achieved.
Among them, the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā) is the means for maturing sentient beings,
because by relying upon it, one matures sentient beings through the supernormal powers (abhijñā).
Furthermore, by way of the means for non-abiding nirvāṇa, there are precisely six perfections.
For a bodhisattva must, by reversing the tendency to abide in nirvāṇa, embrace prosperity within saṃsāra;
and by reversing the tendency to abide in saṃsāra, he must remain undefiled therein.

Therefore, three are the means for attaining prosperity (*abhyudaya*), and three are the means for non-affliction (*asaṃkleśa*); these should be understood according to their respective applications following the previous sequence. Regarding the means for non-affliction, however, there is the cultivation of the antidotes through vigor (*vīrya*) and the suppression of afflictions through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
By means of wisdom, there is the total eradication of the latent tendencies of the afflictions.
"Based on the quality of benefiting all and the quality of being an antidote to the afflictions"—this is another formulation.
In that regard, by means of generosity, the bodhisattva benefits sentient beings by providing them with necessary requisites;
by means of ethical discipline, he benefits them by not causing harm, oppression, or injury.
Respectively, by not inflicting harm upon enjoyments, body, or mind,
one benefits others through patience by enduring their infliction, oppression, and injury; that is,
by enduring the destruction of one's own enjoyments and so forth caused by others.
He favors [them] with these three.
Even though one has suppressed the afflictions through vigor, one applies oneself to the side of the wholesome;
through meditative concentration, one suppresses the afflictions.
Through wisdom, one eradicates the latent tendencies;
these three should be understood as the antidotes to the afflictions.
In that regard, this is the characteristic of the perfections (*pāramitā*):
What is the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) of a bodhisattva?

It is the action of body, speech, and mind consisting in the relinquishment of all possessions by a bodhisattva who is established in the nature of a bodhisattva, relying upon the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) and preceded by a mind of compassion.

And having established it thus, the characteristic of the perfection of generosity should be understood as explained in terms of lineage (*gotra*), aspiration (*praṇidhāna*), intention (*āśaya*), object (*vastu*), and essential nature (*svabhāva*).
That is to say: the nature of a bodhisattva is the lineage;
the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*) is the aspiration.
The mental disposition (*āśaya*) is a mind preceded by compassion; the objective basis (*vastu*) is the relinquishment of all possessions;

and its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) consists of the actions of body, speech, and mind—in this manner, [the perfections] up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) are to be understood in detail.
However, this is the distinction:

it should be understood that within the perfections of ethical discipline (*śīla*), patience (*kṣānti*), and vigor (*vīrya*), "bodily, vocal, and mental action" refers respectively to the undertaking and preservation of all vows, the endurance and acceptance of all harm and suffering, and the complete accomplishment of all wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma*).

Regarding the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*), it should be stated that "in the mastery of all modes of bodily, vocal, and mental action, there is the stability of the mind in all its modes.

Regarding the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), it should be stated that "in the mastery of all modes of bodily, vocal, and mental action, there is the discernment of phenomena in all its modes.
All else is to be understood as being exactly like [the description of] generosity (*dāna*).

Furthermore, that gift which, having set out toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), conduces to omniscience, encompasses omniscience, and performs the function of omniscience, is called the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).

Moreover, these four terms should be understood respectively as: from the perspective of undertaking (*ārambha*), from the perspective of latent impression (*vāsanā*), from the perspective of the body (*kāya*), and from the perspective of natural outflow (*nisyanda*).
Among these, "from the perspective of undertaking" means that it has set out toward omniscience because whatever [merit] arises, it is dedicated (*pariṇāmanā*) therein.
Furthermore, that very same generosity perfumes the mental continuum,
whereby it conduces to omniscience in the future;
when that very same [continuum] becomes fully perfected, it then embraces omniscience through the process of accomplishing the Dharma-body.
Thereafter, by means of the outflow of the *sāmbhogika* and *nairmāṇika* bodies, he performs the activity of omniscience;
in this way, it should be understood up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

The sequence is as follows: based on the state of successive dependence, through the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), a bodhisattva—having practiced the relinquishment of all internal and external things and become indifferent to body and life—renounces even a vast mass of enjoyments and undertakes the vow of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Guarding his morality, he becomes patient through such modes as: "When reviled by others, I must not revile them in return. Thus he becomes forbearing.
Being capable of enduring cold and other such hardships, one initiates vigor by means of the application that abandons those [hindrances].
Having initiated vigor, through the attainment of the fruit of the culmination of application, one accomplishes meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
And having perfected meditative absorption, with a concentrated mind, one attains supramundane wisdom through knowledge of things as they truly are.
Furthermore, by way of being successive supports: ethical discipline is the support for generosity, and so on up to wisdom being the support for meditative concentration.
For it is the case that the generosity of one who possesses ethical discipline becomes pure.
Because one who has been favored by his generosity is not harmed through [the practice of] ethical discipline (*śīla*),

the purification of the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) should be understood as occurring through the power of ethical discipline, since the bodhisattva provides that recipient with the happiness of requisites free from any affliction.
In this way, for one who is patient, there is the purification of ethical discipline.
The purification of patience for one who has initiated vigor occurs because of not breaking the precepts despite injuries inflicted by others;
for, having entered into cyclic existence through the power of enthusiasm, one endures the suffering of the misconduct of sentient beings without difficulty.
The purification of vigor belongs to the meditator,
because of the application toward all wholesome dharmas together with bliss and mental joy;
the purification of meditative concentration belongs to one possessed of wisdom.

One perceives many kinds of phenomena internally through the increase of meditative concentration by means of tranquility (*śamatha*), because it is stated in a verse: "There is no meditative absorption for one who lacks wisdom."
Furthermore, another sequence according to coarseness should be understood:
for giving is established first as the coarsest of all;

immediately after that, among patience and the others, ethical discipline is the coarsest, and so on up to the point where meditative concentration is the coarsest among the perfections ending with wisdom.
Wisdom, however, is the most subtle; therefore, it is established as being at the very end of all.
The etymological explanation: For what reason is giving called the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*)?
Because it is great giving, faultless, and stainless, it is called the perfection of giving.
In this regard, "great giving" consists in the giving of all types of internal and external objects and in giving over a long period of time.
It is "faultless" because it is free from improper seeking and the like; it is "stainless" because of the abandonment of its opposite, stinginess.

As stated concerning the perfection of giving in the *Āryākṣayamatinirdeśasūtra*: "It is stainless because of the abandonment of the opposite along with its latent predispositions (*savāsanā-vipakṣaprahāṇāt*)."
Thus, by means of this threefold supremacy, the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā) is elucidated.
The threefold supremacy consists of: supremacy of intrinsic nature together with its cultivation, and supremacy of skillful means.
And there is the excellence of the fruit. Furthermore, cultivation is to be understood as giving for a long period of time;
in this same way, it should be understood up to the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, the faultlessness of ethical discipline and the other perfections is to be understood, as appropriate, through their being free from the superimposition of a self and so forth;
this is to be seen in the *Akṣayamati-sūtras*.
Furthermore, it is called a *pāramitā* because of its association with twelve kinds of supremacy (*paramatva*).

These twelve kinds of supremacy are as follows: (1) supremacy of magnificence (*audārya-paramatva*), because of having no desire for the prosperities of the entire world and because of being preeminent;
and (2) supremacy of extensiveness (*āyatattva-paramatva*), because of being cultivated throughout three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).

The supremacy of authority is due to being engaged in the task of performing the welfare of all sentient beings. The supremacy of inexhaustibility is because there is no ultimate exhaustion through the dedication toward great enlightenment.
The supremacy of continuity is due to the resolve for the equality of self and others, [expressed] through giving and so forth to all sentient beings.
[The supremacy of ease] is due to the fulfillment of the perfections;
for by mere rejoicing, one fulfills the perfections such as giving performed by others.
[The supremacy of mastery] is due to the fulfillment of giving and the other perfections through the *gaganagañja* samādhi and so forth.
Supreme grasping consists in being embraced by non-conceptual gnosis.
Supreme undertaking occurs at the stage of supreme patience within the level of conduct through aspiration.
Supreme attainment occurs on the first bhūmi.
The supremacy of outflow pertains to the other eight stages;
the supremacy of accomplishment pertains to the tenth stage and the stage of the Tathāgata, by means of the complete perfection of a bodhisattva and the complete perfection of a Buddha, respectively.
Furthermore, they are called *pāramitās* because they are "striven for" (*īhitā*) and "gone to" (*itā*) by the supreme ones;
that is to say, they have been practiced and attained by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, the *pāramitās* are those who have gone to the further shore (*pāraṃgatā*) of the knowable;
the meaning is that they are established in Buddhahood.
Moreover, they are called *pāramitās* because they cause others and themselves to cross over to the further shore (*param*).
The meaning is that they cause both others and themselves to cross over the ocean of suffering.
This, then, is the general etymological definition.
Furthermore, each [of these] is a gift because it removes the poverty of the giver,
or because it removes the burning [suffering] of the recipients.

Ethical discipline (*śīla*) is so called because it brings about the guarding of the doors of the senses through the restraint of the objects of the tranquil faculties; because it leads to rebirth in happy destinies through its immersion in auspicious states; and because it serves as the basis for nirvana through the sequence beginning with the absence of remorse. Patience (*kṣānti*) belongs to those who have been wounded, because it overcomes the saltiness of anger, overcomes the state of a wounded mind, and reveals security.
Furthermore, "wounded mind" (*kṣaticitta*) should be understood as the destruction or humiliation of one who has arrived after having inflicted a counter-injury upon those who have done harm.
Because their enmity has been wounded, they are "the wounded ones" (*kṣatinaḥ*); the manifestation of fearlessness toward them should be understood as the disclosure of security (*kṣema*).
It is "valor" (*vīrya*) because it is not joined with killing, aging, or decline.

In that regard, effort for the sake of abandonment consists of two right abandonments (samyakprahāṇa) directed toward the removal of unwholesome states; and effort for the sake of increase consists of two right abandonments directed toward the full realization of wholesome states.
Meditation (dhyāna) is so called because it sustains, restrains the mind, disciplines, and leads [the mind] [to its object].
In that context, *dhāraṇā* (concentration) is the fixing of the mind upon an object,
the restraining [of it] from distraction,
and the stabilization of the mind.
Discipline should be understood as the suppression of the outbursts of affliction and the leading toward the attainment of mastery,
[which arises] from knowledge not originated by others.
Wisdom (*prajñā*) arises from knowledge of oneself, knowledge of the modes [of reality], and knowledge of the excellence of qualities attained through tranquility (*śama*).
In this context, knowledge produced by others is wisdom associated with proper mental attention (*yoniśomanaskāra*) following the voice of another;
knowledge of oneself is supramundane (*lokottara*).
Knowledge of the aspects is that which is obtained subsequent to the supramundane;
knowledge for the attainment of tranquility is that which serves as the antidote to the afflictions on the path of cultivation;
and wisdom should be understood as the knowledge for the excellence of qualities, for the realization of the distinguished qualities.
Cultivation is fivefold,
ranging from that based on the substratum to that based on mastery.
Therein, that which is based on material support has four aspects:

that based on cause is the repeated practice of the perfections through the power of one's spiritual lineage (*gotra*); that based on maturation is [the practice] through the power of the excellence of one's physical existence;
and that based on aspiration is [the practice] through the power of former vows.
That which relies on the power of analytical discernment is the repeated practice of application toward the perfections by means of the power of wisdom.
The cultivation of the perfections based on mental attention is fourfold:
through the mental attention of resolute belief, for one who has resolute faith in the sūtras associated with all the perfections;
and through the mental attention of relishing, for one who has attained the perfections.
[This occurs] through relishing by way of perceiving virtues;
through the mental application of rejoicing (*anumodanā-manaskāra*), for one who rejoices in the giving and other [perfections] of all sentient beings in all world-systems;
and through the mental application of aspiration (*abhinandanā-manaskāra*), for one who aspires toward the future excellence of the perfections for oneself and for sentient beings.

The cultivation of the perfections based on intention is sixfold: by way of the insatiable intention, the expansive intention, the joyful intention, the beneficial intention, the unstained intention, and the virtuous intention.

In that regard, a bodhisattva’s insatiable intention regarding giving is such that even if a bodhisattva were to bestow world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, filled with the seven precious jewels, and likewise his own bodies as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, at every single moment; [he would still not be satisfied].
Even if one were to provide [gifts] for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges,
and just as for a single sentient being, so too for the entire realm of sentient beings who are to be matured for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment—
if one were to provide for them in this manner, the Bodhisattva’s intention for giving would still remain unsatiated.
Such an intention as this is the bodhisattva’s insatiable intention regarding giving.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva does not let such a succession of giving lapse or be interrupted for even a single moment until sitting at the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
Such an intention as this is the bodhisattva’s vast intention regarding giving.
Moreover, the bodhisattva becomes even more joyful while thus favoring those sentient beings with that gift, whereas those sentient beings, being favored by that gift, do not.
Such an intention as this is the bodhisattva’s joyful intention regarding giving:

that the bodhisattva regards those beings whom he thus assists through his gift as more beneficial to himself than he is to them, because he takes into account that they provide the support for his own unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Such an intention as this is the bodhisattva’s beneficial intention regarding giving.
Furthermore, even after having performed such vast merit consisting of giving toward sentient beings, the bodhisattva does not seek any recompense or karmic maturation;
such an intention as this is the bodhisattva’s stainless intention in the cultivation of the perfection of giving.

That a bodhisattva, even regarding the ripening of such a vast mass of giving, rejoices only for the sake of sentient beings and not for himself, and having made it common to all sentient beings, dedicates it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening—
such an intention as this is the bodhisattva’s virtuous intention in the cultivation of the perfection of generosity.
In that regard, the Bodhisattva’s insatiable intention for the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline up to the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is such that—

even if the Bodhisattva were to undergo as many bodily existences as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges, with a lifespan lasting for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges, constantly deprived of all necessities of life within a great trichiliocosm filled with fire, and yet maintain the four modes of deportment—
Conceptualizing a single moment of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), one should cultivate it up to a moment of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
By this method, one should cultivate the aggregate of ethical discipline up to the aggregate of wisdom—by means of which one awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
One should cultivate the aggregate of ethical discipline up to the aggregate of wisdom.
In this way, the bodhisattva’s intention regarding the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline is insatiable, as is his intention up to the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
Such an intention is the bodhisattva’s insatiable intention regarding the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline up to the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;

it is that the bodhisattva does not fail and does not interrupt that continuous succession of the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline up to the continuous succession of the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom until he sits upon the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
Such an intention as this is the bodhisattva’s vast intention regarding the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline up to the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva becomes even more joyful while benefiting sentient beings through that cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline up to the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom,
than those sentient beings being benefited.

Such an intention as this is the Bodhisattva’s joyful intention (*muditāśaya*) in the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) up to the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Furthermore,

that Bodhisattva regards those sentient beings whom he benefits through such cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline up to the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom as more beneficial to himself than he is to them, because they provide him with support for his unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening (*anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*).
Such an intention as this is the bodhisattva’s beneficial intention regarding the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline up to the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, having performed such vast merit consisting of the perfection of ethical discipline up to the perfection of wisdom, the bodhisattva does not seek a reward for it, nor does he seek its maturation.
Such an intention as this—extending from the perfection of ethical discipline up to the perfection of wisdom—is the bodhisattva’s unstained intention (*nirlepa-āśaya*).

In this regard, when a bodhisattva rejoices only for the sake of sentient beings in the maturation of the mass of merit consisting of the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline up to the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom, and does not do so for himself, but having made it common to all sentient beings, dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; [this is his unstained intention].
Such an intention as this is the bodhisattva’s noble intention regarding the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline, up to and including the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
The cultivation of the perfections based on skillful means has three aspects, by virtue of examining the purity of the three spheres through non-conceptual knowledge;
for such is that skillful means for the accomplishment of all mental orientations.
The cultivation of the perfections based on mastery is threefold: by way of mastery over the body, mastery over conduct, and mastery over teaching.
Among these, mastery over the body should be understood as the two bodies of the Tathāgata: the essential body (*svābhāvikakāya*) and the enjoyment body (*sāmbhogikakāya*).

In that regard, mastery over conduct should be understood as the emanation body (*nairmāṇika-kāya*), by which one displays to all sentient beings every form of conduct in accordance with the Dharma. Mastery over teaching consists in being unimpeded in the teaching of all aspects of the six perfections.
The classification of the six perfections should be understood by way of eighteen supports.
The eighteen supports are: support for the body, support for the mind, and so forth.
The support of the wholesome, the support of a favorable rebirth, and the support of awakening.
The support of compassion, the support of not abandoning sentient beings,
and the support of relinquishing inferior states of mind.
The support for the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena; the support for the application of the roots of virtue; the support for the full realization of the roots of virtue;
and the support for the inexhaustibility of the roots of virtue.
The support of indefatigability; the support for the fulfillment of all intended aims;
the support for attracting a retinue.
The support for entering the stages,
the support for the complete attainment of the Buddha-qualities, and the support for the performance of the Buddha's activities.
It should be understood that each of the perfections, beginning with generosity, is comprised of three types of supports respectively by means of three [factors] each.
In this regard, generosity is threefold: the gift of fearlessness, the gift of Dharma, and the gift of material things.
Ethical discipline is threefold: the discipline of restraint, the discipline of gathering virtuous qualities, and the discipline of acting for the welfare of sentient beings.
Patience is threefold: patience in enduring injury, patience in accepting suffering, and patience in the contemplation of dharmas.
Diligence is threefold: the diligence of armor, the diligence of application, and the diligence in acting for the benefit of sentient beings.

There are three kinds of meditative concentration: meditative concentration for dwelling in happiness in the present life, meditative concentration for the production of supernormal powers, and meditative concentration for acting for the benefit of sentient beings.
There are three kinds of wisdom: that which has conventional reality as its object, that which has ultimate reality as its object, and that which has the welfare of sentient beings as its object.

In this context, the gift of material things (*āmiṣadāna*) is the support for the body, because it benefits the recipient's physical basis through provisions such as food and drink. The gift of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*) is the support for the mind, because it gathers the mind together for the sake of consolation and the removal of specific states of dejection.
In this same way, other cases should also be applied accordingly.

Furthermore, the "inferior mind" of a bodhisattva refers to the mind of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha arising from weariness with the suffering of saṃsāra; the support for its abandonment should be understood as the patience that endures suffering.

The inexhaustibility of the roots of virtue consists in not abandoning all sentient beings until the very end—even in the realm of nirvana without remainder—by virtue of being committed to performing their welfare; the vigor that supports this for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings is to be understood as such.

The activity of attracting a following, based upon realization, consists in providing instruction and counsel for the sake of concentrating the unconcentrated minds of those to be trained, or for the sake of liberating their concentrated minds;
the meditative absorption that supports this is the practice of acting for the welfare of sentient beings.
The entry into the stages (*bhūmi*) is that teaching preceded by faith in the Dharma through which one enters the Stage of Great Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) after completing the accumulations;
its support is the wisdom that takes conventional truth as its object.
The remainder has not been explained because it is easy to apply.

Furthermore, there is a sevenfold classification of giving: (1) giving as a root, which is the perfection of giving of a bodhisattva in the stage of the lineage (*gotra*), because they give by relying on the lineage alone;
(2) giving as a foundation, which belongs to one in the stage of the production of the thought of awakening (*cittotpāda*).
Giving based on the undertaking of a vow;
giving for the sake of assistance for one who is established in the welfare of both self and others;
and unimpeded giving for one who is established in the investigation of the true meaning.
Because there is an absence of grasping through conceptual attachment to the giver and so forth,
giving without possession belongs to one in the stage of power;
for, without external possession of requisites, by means of samādhis such as the "Sky-Treasury," one moves the hand through space and rains down jewels and other things at will.
The gift appropriate to the occasion belongs to one in the stage of maturation, because it is given in accordance with those to be trained;
the great gift belongs to one in the stage of supreme enlightenment.
Because it is unsurpassed;
in this way, up to wisdom, it should be understood according to the appropriate application.
(Abhidh-s-bh 110) "Inclusion" refers to the inclusion of the bodhisattva stages by means of giving and so forth; in this regard, the perfections and so on serve merely as illustrations.
The inclusion of the lineage (*gotra*) is to be understood through its characteristics as the lineage of the perfection of generosity and so forth.
The inclusion of the production of the thought of awakening (*cittotpāda*) is due to the inclusion of the distinguished production of the thought;
for the production of the thought is twofold: undistinguished and distinguished.
In that regard, the undifferentiated [aspiration] is: "O, may I indeed awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment!
The differentiated [aspiration] is: "May I thus fulfill the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom.
It should be understood that by means of this differentiated production of the thought of awakening, there is a gathering of the perfections.
Because they serve as the causes for those [perfections]. The summary of one's own and others' welfare is as follows: that by which one acquires sovereignty through giving is one's own welfare;
furthermore, that by which one benefits others by providing them with necessary aids is also one's own welfare. In this same way, the summary of the remaining [perfections] should be understood.
The Compendium of Ultimate Reality— beginning with the *dharmadhātu*,
because suchness (*tathatā*) is the common characteristic of generosity and the other perfections;
beginning with the accumulation of gnosis (*jñānasaṃbhāra*),...
Because it brings about the state of being a vessel for omniscience;
because, starting from the acquisition of knowledge, it brings to full completion omniscience;
and because it begins with the state of following after knowledge.
Because they follow along with the five perfections of wisdom;
starting from the characteristic of knowledge,
this is because the perfections of wisdom have the nature of correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
Thus, it should be understood that the ultimate truth is subsumed by generosity and the other perfections through their nature as suchness and correct knowledge.
By this mere illustration, the remaining forms of subsumption are to be understood.
The adversaries of generosity and the other perfections are, respectively, stinginess, immorality, anger, laziness, distraction, and faulty wisdom.

Furthermore, whatever wholesome dharmas are subsumed by the perfections, their adversaries—as well as the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)—should be understood as the adversaries of those perfections.
The benefit should be understood as immeasurable by way of its fivefold fruits.
Namely: the abandonment of their respective opposites is the fruit of dissociation;
and in this very life, the assistance rendered to oneself and others is the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra*).
The outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) is the arising of progressively superior and increasingly excellent states in the future.
Great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*) is the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*).

The ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of generosity and the other perfections is, respectively: great wealth, rebirth in the happy realms, abundance of happiness and mental well-being free from suffering, sovereignty over sentient beings, a physical body free from affliction, and great majesty.
It should be understood.
The mutual determination is threefold: that which pertains to application,
that which pertains to the breaking [of the aggregates], and that which pertains to the demonstration of the breaking.
(Abhidh-s-bh 111) In that regard, the preparatory [action] (*prāyogika*) is found to exist in all [the perfections] during the application of giving (*dānaprayoga*).
For example, the application of giving consists in the relinquishing of internal and external things.

In that regard, whatever constitutes relinquishment is the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*). In that very same context, the state of restraint from harming, afflicting, or injuring others through a mind of loving-kindness (*maitracitta*) is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*). In that very same context, the endurance of obstruction, harm, and fatigue is the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*).
In that very context, the repeated exertion of the mind is the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*);
in that very context, the one-pointedness of the mind and its non-dispersal away from the wholesome is the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*);
and in that very context, the thorough grasping of causes and fruits as they truly are, without clinging to views, is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
In this way, up to the perfection of wisdom, one should apply the two kinds of giving as appropriate, considering them to be the knowledge of omniscience.
In that regard, the classification is by way of essential nature (*svabhāva*) and by way of imitation (*anukāra*).

Therein, the essential natures of generosity and the other perfections are, respectively: relinquishment (*visarga*), restraint (*saṃvara*), endurance (*marṣaṇā*), exertion (*abhyutsāha*), stability of mind (*cittasthiti*), and discernment (*pravicaya*).
In that regard, within the applications of generosity and the other perfections, there is the accompaniment of the remaining perfections as previously described.
Therein, the application of generosity and the others consists of causing others to undertake them, speaking in praise of them, and being well-disposed toward them.
Therein, the planting of generosity and the others is their establishment within the mental continuum of another.
In this context, the perfection of generosity consists of the gift of material things; the other five perfections consist of the gift of fearlessness;
and all of them constitute the gift of the sublime Dharma, because they are planted within the mental continuum of another.
In that regard, the demonstration through differentiation is by means of the single-sphere and so forth;
for example, whatever is the perfection of generosity is also the perfection of ethical discipline,
and whatever is the perfection of ethical discipline is also the perfection of generosity.
The "consequent" formulation: Whatever is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), that is also the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*);

however, there may be a perfection of generosity that is not the perfection of ethical discipline—namely, that perfection of generosity which is not subsumed within the perfection of ethical discipline.
In this manner, up to the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of generosity that is not subsumed [within each] should be applied according to the subsequent formulations.
Regarding the statement, "Whatever is giving, all that is a perfection;
whatever is the perfection of giving, all that is giving," there is a fourfold logical alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*).
There may be giving that is not a perfection: namely, that which is not dedicated toward great enlightenment.
There may be that which is a perfection but not giving— namely, ethical discipline and the other perfections when they have been dedicated toward great enlightenment.
There may be both giving and a perfection—
namely, acts of giving and so forth when they have been dedicated toward enlightenment.
There may be that which is neither giving nor a perfection: those phenomena excluded from what has been mentioned.
In this manner, up to the perfection of wisdom, a fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika) should be applied to each one individually.
Regarding the statement, "Whoever practices giving, all such a person produces merit derived from the perfection of giving," there is a fourfold alternative.
The first alternative: one practices giving that is dedicated toward great enlightenment.
The second alternative: [one does so] through the excellence of encouraging others to undertake the perfection of giving and by speaking words that are pleasing to the mind.
The third alternative: by means of giving dedicated toward great enlightenment.
The fourth alternative is: setting aside these aforementioned modes.
In this manner, up to the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), a tetralemma should be applied to each one.

Specifically, in the Vaipulya [sūtras], there is a teaching of vastness and profundity; since the fruit, which is omniscience, is supremely vast and profound, the exposition of the cause should be understood as being in accordance with that fruit.

Some experience fear because they lack conviction in that [teaching]. This is due to a deficiency in the bodhisattva lineage (*gotra*), as they are by nature of inferior mind and thus unable to have conviction in the teaching of profundity and vastness.

Even if they possess that lineage, it is because they have not planted the roots of virtue, such as the aspiration for great enlightenment; or even if they have planted them, it is because they are under the influence of beings who reject the Mahāyāna.

Even among those who have faith, some do not attain deliverance because they fail to seek out the sūtras of definitive meaning; instead, remaining fixed in the dogmatic adherence to their own views, they cling to the literal sense of the words.

For example, there are those who, based on statements regarding the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of all phenomena, deny the existence of all things in terms of their specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

It should be understood that others as well, who cling to the literal meaning, do not attain deliverance in the Mahāyāna, because the Mahāyāna was spoken with various underlying intentions (*abhiprāya*).

And with reference to this, the Blessed One said in the *Mahādharmādarśa* discourse on Dharma: "When a bodhisattva investigates phenomena in an improper manner according to the literal expression, twenty-eight false views arise.
What are the twenty-eight false views?
They range from the view of signs (*nimitta-dṛṣṭi*) up to the view of overestimation (*abhimāna-dṛṣṭi*)."

In that regard, having encountered such proclamations in the Mahāyāna as "all phenomena are without intrinsic nature" and "unproduced," those who are unskilled in its underlying intention (abhisandhi) adhere to the literal meaning; they become fixated on signs such as non-existence, thinking, "The Blessed One has taught that all phenomena are simply non-existent and merely unproduced. This constitutes their "view of signs" (nimittadṛṣṭi).

Adhering thus to signs such as non-existence, they speak of three natures: the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

Among these, this is the imagined nature: that which consists merely of verbal designations, such as "form" up to "nirvāṇa," which is a meaning devoid of substantiality, yet which the foolish superimpose and imagine as having the characteristics of form and so forth.
In this context, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is that which is merely unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpamātra*).
In this context, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is the reality (*tattva*) of all phenomena, namely suchness (*tathatā*).

There are three types of views that deny this: the view that denies designation (*prajñaptyapavāda-dṛṣṭi*), the view that denies imagination (*parikalpāpavāda-dṛṣṭi*), and the view that denies reality (*tattvāpavāda-dṛṣṭi*).
Thus, while negating all phenomena in every respect, they adopt certain arguments in order to establish that view of negation;
even those sūtras of definitive meaning which illuminate the ineffable nature of phenomena, they reinterpret entirely to conform to their own view.
These two constitute their two views: the view of grasping and the view of reinterpreting.

Furthermore, they hold such views as these: "Whoever, relying upon this kind of view, practices either wholesome or unwholesome deeds, is indeed blameless and faultless; all of that becomes auspicious for him, and he escapes from previously accumulated obscurations. Thus, they possess two views: the view of blamelessness (*anavadyatādṛṣṭi*) and the view of escape (*niḥsaraṇadṛṣṭi*). Being thus attached to their own views, they, through a perversion of those views, despise the Śrāvaka Piṭaka which establishes the dharmas such as the aggregates (*skandha*).
Furthermore, those followers of the Śrāvaka vehicle who lack faith in that view of negation (apavāda-dṛṣṭi) harbor hatred toward it;
these two constitute the view of contempt (avajñā-dṛṣṭi) and the view of provocation (prakopa-dṛṣṭi).

Following their own views, while attempting to establish emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness as they truly are, they perceive characteristics where no such characteristics exist and thus establish a perverted definition of them.

And they have such a thought: "All those who enter into or cause others to enter into such a nature of phenomena (dharmatā) produce immeasurable merit. Thus, these two views are the perverted view and the view of production.
However, when they are questioned by others concerning that view, they do not wish to accept anything themselves.
And by means of these six types of fallacies, they interrogate others.

These constitute the view of non-acceptance (*anabhyupagamadṛṣṭi*) and the view of crookedness (*kusṛtidṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, they become conceited, thinking: "Those who practice in this way truly worship and honor the Blessed Buddhas. This is their view of honoring (*satkāradṛṣṭi*).

Even when being distinguished from that view by those skilled in the non-erroneous nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and being made to understand through well-established and renowned reasoning, they do not relinquish that view in any way;

thinking "this alone is true, everything else is false," this is the view of stubborn delusion (*dṛḍhamūḍhatādṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, the corruption (*dausthulya*) consisting of the latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) of these aforementioned views is the root view (*mūladṛṣṭi*).
Furthermore, these same seventeen views are again indicated by means of the remaining views through the method of exposing their faults.

For example, the view regarding what has been seen as a view regarding what has not been seen is called the "view of signs" (*nimittadṛṣṭi*), because one who is actually adhering to signs such as non-existence and so forth is designated as being "non-adherent to all signs."

The view of the denial of designation (*prajñaptyapavādadṛṣṭi*), the view of the denial of the imagined (*parikalpāpavādadṛṣṭi*), and the view of the denial of reality (*tattvāpavādadṛṣṭi*) constitute the view that negates practice (*prayoganirākaraṇadṛṣṭi*), because those who deny everything perceive effort as being ineffective. The view of grasping (*parigrahadṛṣṭi*) and the view of transformation (*pariṇatidṛṣṭi*) constitute the view that does not lead to liberation (*anairyāṇikadṛṣṭi*). (Abhidh-s-bh 114)
Because one who applies themselves to non-expedient means does not attain that fruit; furthermore,
the view of faultlessness and the view of renunciation are views that increase obscurations,
because for one who practices wrongly, the destruction of obscurations is impossible.

The view of contempt and the view of provocation are views that produce demerit, because through the practice of hostility toward the true Dharma and one's fellow practitioners, one incurs great loss. The view of perversion and the view of production are views of futility.

Because one does not attain distinction through the establishment, grasping, or causing others to grasp the incorrect nature of reality, the view of non-acceptance and the view of crookedness are views to be suppressed, since victory is impossible for one who engages in debate by an improper method.
The view of honoring is the view of misrepresentation, because it imputes qualities to that which does not possess them. The view of stubborn delusion is the view of the inexpressible.
Because conversation with one who is dogmatically attached to falsehood is prohibited as being useless;
it is the root view and the great view,
because from it all other modes of view become more nourished and pervasive in the future.
All these twenty-seven views are views of overestimation (*abhimānadṛṣṭi*), because they arise from false overestimation (*abhūtābhimāna*).
For this very reason, it is stated immediately thereafter in that same sutra: "These seventeen, when combined, become ten."
Ten *samāna*s become seventeen;
twenty-seven *samāna*s become one; and one *samāna* becomes twenty-seven.
All phenomena are without intrinsic nature because their existence does not exist of itself;
it is not denied that they have an existence dependent upon conditions.
Or rather, they are "without intrinsic nature" because it is impossible for them to come into being again with that same intrinsic nature by which they previously did not exist.
Even for present phenomena that possess the characteristics of having been attained and not lost, they are without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) because they lack abiding in their own state.

Furthermore, they are without intrinsic nature because they are devoid of that intrinsic nature—which is to say, the characteristic of phenomena as it is grasped by those who have not seen the truth through the medium of the habitual tendencies of verbal proliferation (*abhilāpa-prapañca-vāsanā*)—and which conforms to the way things are apprehended by the ignorant.
Moreover, all phenomena are said to consist of the three natures (*trayaḥ svabhāvāḥ*).

In that regard, the imagined nature lacks even its own characteristic; therefore, it is without intrinsic nature by virtue of the absence of intrinsic nature in its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*).

The dependent nature does not arise of itself because it depends upon conditions; therefore, it is without intrinsic nature because it does not exist as an entity in its own right, being thus without intrinsic nature by virtue of the absence of intrinsic nature in its arising (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā*).

The perfected nature, because it is the object of purification and because its very essence is the absence of the characteristics of the dependent and imagined natures, is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*); and since it is characterized by this ultimate absence of intrinsic nature, it is without intrinsic nature by virtue of the ultimate absence of intrinsic nature (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*).
[They are] without intrinsic nature.
