Having established this, all phenomena should be viewed as being without intrinsic nature,
but not with reference to a total absence of characteristics in every respect.
Furthermore, in the Mahāyāna, all the intentions of the Tathāgata are, in brief, fourfold.
They are as follows: the intention of equality, as when he says, "At that time, I myself was the perfectly enlightened Buddha Vipaśyin."
This is because the *dharmakāya* remains as a residue.

It is with reference to a different time that he said: "Those who shall make a vow for the world-system Sukhāvatī will be reborn there," and that "by the mere grasping of the name of Vimalacandraprabha, one becomes fixed in unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."
The intended meaning is "after some time.
There is also an intention regarding another meaning when he says, "all phenomena are without intrinsic nature, unproduced," and so forth;
this is because their meaning is not according to the literal expression.
The intention regarding the dispositions of individuals is that they praise a certain root of virtue for one person while disparaging it for another who is satisfied with only a small amount.

Likewise, they display the splendor of a Buddha-field to one whose temperament is dominated by passion, whereas to those whose temperament is dominated by pride, they describe the superior excellence of only certain Buddhas.
He says that even those who would commit harm toward Buddhas and Bodhisattvas will all go to heaven if they are covered by remorse (*kaukṛtya*).

He grants the prophecy of Buddhahood for the Great Śrāvakas who belong to the indeterminate lineage (*aniyatagotra*), and he teaches that there is only one vehicle and no second, in order to cause them to abandon their aspiration for the state of a Śrāvaka.
Furthermore, all intentionalities (abhisandhi) are summarized as four, beginning with the intentionality of introduction (avatāraṇābhisandhi).
Among these, the intentionality of introduction is to be seen in relation to the Śrāvakas,
because for the sake of introducing them to the teaching and so that they do not become terrified, he taught the existence of form and other phenomena.
The intention regarding characteristics (*lakṣaṇābhisandhi*) is to be seen in relation to the three natures, such as the imagined (*parikalpita*),
because of the teaching that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature, unproduced, and so forth.
The intention regarding remedies (*pratipakṣābhisandhi*) is to be seen in the subduing of faults, just as the discourse on the Supreme Vehicle serves as the remedy for the eight obscurations.

The eight obscurations consist of contempt for the Buddha and the Dharma, and so forth; their illustrations should be understood as the explanations of the four intentions (abhiprāya) as appropriate. The intention of transformation (pariṇāmanābhisandhi) is to be seen in the profundity of the expression, as it is said:
"Those who perceive the essential in the non-essential, who are well-established in error, and who are thoroughly afflicted by afflictions, attain supreme enlightenment.
Herein, this is the intended meaning: for those whose notion of the essential—that is, their notion of what is primary—is directed toward non-distraction.

For "distraction" (*vikṣepa*) is the wandering of the mind; and "well-established in error" means they are well-established in the error of impermanence and so forth by way of the reversal of permanence, pleasure, purity, and self, and because they do not abandon it; and "thoroughly afflicted by affliction" means they are excessively distressed by the fatigue of long and difficult exertion.

In the *Vaipulya* [sūtras], the instruction for bodhisattvas skilled in the meditative concentration on phenomena (*dharmasamādhi*) should be understood as concerning the benefits of calm abiding (*śamatha*), the benefits of insight (*vipaśyanā*), and the benefits of both together.
In that regard, the benefits of calm abiding are twofold:

first, through the continuous pervasion of the basis by a pliancy (*prasrabdhi*) that reaches its peak moment by moment, there is the dissolution of all underlying dysfunctions (*dausthulya*) in every instant; second, [the attainment of] the state of being a vessel for the noble qualities.

Furthermore, there is the attainment of delighting in the garden of the Dharma, such as the Sūtras and so forth, which is free from the perception of the various forms of objects such as the aggregates, due to the meditative concentration on the resolute conviction that all the dharmas of the teaching are without distinction.
The benefit of insight (*vipaśyanā*) is also twofold.

Through the non-forgetfulness of the dharmas as they have been discerned and by way of mere mindfulness, there arises an immeasurable radiance of wisdom regarding the dharmas such as the Sūtras, whose aspects are undifferentiated;
and there is also the manifestation of signs that are non-conceptual and unconditioned, which constitute the precursor to the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*).
The benefit of both of these is for the fulfillment of the Dharma-body, which is comprised of the revolution of the basis resulting from the abandonment of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

On the tenth stage, for the sake of complete perfection, or on the stage of the Tathāgatas, there is the grasping of the cause by means of the application of the receptacle for the latencies that are the ever-increasing outflow.
Thus it has been demonstrated that the fivefold fruit of this fivefold cultivation is brought forth.
What is the fivefold cultivation?

It is the cultivation of the sign of pliancy (*prasrabdhi-nimitta-bhāvanā*), the cultivation of the sign of non-distinction (*asaṃbhinna-nimitta-bhāvanā*), the cultivation of effortlessness (*anābhoga-bhāvanā*), and the cultivation of the sign of final nirvana (*parinirvṛti-nimitta-bhāvanā*).
For what reason, when they are equal in being outflows of the Dharma-body, is the Vaipulya Dharma to be honored with incense, garlands, and so forth, whereas the Śrāvaka-vehicle Dharma is not?

It is because the Vaipulya Dharma, by virtue of being the basis for the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings, possesses great significance and serves as a source for the production of unsurpassed and immeasurable merit.

(Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya 117) (The Fourth Compendium, titled "The Determination of Attainment") The determination of attainment is to be understood by way of the establishment of the individuals who attain and the establishment of the attainments themselves.
Even though there is no substantial entity (pudgala-dravya), the designation of a "person" (pudgala-vyavasthāna) is established for four reasons. Namely: for the sake of easy conventional usage;

and because, through a single collective designation of a "sentient being," one can easily engage in such conventions as "come" or "go" regarding form and other phenomena, which are numerous and possess diverse, distinct characteristics and names.
This is for the sake of conforming to worldly convention;
for in the world, not all social interaction is established solely through designations of "dharmas," but rather it is mostly conducted through the designation of "sentient beings" (*sattva*).
Therefore, the Noble Ones (*ārya*), when engaging in social interaction with the world, must necessarily conform to that convention.

For the sake of preventing fear— lest those unskilled in the nature of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda-dharmatā) should become terrified upon suddenly hearing that sentient beings do not exist in any way whatsoever—
and for the purpose of manifesting the presence of faults and virtues in oneself and others.

For otherwise, if there were only a teaching on the characteristics of affliction and purification without the designation of a "sentient being," it would not be possible to discern that "in this continuum these faults have been abandoned" or "these qualities have arisen."
Furthermore, the classification of persons (pudgala) is sevenfold, according to the distinctions of their conduct and so forth.

In this regard, one whose temperament is dominated by passion (*rāga*) has intense and prolonged passion, because even toward a lowly object of attachment, he generates excessive passion, and once arisen, it persists for a long time. In this same manner, up to those whose temperament is dominated by discursive thought (*vitarka*), they should be applied respectively to their own respective objects.

"Defilement characterized by equal proportions" (*samabhāgacarita*) refers to defilement abiding in its natural state (*prakṛtistha*), meaning a state of equilibrium free from both intensity and dullness, because the manifestation of defilements occurs in accordance with the actual condition [of those factors]. "One with little passion" (*mandarajaska*) refers to one abiding in their natural state whose defilements are extremely attenuated.
His afflictions are subtler than those of one established in the natural state (prakṛtistha) as previously defined;

he is thus "established in the natural state" because, even toward an intense object, his afflictions manifest only mildly due to the power of his prior cultivation of the antidotes and his innate disposition.

The follower of the Śrāvaka vehicle should be understood as being defined by the distinctions of lineage (*gotra*), faculties (*indriya*), aspiration (*praṇidhāna*), intention (*āśaya*), object (*ālambana*), practice (*pratipatti*), and fruit (*phala*).
Furthermore, his faculties are naturally dull when compared to those of the Pratyekabuddhas and Bodhisattvas;
otherwise, it would contradict the fact that those such as the "Dharma-followers" (*dharmānusārin*) possess sharp faculties.
In this regard, one who has not previously produced the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) and has not previously attained the fruit is one who dwells alone like the horn of a rhinoceros;
others than him are to be understood as Pratyekabuddhas who move in groups.
And "he received a prophecy" means that on the eighth stage he attained the patient acceptance (*kṣānti*) regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*).

Those who have not yet accumulated the provisions and so forth should be understood, respectively, according to whether they are of weak, medium, or superior capacity, as producing the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) and the clear realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*), based on whether this occurs in a fixed or unfixed manner and at a definite or indefinite time.
Among these, the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) are characterized by resolute faith and clarity regarding the teachings that have the truths as their dominant influence.

In that very context, the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) are characterized by the receptivity to the contemplation of phenomena (*dharmanidhyānakṣānti*); they are, respectively, dominated by faith and dominated by wisdom. The supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) are momentary by their very nature; this means they are not continuous.
But it is not due to the abandonment of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), because the roots of merit pertaining to *nirvāṇa* that have already been produced cannot be produced again.
Regarding the weak stage of the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*), the Blessed One said:
"He who possesses even a superior degree of mundane right view does not go to an evil rebirth, even for thousands of births."

Furthermore, there are four types of factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*): those pertaining to the undertaking (*ādhikārika*), those pertaining to resolute conviction (*ādhimokṣika*), those pertaining to aspiration (*ādhikāmika*), and those pertaining to approach (*ābhigāmika*).

That which is performed for the sake of liberation, beginning from the desire for wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharmacchanda*), is that pertaining to the undertaking. That which is accompanied by resolute conviction in the teaching associated with that [liberation] is that pertaining to resolute conviction.

That which is characterized by frequent mental attention directed toward liberation, accompanied by joy and serene confidence, is called "superior" (*ādhikāmika*). That which is certain to produce the stages conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) in that very same lifetime is called "approaching" (*ābhigāmika*).

The path of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) is sixfold: the conformable (*ānulomika*), the protracted (*prākarṣika*), the penetrative (*prātivedhika*), the transformative (*anyapāriṇāmika*), the single-birth (*aikajanmika*), and the single-session (*ekāsanika*).
Among these, that initial weak root of merit which arises having the truths as its object is the conformable.
That which is middling is the protracted.
Because it is even more excellent than that,
that which is superior for the penetration of the truths and which leads to such penetration within that very same lifetime is called "penetrative" (*prātivedhika*).
Furthermore, for those of indeterminate lineage (*aniyata-gotra*), it is for the sake of attaining a specific type of enlightenment (*bodhi-viśeṣa*).
That which is transformed for the sake of the self-awakening of Pratyekabuddhas—without a teacher—is transformed in another birth; that is "transformed in another life" (*tadanyapāriṇāmika*).
That which conduces to the penetration of the Truths in that very same birth is "of one birth" (*aikajanmika*).
That which [conduces to it] on that very same seat is "of one sitting" (*ekāsanika*).
The body-witness (kāyasākṣī) is a non-returner (anāgāmin) who has attained liberation, because he dwells having personally realized and fully entered the eight liberations (vimokṣa).
The eight liberations— beginning with "one possessing form sees forms"— will be explained later.

One liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*) is so called because of having abandoned, without remainder, the obscurations of the afflictions that are the adversaries of wisdom. One liberated in both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*) is one who is liberated from both the obscurations of the afflictions and the obscurations to meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).

One practicing for the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphalapratipannaka*) is one who, starting from the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) practiced in a single sitting, has not yet attained the first fruit.
Furthermore, who attains the first fruit at the conclusion of the path of seeing?

It is one who, though not yet free from passion for the desires through partial detachment (*pradeśavairāgya*), enters the determination of correctness (*samyaktva-niyāma*). However, there is also one who, having previously abandoned the six types of afflictions belonging to the desire realm that are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*) by means of the worldly path (*laukika-mārga*).

In this regard, one who becomes free from passion for a certain level and subsequently enters the certainty of rightness (*samyaktva-niyāma*) becomes a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) at the sixteenth moment of mind.
Furthermore, one who becomes free from passion for the desire realm and enters the certainty of rightness after having abandoned all nine grades [of defilements] becomes a non-returner (*anāgāmin*).

Even though all [defilements] to be abandoned by seeing must be abandoned, the term "stream-enterer" (srotāpanna) is used specifically because of the abandonment of three fetters (*saṃyojana*), since these are primary as they constitute the obstacles to attaining liberation.

For instance, through the view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), one clings to the five aggregates of grasping as self and belonging to a self; thus, due to a delight in the abode [of the mind], one does not rise above suffering.

Even if one has somehow set out toward liberation, through the adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and through doubt (*vicikitsā*), one departs falsely due to an attachment to a wrong path and a lack of certainty regarding the right path; thus, one does not attain true correctness.

Furthermore, through the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), one errs regarding the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), because one superimposes the characteristics of "self" and "mine" upon that which is merely suffering.
By means of the adherence to rules and rituals, one is attached to [wrong] views, because of the conviction that purity is attained through them;
by means of doubt, one is attached to the antidote.
Because there is no certainty regarding the Three Jewels.

The candidate for the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphalapratipannaka*) is that person who, subsequent to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), is on the path of abandoning up to the ninth grade of affliction (*kleśaprakāra*)—the middling-middling grade—of the desire realm.
The once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmī*) is that person who has completed the path of abandoning the eighth grade of affliction—the middling-weak grade.

The candidate for the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphalapratipannaka*) is [that person who, subsequent to the fruit of once-returning, is on the path of abandoning] the weak-strong and weak-middling grades of the afflictions of the desire realm.

The person who, on the path of abandoning the two types of afflictions, is one who has reached the completion of the path for the sake of abandoning the ninth type of affliction, which is the "mild-mild" (mṛdu-mṛdu) category; such a person is a non-returner (anāgāmī).

Even though there is the abandonment of all [defilements] belonging to the desire realm that are to be abandoned by cultivation, the term "non-returner" (*anāgāmin*) is used in the Sūtra with reference to the abandonment of the five lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), because these are predominant as the causes for the lowest states of existence and realms. Furthermore, the lowest states of existence are the realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts.
The lowest realm is the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Within that, the cause [of its being the lowest] is due to the fact that one has not transcended the inferior destinies because of the presence of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the adherence to rites and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*);
and because one has not transcended the inferior realm due to sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and ill-will (*vyāpāda*).

Even though all afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms have been abandoned, the term "Arhat" is used because of the abandonment of the five higher fetters (*ūrdhvabhāgīya*); these are primary because they are the causes for not relinquishing higher rebirth.
In this context, by means of attachment to the form and formless realms, there is "higher rebirth" in the desire realm, meaning birth in the form and formless realms.
Due to restlessness, pride, and ignorance, there is a failure to relinquish the higher [states]; and because of the state of meditating on craving, pride, and doubt, there is affliction therein.

The *kulamkula* (one who goes from family to family) is one who has entered the stream (*srotāpanna*) and is practicing for the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*). Having transmigrated through exactly two existences among either gods or humans, he attains final nirvāṇa.

The *ekavīcika* (one who has one interval) is one who has entered the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*) while still being a once-returner; having transmigrated through only one existence among the gods, he attains final nirvāṇa.
"One interval" (*ekavīci*) means that there is a single interval—an opportunity for birth—between him [and nirvāṇa]; thus he is called an *ekavīcika*.

The one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyī) is one who, having gone to the place of rebirth by means of the impulse of the afflictions (kleśāvedha), would otherwise have taken rebirth; when that [impulse] is exhausted, yet while a mere latent tendency (anuśaya) remains, he does not produce the aggregates after death, but instead produces an intermediate existence (antarābhava).
Upon the remaining [tendency], through the very manifestation of the path previously practiced, he attains parinirvāṇa upon the abandonment of those specific latent tendencies.

Furthermore, with respect to the place of rebirth, he should be understood as being of three types based on whether he has not moved, has only just moved, or remains at a distance, in accordance with the *Satpuruṣagati-sūtra*.

One who "manifests the path without volitional effort" means that because he previously practiced it well, it proceeds spontaneously and thus without exertion. By contrast, one is "one who attains parinirvāṇa through volitional effort."
The one who flows upwards (*ūrdhvasrotas*) is of two kinds: the one who goes to Akaniṣṭha and the one who goes to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

Among these, the one who goes to Akaniṣṭha, due to an abundance of relishing (*āsvādana*), relishes the various grades of dhyāna—such as the soft and so forth—as they arise; beginning from the Brahmakāyika realm, he is reborn successively in all the intermediate stages, being born once in each until he enters Akaniṣṭha, where he attains final nirvāṇa.

One who has reached the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), because he has cultivated the fourth dhyāna without intermingling it, goes only as far as the Peak of Existence, bypassing the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*) entirely, and there attains parinirvāṇa.

However, for one who has cultivated the fourth dhyāna with intermingling—having cultivated its five types, beginning with the weak—one should understand that rebirth occurs in the five Pure Abodes respectively.
"Having willed and having willed" means either proceeding toward oneself by one's own effort or not proceeding [by such effort].

"Falling away from dwelling in happiness in the present life" means falling away from the mundane meditative absorptions (*laukika-dhyāna*). "Refining the faculties" (*indriyottāpana*), moreover, means bringing them to a state of excellence or making them sharp.
For this very reason, it is not stated that one who is of immovable nature (*akopyadharman*) is capable of refining the faculties.
Because of being sharp-facultied by nature.

The Bodhisattva belongs only to the desire realm (kāmāvacara) and the form realm (rūpāvacara), not to the formless realm (ārūpyāvacara); this is because, although he has attained great power, he does not take rebirth there since the formless realm is not a suitable sphere for maturing sentient beings.
"By means of meditation that excludes the formless realm" means by means of a meditative concentration (samādhi) that precludes rebirth in the formless realms.
A bodhisattva dwells in the bliss of meditative absorption without ever falling away from those absorptions, because he is skilled in emerging from them;
it should be understood that for the sake of maturing sentient beings, the bodhisattva takes birth even in the realm of desire.
He displays the entire career of a bodhisattva, beginning from his residence in the Tuṣita heaven up to his defeat of Māra;
and he displays the career of a Buddha, beginning from his perfect awakening up to his great final nirvāṇa.

The bodhisattva who practices through resolute belief is established in the bodhisattva lineage; from the initial setting out toward great enlightenment until he enters the *pramuditā* stage, he does not possess the supramundane realization within himself, because of the absence of such realization. The one who practices through superior intention [acts] throughout the ten stages.
Because his intention is purified through supramundane realization;
he courses in signs on the six stages,
because even though he does not desire it, there is still an intermingling of signs.

One who practices the signless dwells on the seventh stage, because for one who exerts effort, signs do not manifest as long as one desires. One who practices without volitional effort dwells on the remaining stages.
Because of the attainment of the non-conceptual knowledge that is the result of maturation.
The one who attains deliverance all at once abandons the afflictions belonging to the three realms simultaneously.

"By way of categories" means that he abandons the latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the desire, form, and formless realms that are to be abandoned by cultivation, starting from the highest-of-the-high (adhimātrādhimātra) down to the lowest-of-the-low (mṛdumṛdu), including those to be abandoned by vision; however, the meaning is that this is not done separately according to the distinctions of stages and categories as is the case with the worldly path (laukikamārga).

In this regard, there is this scriptural authority as stated in the *Aṅgulyagrasūtra*: "Whatever form, up to consciousness—whether past, future, or present—and so on in detail, whether far or near—all that, having gathered it together into one, makes it a single part, a single mass, a single heap, a single pile; and having made it one, he trains himself thus: 'All this is impermanent, all this is suffering,' and so forth."

It is designated only for the first and last fruits; this is because those two are characterized, respectively, by the complete abandonment of all that is to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation throughout the three realms. However, it is not so designated for the two middle fruits.

This is because, for one who has seen the truths, [the path] is characterized by the abandonment—both with remainder and without remainder—of those defilements belonging to the realm of desire that are to be abandoned through cultivation.

Furthermore, with reference to one who attains liberation all at once (*sakṛnnairyāṇika*), it should be understood that in the *Vibhaṅga-sūtra*, the state of an Arhat is established immediately after the state of a Stream-enterer.

If such a person realizes full knowledge (*ājñā*) in this very life, they do not attain it entirely without remainder because they have not yet become free from passion; therefore, by the power of their vow, they are reborn in the desire realm for the sake of attaining parinirvāṇa quickly.
The establishment of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) is tenfold.

Among these, the clear realization of the Dharma (*dharmābhisamaya*) is the attainment of the highest degree of resolute confidence and faith— which is comprised within the final stage of the aids to liberation— by taking the voice of another as the dominant influence regarding the teachings such as the *sūtras* that have the truths as their governing principle.
For it is thus: through the attainment of faith and resolve regarding that [teaching], those truths are said to have been "realized" by means of the realization of the Dharma (*dharmābhisamaya*).

The "realization of the meaning" (*arthābhisamaya*) is the attainment, with respect to those very same teachings, of the superior patience for the investigation of phenomena regarding the truths (*satyeṣu dharmanidhyānakṣānti*), which is comprised within the final stage of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), having taken proper mental attention (*yoniśomanaskāra*) as its dominant condition.

Furthermore, that patience consisting in the contemplation of dharmas is characterized by three kinds of appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manaskāra*): by the weak-intense [attention] during the stages of "Heat" (*ūṣmagata*) at the time of its arising; by the intense-medium [attention] during the "Summits" (*mūrdhan*) and the "Patience" (*kṣānti*) stages; and by the intense-intense [attention] during the "Supreme Mundane Dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*).

The clear realization of reality (*tattvābhisamaya*) is the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). Furthermore, regarding the conventional cognitions (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) that are established as truths and occur at the conclusion of the clear realization, they are acquired through the nourishment of their seeds by the sovereignty of supramundane cognition (*lokottarajñāna*), but one does not bring them into manifestation because the sixteen moments of mind of the path of seeing proceed without interruption.

Because there is no opportunity for worldly thought, subsequent realization (*pṛṣṭhābhisamaya*) refers to all paths of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) following the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), whether mundane or supramundane.
Realization of the Jewels (*ratnābhisamaya*) is: "The Blessed One is indeed the Truly Perfect Buddha."

Having understood and ascertained that "his Dharma and Vinaya are well-expounded" and "the Saṅgha of disciples has practiced well," the noble disciple possesses serene confidence (*prasāda*) in the Buddha and the others.

This is the realization of non-manifestation; because of the attainment of the restraint of non-action—which is comprised within the morality of one who is intent upon what is beneficial—there is the non-manifestation of its opposites, such as the hells and so forth.

When a certainty arises in this way—such as "My hells are exhausted"—this is the realization of non-manifestation (*asamudācārābhisamaya*). The realization of culmination (*niṣṭhābhisamaya*) is the complete subsiding of all functional rigidity (*dauṣṭhulya*), and so forth, just as the path of culmination was explained in the context of the Truth of the Path.
These same seven realizations, when obtained by Śrāvakas through relying on the voice of another, are called the "Śrāvaka realization."
The realization of a *pratyekabuddha* is so called because it is attained without relying on the voice of another.

Among these seven types of realization, the bodhisattva’s realization is the patient acceptance (*kṣānti*) regarding the attainment [of the path] by a bodhisattva; it is for the sake of skill in means for training *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, and not a direct realization (*sākṣātkriyā*), out of regard for sentient beings and because of not departing via the Lesser Vehicle.
Furthermore, this is indeed called the bodhisattva’s initial clear realization of entering the stages.

And based on this realization, it is said: what is the specific distinction between the realization of a Śrāvaka and the realization of a Bodhisattva? It is distinguished by its object (*ālambana*), because its object is the Vaipulya [sūtras].
It is distinguished by its support (*upastambha*), because it fulfills the great equipment of merit and knowledge throughout complete, incalculable great aeons.

It is distinguished by its penetration (*prativedha*), because through the penetration of the application to the teachings dominated by the selflessness of persons and phenomena, both of these are penetrated by supramundane knowledge. It is distinguished by its acceptance (*abhyupagama*), because of the equality of oneself [with others]...

Because of the commitment to all sentient beings; because of the distinction of departure, due to departing by means of the ten stages; and because of the distinction of embrace, due to embracing non-abiding nirvana.
It is due to the excellence of his station and retinue, from the purification of the Buddha-field and the gathering of those to be trained;
due to the excellence of his lineage, because he possesses the characteristics of a legitimate son who sustains the paternal line;
and due to the excellence of his birth, as he is born within the circles of assemblies.

Furthermore, the distinction of the fruit is due to: (1) the distinction of the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*), because through the abandonment of all types of corruption (*dauṣṭhulya*), whether afflicted or unafflicted, there occurs a revolution of the basis by virtue of its becoming the substratum for all unsurpassed qualities;

(2) the distinction of the abundance of qualities, because of the perfection of immeasurable qualities such as the powers (*bala*), the grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*), and the unique Buddha-qualities (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*);
and (3) the distinction of the five aspects, due to the distinction of purification and so forth.
In this regard, the distinction of purity is due to the abandonment of the afflictions along with their latent predispositions;
the distinction of complete purification is due to the purification of the Buddha-field;
and the distinction of the body is due to the perfect accomplishment of the Dharma-body.
There is a distinction in enjoyment, because Bodhisattvas always experience the diverse enjoyment of the Dharma together within the circles of their assemblies.
There is a distinction in activity, because they carry out the work of a Buddha through emanations as appropriate throughout infinite and boundless world-systems in all directions.

And there is a distinction in the three bodies, because of the attainment of the perfection of the essential body (*svābhāvika-kāya*), the enjoyment body (*sāmbhogika-kāya*), and the emanation body (*nairmāṇika-kāya*).
By way of the distinction of nirvāṇa, because in the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder all qualities are never severed for the benefit of all sentient beings;

by way of the distinction of attaining the power of mixed and intermingled gnosis, because through the single flavor of the utterly pure dharmadhātu, each of the various forms of the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) possesses the capacity of all Buddhas;
and by way of the distinction of the purification of obscurations, because of the abandonment of all afflictive and cognitive obscurations.

Due to the distinction of performing various mixed and intermingled karmic activities for the sake of disciplining each individual sentient being through the sovereignty of all Buddhas; due to the distinction of the specific means for manifesting perfect enlightenment and parinirvāṇa by repeatedly displaying the arising of Buddhas and so forth throughout all world-systems in the ten directions, as appropriate, until the end of time; and due to the distinction of the fivefold protection that brings to maturity and liberates all those to be disciplined. (Abhidh-s-bh 124)
It should be understood [as a protection] because it protects from calamities and so forth.
In this regard, protection from calamities occurs through the entry into cities and so on, by means of obtaining the eyes and other faculties that were previously impaired.
Protection from improper means occurs through the attainment of mundane right view, by means of which all wrong views are eliminated.

Protection from the miserable states (*apāya*) occurs because, by generating the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one completely transcends the lower realms. Protection from the view of a self-identity (*satkāya*) occurs because, by realizing arhatship, one is liberated from the three realms. Protection regarding the vehicles (*yāna*) occurs because it turns bodhisattvas away from the inferior vehicle (*hīnayāna*).

The specific qualities (*vaiśeṣikaguṇa*) are either produced by noble disciples (*āryaśrāvaka*) on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) or on the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*); therefore, it should be understood that these are included within the "subsequent realization" (*pṛṣṭhābhisamaya*) and the "final realization" (*niṣṭhābhisamaya*).
Furthermore, those [qualities] such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and so forth should be understood exactly as they are taught in other sūtras, both in the Śrāvakayāna and the Mahāyāna.

And their definition should be understood, in brief, through five aspects as appropriate: by way of basis (*niśraya*), object (*ālambana*), aspect (*ākāra*), intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and accompaniment (*sahāya*).
In that regard, first of all, the basis for loving-kindness is meditative absorption; sentient beings are the object; and the mental aspect is the thought, "May they be endowed with happiness."

Concentration and wisdom are its intrinsic nature, because all virtues are comprised within calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*); the mind and mental factors are its companions. In this same way, [these elements] should be applied as appropriate to compassion and the other [immeasurables]. Regarding equanimity toward beings who experience pleasure and so forth, one should understand that its aspect is the relinquishing of attachment and so on, thinking: "Oh, may they indeed be liberated from affliction!"
And that is called the dwelling of the intention for benefit.
There are eight liberations (*vimokṣa*).
"Possessing form, one sees forms"—this is the first liberation, and so forth in detail.
In that regard, how is it said that one "possesses form"?

The meaning is that they are to be seen by means of the suppression of the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*) or by the non-establishment of the perception of form, based upon the meditative attainment of formlessness (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), because of the manifestation of the perception of form.
How is it said that one "sees forms"?
It is because one sees forms—such as beautiful or ugly ones—by means of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
How is it called "liberation" (*vimokṣa*)?
It is so called because by means of it one is liberated from the obscuration regarding emanation (*nirmāṇāvaraṇa*).

This means that, based on the internal attainment of the formless (*arūpyasamāpatti*) while being devoid of the perception of form (*adhyātmamarūpasaṃjñā*), there is either the elimination of the perception of form within oneself as the observer, or the establishment of the perception of the formless, or the manifestation of the perception of the name (*nāmasaṃjñā*) within the observer.
The rest is as before.
One dwells having personally realized and attained the beautiful liberation (*śubha-vimokṣa*),

by relying on the perception of mutual dependence and the perception of mutual conformity regarding beautiful and ugly forms, because of the attainment of the perception of their mutual single flavor.

For instance, in relation to beautiful forms, others are considered ugly; or, in relation to ugly forms, they are considered beautiful. This is because, when viewing things of a single kind without such comparison, the notions of "beautiful" or "ugly" do not arise.
Thus, even within what is beautiful there is an underlying ugliness, and even within what is ugly there is beauty;

for even that which is regarded as beautiful, such as the skin, contains thirty-six other impure substances, such as hair and so forth. In this way, having mixed all forms together, one is liberated by means of a perception (*saṃjñā*) that has the single flavor of beauty.

For one who has thus attained mastery over the liberations of form and so forth, the obscuration regarding the emanation of the beautiful and the ugly is abandoned, as is the obscuration regarding the arising of affliction therein.
But what is the affliction regarding emanation?
It is the mental effort (*ābhoga*) involved in the emanation of a beautiful form.
Regarding the creation of an unwholesome form, there is aversion.

As for the four bases of mastery, beginning with the sphere of infinite space, which are pure and conducive to the untainted state for a noble disciple, they receive the designation "liberations" because one is liberated from relishing them.
Those peaceful liberations which, having transcended forms, are formless—non-attachment to them is purification;
the obscuration to that is the relishing of the formless.
The basis for the cessation of perception and feeling is the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
It lacks an object, aspect, or accompaniment because of the absence of mind and mental factors;
its intrinsic nature is the cessation of mind and mental factors,
and it is an abiding state similar to liberation.

Because for the noble disciple (*ārya-śrāvaka*), whose basis has been transformed by means of the supramundane path, there is a state in which even the mind and mental factors no longer function— and because of the supreme tranquility [of that state] and the non-occurrence of the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*)—
these eight liberations are called "abodes" (*vihāra*),
since the noble ones dwell by means of them.
Even there, they frequently dwell by means of these two liberations—

the third and the eighth— because of their preeminence. For this very reason, regarding these two, there is the statement "having realized them with the body and having attained them, one dwells therein," whereas for the other formless and form-liberations, there is no such statement, because [in their case] the obstructions have not been abandoned in their entirety, respectively.
Another formulation is: "by means of the realization of the complete transformation of the basis (āśrayaparivṛtti) of those two."

There are eight spheres of mastery (*aṣṭāv abhibhvāyatanāni*). In this regard, one who possesses the perception of internal forms sees external forms that are limited, beautiful or ugly, inferior or superior;
having indeed mastered those forms, he knows them, he sees them, and he becomes percipient in such a way.
This is the first sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
Perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are vast, beautiful or ugly, and so on in detail, until one becomes conscious through that [perception].
This is the second sphere of mastery.
Thus, these two spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*)—namely, "possessing form, one sees forms"—are derived from this liberation (*vimokṣa*).
Internally perceiving no form, one sees external forms that are limited, and so on in detail up until: "and one likewise possesses such a perception.
This is the third sphere of mastery.
Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are vast, and one becomes percipient of them as such;

this is the fourth sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*). Thus, these two spheres of mastery—in which one not perceiving forms internally sees external forms—are derived from this [fourth] liberation (*vimokṣa*).
Having established this, it should be understood that the four spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) are derived from two liberations (*vimokṣa*).
One who possesses the perception of internal forms sees external forms that are blue, blue in color, appearing blue,
and radiant with blue— just like an *umakā* flower, or a fine cloth from Vārāṇasī that is blue, blue in color, and appearing blue.
In the same way, one who is internally percipient of the formless sees external forms that are blue, up to being blue-appearing;
having mastered those forms, one knows them and sees them, and remains percipient in that manner.
This is the fifth sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are yellow, up to and including those with a yellow luster.
For example, like a *karṇikāra* flower, or a well-woven cloth from Vārāṇasī that is yellow, of yellow color—this is the detailed description.
This is the sixth sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are red, up to and including those with a red luster.
For example, like a *bandhujīvaka* flower, or like a fine cloth from Vārāṇasī that is red, red-colored—
this is the seventh sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).

Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are bright, of bright color, appearing bright, and radiant with brightness— just as the color of a star at dawn, or a Benares cloth that is bright, of bright color, appearing bright, and radiant with brightness; in this very way, not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are bright, of bright color, appearing bright, and radiant with brightness.
Having mastered those forms, one knows them, having mastered them, one sees them, and possesses the corresponding perception;
this is the eighth sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
These [eight] are derived from the liberation (*vimokṣa*) expressed as: "having realized with the body the beautiful liberation and attained it, one dwells therein."

In that regard, by means of the liberations (vimokṣa), one resolves upon the object of focus, such as the limited and so forth; however, by means of the bases of mastery (abhibhvāyatana), one masters it,
based on the power of making it disappear or acting according to one's will.
In that regard, "limited" forms are those comprised within the category of sentient beings because they are small in size;
"excessive" forms are those not comprised within the category of sentient beings, such as houses, celestial palaces, mountains, and so forth, because they are large in size.
Beautiful and ugly forms, comprised within auspicious and inauspicious colors;
inferior and superior, human and divine, respectively—
having indeed mastered those forms, that is, having brought them under one's control.
"He knows" refers to the path of calm abiding (*śamatha*);
"he sees" refers to the path of insight (*vipaśyanā*).
And he "possesses such a perception" because, whether [the object] has been mastered or not yet mastered, he maintains a perception free from conceit regarding it.
"Blue" is the term of designation (*uddeśapada*).
They are blue in color by virtue of their innate blueness (*sahajā nīlatā*);
they are blue in appearance (*nīlanidarśana*) by virtue of their combined blueness (*saṃyoganīlatā*).
They appear blue because of the brilliance resulting from the emission of light from both of them.
Just as it is with the blue, so too should the yellow, red, and white be understood in detail.
Furthermore, there are two examples for each [color] in order to illustrate the manifestation of color that is both innate and produced by combination.
There is another formulation as follows: "blue" is a common term of reference for both a flower and a cloth;
however, "blue-colored" refers specifically to the flower, because in its case there is the possibility of a blue color produced by conjunction (*sāṃyogika*).
It is said to have a "blue appearance" with reference to both the flower and the cloth,

because luminosity is possible in both. Having established this, even in the case of the example, the description— such as "just as the *umakā* flower or a cloth produced in Vārāṇasī is blue, having a blue color," and so forth— is thus rendered appropriate.
In this way, yellow and the other colors are to be applied;
the rest is as in the [sections on] resolute intentions (*adhimokṣa*). What is the rest?
"One possessing the perception of internal forms sees external forms," and so forth.
This, moreover, should be understood according to the explanations such as "one possessing form sees forms," and so on.

Having thus brought the object under control by means of the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), one pervades everything with the totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*); that is to say, one extends it everywhere, infinitely and without limit. Furthermore, those totalities are ten in number, namely:

the earth-totality, the water-totality, the fire-totality, the air-totality, the yellow-totality, the red-totality, the white-totality, the space-infinity-totality, and the consciousness-infinity-totality.

Furthermore, if earth and the other elements were not established within the totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*), then, in the absence of those primary elements as their support, it would be impossible for the derived matter consisting of blue and so forth to pervade [them].
It should be understood that the establishment of these [totalities] occurs by means of the mastery of the pervasion of that supporting form.
The remainder, as far as applicable, is like the liberations, beginning with the totality of the sphere of infinite space.

In this regard, it should be understood that the liberation [factors] constitute the beginning, the spheres of mastery the application, and the spheres of totality the final accomplishment of the liberations.

One who dwells in the state of passionlessness (*araṇā-vihārī*), desiring to come into the range of perception of certain sentient beings, remains in that very dwelling and— observing their future course regarding the manifestation of afflictions within themselves by means of the power of knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhi-jñāna*)—
approaches them or does not approach them in such a way that they do not experience attachment, aversion, envy, or stinginess toward him there.
They do not give rise to the root afflictions (*kleśa*) or the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
Therefore, this is said: "Relying on the *araṇā* meditation, they achieve the dwelling that guards against the arising of afflictions," and so forth.

As for the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*), one who has attained it becomes desirous of knowing whatever account of knowable objects there may be, such as those pertaining to the three times.
Having formed a mental aspiration in each respective case, "May I know this," one enters meditative absorption;
then, upon emerging from it, that aspiration is fulfilled,
meaning that one knows the object to be known.

The analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvit*) is the concentration that, in its full detail, consists in the unimpeded mastery regarding synonyms— such as ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth, beginning with "lack of knowledge," "lack of vision," and "lack of clear realization"— and so on.
The analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvit*) concerns the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena.
And regarding the intention concerning different meanings and so forth, there is the detailed explanation:

"In the analytical knowledge of etymological interpretation (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), [it refers] to the local dialects; that is, in the conventional usage of various mutual designations according to their respective objects, and in the verbal definition of phenomena (*dharmanirvacana*). For example: "It is destroyed (*lujyate*) and utterly destroyed (*pralujyate*), therefore it is the world (*loka*)."

In such cases as "it is called *rūpa* because it is affected (*rūpyate*)," and regarding the distinctions of phenomena within the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), such as [the categories of] "substantially existent" (*dravyasat*), "nominally existent" (*prajñaptisat*), "conventionally existent" (*saṃvṛtisat*), and "ultimately existent" (*paramārthasat*).

Regarding "the supernormal power of psychic transformation (*ṛddhyabhijñā*)," it refers to the perfection of various miraculous transformations, such as, for example, becoming many after having been one, and so forth.
Regarding "the perfection of hearing various sounds," it refers to divine, human, and other such sounds.

Regarding "the perfection of entering into the mental conduct of other beings," this means the perfection of knowing, as it truly is, the movement of the minds of others, such as whether they possess passion and so forth.
Regarding "the perfection of recollecting past conduct": this means the various modes of names, castes, lineages, and so forth, beginning from a succession of past births.

Regarding "the supernormal knowledge of death and rebirth": through the divine eye, there is the perfection of clearly perceiving the death and rebirth of sentient beings—those passing away and being born, those of beautiful appearance and those of ugly appearance, those going to good destinations and those going to bad destinations—beginning from the future limit; herein lie the meditative concentrations and other qualities.

Regarding "the perfection of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows" (āsravakṣayajñānasamṛddhi): the meaning is that it refers to the means by which the outflows are completely destroyed, as well as the knowledge that has the accomplishment of that destruction as its cause.

The primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇānuvyañjana*) are to be understood as having that very nature, for it is through the sovereignty of their meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) that the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, manifest to those to be trained a physical body (*rūpakāya*) resplendent with the thirty-two primary marks and eighty secondary marks.

Because the Blessed Buddhas are manifested through the *dharmakāya*, [their bodies] are of the nature of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). However, for Bodhisattvas who are capable of manifesting themselves in such a way, they are of the nature of meditative concentration and wisdom;
for others born within the circles of assemblies, they should be understood as being of the nature of the maturation (*vipāka*) arising from those [concentrations and wisdoms].
There are four kinds of complete purities belonging to the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and to the Bodhisattvas who have attained the great superknowledges (*mahābhijñā*).
Among these, "the perfection of the appropriation, maintenance, and relinquishing of the basis according to one's wish" means: by taking birth wherever one desires;
and, having sustained the formative forces of life (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*) in that birth, remaining there for as long as one wishes.
When he so desires, through the relinquishing of the life-force and the formative forces (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*) respectively,
and by means of the objects as he wishes, there is the perfection of the knowledges of emanation and transformation; that is, through the emanation of unprecedented forms and so forth,
and through the transformation of previously arisen forms and so forth into gold and the like.

And by way of understanding all modes [of concentration] in their proper sequence, there is mastery over the attainment of the gates of meditative absorption (samādhimukha) according to one's desire; that is to say, for the sake of entering other immeasurable meditative absorptions at will in every moment.

And by way of mastery in the retention of the gates of mnemonic formulas (dhāraṇīmukha) according to one's desire, it means the attainment of the capacity to verbally express any of the forty-two syllables and all their corresponding categories of teachings upon bringing any single syllable to mind.

The ten powers: the power of knowing what is possible and impossible; the power of knowing that actions are one's own; the power of knowing the meditations, liberations, concentrations, and attainments; the power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties; the power of knowing various inclinations; the power of knowing various elements; the power of knowing the path leading everywhere; the power of recollecting former abodes; the power of knowing death and rebirth; and the power of knowing the exhaustion of the outflows.

In that regard, based on meditative absorption (dhyāna), the power of knowing what is possible and impossible consists in the manifestation of concentration and the other [factors] through unimpeded and unobstructed knowledge of all modes of causes and non-causes.

In the same way, this should be applied to the power of knowing the ownership of karma and so forth, as the manifestation of unimpeded and unobstructed knowledge of the ownership of karma in all its aspects.

The four grounds of self-confidence: "While I am a perfectly awakened Buddha, regarding these things that have not been fully awakened to by me, I do not perceive even the slightest ground upon which any ascetic, god, Māra, or Brahmā could rightfully challenge or remind me; and since I do not perceive such a ground, I abide in security and self-confidence, and I declare my noble, preeminent place."
I practice the holy life;
I roar the lion’s roar correctly in the assembly:
"Alas, though I am one whose taints are exhausted, these taints are not yet exhausted! [Such a claim would be made by a false ascetic.]
Furthermore, regarding those things which I have declared to my disciples to be obstructive factors, yet for one who indulges in them, they are not sufficient to constitute an obstruction;

or regarding that path which I have declared to my disciples for the sake of deliverance—the noble, leading-to-deliverance, and penetrative path—by practicing it, one is surely not rightly delivered for the sake of the complete destruction of suffering and the making of an end to suffering; in these matters, [do not misrepresent me].

Whether it be some ascetic or brahmin, [the Buddha says] "I roar the lion's roar," and so on, as should be stated in detail for each [of the four grounds]. These intrepidities (vaiśāradya) are to be understood as pertaining to one's own welfare and the welfare of others. In that regard, one's own welfare is twofold: the excellence of knowledge and the excellence of abandonment.
The welfare of others is twofold: the avoidance of discordant factors and the cultivation of remedial factors.

In this regard, the fearlessness regarding perfect enlightenment—which is essentially knowledge—is directed solely toward one's own welfare; it consists in the fact that, throughout the entire world, one’s claim that "I have perfectly awakened to all aspects of the knowable, including their distinctions and limits," is entirely beyond reproach.
"The concentration that consists in the perfection of establishing [others]" is as previously described.
In this same way, the remaining grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*) are also to be applied.
Furthermore, "outflows in all their aspects" should be understood as the afflictions (*kleśa*) together with their latent tendencies (*savāsanā*).
All factors that constitute obstacles in every aspect should be seen as all defiled factors belonging to the side of the adverse;
the path leading to deliverance in every aspect should be seen as beginning from the path of preparation up to the path of final consummation.
There are three unique foundations of mindfulness.

Here, the Teacher, compassionate, merciful, desiring their welfare, seeking their benefit, and feeling pity, teaches the Dharma to his disciples: "Monks, this is for your benefit; this is for your happiness; this is for your benefit and happiness.
His disciples listen to him, lend an ear, apply their minds to understanding, and practice the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma.
In that regard, the Tathāgata experiences neither elation nor mental gladness, nor does his mind become uplifted; rather, the Tathāgata dwells there equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending.
This is the first unique application of mindfulness, which the Noble One cultivates, and by cultivating which the Noble One is worthy of instructing an assembly.
Furthermore, the Teacher teaches the Dharma to his disciples for their benefit and happiness;
yet those disciples do not wish to listen, up to and including not practicing the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma.
In that situation, the Tathāgata feels no resentment, no impatience, no lack of confidence, and no mental displeasure; he remains equanimous therein—this is the detailed account.
This is the second.

In the third, this is the distinction: some of his disciples desire to hear [the teaching] and even practice the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, while others do not desire to hear it and do not practice the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma; in that case, the Tathāgata does not experience joy, up to and including lack of mental satisfaction.

These three foundations of mindfulness constitute, for the Teacher, in the gathering of the community, the perfection of the non-occurrence of the latencies of attachment, aversion, and both in all their forms, respectively; they consist of meditative concentration and the others.
There are three things that need no protection.
The Tathāgata’s conduct of body is completely pure;
there is no impurity in the Tathāgata’s conduct of body such that the Tathāgata would think it necessary to conceal it, lest others should find out about it.

In this way, the conduct of speech and mind is to be understood. Because he is free from doubt due to being defined by these [qualities], it should be understood that, beginning with the drawing-in of his disciples, the Teacher’s application of restraint, censure, instruction, and admonition proceeds successfully according to his will.

The quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃmoṣadharmatā*) consists of the meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) and so forth, which bring about the perfection of verbal expression regarding all that has been done or spoken exactly as it was, with respect to the task of training all those to be converted.

The eradication of latent predispositions (*vāsanā-samudghāta*) refers to the perfection of the non-occurrence of physical and vocal gestures that indicate the remaining traces of the afflictive and cognitive obscurations in one who has become omniscient; this includes meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and other such qualities.

Great compassion consists of the meditative absorptions and so forth, perfected through dwelling in compassion that takes as its object all forms of uninterrupted suffering among all sentient beings belonging to the three realms.
The eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇikabuddhadharma) are as follows: the Tathāgata has no physical lapse, no vocal outcry,
and no loss of mindfulness.
There is no unconcentrated mind,
there is no perception of diversity,
and there is no equanimity lacking discernment.
There is no decline of zeal, no decline of energy, and no decline of mindfulness.
There is no falling away from concentration, no falling away from wisdom,
and no falling away from liberation.

All the bodily actions of the Tathāgata are preceded by knowledge and follow after knowledge; all his verbal actions are preceded by knowledge and follow after knowledge; all his mental actions are preceded by knowledge and follow after knowledge.
Unattached and unimpeded knowledge regarding the past time, unattached and unimpeded knowledge regarding the future time, and unattached and unimpeded knowledge regarding the present time.
Furthermore, their systematic arrangement is as follows:
for example, an Arhat monk whose outflows are exhausted, while wandering for alms in a village, might once encounter a fierce elephant;
and just as with a fierce elephant, so it is with a fierce horse. (Abhidh-s-bh 132)
With a fierce cow or a fierce dog;
or he crushes a thicket or a thorny fence.
Or he steps upon a water-snake with his feet;
or he enters such a house where a woman invites him with improper conduct;
or again, having left the path in the forest, he goes by a wrong path.

An Arhat Tathāgata has no such lapses whatsoever— such as encountering thieves or bandits, or lions, tigers, or other wild beasts. Furthermore, this Arhat, while once wandering in a forest glade, might stray from the path, enter an empty dwelling,
and utter a sound or raise his voice.
He utters a great roar;
driven by the fault of latent tendencies (*vāsanā*), he laughs a defiled, loud laugh, baring his teeth and displaying a leer.
In this way, such a state of agitation exists for an arhat, but for a Tathāgata, it does not exist in any way whatsoever.

A Tathāgata has no loss of mindfulness; he possesses the quality of recollecting things done long ago and spoken long ago without any defilement. Furthermore, an arhat is concentrated when in meditative absorption and unconcentrated when emerged from it.
For the Tathāgata, however, there is no state in which his mind is not in meditative equipoise.
Furthermore, while an Arhat exclusively perceives the substrate (upadhi) as something to be renounced and perceives the substrate-less Nirvana as peace,
the Tathāgata has no perception of diversity regarding either the substrate or Nirvana.
This is based on his dwelling in supreme equanimity.
Furthermore, an Arhat may neglect the welfare of sentient beings through a lack of analytical discernment;
however, for a Tathāgata, there is no such neglect resulting from a lack of analytical discernment.

Furthermore, an Arhat, with respect to the purification of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), may fall away from what has not yet been attained; he may fall away even from zeal (*chanda*), vigor (*vīrya*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), liberation (*vimukti*), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuktijñānadarśana*).
Such sevenfold falling away does not exist for a Tathāgata.
Furthermore, an Arhat at one time engages in wholesome bodily action, and at another time in neutral action;
as it is with bodily action, so it is with vocal action and mental action.

Because all three types of actions of the Tathāgata are preceded by knowledge and follow after knowledge, there is no indeterminate (avyākṛta) action for him; in this regard, they are "preceded by knowledge" by virtue of being originated by knowledge, and they are "following after knowledge" by virtue of accompanying knowledge.
Furthermore, an Arhat does not comprehend the objects of knowledge belonging to the three times merely through the act of attention, whereby his knowledge and vision become obstructed.
Nor does he comprehend everything in such a way that his knowledge and vision would be obstructed;
rather, the Tathāgata comprehends every object through mere mental attention regarding the three times.
Therefore, these are called the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*aṣṭādaśāveṇikabuddhadharma*).

Among these, the first six—concentration and the others—are for the perfection of the purification of uncommon bodily, vocal, and mental actions. Therein, "there is no stumbling" refers to the purification of bodily action; "there is no clamor" refers to the purification of vocal action.

In this regard, the absence of loss of mindfulness, the absence of an unconcentrated mind, the absence of perception of diversity, and the absence of equanimity without discernment—this tetrad is to be understood with reference to the purification of mental action.

Furthermore, the absence of decline in zeal, up to the absence of decline in the knowledge and vision of liberation, refers to the perfection of the non-attainment and non-decline of the Tathāgata’s faculties together with their bases and fruits; herein, concentration and the other [qualities] are present.
In this context, the basis is aspiration;
the fruit is liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation;
and the faculties are to be understood as diligence and the others.

All bodily action, vocal action, and mental action are preceded by knowledge and follow after knowledge; these three are the meditative absorptions (samādhi) and so forth for the perfection of the uncommon course of action.

Knowledge that is unattached and unimpeded regarding the past, up to and including the present time—these three are the meditative absorptions (samādhi) and so forth for the perfection of the uncommon dwelling in knowledge.

"In the accomplishment of the knowledge of all aspects regarding the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields" means: in the perfection of the knowledge that reaches the ultimate limit of the distinctions between the individual characteristics and specific qualities of the aggregates and so forth.
Furthermore, their actualization (*abhinirhāra*) is elucidated by way of their basis, the person who actualizes them, and the method of actualization.

The method of actualization, moreover, means the frequent mental engagement (*manaskāra-bahulīkāratā*) according to their formal arrangement; that is to say, for one whose mind is concentrated, it is the repeated fixing of the mind upon that [object] in accordance with the instruction.

For example, one desiring to actualize the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), relying on meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), cultivates, attends to, and frequently practices the instruction beginning with "with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness (*maitrī*), free from enmity, free from rivalry," and so forth.

In the same way, one who desires to bring forth the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and so forth should apply the practice as follows: by attending to the established principle that "having been one, one becomes many," and so on, one cultivates it through repeated practice.
These qualities, beginning with the immeasurables, are of two kinds:
those that manifest as their own specific functions, by which the Noble One performs activities such as the abandonment of opposing factors as appropriate;

and those that pertain to dwelling, by which—being comprised within the supremely tranquil non-conceptual gnosis—he dwells in happiness in the present life through the objectless immeasurables and so forth.

In that regard, it abandons its opposites through the immeasurables respectively: ill-will (*vyāpāda*), harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*), discontent (*aratimati*), and both attachment (*anunaya*) and aversion (*pratigha*).
These four immeasurables are called "compassion" (*anukampā*), because by means of them one acts in accordance with what is suitable for the benefit of sentient beings.

Therefore, dwelling among them with a mind abiding in compassion for all sentient beings, he fulfills the equipment of merit; for this very reason, he does not grow weary in the ripening of sentient beings,
because, through his compassion for all beings, he is indifferent to his own self.
(Abhidh-s-bh 134) Among the liberations, one accomplishes the work of emanation by means of two liberations;
by the third, one is not defiled while creating pure emanations.
By means of the four noble liberations, one does not cling to peaceful liberations;
by means of the final, supremely peaceful noble dwelling, one dwells therein.
Liberation should be understood as having the sense of resolve in such and such a manner.
The function of the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and so forth should be applied in the same manner as before, according to their respective explanations.

One becomes a speaker whose words are to be accepted because of the absence of conflict, due to speaking in accordance with what is appropriate through the primary concern for protecting the minds of others.
And by means of the knowledge resulting from aspiration, one becomes highly esteemed by the world,
because one is held in reverence for knowing everything.
Through the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), he satisfies the minds of sentient beings by means of teaching,
because he cuts through their doubts in many diverse ways.

By means of the supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) of psychic power, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of former abodes, death and rebirth, and the destruction of the outflows, one wins over [beings] to the Teaching through bodily action and so forth, respectively.
It should be understood that through the supernormal knowledge of the divine ear, one wins them over by verbal action because of the comprehension of all varieties of sounds.

With respect to the purification of the basis (*āśraya-pariśuddhi*), three [aspects] are to be understood: the intentional assumption of birth in existence (*saṃcintya-bhavopapatti*), the taking up [of a body], and the relinquishing of the basis, according to one's will;
with respect to the purification of the object (*ālambana-pariśuddhi*), one becomes a master of the dharmas;
and with respect to the purification of the mind (*citta-pariśuddhi*), one becomes a master of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Through the purification of knowledge, one upholds the true Dharma.

By means of two powers among the [ten] powers, the Blessed Buddhas teach the path to prosperity (*abhyudaya-mārga*), and by the remaining [eight], they teach the path to the ultimate good (*niḥśreyasa-mārga*); this much is the duty of the Blessed Buddhas.

In that regard, by the power of knowing what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*), the Blessed One refutes the doctrine of causelessness (*ahetu-vāda*) and the doctrine of irregular causes (*viṣama-hetu-vāda*), such as [the claim] that prosperity is without cause or has nature (*prakṛti*), Īśvara, and so forth, as its cause.

By the power of knowing that beings are the owners of their own karma (*karmasvakatā-jñānabala*), he refutes the doctrine of experiencing the results of actions not performed (*akṛtābhyāgama-vāda*), [namely] that karma comes upon one even though it was not personally committed.
For he teaches the path to a happy rebirth correctly and without error;
by the power of knowledge regarding the meditations, liberations, concentrations, and attainments, he penetrates the mental conduct and the movements of the minds of sentient beings;
and by the power of knowledge regarding the superior and inferior faculties, he penetrates their fitness as vessels for the teaching and the ripening of their faculties, such as faith.
By the power of the knowledge of various inclinations, he penetrates the disposition [of beings], whether their inclination be inferior or sublime.
By the power of the knowledge of various elements, he penetrates the state of afflictions that can be eradicated through the destruction of their latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
By the power of the knowledge of the paths leading everywhere, he penetrates the objective support—whether it be the Śrāvaka Vehicle or the Mahāyāna—and the Dharma comprised within the taught Dharma.

By means of the power of the knowledge that recollects past lives (*pūrvenivāsānusmṛtijñānabala*), one penetrates the causal basis for the noble path (*āryamārgahetu*) contained within the accumulation of merits from previous births.
By the power of the knowledge of death and rebirth, one penetrates into the future destiny;
by the power of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows, one penetrates into the departure from the entire triple world, since one thereby teaches the path to liberation exactly as it is.

Furthermore, their power consists in the specific manner of subduing the Māras— the Māra of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*), the Māra of the afflictions (*kleśamāra*), and the Māra of the son of a god (*devaputramāra*). Moreover, this superiority arises because they act as an immediate obstacle even to the abandonment of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*),
and because there is no failure in answering questions posed regarding all topics— from what is possible and impossible up to the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
By means of the grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*), he establishes his own status as a Teacher within the assembly and his commitment to the welfare of both himself and others;
furthermore, he refutes challengers—from those concerning his perfect enlightenment down to the path—by means of the Dharma, including the non-Buddhist teachers.
Through the foundations of mindfulness, he leads the assembly without defilement,
because there is an absence of afflictions such as attachment toward those who wish to listen and so forth.
He constantly exhorts and instructs the community with things that need no protection,
because there is no fear of exposing his own faults, as he has nothing to protect.
By virtue of his quality of non-forgetfulness, he does not neglect the work of a Buddha,
for he does not allow even a moment to pass through negligence when the task of benefiting sentient beings is at hand.

Through the complete eradication of latent tendencies (*vāsanā*), one who is free from afflictions (*niḥkleśa*) does not display any movement resembling an affliction, such as the stumbling and so forth that an Arhat monk might display.
By means of great compassion, he surveys the world six times during the day and night, because he examines it in such ways as: "Who is declining? Who is falling away? and so forth.

This should be applied according to the section on the exposition of characteristics, such as: "the karma of the unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇikabuddhadharma) [is for] the perfection of the purity of uncommon actions of body, speech, and mind."
Through the knowledge of all modes, he cuts through all the doubts of all sentient beings because his knowledge is unimpeded in all respects;
and he establishes the guide of the Dharma for a long time.
Because the compilers have sequentially established the designations for the Dharma-discourses taught in various places for the purpose of cutting through the doubts of those to be trained;
by relying on this guidance of the Dharma, unripened sentient beings are brought to maturity, and those already ripened are liberated.

Upon the attainment of a superior path, there is the abandonment of the inferior path; for example, when the path comprised within the fruit is attained, the path of the candidate (*pratipannaka-mārga*) is said to be abandoned because it is no longer manifested. Furthermore, at the time of attaining the fruit, one realizes the complete abandonment [of defilements], because through the attainment of a specific transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*), there is the total abandonment of the functional rigidity (*dauṣṭhulya*) consisting of the counteragents to those afflictions belonging to the class of the opposites [of that fruit].
"By abandoning through relinquishment" means that he abandons it such that it never again manifests;
however, a bodhisattva does not abandon it in that way, because his path is preceded by the intention to bring all sentient beings to parinirvāṇa.

For this very reason, Bodhisattvas are said to possess inexhaustible roots of virtue and inexhaustible qualities; as it is stated in the *Sūtra*: "Just as with the word 'akṣa,' inexhaustibility is indicated."

Regarding questions such as whether the world is eternal or non-eternal, the classification of these as indeterminate matters (*avyākṛta-vastu*) is due to their being unreasoned (*ayoniśas*) and not conducive to the goal.
Furthermore, what kind of question among those various questions is conducive to the goal?
For example, any question concerning the four noble truths (*catvāry āryasatyāni*).
For it is thus: it is included within the contemplation of cause, fruit, affliction, and purification.

Even upon entering the state of certainty (*nyāmāvakrānti*), a bodhisattva is not established as a stream-enterer (*śrotāpanna*), because they have attained a non-abiding path and, on account of their practice being unestablished, they move against the current.
The object of knowledge is sixfold: error, up to and including the outflow of non-error. Among these, error is the adherence to the grasped and the grasper.

The basis of error is that within the sphere of noble gnosis—which consists merely of the signs of conditioned phenomena and is of the nature of unreal imagination—wherein this adherence of the foolish proceeds.
Suchness (*tathatā*) is the basis for non-delusion, because it is the foundation for non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
The wholesome factors consisting of hearing and so forth (*śrutamayī* etc. are conducive to both delusion and non-delusion, as well as to supramundane knowledge (*lokottara-jñāna*).
Because it is free from conceptualization regarding the objects of knowledge and because it is conducive to non-conceptual gnosis,
non-erroneousness is non-conceptual gnosis.
The outflow of non-erroneousness consists of the wholesome factors acquired subsequent to the noble path.
Furthermore, skill in means is fourfold:
skill in maturing sentient beings consists of the four bases of sympathy, because by means of them one gathers [beings] and establishes them in wholesome qualities.
