The skill in fulfilling the qualities of a Buddha (*buddhadharma*) is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), because of the statement:

"A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fulfill everything from the perfection of giving up to the knowledge of all aspects in their excellence (*sarvākāravarajñatā*) should train in this very perfection of wisdom.

Skill in swift superknowledge (*abhijñā*) consists of the confession of misdeeds, rejoicing in merit, requesting the Buddhas [to teach], and the dedication of roots of goodness six times during the day and night, as described respectively in the *Āryamaitreyaparipṛcchā*.

Skill in the non-interruption of phenomena consists in the non-abiding nirvana, whereby the Buddha’s and bodhisattvas’ conduct is displayed throughout all world-systems in every direction, according to those to be trained, without ceasing again and again and for all time.
Thus, unreal imagination is tenfold.
Among these, root-discrimination is the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
Because it serves as the seed for all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*):

the conceptualization of signs (*nimitta-vikalpa*) consists of the representations appearing as the body, the dwelling place, and objects of enjoyment, because they constitute the objective signs (*grāhya-nimitta*).
Furthermore, these should be understood as having, respectively, the characteristics of the material sense-faculties, the receptacle world, and the objects such as form;
the conceptualization of the appearance of signs consists of the six groups of consciousness and the mind, because they take on the forms of the signs of the aforementioned objects of apprehension.
The conceptualization of the transformation of signs (*nimitta-vikāra-vikalpa*) is the arising of the aforementioned signs of the body and so forth in an altered state.

The conceptualization of the transformation of the appearance of signs (*nimitta-pratibhāsa-vikāra-vikalpa*) is the arising of the aforementioned appearance of signs such as visual consciousness in another state, such as pleasure and so forth.
Conceptualization brought about by others (*paropanīta-vikalpa*) is characterized by the collection of names, phrases, and phonemes included within the teaching.
Furthermore, that [discrimination] is of two kinds: that which consists of a poorly proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, and that which consists of a well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya.

Therefore, it should be understood that the discrimination of proper application (*yoniśo-vikalpa*) and the discrimination of improper application (*ayoniśo-vikalpa*) are respectively subsumed under the mental attention governed by those two.
The discrimination of adherence (*abhiniveśa-vikalpa*) is that discrimination which, arising from the discrimination of improper application, is comprised within the sixty-two types of views.
The conceptualization of distraction is that conceptualization characterized by the grasping at non-existence and so forth, which arises from improper conceptualization.
Furthermore, it is of ten kinds: the conceptualization of non-existence, up to the conceptualization of names according to their referents.
These ten kinds of conceptualization are to be understood with reference to the teaching of the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other texts, as it is said:
"In this regard, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva, while being truly a bodhisattva, does not perceive a bodhisattva."
One does not perceive a so-called "bodhisattva";
one does not perceive the perfection of wisdom;
one does not perceive awakening.
He does not perceive that "he practices," nor does he perceive that "he does not practice";
for indeed, it is empty by way of its own-being, not by way of emptiness.
Form is empty of intrinsic nature, not because of emptiness; up to and including consciousness, it is empty of intrinsic nature, not because of emptiness.
Why is that? That which is the emptiness of form is not that form.
Nor is emptiness elsewhere than form; form itself is emptiness.
Emptiness itself is form;
likewise, it extends up to consciousness.
Why is that?
This is merely a name, namely: the name "Bodhisattva," "Bodhisattva" itself, "perfection of wisdom," "awakening," and so on, up to "form" and "consciousness.

For intrinsic nature has neither arising nor cessation, neither defilement nor purification. Practicing in the perfection of wisdom, a bodhisattva does not perceive even arising, nor does he perceive even purification, up to [the absence of] purification.
For what reason?
Those phenomena are each conceptually constructed as artificial names; they are conventionally designated by adventitious names.
In whatever way they are conventionally designated, in that very way they become attached to them.
The Bodhisattva does not perceive any of those names;
not perceiving them, he does not become attached.
In that regard, as an antidote to the conceptualization of non-existence, it says: "The Bodhisattva, being truly a Bodhisattva," and so forth.

Because the word "real" (sat) has the sense of "existence," [the text] speaks as an antidote to the conceptualization of existence: "He does not perceive a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive anything up to purification, nor does he perceive that 'he does not practice,' because of the negation of the existence of persons and phenomena.
Then, as an antidote to the conceptualization of superimposition, it says: "For indeed, name is empty of intrinsic nature."
Because the intrinsic nature of unreal imagination is negated,
he says "not by emptiness" as an antidote to the conceptualization of denial;
for that name always exists as being devoid of that imagined nature which was imagined by it.
He speaks by way of the antidote to the conceptualization of oneness: "That which is the emptiness of form is not that form," and so on up to consciousness, because they are distinct entities.
For form and the others are the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), whereas emptiness is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*).

As an antidote to the conceptualization of separateness, he says: "Nor is form other than emptiness; up to: emptiness itself is consciousness," because the imagined nature lacks defining characteristics and because its existence is impossible apart from that [emptiness].

As an antidote to the conceptualization of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*), he says: "This is mere name, namely, 'form' up to 'consciousness'," because apart from verbal expression (*abhilāpa*), there is no existence of an expressible intrinsic nature.
As an antidote to the conceptualization of specific qualities (*viśeṣa-vikalpa*), he says: "He does not perceive the arising of an intrinsic nature, nor even its purification."

Because of the negation of specific characteristics such as arising and so forth, he says—as an antidote to the conceptualization of objects according to their names: "Names are artificial; those phenomena are imagined one by one and are designated by adventitious names," and so on.

As an antidote to the conceptualization of names according to their literal meaning, he says: "The bodhisattva, not perceiving any of those names, does not adhere to them," because he neither perceives nor adheres to names as having a corresponding reality.
It is non-conceptual due to the three kinds of contentment, beginning with non-conceptual contentment.

In that regard, when ordinary persons— having taken up some aspect of reality such as impermanence and so forth, and having brought their minds to a conclusion— become satisfied and resolve, "It is thus," that state is characterized by the cessation of all conceptualization known as discursive reasoning (*vitarka*).
The Śrāvakas, as an antidote to the misconceptions of permanence and so forth regarding the aggregates, examine the dharmadhātu—form and the other factors—exactly as they are;
through supramundane gnosis, they penetrate selflessness. Therefore, that is called their non-conceptual state free from misconception.
The Bodhisattvas, however, having realized that even those mere phenomena such as form are conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), eliminate all signs of all phenomena.

Because they penetrate all-pervading suchness (*tathatā*) by means of supremely peaceful supramundane gnosis (*jñāna*), it is said that for them this is "the state free from conceptual proliferation and free from discursive thought" (*niṣprapañca-nirvikalpatā*).
But how, furthermore, is it said to be "free from conceptual proliferation and free from discursive thought"?
If it were by way of non-attention (*amanaskāra*), then it would follow that those who are asleep, intoxicated, and so forth, would possess a state free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpatā*),
because they do not attend to the signs of phenomena (*dharmanimitta*).
Alternatively, if it were by way of transcendence (*samatikrama*), then it would follow that there is a state free from conceptual construction everywhere from the second dhyāna onwards.

Because of the transcendence of the conceptual constructions of applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), there arises a contradiction with the statement that "the body of conceptual construction consists of the mind and mental factors belonging to the three realms.

Alternatively, if it is due to complete stillness (*vyupaśama*), then by that [stillness], the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāveditanirodhasamāpatti*) would result in a state of non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpatā*).
In that case, because of the cessation of the conceptual constructions of mind and mental factors,
it follows that there would be an absence of knowledge.
Alternatively, if by its very nature form were to attain non-conceptuality through that [knowledge], [then...]
Because its intrinsic nature is non-conceptual. Now, if there were a volitional formation (*abhisaṃskāra*) with respect to an object, then by that very fact it would become conceptual;
for this volitional formation "this is non-conceptual" is characterized by the conceptualization of signs (*nimitta*).
Therefore, non-conceptuality is not to be viewed through these modes;
rather, it is to be viewed as the absence of volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāratā*) with respect to the object of focus (*ālambana*).
How so?
For when this bodhisattva, having received conformable instruction, investigates how all signs of phenomena (*dharmanimitta*) are by nature unestablished,

and through the acquisition of the power of that repeated investigation, his mind becomes concentrated— without even volitional effort within himself— upon the suchness of all phenomena in the realm of non-proliferation (*niṣprapañca*) exactly as it is; that is called "non-conceptualization free from proliferation" (*niṣprapañcanirvikalpatā*).
It was stated previously that a bodhisattva is by nature one of sharp faculties; how then is it said that his faculties must be refined from time to time?
It should be understood that this refinement occurs through the successive production of higher stages, based on the threefold classification of weak and so forth among those of the same class.

Otherwise, if the faculties of those belonging to the lineage of sharp faculties were of a single uniform type, no distinction based on faculties would ever be observed among bodhisattvas; yet such a distinction is indeed observed.
The fifth compendium, titled "The Determination of Discourse" (*sāṃkathyaviniścaya*),

should be understood as concerning the determination of meaning within the sevenfold determination of discourse by way of the six meanings, beginning with the meaning of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvārtha*). Therein—
The three natures are the imagined nature, the dependent nature, and the perfected nature.
The meaning of "cause" refers to the three causes:
the cause of origination, as well as the causal, immediately preceding, objective, and dominant conditions,
because they bring about all conditioned phenomena.

The cause of occurrence (*pravṛtti-hetu*) is as follows: it is the sequence beginning with "conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces" (*avidyā-pratyayāḥ saṃskārāḥ*) up to "thus there is the origin and the cessation," because it is through this sequence that defilement (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*) proceed.

The cause of establishment (*siddhi-hetu*) is comprised of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), apprehension (*upalambha*), non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), and authoritative testimony (*samākhyāna*); for by means of these, an unestablished object to be proven (*sādhya*) is established.
The meaning of "fruit" refers to the five fruits:
the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*), such as the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*);
and the fruit of outflow (*niṣyandaphala*), such as the subsequent wholesome and other dharmas within that same continuum which arise from previously arisen wholesome and other dharmas.
The dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*) is, for example, the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) produced through the sovereign power of the collective karma of all sentient beings.

The fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) is, for example, crops and the like. The fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyogaphala*) is, for example, the eradication of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) by means of the Noble Path.
The meaning of "karma" is to be understood as before, namely, as in the exposition on the defilement of karma (*karmasaṃkleśa*).

The meaning of "yoga" consists of five types of yoga. First, collective yoga (*sāmūhika-yoga*), such as that of the wood, bricks, and so forth used for a house. Second, consequential yoga (*ānubandhika-yoga*), such as the cause consisting of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and so forth;
for when these exist, one is said to be "endowed with" (*yukta*) afflictions and the like, even if they are not currently manifesting.
Connection by relation (*sāmbandhika-yoga*) is, for example, the mutual connection among those born of the same lineage.
Connection by state (*āvasthika-yoga*) refers to the various states of the continuum, such as being favored;
for one existing in those states is said to be "endowed with happiness" up to "endowed with suffering or neither-suffering-nor-happiness."
The "transformative" (vaikārika) yoga is the manifestation of adventitious secondary afflictions and the like;
for when that is present, one is said to be "endowed with" passion and so forth, as well as faith and so forth.
The meaning of "functioning" (*vṛtti*) refers to the five functions.
The "functioning as characteristic" (*lakṣaṇavṛtti*) pertains to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), consisting of the three characteristics beginning with arising;
it is so called because [the conditioned] proceeds by way of those modes.
The function of abiding is the establishment of that which is supported within its support.
The function of perversion is the occurrence of defiled phenomena in a manner that does not correspond to reality.
The occurrence of non-perversion pertains to the dharmas of purification;
the occurrence of differentiation pertains to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), because they proceed through various modes such as past, future, and present, or internal and external.

The *Vyākhyāviniścaya* (Ascertainment of Exegesis) is that by which one explains the meaning of the sūtras; it does so by demonstrating, according to each sūtra and as appropriate, six types of meanings, beginning with the objects to be fully known (*parijñeya-vastu*). Among these, the object to be fully known consists of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth.
The object to be fully known is impermanence and so forth;
the proximate cause for full knowledge is the guarding of the doors of the sense faculties through ethical discipline and so forth;
and full knowledge consists of the factors conducive to awakening.
The fruit of full comprehension is liberation;
the clear realization of that is the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Furthermore, there are indeed fourteen aspects of exposition.

The "Gateway of the Compendium of Explanations" is that wherein the origin and purpose of the Sūtra, the meaning of its words, the thematic connection, the underlying intention, and the resolution of objections are described.
The gateway of the compendium of entities (*vastusaṃgrahamukha*) is that wherein the gateway of the sūtras is set forth in relation to the trainings, the noble truths, the entities, and so forth;
for example, the three verses beginning with "The non-doing of all evil," which are taught with reference to the trainings, and so on.
The "face of the primary and secondary members" (*aṅgopāṅgamukha*) is that wherein a summary is presented by one word, while the detailed exposition is shown by the remaining words.

For example, in the teaching on the twelvefold conjunction of conditions (*dvādaśāṅgapratītyasamutpāda*), there is a summary stating "perfection of oneself and perfection of others," and these two are then respectively explained in detail by the five subsequent phrases for each.
The gateway of successive accomplishment is that wherein it is demonstrated how these very dharmas are taught as the basis for the successive accomplishment of each subsequent stage;
for example, the five faculties.
For instance, one who possesses faith initiates vigor.
For one who has initiated vigor, mindfulness becomes established;
for one whose mindfulness is established, the mind becomes concentrated;
and for one whose mind is concentrated, they understand things as they truly are.
The "gateway of refutation" is that wherein, having introduced a certain subject, its refutation is demonstrated.
For example, in the *Vāsyopamya-sūtra*, with reference to the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), four types of persons are refuted:
one who is outside this Dharma; one who belongs to this Dharma but is satisfied merely with hearing and reflection; one who is weary of cultivation; and one whose equipment is incomplete.
By the passage from the sutra beginning with "O monks, for one who knows and sees, I declare the destruction of the outflows," the first type of person is refuted;
by the passage beginning with "for one devoted to the practice of cultivation," the second;
and by the simile of the raft, the third.
And the fourth [member] is not stated by way of an example.
(Abhidh-s-bh 143) The method of the transformation of syllables (*akṣaraparīṇāma*) is that where syllables well-known in one sense are transformed into another;
for example, in the verse: "One who is faithless and ungrateful... [and so forth].
Therein, the aspects of destruction and non-destruction, as well as perishing, non-perishing, the means for both, and the distinctions between both, are demonstrated.

For example, in the *Sujāta-sūtra*, "perishing" (*praṇāśa*) refers to attachment to external and internal acquisitions (*upadhi*). Among these, external acquisition is characterized by such things as house, wife, and so forth; [internal acquisition is characterized by the aggregates].
The internal [destruction] has the characteristic of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*).
Non-destruction is the cessation of attachment to both of these.
The means of destruction are: not going forth into homelessness, and for one who has gone forth, negligence regarding the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).

The means for non-destruction should be understood as the opposite [of the aforementioned]. In this regard, it is said: "Ah, this well-born son of good family shines forth from both sides: on the one hand, because he has shaved off his hair and beard and gone forth [into homelessness], and on the other, because through the destruction of the outflows (āsrava), he understands up to [the realization that] 'I know'. By this teaching of non-destruction and its means, the destruction and its means—characterized as being the opposite of those—are indicated.
The classification of non-perishing is shown by means of verses in song: "O, how this monk shines—tranquil and free from outflows!
Thus, both renunciation and the destruction of the outflows have been elucidated.
Furthermore, that destruction of the outflows—
Free from passion, detached, and extinguished through non-clinging,
he maintains this final body after having conquered the army of Māra.
By this [it is shown]: through detachment by means of the mundane path;
through the abandonment of the fetters pertaining to the lower realm by means of the supramundane path;
and through the abandonment of the fetters pertaining to the higher realm.
It is elucidated by way of the abandonment of internal acquisitions (*ādhyātmikopadhi*).
This exposition should be understood as pertaining to the cessation of cause and fruit;
conversely, the various types of ruin (*praṇāśaprabheda*) should be seen as indicated by the opposite of this.
The section on the classification of persons (*pudgalavyavasthānamukha*) demonstrates that this teaching was spoken with reference to a specific number of persons.

For example, in the *Audakopama-sūtra*, it is taught with reference to two types of persons, further divided into three or four categories: the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and one who has seen the truth (*dṛṣṭasatya*).
The ordinary person is of three types: the non-white, the slightly white, and the largely white.
Those who have seen the truth are of four types: the four who are practicing for the fruits and the four who abide in the fruits; three of these are those still in training (śaikṣa).
One is the one beyond training.
The gateway of the formal establishment of distinctions (*prabhedavyavasthānamukha*) is that wherein the meaning is described by means of questions such as the fourfold alternatives (*catuṣkoṭika*).
For example, in the *Anityasūtra*: "Whoever perceives this 'existent'—does everyone such a person perceive form?"
Regarding the statement, "Whoever perceives form, all such persons perceive this as existing," there is a fourfold logical alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*).

The first alternative refers to one who perceives the four aggregates beginning with feeling—without superimposing the distortions (*viparyāsa*) of permanence, purity, pleasure, and self—and perceives them as things to be fully understood and abandoned.

The second alternative refers to one who perceives form by superimposing the distortions of permanence, purity, pleasure, and self, and perceives it as something not to be fully understood or abandoned.

The third alternative pertains to one who, without superimposing the perversions of permanence, purity, pleasure, and self upon form, perceives it as something to be fully understood and abandoned; the fourth alternative pertains to one who, having superimposed the perversions of permanence, purity, pleasure, and self upon the four aggregates beginning with sensation, perceives them as not to be fully understood and not to be abandoned.

Just as it is with the fourfold alternative regarding form, so it should be understood in detail for all [aggregates] beginning with feeling, up to: "For whom what was to be done has been done, he understands there is no further existence beyond this;
for one who understands there is no further existence beyond this, for him everything that was to be done has been accomplished."
He said: there are four alternatives.
The first alternative is that of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who practices good conduct throughout his life. The second is that of those who hold views such as nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).
The third [alternative] refers to one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
The fourth [alternative] is established by excluding those modes (ākāra).

The "Entrance to Method" (*nayamukha*) is that wherein the meaning is described by means of six methods: the method of the true meaning (*tattvārthanaya*), the method of attainment (*prāptinaya*), the method of teaching (*deśanānaya*), the method of avoiding the two extremes (*antadvayavivarjanānaya*), the method of the inconceivable (*acintyanaya*), and the method of intention (*abhiprāyanaya*).
Among these six methods, the first three are to be understood respectively through the latter three methods.

For example, in the *Āsvādanasūtra*, by stating, "O monks, there is enjoyment (*āsvāda*) in form," and so forth, the method of the true meaning is elucidated, having avoided both the extreme of denial (*apavādānta*) and the extreme of superimposition (*samāropānta*).
By stating "there is gratification, there is danger, there is an escape," the extreme of denial (*apavādānta*) is avoided;
by stating "from form up to consciousness," the extreme of superimposition (*samāropānta*) is avoided;

and by demonstrating that defilement and purification reside in the mere aggregates (*skandhamātra*) and not in a self (*anātman*), [the Buddha] said, "O monks, as long as... up to the unsurpassed..."
By the statement "I have realized full and perfect awakening," the method of attainment (*prāptinaya*) is elucidated through the inconceivable method (*acintyanaya*),
because it indicates an realization to be personally experienced within oneself (*pratyātmavedanīya*). This entire sutra, moreover, is the method of teaching (*deśanānaya*).
And that intention is to be understood;
it is the object to be fully known and the meaning to be fully known.
This sutra was spoken with reference to full comprehension, the fruit of full comprehension, and the proclamation thereof.

In this context, the thing to be fully understood (*parijñeya-vastu*) consists of form (*rūpa*) and so forth; the meaning to be fully understood (*parijñeyārtha*) consists of its relish (*āsvāda*) and so forth,
because that thing— form and so forth— is fully understood by way of those aspects.
This is the thorough knowledge of these five aggregates of clinging through three revolutions, which is the knowledge of things as they truly are.
The fruit of this thorough knowledge is the liberation of wisdom—from this world with its devas, up to the world with its devas, humans, and asuras—up to complete deliverance.
Through the realization of that, I directly knew: "I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

(Abhidh-s-bh 145) The entrance of thorough knowledge and so forth is that wherein, starting from the characteristic of reality, there is [an exposition] by way of the characteristic of thorough knowledge, the characteristic of abandonment, and—
By means of the characteristic of direct realization;
by means of the characteristic of the various modes of these very [topics] such as the characteristic of reality;
and by means of the characteristic of the relationship between the basis and that which is based upon it.

The meaning is explained by means of the characteristics of obstructive factors regarding thorough knowledge and so forth, the characteristics of factors that are in accordance with the natural order, and the characteristics of the disadvantages and benefits regarding the lack of thorough knowledge and so forth.
For example, as in this very *Āsvādanasūtra*:
therein, the characteristic of reality is the truth of suffering comprised within the aggregates of clinging;
the characteristic of full comprehension is the thorough knowledge of that very [suffering] as it truly is, by way of its gratification and so forth.
Full comprehension;

the characteristic of abandonment and the characteristic of realization, which is liberation from the entire world through the direct realization of the transformation of the basis upon the abandonment of obscurations; and the characteristic of cultivation, which is dwelling extensively with a mind free from cognitive distortions.
The characteristic of the distinction of types consists of the fivefold division of the characteristic of reality, from form up to consciousness.
The characteristic of thorough knowledge has a threefold division: one knows as it truly is the relishing of what is relished, up to the departure from what is departed from.
The characteristic of abandonment and the characteristic of realization each have a twofold division: liberation from the afflictions and liberation from suffering.

In this context, there is liberation from the afflictions for the world including its gods, up to the entire generation including gods and humans; therefore, for the sake of specifying that very point, he says "emerged" (*niḥsṛta*).
For as it is said elsewhere in a sutra: "What is emergence?
It is the disciplining of desire and passion, the abandoning of desire and passion, and the transcending of desire and passion."

Thus, when there is dissociation from the afflictions that produce future suffering, one becomes liberated even from suffering; for the sake of this distinction, he says, "dissociated" and "liberated.
There is a twofold division of the characteristic of cultivation: the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Among these, by the phrase "with a mind free from distortions," he indicates the path of seeing.
By the phrase "I have dwelt extensively," the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is indicated;

for this suggests that the successive [stages] beginning with the characteristic of reality (*tattvalakṣaṇa*) serve as the basis (*āśraya*) for those that follow, characterized by the relationship between the basis and what is based upon it.

Furthermore, the characteristic of being an obstacle to thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) and so forth is likewise the non-thorough knowledge (*aparijñāna*) of things as they truly are, according to the three turnings (*triparivarta*).

The characteristic of conformity (*anulomika-lakṣaṇa*) is the investigation of these very things—form and so forth—from the perspective of their gratification (*āsvāda*) and so on, according to how they are established.
The characteristic of fault (*ādīnava-lakṣaṇa*) consists in non-thorough knowledge and so forth, up to the lack of liberation and the lack of awakening to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
It should be understood that the characteristic of benefit (*anuśaṃsa-lakṣaṇa*) is the opposite of this.

The aspect of relative strength and weakness (*balābala-mukha*) is that wherein, if even a single word were not uttered, this meaning would not be conveyed; thus, the efficacy of every individual word is demonstrated.

For example, in this *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*: "When this exists, that comes to be; from the arising of this, that arises—namely, with ignorance as condition, the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) arise," and so forth.
The individual significance of these terms should be understood as before, just as in the explanation of the characteristics of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
The entrance of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) is that wherein, having taken up a single word from a sutra, its meaning is explained in detail.
For example: "A monk endowed with six qualities could, by the breath from his mouth, shake even Himavat, the king of mountains."
How much more so, then, regarding ignorance together with its latent tendencies?
By which six [qualities]?
Here, monks, a monk is skilled in the arising of the mind; here, a monk, secluded from sensual desires, attains and dwells in the fourth dhyāna.
In this way, a monk becomes skilled in the arising of the mind.
And how does a monk become skilled in the stability of the mind?
Here, through the sequence of cultivation, a monk transforms that meditative absorption which belongs to the side of decline into one that belongs to the side of stability.
In this way, a monk becomes skilled in stability.
And how does a monk become skilled in emergence?
Here, through the sequence of cultivation, a monk transforms that meditative absorption which pertains to stability into one that pertains to distinction.
In this way, a monk becomes skilled in emergence.
And how does a monk become skilled in application?
Here, a monk [exerts himself] for the sake of unarisen wholesome states, and so on in detail; these are the two right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).
In this way, a monk becomes skilled regarding the acquisitions.
And how does a monk become skilled regarding the states of woe?
Here, a monk [exerts himself] for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states, and so forth; thus, in detail, there are two right abandonments.
In this way, a monk becomes skilled in the unfavorable states.
How does a monk become skilled in the favorable means?
Here, a monk cultivates the basis of psychic power endowed with concentration of desire and the formative forces of exertion; thus, in detail, are the four bases of psychic power.
For in this way, a monk becomes skillful in means.
The "gateway of accomplishment" (*abhinirhāramukha*) is that in which each successive step is explained by means of sets of four and so forth.
Within those very sets of four and so forth, it should be understood that each individual term has an infinite accomplishment through further sets of four and so forth.
For example, in the *Buddhākṣepasūtra*: "These four are the qualities that purify the enlightenment of bodhisattvas: the cultivation of emptiness..."
It consists of an unimpeded mind toward all sentient beings,
the constant bringing about of benefit for bodhisattvas, and the thorough proclamation of the gift of Dharma with a mind free from worldly motives.
This set of four should be understood as the antidotes to the four opposing factors for the sake of purifying enlightenment, starting from one's own welfare and the ultimate truth.
The four opposing factors are: relishing meditative attainments (*samāpatti-āsvādana*), ill-will (*vyāpāda*), [laziness], and [distraction].
Pride and craving for gain and honor.
Another interpretation: by the first quality, the antidote for the abandonment of afflictions is shown;

by the remaining three reasons, the avoidance of the Lesser Vehicle is elucidated: through the adoption of all sentient beings by means of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), and through the ripening of those who have entered [the path].
And by means of causing those who have not entered [the path] to enter.

Another interpretation: by the first [verse], the accumulation of knowledge (*jñāna-saṃbhāra*) is illuminated; by the three [verses] concerning grasping, maturation, and introduction, the accumulation of merit (*puṇya-saṃbhāra*) is illuminated, because each produces a specific excellence of merit.
Furthermore, it is by two causes: by way of intention, through a mind of loving-kindness;
and by way of practice, through both the realization of what has been attained and the instruction of the scriptures.

Endowed with four qualities, bodhisattvas cultivate emptiness: through the non-fluctuation of the internal mind; through the application of the power of resolute conviction and analytical investigation;
through the penetration of the true nature of all phenomena;
and through liberation from all obscurations.
That upon what they rely and how they cultivate [the path] has been elucidated by this.
Relying on what? On the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).
How do they cultivate it?
By means of the path of ordinary beings through the empowerment of the powers of hearing and reflection, and by means of the path of learners and the path of no-more-learners.

Endowed with four qualities, bodhisattvas possess minds that are unimpeded toward all sentient beings: through the cultivation of loving-kindness, through non-disturbance in practice, and through non-conceptualization of signs.
And because of their inability to endure weariness;
here too, it is illuminated what they rely upon and how they come to have an unimpeded mind.
Relying on what?
[They cultivate] the cultivation of friendliness from previous lives.
How do they become unobstructed in mind? By not disturbing their own minds toward those who abide in wrong practice.
By not conceptualizing the cause of harm toward those who have caused injury,
and by being untiring in one's exertion for the sake of the welfare of others.
Endowed with four qualities, bodhisattvas always provide benefit to other bodhisattvas: by means of self-examination,
by means of imparting correct instruction,
and by means of being pleasant and agreeable to live with.
And by means of providing worship, gain, honor, and service; herein too, that upon what basis and in what manner one provides these is elucidated. Upon what basis?
How does he bring about the state of having destroyed pride?
As it has been said, by means of three modes, respectively for bodhisattvas who are inferior, equal, and superior.

Endowed with four qualities, Bodhisattvas proclaim the gift of Dharma with a mind free from worldly desire: by means of penetrating the ease that lies in the absence of obstacles, by skill in removing the lethargy of delusion, and by delighting in the Dharma that acts as a protector.
Here too, that upon which they rely and how they reveal it has been elucidated. Upon what do they rely?
How do they reveal the realization that gain and honor act as obstacles? By means of instruction for those who are deluded.
By means of instigating and inciting those who are dejected due to attachment to negligence or self-contempt;
by means of gladdening those who have correctly entered the path;
and by means of naturally delighting in the Dharma.
The accomplishment of the first [perfection] should be understood through the differentiation of its terms and so forth by means of the other fourfold set.

(Abhidh-s-bh 148) *Prabhidyasaṃdarśanaviniścaya* (the determination through detailed exposition) refers to [questions concerning] the phenomena such as the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, as previously specified, according to their respective applications, beginning with those that range over a single category (*ekāvacāraka*). In this context:

a "question ranging over a single category" is one by which, having questioned one phenomenon individually in conjunction with the remaining ones, and having set that aside, one questions the second [phenomenon] in conjunction with that [first] and the others, and so on for each one individually.
He asks all [the following questions]:
namely, "Is one who is endowed with the sense-base of the eye also endowed with the sense-base of visible form?
or "Is one who is endowed with the sense-base of visible form also endowed with the sense-base of the eye? This is the first part of the formulation (*pūrvapādaka*).
Regarding the question, "Is one who is endowed with the sense-base of the eye also endowed with the sense-base of the ear? there is a fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika).

In this manner, up to the question, "Is he also endowed with the sense-base of the mind? it should be applied accordingly. Regarding the question, "Is he also endowed with the sense-base of mental objects (dharmāyatana)? the first alternative (pūrvapādaka) applies.

Whoever is endowed with the sphere of visible form is also endowed with the sphere of the eye, or whoever is endowed with the sphere of the eye is also endowed with the sphere of visible form; this is the "subsequent member" (paścātpādaka).
Furthermore, whoever is endowed with the sphere of visible form is also endowed with the sphere of the ear; here too, this is the "subsequent member."

In this manner, the same should be applied accordingly up to the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*). Regarding the question, "Is one who is endowed with the sphere of the ear also endowed with the sphere of the eye? there is a fourfold alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*).
In this way, it should also be applied up to the sphere of mental objects.
In this manner, by means of each individual desire-to-know (*kāmarṣa*), all bases (*āyatana*) should be joined with one another in succession.

A "prior-phrase" (*pūrvapādaka*) occurs when, having begun with some dharma among two dharmas, an answer is given regarding the prior dharma as the basis for those two dharmas that have been mutually questioned.
For example: "Is whatever is knowledge also an object of knowledge (*jñeya*), or is whatever is an object of knowledge also knowledge?"
The first alternative: that which is knowledge is also the object of knowledge.
There may be that which is the object of knowledge but not knowledge;
these are other phenomena (dharmas).

The *paścātpādaka* (subsequent-member [formulation]) is likewise that which, when two dharmas are mutually questioned, is explained by relying on the latter one; for example: "Is whatever is the apprehended also the apprehender? Or is whatever is the apprehender also the apprehended?
The *paścātpādaka* is: "Whatever is the apprehender is also the apprehended."
There may be that which is the object of apprehension (grāhya) but not the subject of apprehension (grāhaka):
namely, the five objects such as visible form (rūpa) and so forth, and the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana), excluding the associated factors (saṃprayuktaka).

A "two-pointed" [question] is one where two alternatives are explained because others are impossible; for example, having concluded the establishment of the aggregates (*skandha*) and the establishment of the elements (*dhātu*), it is said: "Is the number of the aggregates also the number of the elements, or is the number of the elements also the number of the aggregates?"
The two-fold alternative: there may be a number of aggregates (*skandha*) without a corresponding number of elements (*dhātu*).
This is the case with the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).

For instance, there is no single element that possesses the complete characteristics of the entire aggregate of form, nor one that possesses the complete characteristics of the entire aggregate of consciousness.
The enumeration of the elements (dhātu) is not the enumeration of the aggregates (skandha);
it is the dharma-element (dharmadhātu).
(Abhidh-s-bh 149) A "threefold alternative" (*trikoṭika*) is that in which exactly three alternatives are explained;
for example: "Is that which is the enumeration of the aggregates also the enumeration of the bases?"
Whatever is the enumeration of the bases (āyatana), that is also the enumeration of the aggregates (skandha).
There is a threefold classification: there may be an enumeration of aggregates that is not an enumeration of bases, namely, the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha).

There may be that which is counted as a sense base (*āyatana*) but not counted as an aggregate (*skandha*), namely the sense base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*). There may be that which is counted both as an aggregate and as a sense base, namely the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) and the sense base of mind (*manāyatana*).
The enumeration of neither [of these two] is simply impossible within the aggregates and sense-bases.
A fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika) is one in which all four alternatives are explained;
for example: "Is one who is endowed with the eye faculty also endowed with the ear faculty, or is one who is endowed with the ear faculty also endowed with the eye faculty?"
There are four alternatives: the first alternative is one who has produced and not lost the eye-faculty but is deaf; the second is one who has produced and not lost the ear-faculty but is blind;
the third is one who has produced and not lost both the eye- and ear-faculties.
The fourth [alternative] is excluding those aforementioned modes.
"Answered with *oṃ*" means that in a certain question, the answer is given as "Oṃ," which signifies acceptance, meaning "it is so.
For example, when asked, "Are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) impermanent? or "Are all impermanent things conditioned phenomena?", one must answer "Oṃ."
The *prātikṣepika* (rejection-based) is that wherein "no" is rejected;
for example: "By how many truths are the formations dissociated from the aggregates subsumed?
The rejection-based [answer] is: "There are no formations dissociated from the aggregates."
The Determination of the Thorough Inquiry—consisting of eight aspects—is the teaching on non-apprehension (*kāpadeśa*), as follows: Who does not apprehend?
A bodhisattva who has attained the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
What does he not apprehend?
The characteristic of the apprehended and the characteristic of the apprehender—
by what does one not perceive them?
By the perfection of wisdom.
For what purpose does he not apprehend anything?
For the sake of protecting all sentient beings and for the sake of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
From what does he not apprehend anything?

It is through encountering the arising of a Buddha, hearing the true Dharma, proper mental attention, and practicing in accordance with the Dharma that one does not perceive anything; what is it that one does not perceive?
All phenomena.
Where is it not apprehended?
From the stage of practice through aspiration up to the tenth bodhisattva stage.
And how many kinds of non-apprehension are there?
It is of eleven kinds: that which has arisen and is opposed, that which has not yet arisen,
and that which is present before one.
Arising through the power of causes, arising through the power of friends,
and the non-apprehension of all phenomena.
The non-apprehension of emptiness,
with the conceit "I am," and without the conceit "I am."
This applies both to one who has not accumulated the provisions and to one who has accumulated the provisions.
Furthermore, these non-apprehensions— whatever is past, future, or present, and whatever is far or near— are to be understood according to this sequential order.
(Abhidh-s-bh 150) Just as with the designation "kā" (*kāpadeśa*), so it is with the designation "yā" (*yāpadeśa*):
that which one does not perceive, by what means, for what purpose, from what cause, whose, where, and in what manner— that is non-perception (*anupalambha*) in its various forms.
Furthermore, there are four paths of determination, beginning with the refuter (*dūṣaka*).

Among them, the refuter is one who negates an ill-proclaimed position of another, saying, "This is not correct. The establisher (*sādhaka*) is one who confirms a well-proclaimed position of one's own, saying, "This is correct."
He is the cutter away of the doubts that arise in others, providing them with certainty;
he is the awakener of those who are deluded regarding those matters, explaining their true meaning.
The determination regarding the performance of duties has as its purpose the mutual support of the means of livelihood and so forth for worldly beings.
The determination regarding entry is the investigation as to which of the three vehicles one should enter oneself and which one should cause others to enter.
The determination regarding inclination is the conviction, through wisdom consisting of hearing, in accordance with the teaching.

*Yuktiviniścaya* (ascertainment through reasoning) is the investigation of the underlying intention by means of wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī prajñā*) through [examining] what precedes and what follows.

*Sāṃkathyaviniścaya* (ascertainment through discussion) is the mutual enjoyment of the Dharma through the practice of asking questions and receiving answers regarding what has been heard and reflected upon.
*Prativedhaviniścaya* (ascertainment through penetration) is the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), because by means of it there is the penetration of the truths.

The determination of purification is the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), because by means of it, the remaining afflictions are purified. The determination of accomplishment is the path of distinction (*viśeṣamārga*), because by means of it, the extraordinary qualities (*vaiśeṣikaguṇa*) are brought forth.
The determination of the differentiation of terms is the boundless teaching of the Dharma by way of bringing forth various modes such as pairs, triads, tetrads, and so forth.
The Tathāgata’s knowledge is the definitive realization of the accomplishment of all aims through mere effortless exertion;
for, without prior exertion, there occurs the manifestation of unattached and unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding all objects simultaneously with that exertion.
The determination of debate is skillfulness regarding debate, the proponent, the opponent, the forum, and so forth.
In this context, all speech is *vāda* (discourse). Discourse that proceeds according to specific modes in the world is *pravāda* (rumor or common talk).
Contradictory discourse is *vivāda* (dispute).
*Apavāda* is a censurable statement;
*anuvāda* is a conformable statement, which is the determination of a discussion (*sāṃkathyaviniścaya*);
*avavāda* is a statement for the sake of comprehension.

[The Basis for Debate] This is because debate is conducted herein. A royal court is where the king himself is present; a judicial court is where those appointed by the king are present; and an assembly refers to merchant guilds and the like.
They are authoritative assistants whose words neither the proponent nor the opponent doubt;
they are ascetics and brahmins skilled in both Dharma and worldly affairs, whose intellects are proficient in those treatises by way of both the letter and the meaning.
The basis of debate is that upon which the debate is conducted, namely: the thesis to be proven (*sādhya*) and the means of proof (*sādhana*).
In that context, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) to be proven is whether the intrinsic nature of the self or the intrinsic nature of phenomena exists or does not exist.

The "particular" (viśeṣa) to be proven consists of specific attributes of the self and specific attributes of phenomena, categorized by such modes as being omnipresent or non-omnipresent, eternal or non-eternal, possessing form or formless, and so forth.
A thesis (*pratijñā*) is the communication intended to bring about another's understanding of a matter that one has accepted for oneself as something to be proven (*sādhya*).

If the term "to be proven" (*sādhya*) were not employed, it would follow that even the teaching of one's own position when it is already established would constitute a thesis. If the term "matter accepted for oneself" (*svarucitārtha*) were not employed, it would follow that even the statement of an opponent's position, if it were something to be proven, would constitute a thesis.

If the term "seizing" (*paragrahaṇa*) were not used, then even for one who speaks alone, that speech would result in being considered a formal proposition (*pratijñā*). If the term "bringing about" (*saṃprāpaṇa*) were not used, then even a physical indication of that meaning would result in being considered a formal proposition. If the term "making known" (*vijñāpanā*) were not used, then even when the meaning is not understood by the listeners, it would result in being considered a formal proposition.
However, when established in the manner described, none of these faults occur;
therefore, its establishment should be understood as follows:

the reason (*hetu*) is the designation of perception (*pratyakṣa*), apprehension (*upalambha*), and non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) as the cause for the conviction regarding a matter not yet known, with respect to that very same probandum (*sādhya*).
He shows that here the meaning of "reason" (*hetu*) is for the purpose of producing conviction.
For, by this designation—namely, "from perception and non-perception" or "from perception"—conviction arises regarding an object not previously understood in that which is to be proven (*sādhya*).
Therefore, that [designation] is called a "reason" because it is the cause (*nimitta*) for that [conviction].
Furthermore, perception and non-perception are to be understood as being based upon either an essential nature (svabhāva) or a logical mark (liṅga).
An example (dṛṣṭānta) is the designation of an equalization between a seen end and an unseen end;
the meaning is the designation for the sake of making known an unperceived portion by means of a perceived portion.
The application (*upanaya*) is the designation of "application" for the purpose of leading [the conclusion] so that the remaining members of that same class may accept that property.

Just as the object to be proven has been established by means of the three members [of the syllogism], so too is there the designation of "application"—which is the extension of the logical reason (*yuktyātideśa*)—for the purpose of leading the remaining members of that same class who are to be proven to accept the property of the object already established. This is the application.
The conclusion (*nigamana*) is the statement of having reached a final determination.
Because it is thus well-established by reasoning, one should understand that "this is exactly so" constitutes the conclusion.

This is presented merely as an illustration of these [members], such as the thesis and so forth. For example, for a proponent of selflessness, in that specific context involving an opponent, the statement "there is no self" is the thesis (*pratijñā*).
The reason is that when the aggregates (*skandha*) are examined, four types of faults are found.
For if that self were being designated, it would have to be designated either as having the characteristics of the aggregates or as being within the aggregates.
Or [is it] apart from the aggregates, or is it without aggregates?

If it has the characteristic of the aggregates, then the aggregates—being dependent on others, having arisen through conditions, and being subject to the nature of arising and passing away—are not independent; thus, the fault follows that a self with such a characteristic is untenable.
Now, if [the self] were based on the aggregates, then the fault would be that the self, being dependent on impermanent aggregates, would itself become impermanent.

If it were other than the aggregates, then the fault would be that the self would be bodiless and thus devoid of purpose. If it were not composed of aggregates, then the fault would be that for one who is liberated by nature alone—a *kevalin*—exertion toward the goal of liberation would be useless.
The illustration is: "like the designation of the past with respect to the present.

For that [past], being designated by way of having a presently existing characteristic, would either be designated as having a present characteristic, or it would be designated elsewhere than in the present—either as independent of the present, or as something other than the present.

In that case, if it has the characteristic of the present, then by that [reasoning] the present would be that which has arisen but not yet ceased; whereas the past consists of what has arisen and ceased—this is a fault.
Alternatively, if it is in the present, then as long as it has not ceased, a connection with that which is of the nature of having ceased is not logical—this is a fault.
Or else, apart from the present, if one sets aside the present, no such entity whatsoever is perceived where that [past] could be designated—this is a fault.

Alternatively, if it were independent of the present, then the fault would follow that even the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) would be past. Furthermore, it is established that this past [entity] does not exist by way of its own characteristic because its characteristics have perished.

Therefore, since these four faults regarding the designation of the present are established, the self—which is unestablished—is proven to be non-existent through the perception of these fourfold faults in the designation of the aggregates (skandha).

Having thus refuted the misconception of a self, the application [of the argument] is the extension [of the same reasoning]: by this very logic, permanence and the other [attributes] do not exist either.
Since this is so, therefore the five aggregates are impermanent, up to being selfless; this is the conclusion.
Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is an object that is self-existent, luminous, and non-erroneous.
Among these, "self" (*sva*) refers to its own object; for example, visible form (*rūpa*) is the object of the eye.

The inclusion of the term "existent" (*sat*) is for the purpose of excluding from the category of direct perception those things such as jars and other substances which, though commonly accepted as perceptible in the world, are in fact mere conceptual designations (*prajñaptimātra*).
The inclusion of the term "manifest" (*prakāśa*) is for the purpose of excluding objects that have not come into appearance due to causes of non-apprehension such as being obstructed;
the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) is for the purpose of excluding [cognitions of] a whirling firebrand, illusions, mirages, and the like.
Inference is the conviction regarding that which remains after direct perception.
That which remains other than what is directly perceived— the imperceptible— is established for the observer as necessarily coexisting with it, having been previously experienced.

For one who perceives that directly, there arises a conviction regarding another [factor] based on the authority of the learned: "Because this co-occurring factor exists here, that other must also exist. This is inference preceded by perception, just as for one seeing smoke, [there is the inference] of fire.
Authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*) is instruction that is not contradicted by those two [perception and inference].
That instruction in which both perception and inference are in no way contradicted nor do they deviate is authoritative scripture, because it inspires confidence.
The ornament of debate is that by which an advocate, when engaging in debate, shines exceedingly; it consists, moreover, of such qualities as knowledge of one's own and others' systems.

Among these, knowledge of one's own and others' systems refers to the continuous ripening of proficiency—both in terms of the literal text and its meaning, and with respect to the sequence of earlier and later parts—concerning both one's own established tenets and those of others.
Perfection of vocal expression (*vākkaraṇasaṃpat*) is the quality of speaking without confusion and so forth, which is the opposite of the faults of speech to be described for one who speaks words.
Fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*) is the state of being free from hesitation and free from distress while speaking even when surrounded by learned people intent on citing numerous examples.
Steadfastness (*sthairya*) is the quality of speaking without haste, waiting for the conclusion of the opponent's speech.
Courtesy is natural goodness and the adaptation of one's mind to that of the judges and the opponent.
Defeat in debate is that by which a debater is said to be defeated;
furthermore, this occurs through such means as the abandonment of the discussion.

Among these, the abandonment of the discussion consists in the admission of faults in one's own argument or merits in the opponent's argument through such modes as saying, "My [position] is not good, yours is good," and so forth.
The collapse of discourse (*kathāsāda*) means distraction through such means as shifting from one point to another;

as it is said in the Sūtra: "The Venerable Cundika, while engaging in debate with the heretics, having denied something, then asserts it; having asserted it, then denies it. The fault of discourse (*kathādoṣa*) refers to confused speech and the like.

In that context, "confused" refers to that which, having abandoned the relevant subject matter, is an expansion of various irrelevant discourses; "agitated" refers to that which is characterized by the outburst of anger or the outburst of levity;
and "unintelligible" refers to that which is not grasped by the assembly or the speaker, either in terms of the Dharma or its meaning.
That which is "immeasurable" (amita) refers to what is excessive, redundant in meaning, and already known.
That which is "meaningless" (anartha) is that which is joined with what is purposeless;
this should be understood as having five aspects.
Meaningless, irrelevant, and lacking logical consistency.

It is equivalent to the probandum (*sādhyasama*), associated with futile rejoinders (*jāti*) and quibbles (*chala*), because the meaning is unperceived, because the meaning is incoherent, because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because the means of proof itself is what remains to be proven, and because it follows all improper and unrefined arguments.
Speech that is mis-timed (*akālayukta*) is that which should have been said first is uttered later, and that which should have been said later is uttered first.

Unsteady speech (*asthira*) is that which, having been promised, is then disregarded, or having been disregarded, is then promised; it is that which is hastily grasped through speech that is too rapid.

[A] "Non-flaming" speech refers to that which transcends the characteristics of the *śabda* (linguistic) system, which provides an answer without restating [the opponent's position], and which begins in Sanskrit and concludes in Prakrit,
or begins in Prakrit and concludes in Sanskrit.
That which is unconnected, interrupted by what is internally presided over, is called the manifestation of speech (*vākpratibhāna*).
The exit from debate is that by which one emerges from debate:

either by not engaging in it after having examined the merits and faults, thus avoiding the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) in debate; or by engaging in it and successfully carrying it through to completion.
In that context, [the opponent's] lack of receptivity consists in the impossibility of turning them away from an unwholesome position and establishing them in a wholesome one.
The deficiency of the assembly consists in its being undisciplined, biased, or attached to a particular side.

One’s own lack of skill consists in being untrained in everything from the debate itself up to the ornaments of debate. By contrast, the receptivity of the opponent and so forth should be understood as the opposite of these.
The factors that are highly beneficial for debate are those which are necessarily employed in debate.
For example, knowledge of one's own and others' systems is a factor highly beneficial for debate, by means of which one engages in debate on every subject of discourse.
The remainder is easy to understand.

Having stated "by one engaged in the side of the wholesome" (*kuśalapakṣaprayuktena*), the statement "by one for whom practice is the essence" (*pratipattisārakeṇa*) is intended to make known the purity of intention; it means "by one engaged in the side of the wholesome, such as learning and so forth, not for the sake of gain, honor, and the like.
By "by one who gathers beings" (*sattvasaṃgrāhakeṇa*), the distinction from the Śrāvakas and others is indicated; it means "by one for whom the practice of benefiting others is primary.
Thus, one who has practiced for both their own benefit and the benefit of others quickly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment—this is to be understood as the connection between these terms.
Even when a debate is conducted without contention, because the Mahāyāna Dharma is inherently profound, it is difficult to gain understanding; how much more so when it is conducted with contention!

Furthermore, those opponents with whom one debates do not respond with the intention of seeking knowledge, but rather with the intention of finding fault. Moreover, the members of the assembly before whom that debate is held may themselves be uncivilized, unlearned, or dogmatically biased.
Moreover, almost every debate is characterized by six faults.

For instance, one engaged in debate may, out of excessive impetuosity, adopt even an untenable position and, through dogmatic attachment, employ quibbles (*chala*), futile rejoinders (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
Furthermore, without concluding the completion of one's speech, one begins to speak at an improper time.
It means that one causes the opponent’s speech— even when it is correctly stated— to fall into error or disparages it; they speak even harshly,
by which the opponent and others become deeply provoked in mind.
And he personally corrupts his mind toward them; thus, he becomes possessed of these six faults.
For one who is tranquil, speech is difficult to find;

and when there is no tranquility, it is difficult to protect the minds of others and to protect one's own mind, by means of which others might gain confidence and one's own mind becomes concentrated through the application of the bases of liberation (*vimuktyāyatana*).
Generally, in debate, the thought arises: "How might I win and how might my opponent be defeated?
When that [thought] exists, there is the affliction of the suffering of burning anguish;
when that exists, there is dwelling in discomfort.
Then, due to the inability to apply oneself continuously to the side of wholesome qualities, there occurs a falling away from what has been attained with respect to further distinguished realization.
In this verse, "Having killed mother and father," these syllables—which denote that which is most blameworthy and sinful in the world—have been transformed for the sake of purification.
Furthermore, what is considered most blameworthy in the world?
It is the killing of one's elders and the killing of the great multitude.
Furthermore, that venerable person (gurujana) is of two kinds: the specific and the common to the world.
The one common to the world is also of two kinds: the protector and the one worthy of offerings (dakṣiṇīya).
Among these, the specific venerable persons are the mother and the father.
King Pālaka and the learned Brāhmaṇas worthy of offerings,
because they possess a state of purity that is even more sublime.
Thus, the killing of all these is called "the killing of one's elders.
The "killing of the great multitude" refers to the destruction of the kingdom along with its followers.
Furthermore, the "followers" should be understood as cattle, horses, buffaloes, camels, and so forth.
Furthermore, how are these syllables transformed into purification?
The transformation of the words "killing mother" and so forth into the abandonment of craving and so forth is, respectively, [the abandonment of] craving (*tṛṣṇā*),
karma-existence (*karmabhava*), and so on.
With reference to consciousness accompanied by grasping,
the two types of clinging to views and to rules and observances,
and the six sense bases together with their respective objects, one should understand [the factors] beginning with "mother."
Because of their similarity:
therein, craving is the cause of manifestation,
while karmic existence is the cause of arising.
And that [craving] should be regarded as being like a father by way of its connection with the striking of the seed of cultivation.
Through these two causes, consciousness proceeds together with grasping (*sopādāna*).

While it is proceeding in this manner, even though there is a desire for liberation, there are two types of misapprehension (*parāmarśa*) which act as obstacles to the attainment of liberation, leading one to believe in what is not the means and in what is not supreme purity.
This alone should be understood as the similarity between these two and the *śrotriya*: namely, their adherence to a supreme purity.
Furthermore, that very consciousness, by way of being the basis and the object, should be understood as the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) together with their respective domains.
In this verse, "one who lacks faith" (*aśrāddha*) and "one who is ungrateful" (*akṛtajña*), syllables expressing inferior meanings are illuminated as having the highest meaning.
There are four types of inferior persons in the world: one who is deficient in mental action, one deficient in bodily action, one deficient in verbal action, and one deficient in enjoyment.
Furthermore, one deficient in mental action is of two kinds: the one who lacks faith, by way of being contrary to the engagement in the wholesome; and...

Because one does not apply oneself to giving and other virtues due to a lack of conviction in the existence of future worlds and so forth; and because one is ungrateful by being inclined toward the practice of unwholesome deeds,
since one lacks restraint in committing misdeeds such as matricide due to a disregard for benefits received.
One deficient in bodily action is a thief or a housebreaker, because his livelihood is exceedingly contemptible;
one deficient in verbal action is primarily characterized by lying and so forth, because such a person is excluded from entering assemblies and the like.
"Is this a dog, a crow, or a hungry ghost (preta) that has come to enjoy us?"—
such [thoughts arise] because of eating what has been vomited.
(Abhidh-s-bh 156) But how, then, are these syllables transformed into the ultimate meaning?
Because they transform words such as "faithless" and so forth into the state of an Arhat.
In that regard, he is "lacking faith" because he relies on his own personal realization through the yoga of the knowledge and vision of liberation;
he is "ungrateful" because of his knowledge of the unconditioned emanation;
and he is "one who cuts the connection" because of his abandonment of the afflictions that cause the reconnection of rebirth.

It has its opportunity destroyed because it does not bring about suffering in all future states of existence; it has vomited out its desires because, even while sustaining the body through the power of requisites in the present life, there is no longer any hope for wealth or life.
And as it has been said: "Those who perceive the essence in the essenceless.
The explanation of the meaning of this verse should be understood as before.
Furthermore, its body refers to the fact that, by relying upon meditative concentration (*samādhi*), Bodhisattvas touch great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*) through the paths of seeing and cultivation.

"He increases the nature of stinginess" means that by abandoning the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of stinginess along with their residual impressions (*savāsanā*), he realizes the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*) into that very suchness (*tattathatā*).
Furthermore, "he becomes weary of giving" because for a long time he has undertaken the most difficult exertion for the sake of giving.
And he hates the supplicant because, due to his own attachment to what he desires, he is averse to the supplicant; thus,
he never gives anything at any time.
Because one gives every kind of thing at all times,
and because one is far from giving, having abandoned the practice of giving only when [the object] is near.
In this context, "endowed with the supreme holy life" means by means of the supramundane path.

"He does not seek an escape from sexual intercourse elsewhere than through sexual intercourse itself" means that he abandons it through the thorough knowledge of it as it truly is (*yathābhūtaparijñāna*). Furthermore, his thorough knowledge of things as they truly are should be understood as arising from the penetration of suchness (*tathatā*).
By abandoning sexual intercourse,
one becomes equanimous through the relinquishment of non-celibacy;
yet, one tolerates the arisen passion for sexual intercourse.
Because he expels internally arisen sensual desire to the outside, and because—

through the Dharma that serves as the antidote to sexual intercourse— he is not terrified by it, but instead resolves to cross over all sentient beings by means of the path that serves as its antidote;
and because he frequently enters into the union of the two-by-two, consisting of the four truths through the distinction of cause and fruit, and through the pair of affliction and purification.
Furthermore, it is because one repeatedly enters the two paths—the mundane and the supramundane—by means of the non-duality of calm abiding and insight.

On what basis does this treatise receive the name *Abhidharmasamuccaya*? According to the principle of etymology (*nirukti*), it is because of its "collecting together" (*sametyoccayatām*). The meaning is that it is so called because Bodhisattvas, having collectively realized and attained reality (*tattva*), perform a compendium (*saṃkalana*) of it.
The meaning is that it is based on its being a universal compendium, because it encompasses all subjects of inquiry according to the *Abhidharma-sūtra*.
Furthermore, the meaning is that it serves as a basis for correct accumulation, because it leads to the attainment of Buddhahood through unerring means.
Thus ends the fifth compendium, titled "The Determination of Discussion," from the *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya*.
This was caused to be written by the learned physician Śrī Amaracandra, for the sake of the world’s attainment of the perfection of Buddhahood.
